title: Loyal to the look: why Zohran Mamdani wears a suit in all seasons | New York | The Guardian
description: Around town, on the pitch and even in the pool, the New York mayor keeps his suit on – what do his sartorial choices tell us?
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: Around town, on the pitch and even in the pool, the New York mayor keeps his suit on – what do his sartorial choices tell us?
Content: Zohran Mamdani with his wife, Rama Duwaji, during the ticker-tape parade for the NBA champion New York Knicks in June.Photograph: Angelina Katsanis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenZohran Mamdani with his wife, Rama Duwaji, during the ticker-tape parade for the NBA champion New York Knicks in June.Photograph: Angelina Katsanis/Getty ImagesNew YorkLoyal to the look: why Zohran Mamdani wears a suit in all seasonsAround town, on the pitch and even in the pool, the New York mayor keeps his suit on – what do his sartorial choices tell us?Adam Gabbattin New YorkSun 26 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlaying football.Playing in the sand. Dancing on a stage with Alicia Keys and the entire New York Knicks roster. Swimming in a swimming pool. Swimming in the ocean.Traditionally, a suit and tie would be considered inappropriate attire for each of these activities. Yet over the past yearZohran Mamdanihas seemingly been on a one-man crusade to prove otherwise: to convince people that a formal suit is, actually, suitable for all activities.What Zohran Mamdani’s suit tells us about the man and the way society is changingRead moreThat’s because theNew Yorkmayor hardly ever wears anything but a suit: frequently purchased from Suit Supply, almost always in a dark colour and worn with a formal tie, mostly paired with smart black boots. He’s hardly the first male politician to embrace the suit – it’s the de facto uniform, after all, of those seeking to project seriousness and solemnity – but few, if any, have been quite as wedded to the formal blazer and matching trousers.Cheering on the Knicks at Madison Square Garden in May, Mamdani stood out for his decision towear a dark suit and tie. After the Knicks won, he took the unusual decision to wear the team’s jersey over his shirt and tie, but under his suit jacket. In June, he wore a navy suit, white shirt, and blue striped tie for a press opportunity with childrenat the beach.Those aren’t even the most unusual examples.On New Year’s Day 2025, while running for mayor, he wore a suit to take part in the Polar Bear Club plunge, a New York tradition whereby people go swimming in the frigid Atlantic. “I’m freezing … your rent as the next mayor of New York City,” Mamdani said inan accompanying TikTok video, a message that was rather on the nose, but won him lots of press coverage.View image in fullscreenMamdani in his suit on the football field.Photograph: Ira L Black/Fifa/Getty ImagesWater proved again to be no obstacle when Mamdanileaped, fully suited, into a swimming poolin Harlem last month, to announce the opening of the city’s pools for summer. (Mamdani “broke the rules in the process”, the rightwing New York Postreported, “which requires all swimmers to wear bathing suits in the water”.)The mayor is trapped, it seems, in a wool or possibly wool-blend prison of his own making. But why?Mamdani’s most recent predecessors weren’t as tied to the suit. Bill De Blasio was keen on shorts – although, in a furore that won’t have gone unnoticed by Mamdani, the former mayor was mercilessly ridiculed forwearing the cargo variety– while Eric Adams waspartial to a polo shirt, and sometimesa woolly cardigan.“I think Mamdani wants to double down on appearing as a working mayor, as someone who is always on the job and on the clock,” said Ella Devi, a fashion commentator and, like Mamdani, Democratic Socialists of America member whose (typically negative) assessments of Republicans’ style have made her a target for conservatives.“I think that he kind of wants to convey that he is committed to the job, through his sartorial choices. I think that is reflected in his attachment to the suiting.”Devi added: “It’s also that he’s a young, Muslim, socialist.”View image in fullscreenZohran Mamdani with Barack Obama at an educational event in the Bronx in April.Photograph: Getty ImagesIt seems likely that Mamdani, the repeated focus of rightwing media, is held to a higher bar than white centrist politicians. It’s an issue Hasan Piker, the Turkish American leftwing streamer,brought up recently, when he said conservatives are “more receptive to what I have to say” when he dresses smartly.“I used to wear T-shirts all the time,” hetold Dazed. “But then I figured I should start wearing a suit and a tie because there are a lot of adults watching on Fox News [the rightwing channel frequently airs clips of Piker speaking] – if they see me saying something in the clips, they’ll be more receptive to what I have to say if I’m in a more appealing format.”The mayor’s office declined to comment on Mamdani’s wardrobe, but he addressed his penchant for suit-wearing in a recent interviewwith CNN.Asked about his decision to jump into a swimming pool wearing a suit, the mayor said: “I think I misunderstood the term swimsuit. I do also have to say thank you, though, to Goodwill [a charity known for its shops that sell used clothing], because I got that suit for 30 bucks, because you can’t go ruining the other suits that you have. But I’m clearly learning that there might be a different way to dress when it’s 100-degree weather.”How Zohran Mamdani makes affordable suits look expensive – and you can tooRead moreLeftists have not always been known for formal dresswear. That remains true in some cases – the disgraced Maine senatorial candidate Graham Platner wore sweaters and T-shirts during his campaign; John Fetterman, the Democratic senator from Pennsylvania, has a passionate commitment to wearing basketball shorts – but that might be changing.“If there’s a visual language that connotes credibility and authority, why not take advantage of it?” Nathan Robinson, the editor of the leftwing Current Affairs magazinewrote this month.“You might see someone in a suit as serious, professional, ready to do business. You might think they belong in the Senate or a boardroom. That’s certainly what Mamdani is trying to convey with his suits. He understands that socialists face a challenge: we’re considered fringe. People think we don’t belong among those making important decisions. The suits are a subtle way of asserting the legitimacy and authority of socialist ideas.”View image in fullscreenMamdani (middle) with Mrs and Mr Met at Citi Field in April.Photograph: Caean Couto/Getty ImagesMamdani has taken the concept further than most. A keen football player, he wore a black suit with a grey tie whiledoing keep-upswith a football in July, and when he played in a game that same month, Mamdani simply threw a football shirt over his suit – although he did ditch the jacket.It was not always thus. A source who played for the same team as Mamdani before his election said that he did not play in a suit and tie, although they added: “He always showed up in a suit, or at least suit pants, and hisfamous boots, and would change on the pitch because he was also always running late.”The source, who asked not to be named, but who now plays for a football team with the author of this article, continued, “But he never missed a tackle” – a remark which was possibly aimed at this writer.The source said Mamdani used to play in “black shorts”. Asked if a suit would be appropriate attire for a football match, they said it would not. They explained: “Limited stretch in the materials, restricted range of motion, you get sweaty and probably don’t want to have to dry-clean a suit as often for cost and longevity purposes, likelihood of it getting grass stains or torn up during play, excessive wear from friction which would also compromise longevity of a likely costly piece of clothing less easily replaced, too hot to play in (comfortably).”Having become so intertwined with the suit, the question might be: can Mamdani ever wear anything else? Can the mayor ditch the formalwear?View image in fullscreenMamdani smiles after leaving a pre-World Cup event in Harlem.Photograph: Adam Gray/AP“I think that now he’s kind of trapped in the suit, and he knows that he’s trapped in the suit, because he’s made it his thing to always wear the suit,” Devi said.“He has to stick with the bit, the suit bit. If he wears jeans, then the New York Post is just going to write about that for the next three weeks.”With temperatures in New York recently hitting 38C (100F), Mamdani might be wishing he could wear something else – although Devi had a suggestion should the heat become too unbearable.“He would never go for this, because it would not be seen as very socialist, but Thom Browne does some very good suit shorts for the future heatwaves. So that’s my advice to Mayor Mamdani,” she said.It’s a fine idea, except according to Thom Browne’s website, those shortsretail at about $1,300, which might raise questions over Mamdani’s socialist credentials. It seems that, at least for now, Mamdani is stuck in the suit.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkZohran MamdaninewsShareReuse this content

title: The Rapture review – this apocalyptic drama couldn’t be here at a better time | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s set in a UK racked by an unbearable heatwave and the rise of extremism – this adaptation of the 2010 novel feels horrifyingly apt
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: It’s set in a UK racked by an unbearable heatwave and the rise of extremism – this adaptation of the 2010 novel feels horrifyingly apt
Content: India Amarteifio as Bethany Krall in The Rapture.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Mammoth ScreenView image in fullscreenIndia Amarteifio as Bethany Krall in The Rapture.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Mammoth ScreenTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Rapture review – this apocalyptic drama couldn’t be here at a better timeIt’s set in a UK racked by an unbearable heatwave and the rise of extremism – this adaptation of the 2010 novel feels horrifyingly aptLucy ManganSun 26 Jul 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen The Rapture by Liz Jensen was first published, in 2010, it was set in a near-future when temperatures in the UK are rising to unbearable heights, culty-Christian groups with apocalyptic bents are springing up all over the place and there is a growing sense that the world is going mad. Swap out “culty-Christian” for “political extremists bent on embracing the apocalypse rather than trying to save us from it” and it would be a deluded soul indeed who wouldn’t place it among fiction’s more prescient offerings.The adaptation that has arrived on our screens 16 years later – a study in physical and mental discomfort – is the perfect accompaniment to our current record-breaking, fear-inducing heatwave, and gains a lot of power from our growing collective awareness that the future is finally here.Clinical psychotherapist Dr Gabrielle Fox (Ruth Madeley) is still coming to terms with an apocalyptic event in her own life: a car accident that killed her husband and left her paralysed from the waist down. She was the driver and is pursued by guilt, which she discusses in weekly sessions with her own psychotherapist (Ruth Jones) – because physicians are the worst at healing themselves. But after two years, she must go back to work.Her first case, at the adolescent secure psychiatric unit at Oxsmith hospital, is a humdinger. Seventeen-year-old Bethany Krall (India Amarteifio) was convicted of killing her mother Carys (screwdriver, eye) when she was 15, and has been locked up on the unit, pretending to take her anti-psychotic meds, ever since. She has no memory of attacking her mother and denies doing it. There were no witnesses but she was the only one in the house at the time, definitely the only one covered in blood immediately afterwards and certainly the only one who had drawn a picture of her mother with a screwdriver poking out of her face a week before it happened.Bethany claims her drawings are of her visions, not plans. She does them with her eyes closed and they usually involve death or destruction. Her nurse Rafiq (Naby Dakhli) says that the scenes they depict come true and is convinced she is a prophet. Gabs, as a woman of science and observer of human complexities rather than supernatural forces, suspects that Bethany is at best disturbed and at worst mentally ill – and, in either case, in need of treatment rather than obeisance. But then Bethany reveals knowledge of some private details of Gabs’ life, and seems to have drawn a picture of her long before anyone knew she would be assigned her case.Bethany’s father, Leonard (Sam Hazeldine), just wants to help his daughter. “I’m desperate to see and support her,” he assures Gabs when she visits him at the well-appointed Faith Way centre, where he leads a sect united under the exhortation “Choose hope”. Leonard broadcasts sermons online and preaches against environmental activist groups such as the increasingly militant Climate Front, who, he believes, are frightening people with their doom-mongering ways. We do not like Leonard. In this we are joined by his daughter, who has been refusing visits from her unsettling papa ever since she was arrested. She is unwilling to be used – as she believes her mother was – as a pawn in his game of “playing the good Christian”.There is an awful lot going on in The Rapture. To all the above we must add an investigative journalist, alternately clarifying and muddying waters; a charming (possibly too charming) new love interest for Gabs; and a mystery woman who might be able to tell them more about Carys’ death, if Gabs can identify her from one of Bethany’s vision-sketches. And that’s just the first two episodes, which were all that were available for review of the total five.It is clearly aiming for a lot thematically, too. How do we account for the destabilising forces of grief and guilt? How do guilt and grief manifest at a collective rather than individual level? Where do the lines between madness and sanity, impassioned but rational belief (in the climate crisis, say) and religious fervour lie? The overall effect is chaotic. Much is gestured at, and the story has some promising leads, but unless the remaining three episodes become much leaner and clearer, we are probably doomed to frustration.Nevertheless, the Rapture has smaller-scale scenes and moments that work incredibly well. One is the first crack in Bethany’s wall of denial regarding her part in Carys’s death. Another is Gabs negotiating the new mental and physical territory that comes with her first potential relationship – with Frasier (Jack Farthing) – since she became a widow and a wheelchair (and catheter, it is unobtrusively noted) user. Yet another is journalist Dick (Iwan Rheon) drinking but trying to keep bitterness and collapse at bay. A little less all round could have made The Rapture into a lot more than it – so far – is.The Rapture aired on BBC One and is on iPlayer now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDramareviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was like something was crawling over me’ – the worrying rise of shingles among millennial women  | Health | The Guardian
description: Stress, the cost of living, long working hours and even excessive exercise have all been touted as reasons the illness is rising among women in their 30s and 40s. What can be done to help them?
Author: Emily Retter
Headline: Stress, the cost of living, long working hours and even excessive exercise have all been touted as reasons the illness is rising among women in their 30s and 40s. What can be done to help them?
Content: ‘The pain took my breath away’ – Francine Jones, 39, had shingles earlier this year.Photograph: Joann Randles/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The pain took my breath away’ – Francine Jones, 39, had shingles earlier this year.Photograph: Joann Randles/The GuardianHealth‘It was like something was crawling over me’ – the worrying rise of shingles among millennial womenStress, the cost of living, long working hours and even excessive exercise have all been touted as reasons the illness is rising among women in their 30s and 40s. What can be done to help them?Emily RetterSun 26 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe “lightning strike” pain was like nothing Francine Jones had experienced before. “That is the only way I can describe it,” she says, of the stabbing in her torso that would occur every 10 minutes or so. “It was a really sharp, intense pain, as if someone was giving me an electric shock … it took my breath away.”It had started in May with a strange pricking sensation under her bra. Then 10 large blisters, plus a host of smaller ones, formed in a band from her stomach to her back. They burned, “like someone was putting an iron on me. I don’t think I wore underwear for five or six weeks.” Showering, or even a cold flannel, would make her skin burn. Then came “the itch”, which lasted for five weeks and was so intense that she was lucky if she slept for four hours a night. “It was like something was crawling all over me all the time.” I can hear her wincing.Jones is describing the stages of shingles she experienced. “Stages” is her terminology; there is no set pattern. It is her way of describing how the illness progressed. One night, she even feared she was having a heart attack. “I felt like I had a constant stitch and it intensified to where I was unable to walk,” she recalls. “I tried to take a deep breath and then the pain got worse. I was crying my eyes out.”The healthcare assistant from Hereford is 39, not an age at which you might expect someone to get shingles. Yet she is not as much of a rarity as you might expect. Her story reflects a concerning trend: a 2019 US research paper reported that the sharpest rise in shingles cases was among those aged 30 to 49. Between 1998 and 2017, cases of shingles in this cohort more than doubled, overtaking the trajectory of older groups, although the latter experienced more cases overall. (Cases across all groups have been rising steadily in the US for decades, a trend for which experts do not appear to have a clear explanation, although they speculate that increased stress and depression, contributing to weakened immunity – a key cause of shingles – may play a role.)After being diagnosed by a pharmacist, Jones was prescribed antiviral medication for seven days, then the nerve pain medication Gabapentin, which she is still taking. She has been off work for two months and still experiences sporadic aching in her side, as if she has twisted badly.View image in fullscreenFrancine Jones had a band of painful blisters from her stomach to her back.Photograph: Handout“I always thought it was old people who got shingles,” she says. In fact, a US study published in the journalClinical Infectious Diseasesthis year found that those aged 30 to 39 with certain conditions, including asthma, diabetes, depression and stress, had a higher risk of shingles than those aged 50 to 59 who were immunocompetent. Experts say the uptake of the shingles vaccine in the over-50s in the US is still too low to offer an explanation for this.Shingles, also known as herpes zoster, is a reactivation of the varicella zoster (chickenpox) virus, which lies dormant in the sensory dorsal root ganglia – a cluster of neuron cell bodies just outside the spinal cord – after the contraction, often in childhood, of chickenpox. Reactivation can be triggered when immunity is impaired and T-cells in our blood can no longer keep it in check. The first symptom is usually pain or tingling in one area of the skin, sometimes accompanied by headaches and generally feeling unwell. This is typically followed by blisters. Pain is caused by inflamed nerves – one complication can be postherpetic neuralgia (persistent pain for more than 90 days), which occurs in around20% of patients.View image in fullscreenAn illustration of the varicella zoster virus.Photograph: Roger Harris/Science Photo Library/Getty Images/Science Photo Library RFAccording to the NHS,around a quarter of uswill experience shingles in our lifetime and the incidence increases with age, which is why the shingles vaccination is offered to those over 65 in the UK and those over 50 in the US. Cases in the UK are above the five year average, according to the Royal College of GPs Research and Surveillance Centre. It believes this may, in part, reflect additional diagnoses through the Pharmacy First scheme, which allows pharmacists as well as GPs to diagnose shingles and prescribe treatment.“I’ve had shingles eight times in the last two years. I’m 38 years old,” wrote one woman, in a Facebook support group for those with shingles. “I had shingles in April for the first time at 36,” said another. Others have similar stories: “I got it last year at 32”; “I had it at 41 this time last year but I’ve only just finished recovering”; “I’m 44, got shingles last year and it was horrific, the pain!” The majority of voices are female.Across most age groups, women have a 56% higher chance of developingshingles, thought to be because their immune systems work differently from men’s (women are more prone to autoimmune conditions, for example).In the US, one hypothesis for the rise in shingles is that the introduction in 1995 of the chickenpox vaccine for children, which eventually lowered rates of infection in young age groups, means adults who have not been vaccinated are missing out on exposure to chickenpox, and therefore the boosts to their own resilience to shingles.Indeed, the 2019 study expected to find this, especially when it came to explaining the rise in shingles in the millennial cohort, who are too old to have had the chickenpox vaccine and too young for the shingles vaccine.The less chickenpox, the less shingles resilience hypothesis sounds plausible, but Jennifer Moffat, associate professor ofmicrobiology and immunologyat the State University of New York Upstate Medical University, explains that this theory was disproved in the 2019 study because chickenpox and shingles rates did not tally as expected. “As chickenpox decreased, the rate of zoster was on the same trajectory in 30-year-olds as it always was,” she says. She adds that it is now believed that resilience is naturally built, with or without exposure to chickenpox. “Scientists and physicians now believe the virus occasionally reactivates without symptoms, which provides an internal immune boost. Only when that person has impaired immunity does it cause a rash and the symptoms of shingles.”Moffat adds: “It only takes a small gap in your immune function to let this virus pop out. Having a respiratory disease like Covid or flu … getting a bad sunburn, having type 2 diabetes or even treatment with steroids (which suppress immune system responses) can lead to an eruption of shingles.” She also believes, “something else is happening on a very large scale that is putting people at higher risk for reactivation – the declining health of humans in general. Less activity, poor diet, more stress, even maybe a warming climate.” Her list goes on: “Lack of social supports, eating ultra-processed foods, not cooking at home, not sleeping enough, higher income inequality, lack of access to healthcare – this last [one] is a major problem for young people in the US,” she points out.But why are millennial women especially struggling? Coupled with their immune systems being more prone to shingles than men’s, Moffat speculates that their health and mental health may be more compromised as they face a wide range of lifestyle pressures in midlife. “Well, if you looked at their general health, I imagine you’d find higher rates of high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes,” Moffat says. She finds the Clinical Infectious Diseasesstudy compelling. “Having depression at ages 30 to 39 puts you at as high a risk for shingles as a person in their 50s,” she says. “How many women do you know who feel great? They’re trying to earn, to care for their families, maintain homes. They have [older] parents, small children. There’s so much pressure on women, and I think health is not as easy to obtain any more. I think women are very squeezed in that age group.”Jones faced an acute period of personal stress before her shingles, but says life is generally quite stressful anyway. “The cost of living goes up, people are working more hours.” She says she would force herself to get to the gym at 8.30am on Sundays and sometimes do two classes a day. Studies have observed that exercising seven days a week canpotentially increase the risk of developing shingles.It is stress that Daisy, now 51, believes may have been behind her three shingles flare-ups. She was 43 when she first had it in 2018. She noticed half her body felt sore and that there was a rash “the size of a penny under my arm”. Her GP initially gave her cream for heat rash. “I had post-shingles pain for a couple of years … dots and bolts of pain,” she says. She had recently started a new job and suffered a bereavement.In 2022, her shingles returned. “I was managing quite a demanding day job, studying, going to the gym, living life as a single woman,” she says. In 2023, it emerged a third time after a period of illnesses including laryngitis and Covid. She was also taking exams and had started perimenopause.Consultant dermatologist Dr Adil Sheraz explains that early diagnosis, pre-rash (some shingles cases never display one), can be missed and younger people can also be overlooked. This is problematic because antivirals are most effective if taken within 72 hours of the first symptoms. “I have seen it missed many times,” he says. “If the patient comes in quite late, we still treat them, but often you miss the treatment phase.”Antivirals are taken for around 7-10 days, “after which the active infection goes away”, Sheraz explains. “You are then left with redness for quite some time. And then a certain percentage of patients will be left with nerve pain that may go on for many years.”His younger patients do tend to be immunocompromised – although the shingles vaccine is now available for people aged 18 and over who have a severely weakened immune system or take immunosuppressant medication. It is growing use of the latter, he speculates, due to significant advances in drug technology and the treatment of autoimmune conditions, that may be another reason for the rise in cases of shingles. “Up to 10 years ago, we would never use these types of immune suppressants for eczema, for example, or for blistering conditions,” he says.While shingles usually presents on the torso, it can appear anywhere, including the face. Proximity to the eye can risk blindness. Hayley, 42, from north Wales, suffered corneal scarring after her shingles was repeatedly missed. Aged 38, she began feeling an ache near her ear, jaw stiffness and then her eyebrow swelled. “Then my whole eye swelled,” she says. “It looked like I’d been punched.”Her GP diagnosed an infected salivary gland. A week later, a rash appeared under her eyebrow and her eye also felt sore, akin to a “chopping onions” sensation. The rash and swelling subsided (the blisters have left a scar), but then her GP diagnosed allergic conjunctivitis. “I had trouble looking up,” she recalls. “I was sitting in a dark room. I couldn’t really watch TV, read a book. Doing computer work, I had to keep walking away.”It was an optician who referred her to the hospital, where shingles was diagnosed almost two months later, and antivirals and steroids were prescribed. Thankfully, the corneal scarring was outside her field of vision.Moffat would welcome shingles vaccination at a younger age. “Shingles is terrible, it’s painful, it’s disfiguring,” she explains. For now, looking after your wellbeing is the best prevention for younger people, she believes.When we speak, Jones admits she is taking a rest day due to the re-emergence of her twisting pain. “I try to listen to my body now,” she explains. She won’t be at the gym on a Sunday morning any time soon.*Some names have been changedExplore more on these topicsHealthWomenImmunologyMedical researchfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Am I a chicken-shop lefty? Here’s what a French fast food row taught me about politics | Coco Khan | The Guardian
description: Feathers are flying over the halal chicken chain Master Poulet opening a branch in gentrified Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine – it’s an issue of wealth and class we know only too well, says writer and podcaster Coco Khan
Author: Coco Khan
Headline: Feathers are flying over the halal chicken chain Master Poulet opening a branch in gentrified Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine – it’s an issue of wealth and class we know only too well, says writer and podcaster Coco Khan
Content: The Master Poulet rotisserie in Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine, near Paris.Photograph: Apaydin Alain/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Master Poulet rotisserie in Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine, near Paris.Photograph: Apaydin Alain/ABACA/ShutterstockOpinionFranceAm I a chicken-shop lefty? Here’s what a French fast food row taught me about politicsCoco KhanFeathers are flying over the halal chicken chain Master Poulet opening a branch in gentrified Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine – it’s an issue of wealth and class we know only too wellSun 26 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareHow do you like your progressive politics? Are you net-zero left or anti-identity politics left? A “legalising drugs” kind of radical or someone whose public sector solidarity includes police? Nato or Nat-no?The reputation for infighting in lefty spaces – where policy disagreements harden into personal tests of morality – needs neither introduction nor encouragement.But reading about the left-on-left battle at Master Poulet, a French chicken chain that just opened its first UK branch, I found myself mulling a question that felt more than a little personal: am I chicken shop left?OK, OK, this might just be ameproblem. I’ve always had an interest in chicken shops. Maybe it’s personal: chicken shops, offering cheap halal takes on mainstream fare, have long been a pursuit of south Asian immigrants who hoped, like my own family, for a better life in this brave new world (talk about a wing and a prayer). But they are also bound up in Black British youth culture: neighbourhood incubators for music, affordable places to hang, landmarks of “the ends”. Chicken shops tell the story of a mixed, working-class Britain, with all its whimsy.Populism unites Le Pen and Farage. But she is a step closer to powerRead moreThere’sMorris CassanovaAKA “Mr Chicken”, the late graphic designer who claimed to have designed 90% of the chicken shop signs in London. Or just the sheer nerve of the Americana. I still chuckle whenever I pass a Dixy Chicken, imagining what the Confederate south might think of a halal business from Solihull bearing its name. Add the peri boom, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s hit YouTube channelChicken Shop Dateand Rishi Sunak discussing his Nando’s order (“It’s good broccoli,” he said), and the chicken shop’s modern cultural legacy is something to crow about.Anyway, back to the boeuf–sorry, I mean poulet – in France. Back in April, Karim Bouamrane, the Socialist party (PS) mayor of Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine, near Paris,tried to block a Master Poulet branchthat had opened outside the town hall. Literally, with concrete blocks at the doors. A court ordered them removed, so he swapped them for giant colourful plant pots. The shop responded withquippy signs(“we are open … no offence to Karim”, read one), delighting French social media with this meta game of chicken. Bouamrane insisted it was all about quality of life, as late deliveries and cooking smells disturbed residents. Not everyone was convinced.Saint-Ouen has transformed in recent years, not least due toregeneration pegged to the Paris Olympics. Critics accuse the mayor of overseeing a gentrification drive that has seen property prices surge, arguingthat’shis real issue: he wants to chase out cheap food (and the sorts of people who eat it). Master Poulet serves a drumstick of rotisserie chicken and potatoes for €4 (£3.40) – cheaper than a McDonald’s and probably no less healthy, yet McDonald’s is not a target. And given the tradition of rotisserie chicken in France, you do have to ask whatexactlyit is about the halal version that prompts complaints about bad odours.Which may explain why politicians from the further-left LaFranceInsoumise (LFI), have waded in, questioning whether Islamophobia and classism are at play, and accusing the mayor of abusing his power. One MP visited the shop in solidarity. His name? Éric Coquerel. I’ll just leave that there.To be clear, I am far from an expert on French politics. The last time I thought much about the LFI and PS was in 2024, when they joined forces in the Nouveau Front Populaire (NFP) to hold back Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally. It worked, prompting many of us in the UK to ask, with Nigel Farage tipped for No 10, shouldn’t we – red, green, yellow or bin – be doing the same?Bouamrane announced last month he would berunning for president. But as I pecked at pommes frites on a warm London evening, it was hard to see how that successful arrangement of NFP could happen again. Bouamrane has since called LFI a colonialist party, for undermining French republicanism with its talk of race; while allegations of racism from LFI continue. Meanwhile, opinion polls put Le Penon trackfor presidential glory. What leaves me crestfallen (at this point the puns are involuntary) isn’t the disagreement but what it heralds.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo am I part of the chicken shop left? I don’t know, maybe. But perhaps that’s the wrong question. After the almighty flap over Master Poulet, I’m left feeling that politics should be less “ruling the roost” and more “birds of a feather”. Especially with a far-right fox prowling outside the henhouse.Coco Khan is a freelance writer and co-host of the politics podcast Pod Save the UKDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Lena Headey looks back: ‘I told Harvey Weinstein where to go. A decade of possibilities disappeared’ | Lena Headey | The Guardian
description: The Game of Thrones actor on her feral youth, not playing the fame game, and being protective of her daughter
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The Game of Thrones actor on her feral youth, not playing the fame game, and being protective of her daughter
Content: FlashbackLena HeadeyLena Headey looks back: ‘I told Harvey Weinstein where to go. A decade of possibilities disappeared’The Game of Thrones actor on her feral youth, not playing the fame game, and being protective of her daughterHarriet GibsoneSun 26 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLena Headey in a yellow onesie opening boxes of Christmas presentsLena Headey in 1976 and in 2026. Later photograph: Simon Webb/The Guardian. Styling: Andie Redman. Hair and makeup: Neusa Neves at Arlington Artists. Archive photograph: courtesy of Lena HeadeyBorn in Hamilton, Bermuda, in 1973 and raised in West Yorkshire and Somerset, Lena Headey is an actor, writer and director. She made her film debut in Waterland in 1992. Her career spans 300, Terminator: The Sarah Connor Chronicles andGame of Thrones, in which she played Cersei Lannister from 2011 to 2019, earning five Emmy nominations. Intimacy, which she writes, directs and stars in, is an eight-part comedy audio drama for BBC Sounds and Radio 4.I was an OG onesie wearer. This was taken on Christmas Day in our house in Bermuda. My parents were in the police force, and for some reason one day the Yorkshire branch decided: “We’re all going to go to Bermuda for some training.” I don’t remember much from that time, but I know that it was hot, everyone had scooters, and that it was fun.My mum says I was an independent kid. If my parents ever tried to help me, I’d shout at them: “Leave it, leave it, leave it!” I was playful and adventurous and liked to wander far from home. We left Bermuda when I was six and moved to Somerset, where my brother was born. Having police as parents didn’t make them rule-abiding or strict. Instead – being a kid of the 70s and 80s – they would go to work while us kids were allowed to do whatever we wanted. I had a feral decade, one full of dangerous things done outside, and I feel very grateful for it.I had no ambitions to become an actor as a child, but I was obsessed with films and loved drama classes, mainly because they were the easy part of school. I found the academic side of learning difficult, but socially I survived. I had friends, and was always down for a good time.double quotation markI don’t miss being leered at, at all. There’s a liberation to getting olderFrom 11 to my late teens, I had a particularly difficult time mentally, to the extent that when I was 14 I ran away from home. I got on a bus to Birmingham to meet some older guys that I’d met on holiday. I had their addresses as we had sent letters to each other. What happened next? I smoked a bunch of weed, ran out of money and went back home. After that, my parents took me to the doctor. When he asked what was wrong, why I ran away, I said: “I don’t know. Everything just feels shit.” The doctor’s response was: “You seem depressed.” That was that, no further help.When I started acting properly in my late teens,the whole world opened up and I felt much happier. I was 17 when our school entered a play into a competition, and we went to the National Theatre to perform it. They put our photographs up in the lobby, and some casting directors saw them and asked a bunch of us to audition for a film called Waterland. I didn’t have an agent, but I drove to London for the audition at the Groucho Club. I got the part and remember thinking: “Great! Now I get to leave school.”Even though I was green and clueless, my memories of making that film are of joy and collaboration. The director, Stephen Gyllenhaal, was brilliant and the cast were all young and we got on with each other. On set, there was no hierarchy, no distinction between cast and crew – we were all in it together. On the other hand, I felt deeply vulnerable and uncomfortable being naked and pretending to have sex with another actor. Nothing’s changed – I’m still never the most enthusiastic with that side of the job. I don’t think any actor wakes up and goes: “Oh my God, today’s the day I get to wear a thong and shag someone.”After Waterland I embarked on a decade of auditioning. Sometimes it was heartbreaking, and sometimes I’d nail a job and feel fantastic. But in general, my 20s and 30s were tough. I hadn’t found my own value as a woman and was trading on external, social value rather than who I really was.Throughout my career, I’ve had great experiences in the industry, and some really bad ones too. I was lucky with Harvey Weinstein. He didn’t get his hands on me because his keycard didn’t work for the hotel room he had taken me to. I was young, cocky and drunk in our first encounter – and so when I realised what was happening I essentially told him to fuck himself. While I was fortunate nothing worse happened, I didn’t ever get another Miramax film after that. A decade and a half of possibilities disappeared. I felt I was blacklisted because I refused to do what he wanted.I was 35 when Iauditioned for Cersei in Game of Thrones.It was in a tiny room at HBO in LA. I put everything I had into it. Then I heard a phone go off – it was one of the exec’s. She got up and answered the call and left the room. I watched her walk out, and said: “Are you joking?” At that moment I thought: “I’m never getting this. I am obviously very uncharismatic and unengaging.” Turns out that is quite normal, and I was wrong.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGame of Thrones threw me into visibility on a scale I hadn’t experienced before and it was a strange dynamic to contend with. The show ran for a decade of my life, one in which I went through a divorce and became a mother, twice. Even though I was in a big show and making money, and had financial security for the first time as an actor – and for the last time, it turns out – I was still wrangling with major life changes while being in the public eye. There were lots of weird moments, such as going on holiday with the kids, being half-naked in the sand and someone coming up to me and saying: “Can we do a quick video?” I’d have to say: “Nah, not really.”Rita Wilson looks back: ‘Cancer was terrifying, but now I see it as a gift. It gave me an extra lease on life’Read moreFame is not for me. I could employ a stylist and go to the opening of this and that. But I’m really lazy. I look at people who seem to get lots of work and opportunities and ask: “Why didn’t I get that job?” My agent will reply: “Well, if you did a bit more press or agreed to having a publicist, things might be different.” After that, I often think: “Nah, forget it.” The trade-off for having lots of work is that you have to get out there, always pushing to be seen. Which is tough when you have Jomo: the joy of missing out.It’s often said that women become invisible when they reach midlife.While it is true, I’ve never liked being available; that feeling of shrinking under the weight of feeling scared and alone when you’re by yourself on a train or in a cab. I’ve had way more horrible experiences than what happened with Harvey, but that is life. My main takeaway is that I never, ever, want those things to happen to my children. The biggest stress of being a parent is wanting your children not to feel the same pain or disappointment or violence or sadness. When I’m out with my daughter, who is gorgeous and only 11, I see the power of her beauty in the eyes of men that really shouldn’t be looking at her. I hate it. So I don’t miss being leered at, at all. There’s a liberation to getting older.When I see that photo, I wish that I could protect my younger self from some of the things she would go through. But I can’t. Instead, I’m appreciative that I can protect my girl instead.Explore more on these topicsLena HeadeyFlashbackFamilyPhotographyGame of ThronesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why does everything feel so joyless? Welcome to the age of decadence without pleasure | Society | The Guardian
description: Decadence in our era comes in technologically mediated forms, emptied of desire and obsessed with self-optimisation
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Decadence in our era comes in technologically mediated forms, emptied of desire and obsessed with self-optimisation
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignThe featured essaySocietyWhy does everything feel so joyless? Welcome to the age of decadence without pleasureDecadence in our era comes in technologically mediated forms, emptied of desire and obsessed with self-optimisationMichèle Mendelssohn and Charlie TysonSun 26 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTShareDo you want to have a good time? You know, really enjoy yourself? Click here, and tell us your desires. Maybe it’s a new outfit, or some exotic cuisine delivered anonymously and steaming hot to your door. Maybe it’s porn or gambling. Perhaps you prefer the infinite scroll, the endlessly unfurling ribbon of glossy images and videos starring people you’ll never meet doing things you’ll never do. Or maybe you favor talking to a chatbot who will assure you that you are the most special of all its users.For anyone with an Internet connection and a little discretionary income, the contemporary moment offers a superabundance of seductive distractions. Why then the pervasive mood of emptiness? Why are so many at once overstimulated and bored?Welcome to the era of decadence without pleasure.The concept of decadence as a marker of cultural decline coinciding with a high level of wealth has been around since the twilight of the ancient Greeks and Romans. After the Roman emperor Elagabalus took the throne at 14, he served flamingo brains, seasoned his food with pearls, and, according to one account, smothered guests to death with an avalanche of rose petals. But his vices were outdone by Nero, who had his enemies sewn into wild animal skins and devoured by dogs in an elaborate garden spectacle.So decadence has an inescapably pejorative ring, suggesting decay, excess and a falling away from norms and ideals. Critics of decadence have usually hailed from the political right, and the same is true today: consider conservative New York Times columnist Ross Douthat’s critique of cultural and economic stagnation in his 2020 book The Decadent Society, or billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s complaints about faltering innovation and the supposed decline of the west. JD Vance likes to invoke the fall of Rome,warning, inhis 2026 memoir Communion, that the US is “a great civilization” tumbling into “disrepair”. But plenty of thinkers on the left also worry that modern wealthy societies have entered a period of paralysis, under the shadow of what the Italian theorist Franco “Bifo” Berardi calls “the slow cancellation of the future”.View image in fullscreenThe Roses of Heliogabalus (1888) by artist Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema, depicting the young Roman emperorElagabalushosting a banquet.Photograph: Studio SebertThat all sounds bad. Yet a passionate minority has sometimes found, in decadence, reasons for hope.Cultures later judged decadent produced extraordinary upwellings of art, like the flare of a dying star. Think of the undulating arabesques of Rococo painting before the French Revolution, or the lush shimmering silks of the late Ottomans, or the experimental cinema and nightlife of Weimar Berlin.Nowhere was the cultural potential of decadence more visible than in the late-19th century. In France, Britain and (with less gusto) in the United States, artists such as Oscar Wilde, Aubrey Beardsley, Joris-Karl Huysmans and Rachilde developed new literary and visual styles championing extravagance, sensuousness and the superiority of artifice. It is to these avant-garde experiments that we owe green carnations (the fakest of flowers), frivolous dandies obsessed with perfumes, a bejeweled tortoise crushed to death by the weight of its splendor, and erotic nightmares including a woman with monstrous flowers growing between her thighs and a male anatomical model whose legs spread at the click of a spring so that he can be penetrated by his female lover. Such taboo-busting grotesquery protested against the inertia of modern civilization by applying moral and aesthetic shock treatment.The decadents, however, were not just provocateurs. Their revolt against Victorian society’s deadening enslavement to usefulness, materialism and conventionality put forward a positive philosophy of life, a certain way of thinking about pleasure. Against their era’s obsession with use-value and profit, the decadents insisted that pleasure was, or ought to be, “useless”, enjoyed for its own sake in life’s passing moments. “Not the fruit of experience, but experience itself, is the end,” intoned the essayist Walter Pater, one of the guiding lights of English decadence, in his masterpiece The Renaissance. A reclusive Oxford don, Pater was said to have once stopped High Street traffic to stroke a cat. Why? For the sensation of fur beneath his fingers. The virtue of decadent pleasure is that it is useless, an end in itself.Our tech overlords are planning for conscious AI to conquer the cosmos. What could go wrong? | Eduardo PorterRead moreThe fixations of fin-de-siècle decadence that inspired Oscar Wilde and company are still with us, but in shrivelled, technologically mediated forms. GLP-1s turn the delights of eating into a problem to be managed. Anti-ageing remedies and “looksmaxxing” turn decadence’s preoccupation with self-styling into a (literally painful) form of self-optimisation. AI restages decadence’s love of artifice by outsourcing human thinking to a chatty, eager-to-please machine butler.The problem with contemporary culture isn’t that we’re too decadent. We have inherited the surfaces of decadence – luxury, excess, artifice, bodily display – but have surrendered the fin de siècle’s commitment to pleasure. The result is a culture in which pleasure is subordinated to programs of optimisation and replaced at scale by numbing algorithmic stimulation and promises of instant gratification. Whether you’re after goods, food, art or ideas, you can get more, faster, now.But quantity and speed can’t make up for the paradox at the heart of today’s decadence: the fact that it’s often “meh” and oddly joyless. It’s a sign of the times that this spring,Amazon’s Chinese rival launchedin the UK and Europe under a name that promises to deliver emotional fulfilment: Joybuy.The ‘looksmaxxing’ eraBryan Johnson, the frequently shirtless tech tycoon who has funnelled his fortune into what he calls the“Don’t Die” movement, has turned his quest for immortality into a prolonged exhibition of ascetic self-management. His lifestyle is harrowingly spartan: he doesn’t drink alcohol, avoids the sun, never goes out in the evening, and subsists primarily on lentils, boiled broccoli and macadamia nuts. Yet his regimen is, in its peculiar way, one of prurient excess. He swallows up to 111 pills a day, tracks his night-time erections, and once tapped his teenage son for blood plasma. His fight against death costs a reported $2m a year.Johnson presents himself as a man of the future, but he has a 19th-century double. While pallid, faintly androgynous men with money and strange habits are not rare in decadent literature, the most famous is Duke Jean des Esseintes, the hero of Joris-Karl Huysmans’s 1884 novel Against the Grain, a work considered the Bible of decadence. The last scion of an aristocratic French family, des Esseintes creates for himself a cloistered world of voluptuous artifice: padded walls, rare books, exotic flowers, fragrant bonbons, subtle liqueurs, perfumes so sweet they verge on rancid.View image in fullscreenBryan Johnson wearing a brain-scanning helmet called Flow during a pilot study involving a ketamine-induced altered state of consciousness.Photograph: Business Wire/APLike Johnson, des Esseintes is medically fragile, obsessed with death, and preoccupied with the minutiae of his private sensations. Like Johnson, he sees his retreat from ordinary society into a tightly controlled artificial environment as an experiment that tests the limits of human possibility. But whereas des Esseintes’s withdrawal is an immersion into the subtleties of sensation, Johnson’s “Don’t Die” movement treats the delights of the senses as suspect, even fatal. Des Esseintes hosts a funeral banquet for his “dead virility” in a dining room draped in black, opening on to charcoaled gardens, with guests dining on black-bordered plates filled with black food (rye bread, caviar, black pudding, cuts of meat dripping with liquorice-coloured sauce). Johnson, by contrast, treats impotence as a technical problem,repeatedly shockinghis penis to increase his erections.double quotation markThese attitudes reflect the fantasies of a narrow elite obsessed with human enhancementJohnson’s programme is extreme, but he is not an anomaly. His lifestyle makes visible, in exaggerated form, new attitudes toward pleasure and embodiment being pushed by today’s tech billionaires. While some superwealthy people in or around Palo Alto are biohacking for longevity with the help of concierge medics, others are treating even sexual pleasure as a domain to be perfected through medical interventions. For example, at Dr Sally Greenwald’s exclusive OB-GYN practice, nicknamed the “Billionaire’s Vagina Club” – Greenwald describes her clientele as “the top 0.001%” – middle-aged women can improve their “sexspan” through bespoke advice, hormonal cocktails and tracking devices. “Sex equals sleep, stress reduction, cardiovascular engagement, relational fulfilment, and pelvic-floor health, and each of those equals health,”Greenwald says.These attitudes reflect the fantasies of a narrow elite obsessed with human enhancement and – above all else – the prolongation of their own survival. The class politics of pleasureless decadence can be roughly summarized as: biohacking and quantified asceticism for the rich, algorithmic stimulation for the rest.In contexts of extreme inequality, rich people tend to set the terms by which pleasure is understood and experienced. The very fact of inequality injures pleasure, because in a stratified society, food, art, travel and other delights can devolve into occasions to demonstrate rank or taste. Our present social order, however, is not just radically unequal; it’s dominated by a ruling class that distrusts pleasure and sensation. What passes for “fun” among today’s top 0.001% amounts to anything but: think of the 80-hour workweeks championed by tech titans like Elon Musk, or Equinox gym’s “Optimize” longevity membership costing $40,000 a year, or courtside seats at Knicks games inside the miniaturesurveillance statethat is Madison Square Garden. And because of their outsized political and cultural influence, their sway over public and private investment, and their habit of not paying their share of tax, the pleasurelessness of the ultra-monied classes trickles down to the rest of us.“I think trying to optimise things … is actually the divine spark within us,” recentlyprofessedthe German biotech billionaire Christian Angermayer, a champion of “humanmaxxing”, the use of drugs and supplements to enhance the body. Divinity aside, it seems pertinent to mention that the person content with every day sensations makes for a poor consumer. But get people outside the plutocratic class to reconceive their minds and bodies as sites of perpetual self-improvement, and you have, in Angermayer’s words, “a total addressable market of ideally 100%”.The most culturally revealing such market is for GLP-1s such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro. One in eight American adults report taking GLP-1 injectables for weight loss, according to a 2025 Galluppoll, and far moreexpress interestin taking them. The global market for this class of drugs isexpectedto reach $190bn by 2035. For many, these medications confer real benefits. Yet it seems fair to ask: what does the widespread embrace of appetite-governing pharmaceuticals suggest about our culture’s handling of pleasure and desire?GLP-1s reshape the felt relation between desire and satisfaction, as research has already begun to show. While more studies are needed, some usersreporta diminution of pleasure across several areas of their lives: they complain of lethargy, decreased libido, emotional flatness and a weakened connection to the social dimensions of eating.View image in fullscreenThe Fruit Bearers (1896) by Aubrey Beardsley.Photograph: AlamyThe decadence of the fin de siècle celebrated cornucopian abundance. Take for example Aubrey Beardsley’s1896 drawingThe Fruit Bearers, depicting two figures bearing colossal bowls of fruit, lush grapes overhanging, a peacock in the background observing the opulent procession. In contrast, today’s anhedonic decadence celebrates the inhibition, even the transcendence, of appetite. While in haute cuisinethe trappings of indulgence are preserved – some upmarket eateries nowoffer“small appetite” menus featuring caviar and foie gras – the tendency is toward delicate minimalism. Because eating is a quintessentially communal activity, an intervention in how people eat is also an intervention in how we socialize.It seems reasonable to expect, meanwhile, that the widespread uptake of such drugs may contribute to a tightening not just of belts but of beauty norms. Looksmaxxing, an online subculture aimed primarily at young men, presents a darker strain of physical perfectionism, treating the body as a site of correction. Of course, women have long been ground down by painful and impossible beauty standards. What’s striking about looksmaxxing is the migration of this kind of disciplinary logic into a male subculture that speaks of beauty in terms of brutal domination: anyone can be “mogged” (outshone by a more handsome man), and one of the purposes of maxxing is to increase one’s “sexual market value”. Key to this subculture is the rejection of subjective taste in favor of mathematical norms (looksmaxxers prize certain ratios of facial proportion, measuring, for instance, the height of the forehead or the distance between the pupils).“[T]o make oneself beautiful is a universal instinct,” a young Max Beerbohm wrote in his 1894 essay A Defence of Cosmetics, a send-up of decadence’s cult of artifice. Whereas the fin-de-siècle decadents with their love of makeup treated the face as a mask to play with or an enigma to contemplate, looksmaxxers recast the face as a set of homogenizing metrics requiring arduous correction. “The men are weeping in the gym,” writes Andrew McMillan in his prescient 2015 poem about punitive male beauty standards:they have got too close to the glassand now they are layingin the broken pools of their own faces.View image in fullscreenThe pleasureless decadence machineThe fin de siècle had its own cult of masculine self-display in the form of the dandy, with his carefully tailored coat, polished shoes and pigskin gloves. The dandy’s concern for appearance was just part of the era’s wide-ranging love of stylization. “The first duty in life is to be as artificial as possible,” Oscar Wilde proclaimed. “What the second duty is no one has yet discovered.” Wilde and other decadents prized the made over the natural. Artifice was a way of intensifying the given world, overlaying the hard facts of life with a glittering sheen or a more pleasant smell. After all, what is the dandy’s perfume but a victory for pleasure over necessity?AI marks a triumph of artifice more sweeping than the old decadents could have imagined. Yet far from bolstering our capacity for perceptual intensity, AI presents new threats to both. Its productions – LinkedIn posts about the virtues of entrepreneurship, cartoon soap operas about the infidelities of anthropomorphized fruits – are eerily hollow, with no felt experience, embodiment or sensation behind them. AI is the pleasureless decadence machine.double quotation markThere is no pleasure or pain for an AI, no skin in the gameCarissa VélizAlready our algorithmically driven culture is saturated with a deluge of slop that promises numbing, empty stimulation. The old decadents were fascinated by the prospect of mental oblivion, the loss of self-control in the face of overwhelming beauty. Today, AI researcherswarnof “human enfeeblement” as tech companies seek to draw users into relations of dependency and infantilization, with machines to do their “thinking” for them.While the fin-de-siècle left imprints on visual art, fashion, music and other art forms, it was primarily as a literary movement that its decadence made cultural interventions. Crucial to decadent writing was a taste for language – lilting rhythms, overheated exclamations – that would affect the reader viscerally, leaving her trembling, her moral assumptions upended. In contrast, LLMs leach language of pleasure by blandifying it: the algorithm steers language away from the idiosyncratic and toward the predictable.Pleasure isn’t just about hedonism or indulgence in “useless” objects. It is one of the principal ways we, as embodied beings, perceive value. Pain teaches us not to touch the hot stove twice; pleasure guides us toward the sweetness of clean water and fresh air. Pleasure is not infallible: some things that feel good are cruel, addictive, or destructive. But the embodied experience of pleasure is crucial to how we learn and how we make judgments about what is good, beautiful and worth pursuing. These are not judgments we can wisely cede to disembodied machines.“There is no pleasure or pain for an AI, no skin in the game,” the philosopher Carissa Véliz writes in her recent book Prophecy. As a result, an AI “cannot care, and therefore cannot value”. Without some felt relation to pleasure and pain, judgments of value and taste become abstract and bloodless.View image in fullscreenReclaiming everyday pleasuresBecause of its commitment to embodied pleasure, fin-de-siècle decadence offers powerful lessons for the increasingly disembodied, tech-optimised world championed by elites. This is not to suggest, however, that the old decadents were living uncomplicated lives of satisfaction and joy. WB Yeats called the poets of 1890s London “the tragic generation”. The decadents could be moody and morbid, susceptible to ennui, spleen and other Baudelairean ailments. In other words, they were all too human. Some died young, succumbing to alcoholism or tuberculosis; others abandoned the religion of art to join the Catholic church. Fin-de-siècle decadence had, moreover, an aristocratic and misogynistic bent. Many of its most influential English champions were highly educated men who regarded ordinary life with aloofness, even contempt.From the start, however, decadence was both an elite and a minoritarian movement, spearheaded largely by men (and some women) of privilege – but responsible for injecting a new awareness of queerness into public consciousness.Oscar Wilde’s 1890 novel The Picture of Dorian Gray is a story of a thrill-seeker’s descent into decadent squalor – hedonism, moral bankruptcy, irresponsible self-indulgence and the exploitation of others – in the name of never ageing. But when Victorian society raged at Dorian’s monstrosity, Wilde countered that “vice and virtue are to the artist materials for an art” that can reveal humanity to itself. Sure, Dorian was a perverted Peter Pan, a bad boy who didn’t want to grow up and face consequences. But his scandalous romp reflected society’s concealed desires back to itself.In fin-de-siècle decadence, we can also see a growing appreciation of female desire. The 1892 poetry collection Sight and Song by Michael Field – the pen name of two lesbian lovers who wrote as one – turns an explicitly female gaze on the art-historical canon. A poem in response to Leonardo da Vinci’s drawing of Leda, the princess seduced by Zeus in the form of a swan, grants Leda all the power: “She draws the fondled creature to her will.” Their Saint Sebastian is, by contrast, a passive icon of masculine beauty, “with body fresh for use, for pleasure fit, / With its energies and needs together knit”.View image in fullscreenLeda and the Swan, 16th century, attributed to the followers of Leonardo da Vinci.Photograph: Heritage Images/Getty ImagesSo too have Black and postcolonial artists drawn from late-19th-century decadence in asserting their own claims to pleasure. Bruce Nugent’s homoerotic story Smoke, Lilies and Jade (1926), one of the more audacious works of the Harlem Renaissance, opens with the Black hero, Alex, lying on his bed, exhaling blue smoke from a cigarette. Alex idly ponders Wilde’s remark that “a cigarette is the most perfect pleasure because it leaves one unsatisfied” before passing into the streets in search of more gratifying pleasures. He meets a white man he callsBeauty, and the two embrace: Alex “could feel Beauty’s body … close against his … hot … tense … white … and soft”. That sentence’s panting prose gives away the game – Alex knows that enjoying the pleasure forbidden to him is the ultimate decadent act.double quotation markIf a New Decadence is to emerge, we need artists to invent it and individuals to ... appreciate its disruptive energiesAnd now? A renewed, democratic decadence could stage a revolt against optimisation, encouraging ordinary people to brace themselves against the siren simulations of the digital world. Because contemporary culture looks decadent but feels punishing and devoid of meaning, a New Decadence could respond powerfully to this essential contradiction. Every day acts of aesthetic perception – such as Walter Pater stopping traffic to stroke a cat – matter. But if a New Decadence is to emerge, we need artists to invent it and individuals to pause and appreciate its disruptive energies.So far, neodecadent energies in art have been submerged in satirical entertainments about rich people behaving badly – films like Saltburnor TV shows like The White Lotus that reproduce the structure of pleasureless decadence by equating pleasure with status, power and consumption.There are signs, however, of something more original and less reactive emerging, an art that foregrounds the senses for an era that distrusts the body. The sensuous cinema ofPeter Strickland; the frightening but gorgeousblood-coloured sculpturesof Anish Kapoor; the reinvigoration of Black decadence in Shola von Reinhold’s novelLote; the Dionysian reimagining of the fin de siècle in John Corigliano’s operaThe Lord of Cries– none of this amounts to a coherent movement. Yet all these works offer, to their respective artforms, materials from which a New Decadence could arise – a movement that could give pleasure back to people, make the social body’s pulses race again, and force fresh blood through today’s complacent, anemic culture.View image in fullscreenA gallery worker poses with the work Mount Moriah at the Gate of the Ghetto by Anish Kapoor at the Hayward Gallery in London on 15 June 2026.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAWalter Pater prefaced his study of the Renaissance with a sort of epicurean pleasure script, a series of diagnostic questions you can ask yourself to get a better handle on what you experience:What is this song or picture, this engaging personality presented in life or in a book, tome? What effect does it really produce on me? Does it give me pleasure? and if so, what sort or degree of pleasure? How is my nature modified by its presence, and under its influence?Your answers to these questions, he argues, have the virtue of satisfying your soul. Giving your attention to what you are feeling, analyzing your impressions, being moved and attentive to life’s everyday experiences – this is where real pleasure lies, so long as your pleasure harms no one else’s.Why strive for pleasure? Why long for it? Because – contra the Bryan Johnsons of the world – we will die. “A counted number of pulses only,” Pater writes, “is given to us of a variegated, dramatic life.” Like Johnson, like the humanmaxxers, Pater counts his pulses. “Our one chance lies,” he writes, “in expanding that interval, in getting as many pulsations as possible into the given time.”How different Pater’s pulse-counting is from that of the biometric ascetics. Against the pressure to optimise life, decadence issues a different command:feel it.View image in fullscreen.

title: Ed Miliband indicates development and climate will be at heart of UK foreign policy | World Bank | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Foreign secretary to take up World Bank seat and play active role in shaping changes to global lender
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Exclusive: Foreign secretary to take up World Bank seat and play active role in shaping changes to global lender
Content: Experts have welcomed Miliband’s move as a boost to climate action.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenExperts have welcomed Miliband’s move as a boost to climate action.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.World BankEd Miliband indicates development and climate will be at heart of UK foreign policyExclusive: Foreign secretary to take up World Bank seat and play active role in shaping changes to global lenderSupported byAbout this contentFiona HarveyEnvironment editorSun 26 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s foreign secretary,Ed Miliband, is to indicate he will put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations by taking up the country’s seat on the board at the World Bank.The position, which is usually delegated to a junior minister, means Miliband will play an active role in shaping the changes to theWorld Bankthat developing countries have called for, and ensuring the climate remains a core focus for overseas aid.Miliband, who was energy and net zero secretary under Keir Starmer, will say: “International development is not an add-on to British foreign policy – it is central to it. By taking on the role of UK governor to the World Bank, I want to send an unambiguous signal that this government is serious about its global leadership on development and climate.”His announcement comes as fires continue to devastateswathes of France and Spain, and after Scotland called formilitary aidto tackle a blaze that engulfed the Cairngorms. Conditions approachingdrought across England and parts of Waleshave prompted hosepipe bans, and the heatwave that swept across Europe in June isestimated tohave cost the continent’s grain farmers €2bn (£1.7bn) in lost revenue.By taking up the World Bank seat personally, Miliband is sending a clear signal that while other politicians even now argue against net zero policies, the Foreign Office will continue to drive climate action.The move comes at a crucial time for the international lender, which has come underheavy pressure from the Trump administrationto reverse a previous focus on climate finance. Last month, the publicly funded bankscrapped its goalfor 45% of its finance to be directed to climate-related ends.Experts welcomed Miliband’s decision as a boost to climate action. Lord Stern, a professor of economics at the London School of Economics, said the foreign secretary’s take-up of the UK governor’s seat would “send a powerful and important signal” to the world.“As a former chief economist and senior vice-president of the World Bank, I know that the UK can punch above its weight,” he said. “But only if the leadership is there from the top. In recent years, that has slipped. Ed Miliband will be restoring development and climate to the priority in our international relationships that they must have, in a world facing climate and biodiversity crises, and with real and growing threats to the wellbeing of the world’s poorest.”Other countries have been wary of challenging the US on its anti-climate stance, for fear of reprisals and after widespread cuts to developed countries’ overseas aid. The UK is one of six countries with its own seat at the World Bank board.Mohamed Adow, a director of Power Shift Africa, a thinktank, said Miliband could champion changes at the lender that would help the poor.“The real test is whether the UK uses its influence to push the World Bank to deliver far more finance for climate action and adaptation, to get money to countries faster, and ensure the poorest nations are not forced deeper into debt to respond to a crisis they did least to cause,” Adow said. “If this appointment marks the start of renewed British leadership on global climate and development, it will be warmly welcomed across Africa.”Miliband will face a shrinking aid budget and tough decisions over allocation. Starmerslashed overseas aidto 0.3% of gross national income, a sharp reduction from 0.5% under the Conservatives and the 0.7% reached under the last Labour government.Climate finance was also cut by 14%, from £11.6bn for the period 2021 to 2026 to £2bn a year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, wascriticised last weekfor saying his planned £2 cap on bus fares in England would be funded mainly by changing international climate finance grants into repayable loans. The loans will go to theTropical Forests Forever Facility, an investment fund set up by the Brazilian government.Jonathan Hall, the managing director of the charity Conservation International UK, said that to restore its credibility, the government should rescind the cuts Starmer madeto funding for nature protectiondespiteBritain’s spy chiefs sayingthat ecosystem collapse overseas threatened national security.“Miliband now needs to reintroduce a clear target for a third of the UK’s £6bn climate aid budget tofinance natural ecosystems and tropical forests, a goal which was lost under his predecessor,” said Hall.The UK will take over the leadership of the G20 group in November.Rachel Kyte, the UK’s climate envoy and a former senior World Bank official, said: “We will be in the midst of an energy and food security crisis from the blockage of the strait of Hormuz. Compounding that is a severe El Niño. We will need every ounce of capacity in the international financial architecture to help some parts of the world through the severity of these impacts. Ed has seen what it takes to mobilise the world to action before, pulling every lever we have available to us. If needed, we will do it again, for our own and everyone else’s security.”Explore more on these topicsWorld BankClimate financeClimate crisisEd MilibandForeign policyAidGlobal economynewsShareReuse this content

title: Pedro Sánchez says Spain is suffering effects of climate crisis as firefighters battle wildfires in France | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Blazes near Madrid coming under control but efforts to contain huge fire near Bordeaux hampered by windy conditions
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Blazes near Madrid coming under control but efforts to contain huge fire near Bordeaux hampered by windy conditions
Content: A home in the village of Le Porge in south-west France is consumed by flames.Photograph: Clement Viala/infobassin.com/Abaca/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA home in the village of Le Porge in south-west France is consumed by flames.Photograph: Clement Viala/infobassin.com/Abaca/ShutterstockWildfiresPedro Sánchez says Spain is suffering effects of climate crisis as firefighters battle wildfires in FranceBlazes near Madrid coming under control but efforts to contain huge fire near Bordeaux hampered by windy conditionsAngelique Chrisafisin Paris,Sam Jonesin Madrid andJennifer RankinSun 26 Jul 2026 08.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 22.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAuthorities inFrancebattled to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux in the south-west as Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, warned Spain and the Iberian peninsula were suffering the effects of the climate emergency.Efforts to extinguish the blaze in the Gironde region of France – which has consumed an area four times the size of Paris and caused nearly 220,000 people to be evacuated – were hampered by windy conditions on Saturday night.InSpain, fires west of Madrid were being brought under control, but Sánchez spoke of “difficult hours”.Wildfires have forced about 375,000 people to flee their homes in France and Spain. In France nearly 260,000 have been forced to flee, while in neighbouring Spain 116,000 have been evacuated this week.0:59Firefighters in Spain and France battle raging wildfires – videoBordeaux’s mayor, Thomas Cazenave, described the Gironde blaze as being “at the gates of the metropolitan area”, between 15 and 20 miles (25-30km) from the city itself, which has a population of 268,000. An evacuation of the city was not on the cards, he said.Nearly 260,000 people have been evacuated across France as a whole, including 36,000 ordered to leave another wildfire zone in the Landes region farther south earlier this week.Map showing the location of wildfires in France and SpainSophie Brocas, the prefect of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, which includes the Gironde, said that the highly unpredictable nature of this wildfire was a phenomenon never seen before in France. “I urge tourists not to come to Gironde as long as the fire has not been contained,” she said. “I invite tourists who are already here to think about going to another destination. We don’t know where the fire is going to go.”France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, was due on Monday morning to hold a crisis cabinet meeting to discuss the emergency.France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Sunday the previous night had been difficult and “the situation remains very unfavourable”. He said the Gironde fire had become “extremely virulent and unpredictable again” on Saturday night, generating its own wind and spreading erratically towards the Bordeaux metropolitan area. It had become calmer by the end of the night, he said.Since Wednesday, the fire in Gironde has injured 84 firefighters, 10 of whom have been evacuated, according to the latest situation report published on Sunday by the prefecture.Sebastien Bouvier, federal secretary of France’s CFDT union, said firefighters did not have adequate equipment to protect themselves from the fires’ toxic fumes.About 2,500 firefighters (including a Swiss team), 1,500 military personnel and about 1,200 police had been deployed to Gironde, Nuñez said, as he praised the contribution of 450 volunteers from civil security organisations.He said another five Gironde municipalities had been evacuated overnight.View image in fullscreenA drone view of an area burned by the wildfire in the village of Le Porge, Gironde.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersOne firefighter told Agence France-Presse that the fire had formed a pyrocumulonimbus, a fire-generated thunderstorm that “creates its own wind, with whirlwinds, becoming erratic and uncontrollable”.A spokesperson for the National Firefighters Federation of France said that while known in wildfire-prone Australia and Canada, one had never been seen before in France. The federation’s Lt Col Éric Brocardi told AFP there was a need to understand a “natural force beyond our control”.
