He said: “It’s a David v Goliath scenario: the idea is that, at some point, we’ll find a weak spot and strike there.”Police in Gironde made three arrests over the weekend, including one man smoking in the forest and two having barbecues in a forest area.View image in fullscreenSmoke rises from a wildfire near San Martin de Valdeiglesias, west of Madrid.Photograph: Ana Beltran/ReutersAuthorities in Spain said major areas of fire near Madrid had been contained and cooled down, according to a senior officer with Spain’s military emergencies unit.“We’re facing some difficult hours, although it’s true that the latest update has shown that last night was very positive in terms of the fire’s evolution and efforts to control it,” Sánchez said.Speaking at an advance firefighters’ command post west of Madrid, the prime minister warned that Spain and Portugal were experiencing the varied consequences of the climate emergency, from fires and storms to heavy snowfalls. “The entire Iberian peninsula is suffering the effects of the climate emergency in a very specific way,” he said.While the fire near Madrid was being brought under control, emergency workers battled to extinguish a new fire near the Mediterranean port city of València, where at least 15,000 people were evacuated. “The fire is beyond our capacity to extinguish, it has a perimeter of about 21km,” the València region’s president, Juanfran Pérez Llorca, said late on Saturday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSpain’s interior ministry said on Saturday evening that a man had died in a fire in the Valèncian town of Manises. He had been found in a car in a ravine, officials said. Sánchez was due to visit València on Monday.0:57Spain wildfire burns ‘out of extinguishing capacity’ as fires engulf parts of Europe – videoAuthorities also ordered the evacuation of eight more municipalities near Toledo, south of Madrid, on Saturday, bringing the number of people forced to flee their homes by wildfires in Spain in recent days to 116,000, the Associated Press reported.Spain’s environment minister, Sara Aagesen, said the wildfire that had burned through 50,000 hectares of land in the central province of Ávila was “the largest forest fire in our country’s recent history”. The civil protection chief, Virginia Barcones, called the Ávila fire a “monster”.Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said on Sunday evening the fires were advancing but slowly.The blazes are the latest episode in a summer of wildfires that threaten to burn an unprecedented expanse of land. Europe has endured a series of heatwaves since the spring, fuelled by the climate crisis, includingthe hottest-ever June, leaving vegetation tinder dry.The EU commissioner for crisis management, Hadja Lahbib, told the BBC it was likely that damage from wildfires would exceed previous records. “Last year, one million hectares burned during the summer and so we are expecting to face another historic, sad record because the season has started earlier in the year,” she said.View image in fullscreenFirefighters battle a blaze in Ares, south-west France.Photograph: Damien Rembert/EPASpain’s environment ministry said 32 major fires affecting 152,678 hectares (377,276 acres) had been recorded so far in 2026, compared with seven affecting 24,133 hectares in the same period in 2025.The Gironde fire in France has so far burned 42,000 hectares, an area four times the size of Paris and one of the biggest devastations of land since the second world war. At least 240 homes had been destroyed and many more damaged, a gendarme told BFMTV.View image in fullscreenFirefighters prepare to join efforts to contain the Gironde fire.Photograph: Astrid Lagougne/EPAFirefighters are battling to slow the fire’s progression toward Bordeaux from the ground and air, with planes dropping water and retardants. Jérôme Steffe, the mayor of Cestas commune, 10 miles from Bordeaux city centre, told French media: “We are working together to put in place a firewall to block the advance of the flames.”An exhibition centre in Bordeaux has been turned into an emergency shelter, providing camp beds and food for thousands of people, including hundreds of older people evacuated from care homes.Cazenave said he had asked the central government for an economic crisis plan for the area because many businesses and workers had been evacuated from areas west of Bordeaux and the tourism industry had been heavily affected. He said it was impossible to say when people evacuated as a precaution could return to their homes.“We don’t know how long this crisis will last, whether several days or several weeks,” he said.The Landes fire has consumed 3,600 hectares and a rekindling of flames on Saturday had to be tackled from the air, Nuñez said. French authorities are also dealing with wildfires in the south-eastern Var region, where 3,000 people have been evacuated, as well as the Hautes-Alpes and Corsica.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresFranceSpainExtreme heatExtreme weatherClimate crisisEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to meet Zelenskyy at UK naval base in show of ‘unwavering’ support | Volodymyr Zelenskyy | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president will be first overseas visitor for new British prime minister
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Ukrainian president will be first overseas visitor for new British prime minister
Content: Volodymyr Zelenskyy was one of the first world leaders Burnham spoke to when he entered No 10 last week.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAView image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy was one of the first world leaders Burnham spoke to when he entered No 10 last week.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAVolodymyr ZelenskyyBurnham to meet Zelenskyy at UK naval base in show of ‘unwavering’ supportUkrainian president will be first overseas visitor for new British prime ministerPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentSun 26 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy will become Andy Burnham’s first overseas visitor as prime minister, in a visit that Burnham said underlined Britain’s “unwavering” backing for Ukraine.Less than two weeks after Keir Starmer travelled to Kyiv for the final foreign visit of his prime ministership, the Ukrainian president will on Monday join Burnham at a naval base where Ukrainian forces have been receiving training.Zelenskyy was one of the first world leaders Burnham spoke to when he entered No 10 last week, and the prime minister has promised to maintain Starmer’s strong support for the country in pushing back against Russia’s invasion.Andy Burnham says he will disagree with Trump in public if necessaryRead moreOn the visit to the base, the pair will speak to Ukrainian and British military personnel who have taken part in Exercise Sea Breeze, a 15-country training deployment based on mine exercises and other maritime operations in the Black Sea.The second part ofthis year’s exercise, which took place in Portland, Dorset, finished on Friday and involved more than 200 Ukrainian personnel.Burnham and Zelenskyy are also due to discuss joint projects including Stone Cloak, an electronic jammer for which the UK has shared the intellectual property, allowingUkraineto use the system immediately.Thousands of the jammers, each about the size of a tablet computer, have been sent to Ukraine to be fitted to drones, with the aim of stopping Russian air defence systems from tracking and targeting them.Ukraine is now able to mass produce the devices itself. After being initially used there, the jammers are due to be fitted to new UK weaponry, including cruise missiles.Burnham, in a comment released by Downing Street before the visit, said: “Britain stands with Ukraine, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering. Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve, and we will not back down until we achieve a long-lasting and just peace for Ukraine.“Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAccording to statistics released by No 10, since Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, total UK support for the country has totalled £25bn, including £16bn in military assistance.Starmer visited Ukraine a number of times, and hosted Zelenskyy regularly. In one of the most telling displays of UK support, after a March 2025 visit to the White Houseduring which the Ukrainian leader was publicly beratedby Donald Trump, he thentravelled to the UKand met not only Starmer but also King Charles at Sandringham, which is primarily a royal home and rarely used for official events.During Starmer’s final visit to Ukraine, Zelenskyy presented him with the country’s Order of Freedom, the most prestigious honour that can be given to an overseas national.During a press conference with Starmer, the Ukrainian president said he hoped to build a strong relationship with Burnham, and to arrange a meeting “as soon as possible”.Explore more on these topicsVolodymyr ZelenskyyForeign policyAndy BurnhamLabourMilitaryUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Police shoot dead Berlin Pride van and knife rampage suspect, officials say | Germany | The Guardian
description: Abdul Ballout, 21, reportedly shot in operation at allotment in Spandau district after fatal attack in Tiergarten park
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Abdul Ballout, 21, reportedly shot in operation at allotment in Spandau district after fatal attack in Tiergarten park
Content: Police officers secure the area at an allotment garden complex in the Berlin suburb of Spandau where the man suspected of the attack was shot and killed.Photograph: Christian Mang/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice officers secure the area at an allotment garden complex in the Berlin suburb of Spandau where the man suspected of the attack was shot and killed.Photograph: Christian Mang/ReutersGermanyPolice shoot dead Berlin Pride van and knife rampage suspect, officials sayAbdul Ballout, 21, reportedly shot in operation at allotment in Spandau district after fatal attack in Tiergarten parkDeborah Colein Berlin andJennifer RankinSun 26 Jul 2026 13.53 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by police, German officials have said.Police confirmed on Sunday evening that the chief suspect had been shot dead, reportedly during an operation at an allotment garden complex ⁠in the capital’s Spandau district.One woman was killed on Saturday evening and 29 others were injured after a man drove a rented minivan into a crowd of pedestrians, then attacked people with what appeared to be a machete. The attack took place in the Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate at about 10pm local time on Saturday, close to one of Europe’s biggest LGBTQ+ celebrations.The attack forced organisers to cut short one of Europe’s largest Pride events and came asGermanyremained on edge after a series of deadly vehicle and knife attacks.map showing the location of the attack in the Tiergarten and the park’s location within Berlin city centre.View image in fullscreenThe 21-year-old suspect was identified by police as Abdul Ballout, a German national with Lebanese roots.Photograph: Polizei Berlin/ReutersThe German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, named the chief suspect as 21-year-old Abdul Ballout. “We are dealing ​here with ‌a suspected ‌perpetrator, who had previously drawn attention ‌to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene,” he told ‌a press conference near the site of the attack. He said Ballout had a criminal conviction and had been sentenced as a juvenile to a year and 10 months in prison, but that the sentence had been suspended.German media reported that Ballout, a German national with Lebanese roots, was a supporter ofIslamic Stateand last year travelled to the Middle East in a failed attempt to join the group. He was then convicted in Germany of “preparing a serious act of subversive violence”, the news outlets Bild and Der Spiegel reported.Police and prosecutors had asked for help in finding Ballout, but warned the public to avoid “direct contact” with him, saying he may be armed and dangerous. Police searched an apartment in the Schöneberg district of Berlin near the scene of the attack in the early hours of Sunday, but said they had found no one there.View image in fullscreenPolice officers secure the scene where the suspect was killed.Photograph: Michael Kappeler/DPA/APBefore Ballout was shot,Der Spiegel spoke with his father, Tawfik,by telephone from Lebanon, where he was visiting relatives.Describing Ballout as “generous, emotional, loving”, he said his son had lived with his mother, from whom Tawfik is divorced, and two of his three sisters. Ballout attended school until 10th grade, then bounced from job to job, in security or as a driver.Tawfik described the family asShiabut “not extremely religious” and said it “does not support Islamic State”, an extremist Sunni group.He and Ballout had fought about his hair and beard. “I did not allow him to wear a long beard,” he told Spiegel, calling it a symbol of extremism. Asked about a possible motive for the attack, he said: “He was brainwashed.”Tawfik spoke with Ballout on Saturday, the day of the attack. “He called me and we spoke normally, like every day. He said he missed me and wished he was with us in Lebanon.”The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, urged Germany to avoid division and intimidation in the aftermath of the attack. “We ​will think ​about ​consequences, we ​will ‌defend ​our freedom,” he said in a news conference.Earlier, Merz vowed to punish those responsible, describing the “heinous act” as an “attack on our society” in a social media post. The flag at the German Bundestag was ordered to be lowered to half mast.Police said the vehicle had struck multiple ⁠people after being driven into the Tiergarten. Shortly before 10pm the driver of the white minivan swerved into the park, close to where the route of the Pride march had been earlier in the day, hitting people on a path and crashing into a tree.Bild cited a witness as saying that a man had emerged from the vehicle and fled on foot. A hunt involving helicopters and officers from several German states was under way across the capital on Sunday.View image in fullscreenEmergency personnel work near the scene where a group of people were injured.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAJulian Methig, who attended the event, described it as a nightmare come true. “It’s one of the worst days for the queer community and a day I personally hoped I’d never have to experience … I’m shocked,” he said.Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered in Berlin in warm summer sunshine to celebrate the Pride parade. It is known in Germany as Christopher Street Day (CSD), named after the site of the Stonewall Inn in New York City where riots against police raids touched off the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. CSD was first held in West Berlin in 1979.View image in fullscreenPeople attend the annual Christopher Street Day parade.Photograph: Maryam Majd/ReutersBerlin’s mayor, Kai Wegner, called the deadly assault “an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society”.“Following a peaceful and colourful CSD, the rally for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal manner,” he said on X. “Berlin is the city of freedom – and our freedom has today been attacked in the most appalling way. My thoughts are with the victims, their families and friends.”View image in fullscreenTwo people embrace as they stand near emergency personnel in Berlin.Photograph: Markus Schreiber/APFor the first time in its history, CSD began on Friday night this year with a pro-democracy political rally. Berlin will hold a regional election in September along with two other states.The parade on Saturday ran under the motto “taking a stand is hot”, which organisers said was “in response to increasing hostility” to LGBTQ+ people in Germany.More than 80 floats and 50 groups on foot joined the procession through the city centre past Potsdamer Platz and the Victory Column monument in the Tiergarten, culminating in a rally at the Brandenburg Gate.View image in fullscreenEmergency personnel and police gather in Berlin.Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/APEarlier in the day one person was arrested for resisting police orders at a far-right counterprotest.Before last year’s parade, Berlin LGBTQ+ organisationssounded the alarmthat attacks had become more frequent while hard-won rights were under threat. Campaigners said a rise in hostility had accompanied the surge in support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), now the most popular party in national opinion polls, as well as an increase in Islamist-inspired attacks.European leaders offered solidarity, including heads of government in Belgium, the Netherlands and Sweden. “Italy firmly condemns and opposes all forms of hate and extremism,” the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, wrote on X, adding: “We stand with Germany and the German people.” The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said: “Faced with hatred and violence, our response will always be unity, freedom, and resolve.”The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, a German centre-right politician allied with Merz, sent her deepest sympathy to the victims of the attack, describing the CSD parade as standing for “freedom, dignity and equality – the fundamental values of the EU”.View image in fullscreenThe vehicle used in the attack on the parade was removed from the scene in the Tiergarten park on Sunday.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersBritain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said he was “horrified by the appalling attack in Berlin” and had spoken to his counterpart, Johann Wadephul, “to convey the UK’s solidarity: we stand with Germany”.Far-right leaders were also quick to comment on the attacks. The co-leader of the AfD Tino Chrupalla wrote on X: “We will not allow religious extremists to divide our country with violence and intolerance!”The president of France’s far-right National Rally, Jordan Bardella, wrote: “The Islamist threat remains a major issue in Europe and continues to target what they hate most about our civilisation – and what we cherish so much – freedom.”Explore more on these topicsGermanyIslamic StateLGBTQ+ rightsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Rising oil prices could force up UK interest rates, say economists | Interest rates | The Guardian
description: Bank of England expected to keep rates on hold on Thursday but renewed Iran conflict casts shadow over energy costs
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Bank of England expected to keep rates on hold on Thursday but renewed Iran conflict casts shadow over energy costs
Content: A US warship stops a tanker under a blockade of Iranian ports and vessels. Renewed fighting has pushed up oil prices.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA US warship stops a tanker under a blockade of Iranian ports and vessels. Renewed fighting has pushed up oil prices.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesInterest ratesRising oil prices could force up UK interest rates, say economistsBank of England expected to keep rates on hold on Thursday but renewed Iran conflict casts shadow over energy costsPhillip InmanSun 26 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Bank of Englandcould be forced to tear up its economic forecasts and raise interest rates later this year if oil prices return to above $100 a barrel, according to City economists.Before a meeting of Bank officials on Thursday, economists said that while an interest rate hike would probably be avoided this week there could be some in the future because of conflict in the Middle East.The UK economy has remained relatively resilient since Donald Trump’s war on Iran began in March, but this could be at risk after fighting reignited last week, the economists added.The breakdown of the fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran sent oil prices back to the highs seen in April and May, sparking fears that higher prices at the pumps would send inflation soaring.A barrel of Brent crude jumped above $100 a barrel (£75) on Thursday before falling back to $96 on Friday, well above the $71 recorded earlier this month.Gas prices have soared before the crucial period when most European countries refill their storage facilities in time for winter heating demand.All the major central banks say they are concerned about the impact of the war in the Middle East and its influence on rising prices.The Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee is expected to vote on Thursday in favour of holding interest rates, and to continue maintaining them at 3.75% until at least December, by a margin of seven to two. This echoestheir last meeting in Junewhen two officials on the committee voted to increase rates to head off rising inflation.Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said that calculation might change if the intensity of airstrikes was maintained and the sea channels allowing tankers to enter and exit oil terminals remained blocked.He said: “We see upside risks to the interest rate outlook in the near term, with much dependent on the duration of the unfolding energy shock. A second energy wave will likely amplify uncertainty around the inflation path and the risk of second-round effects.”View image in fullscreenThe Bank of England’s monetary policy committee is expected to vote on Thursday in favour of holding interest rates.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/ReutersGeorge Buckley, the chief UK and euro area economist at Nomura, said financial markets were giving a clear signal that higher oil prices would translate into higher interest rates. “At $90 they would see the need for one and a half quarter-point hikes. At $100 there would be a need for two 25 basis point hikes,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK inflation falls by more than expected to 2.6% in lift for Andy BurnhamRead moreMohamed El-Erian, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania and a former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, suggested a sustained increase in oil prices to $90 a barrel could be enough to rewrite UK policymakers’ forecasts.He said: “Should oil prices remain above $90 a barrel, an important ‘if’, then headline inflation would face significant upward pressure. This, in turn, would heighten concerns over immediate indirect effects, including rising food prices driven by diesel transportation costs, and broader second-round effects over time.“The result would be heightened market expectation of aBank of Englandrate hike, even as higher energy prices act as a tax on economic activity.”Ruth Gregory, the deputy chief UK economist at CapitalEconomics, said a worst-case scenario showed that if inflation rose to 7% over the coming months in response to the Middle East conflict, UK interest rates would probably rise from 3.75% to 4.75%.Harvinder Kalirai, the chief global currency strategist at Alpine Macro, a division of Oxford Economics, said he expected the Bank to “look through the oil shock and political noise” to hold rates steady for now before resuming cuts next year.He said the UK was not strong enough to withstand a rise in the cost of fuel and higher interest rates: “Demand is not strong enough to sustain a pass-through from the energy shock, forcing firms to absorb higher input costs.”Kalirai said once volatile elements of the inflation basket – including fuel and food – were excluded, prices were growing slowly while pay packets were rising at a slower pace.Costas Milas, an economics professor at the University of Liverpool, said oil price shocks triggered long bouts of inflation and should be tackled quickly.He said: “This is too uncomfortable for the BoE to stay inactive not least because the public remainsdissatisfied with the BoE. Since dissatisfaction increases with inflation, the BoE should act soon by raising interest rates, possibly as early as September.”David Aikman, the head of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said: “The longer inflation remains above target, the greater the change inflation expectations shift and wages respond – and hence the Bank needing to hike rates.”Financial markets also anticipate a hike at the European Central Bank governing council’s next meeting on 10 September. It raised interest rates in June for the first time since 2023 in response to higher inflation caused by the war in Iran.Central banks have come under fire for considering a rise in the cost of borrowing, with critics arguing increases in interest rates will only make a bad situation worse.Explore more on these topicsInterest ratesBank of EnglandInflationUS-Israel war on IranEconomicsOilCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: RAF Chinook crash victims’ families ask Andy Burnham for review of disaster | Military | The Guardian
description: PM urged to end ‘cover-up culture’ and order independent review taking in evidence that has emerged on 1994 crash
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: PM urged to end ‘cover-up culture’ and order independent review taking in evidence that has emerged on 1994 crash
Content: The Chinook Justice Campaign, made up of more than 55 family members of 25 of the victims, delivering a letter to Andy Burnham.Photograph: Chinook Justice Campaign/PAView image in fullscreenThe Chinook Justice Campaign, made up of more than 55 family members of 25 of the victims, delivering a letter to Andy Burnham.Photograph: Chinook Justice Campaign/PAMilitaryRAF Chinook crash victims’ families ask Andy Burnham for review of disasterPM urged to end ‘cover-up culture’ and order independent review taking in evidence that has emerged on 1994 crashJosh HallidayNorth of England editorSun 26 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe families of those killed in an RAF Chinook crashin 1994have urged Andy Burnham to end Britain’s “cover-up culture” and order an independent review intothe disaster.Twenty-nine serving military personnel died when the Chinook HC2 helicopter crashed on the Mull of Kintyre in south-westScotlandduring a flight from Northern Ireland.The two pilotswere initially blamedfor the crash butexonerated after an inquiry in 2011, which did not determine its cause.Liam Fox, the former Conservative defence secretary who orderedthat official review, said last month there were now “deep concerns” that “vital information” could have been withheld.Fox, who is backing the calls for a fresh independent review, said there was now a “strong enough belief” that a deliberate cover-up had taken place. There were concerns, he said, that details provided by the Ministry of Defence (MoD) onthe airworthinessof the Chinook that crashed were “not correct”.View image in fullscreenAll 29 personnel on the Chinook HC2 were killed when it crashed on the Mull of Kintyre, south-west Scotland, in June 1994.Photograph: Chris Bacon/PAA high court judge ruled this month that the families of several victims of the crash could not bring a legal claim against the MoD over the incident because it had been brought too late.The Chinook Justice Campaign (CJC), which is made up of more than 55 family members of 25 of the victims, said it would take the case to theEuropean court of human rights.However, Matt Tobias, whose father, Lt Col John Tobias, was killed in the crash, said the families “do not want years of further litigation” and urged the prime minister to help by ordering a fresh independent review.He said: “We would urge Mr Burnham to meet us within his first 100 days in office so we can present the evidence that has emerged over recent years and explain why we believe a fresh review, independent of theMinistry of Defence, is now essential.Mull of Kintyre crash: The last flight of Zulu Delta 576Read more“Mr Burnham’s speech in the House of Commons, in which he spoke about ending Britain’s cover-up culture and strengthening the duty of candour, gave our families real hope.”In a letter delivered to Burnham, the Chinook families said it could be a “test case” forthe new Hillsborough law, which was unanimously backed by MPs this month and creates a legally enforceable duty of candour compelling public officials and authorities to act transparently during investigations.Tobias said: “We ask that he and his ministers give the Chinook families more respect than we received from his predecessor, who denied us a meeting and an inquiry – believing MoD lies instead. After 32 years, we are not asking for special treatment. We are simply asking for the truth.”The CJC group said it wanted Burnham to establish a fresh review, independent of the Ministry of Defence, withfull access to all relevant documentsrelating to the airworthiness of the Chinook helicopter and the circumstances leading up to the crash.An MoD spokesperson said: “Our thoughts and sympathies remain with the families, friends, and colleagues of all those who died in the Mull of Kintyre crash.“We understand the recent court judgment will be disappointing for those involved. Defence Ministers have previously met with the CJC and we will continue to engage to hear concerns and discuss this important matter.”Explore more on these topicsMilitaryMinistry of DefenceLiam FoxScotlandEuropean court of human rightsAndy BurnhamHelicopter crashesnewsShareReuse this content

title: US pauses Iran attacks for second night after Trump advised to halt bombing | Iran | The Guardian
description: Top military officials say campaign has reached its limit of effectiveness and warn of dwindling stocks of munitions
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Top military officials say campaign has reached its limit of effectiveness and warn of dwindling stocks of munitions
Content: US naval forces carry out an operation as part of their blockade on Iranian ports and ships.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUS naval forces carry out an operation as part of their blockade on Iranian ports and ships.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesIranUS pauses Iran attacks for second night after Trump advised to halt bombingTop military officials say campaign has reached its limit of effectiveness and warn of dwindling stocks of munitionsAndrew Rothin JerusalemSun 26 Jul 2026 14.45 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 07.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has paused strikes on Iran for a second night as top military officials advisedDonald Trumpto halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war.Trump is said to be weighing up diplomatic and military options in the nearly five-month-old conflict, withBenjamin Netanyahuexpected to visit the White House on Tuesday. The Israeli prime minister is a vocal critic of Washington’s negotiations with Iranian leaders and has pressed for the US to continue its strikes against Iran.Netanyahu is under considerable political pressure to show that his military campaigns againstIranand Hezbollah in Lebanon have yielded results before elections scheduled for October.Tehran said on Sunday it would pause what it called “retaliatory” attacks against US allies in the region. “These [US] attacks continued until two nights ago, but over the past two nights the Americans have stopped their attacks,” said the army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia. “Our strategy has essentially been retaliatory, we have also halted our retaliatory operations.”‘Shameful’: Pentagon accused of cover-up over US military casualties in Iran warRead moreSenior officials in the Trump administration are reported to have told the president about dwindling munitions stockpiles that could hamper a sustained military campaign in the region.Axios reported on Sunday that Adm Bradley Cooper, the top US military commander in the region, had told Trump the US military campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness.The message was said to affect Trump’s decision to hold strikes on Iran for the first time in nearly two weeks. Cooper told Trump the US had nearly exhausted the list of targets that it had developed to attack in Iran, and without a return to major combat operations there was little point in continuing the bombing campaign, the news website reported.Asked on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press whether Trump was ruling out additional strikes in Iran, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz said: “I wouldn’t go that far at all. The president is keeping all options on the table.”The lull in fighting, which began on Friday evening, follows nearly two weeks of strikes against Iran and the collapse of a ceasefire brokered by Trump. Washington blamed Iran for strikes on US forces and allies in the region and its closure of the strait of Hormuz, a conduit for an estimated 20% of the world’s oil and gas.Senior diplomats from Iran and Oman were said to be holding negotiations on Sunday on reopening the vital waterway and an official in Tehran confirmed colleagues had been in touch with US negotiators to prevent a return to war. Iran has demanded payment and control over which ships pass through the strait.“Mediators are working and trying to prevent tension from escalating,” the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, told a press conference on Sunday.But an Iranian army spokesperson signalled defiance, saying the US had no clear strategy and was “experiencing strategic decision-making fatigue”.Graph showing how fighting has stopped ships transiting HormuzThe US vice-president,JD Vance, and Dan Caine, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff, warned Trump of the risks of a renewed military campaign against Iran at an Oval Office meeting on Friday, according to media outlets. The president then ordered the military to call off new strikes, which he had warned could “knock out everything they have”.“We’re talking to [the Iranians] right now,” Trump told reporters on Friday. “I think they’re getting more and more serious as the days go by. We’re locked and loaded and ready to go, but we’re talking to them.”At a White House Correspondents’ Association dinner that evening he said he did not think Iran was ready to make a deal but he was ready to listen.View image in fullscreenIsraeli army units stage a raid near Nablus in the occupied West Bank after the deaths of four Palestinians and two Israelis when armed settlers entered a village.Photograph: Mohammed Torokman/ReutersCaine warned Trump about dwindling munitions stockpiles, which include Patriot missile interceptors and offensive weapons like Tomahawk cruise missiles. Vance campaigned on his opposition to US military interventions in the Middle East and has grown more vocal in his opposition to the war in Iran.Netanyahu’s office announced on Sunday that he would convene a meeting of his security cabinet before leaving for Washington on Monday. He played a crucial role in lobbying Trump to launch joint strikes against Iran in February and has said that US negotiators must take a strong line on Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programme. US negotiators have instead prioritised opening the strait of Hormuz.Netanyahu will travel to Washington amid some of the worst violence this year in the West Bank, where his military is launching an “extensive” operation after the deaths of four Palestinians and two Israelis when armed settlers entered a Palestinian village on Thursday.The US and the UK under its new prime minister, Andy Burnham, are discussing plans for a high-level meeting in London this week to discuss the potential for a coalition to protect ships in the strait of Hormuz and de-mine the waterway. The discussions will be an early test for Burnham’s administration. The Labour government has so far refused to allow Washington to use a British airbase for offensive operations against Iran.Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpUS foreign policyIsraelPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Boy, 16, charged with murder of teenager stabbed in Luton park | UK news | The Guardian
description: Four others arrested on suspicion of same murder in Luton after death of 17-year-old
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Four others arrested on suspicion of same murder in Luton after death of 17-year-old
Content: Bedfordshire police said officers were called to Kingsway recreation ground shortly after 6.30pm on Friday.Photograph: GoogleView image in fullscreenBedfordshire police said officers were called to Kingsway recreation ground shortly after 6.30pm on Friday.Photograph: GoogleUK newsBoy, 16, charged with murder of teenager stabbed in Luton parkFour others arrested on suspicion of same murder in Luton after death of 17-year-oldNadeem BadshahSun 26 Jul 2026 18.26 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 16-year-old boy has been charged with murdering a teenager who died from multiple stab wounds at a park in Luton, police said.Four other teenagers have been arrested on suspicion of the same murder.Bedfordshire police said officers were called to Kingsway recreation ground shortly after 6.30pm on Friday following reports that a number of teenagers were seen “carrying large knives”.The 17-year-old boy, who has yet to be identified, was taken to hospital but died a short time later.Police said two boys, aged 16 and 17, had been arrested on suspicion of murder on Saturday after they were initially arrested on suspicion of violent disorder.The younger male has since been charged with murder and remanded in custody, the force said.Another three 17-year-old boys have also been arrested, each on suspicion of murder, violent disorder and carrying a weapon, it added in its statement on Sunday.DCI Nick Gardener said: “We are progressing our investigation and we are continuing to appeal to anyone who was in the area, or witnessed the events leading up to the disorder, to please get in touch.“Our officers are continuing to carry out additional high-visibility patrols, and we are continuing to engage with local members of the public.“We would also like to remind the public not to share any distressing videos or images as this can be concerning for families involved, but also form a vital part of the police investigation.”Zanib Raja, a councillor in Luton, has also encouraged people not to share alleged videos of the incident online.Raja wrote on Facebook: “Like many of you, I became aware of this horrific attack through disturbing videos circulating online.“Let me say this clearly: Do not share them. They traumatise the family, fuel fear, & do nothing to help.”She added: “A tragic incident took place … in Kingsway Park, a place many of us grew up in, played in, & built memories in.“A place that should be safe for families, children, & every resident of our town. Instead, a man lost his life in broad daylight. A family has been shattered. Luton is hurting.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gary Stevenson to quit YouTube channel, citing health concerns | Economics | The Guardian
description: Former City trader’s weekly Gary’s Economics videos took off during the Covid pandemic
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Former City trader’s weekly Gary’s Economics videos took off during the Covid pandemic
Content: Gary Stevenson stands with Canary Wharf buildings behind himPhotograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGary Stevenson stands with Canary Wharf buildings behind himPhotograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianEconomicsGary Stevenson to quit YouTube channel, citing health concernsFormer City trader’s weekly Gary’s Economics videos took off during the Covid pandemicGwyn TophamSun 26 Jul 2026 12.11 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe City trader turned wealth tax campaigner Gary Stevenson has announced he is quitting theYouTubechannel that made his name, citing health concerns.His announcement, in a 48-minute address to camera, came after a mixed reaction to a televised documentary that brought him to a wider audience but drew some scepticism from left-leaning tax experts as well as more rightwing critics.Stevenson, whose weeklyYouTube channelGary’s Economics took offduring the Covid pandemicand grew to 1.64 million subscribers, posted an abridged 18-minute signoff on social media on Sunday morning entitled “It’s time to say goodbye”.He said it would be the last weekly video, saying they had become “harder and harder as he had got more tired”.Theformer City trader, born in 1986 in east London, came to wider prominence through the channel and his published memoir, Trading Game, in which he described how he made millions as a Citibank employee in the years after the financial crisis.Retiring with burnout and disillusioned by the City, the self-styled anti-inequality campaigner argued for a 2% tax on individual wealth over £10m, which he said would raise £24bn a year for the Treasury.Stevenson has been an influential online voice in raising awareness of inequality and linking it to falling living standards, predicting the rises in the cost of living and warning about the danger to society of constant accumulation by the growing billionaire class.However, a Channel 4 documentary released last month, How to Get Filthy Rich with Gary Stevenson, in which he took his arguments to those who would incur the tax, was poorly received.The Guardian’s Lucy Mangan wrotethat the presenter was “outdone and undone by almost all of his interviewees … left floundering, without convincing comebacks”, concluding that it was “a faintly embarrassing waste of time”.The expert tax lawyer and investigator Dan Neidle told Stevenson “to separate your emotional reaction to inequality from a rational assessment of the best tools for it” and described his plans as “populist claptrap”.A slightly more sympathetic review in the Telegraph said Stevenson had “all the traits of the self-aggrandising online influencer class … so used to addressing his followers straight down the camera that engaging in debate with people of differing views leaves him floundering”.Despite the reception to the documentary, Stevenson’s proposal for a wealth tax is gaining traction. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, is fielding growing calls to increase taxes on the ultra-rich.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA proposal to tax the 1,000 UK households with wealth of more than £100m could raise £10bn,according to one recent study. Last week ex-footballer Gary Lineker was among 120 other millionaires who wrote an open letter in favour of a wealth tax,urging Burnham to tax them more, saying “we can afford it”.Stevenson gave some notice of his intentions in a Newsnight interview when the documentary aired earlier this month. He told the BBC he was quitting public conversation, saying: “It’s tiring. I do this because I don’t want this country to go down the toilet. Living standards are going to get worse … You cannot have a situation across [Britain and] the western world where the working class, the middle class and the government all very rapidly lose all of their wealth to 1% of people.”However, the valedictory video on Gary’sEconomicssuggested that, after a break in Japan, he might make a return to public life in some form. Stevenson said he was now looking at a podcast format and did not rule out doing more videos on a monthly basis.He said: “The very richest people in the world are going to fight this … We need a big chunk of the population to understand that living standards are falling because of rising inequality.”Stevenson ended by saying: “I cannot be the only educator on this. We need to accept this will not be a short-term battle ... And I need to rest.”Explore more on these topicsEconomicsYouTubeBankingShareReuse this content

title: Burnham v Starmer: one week in, how do their leadership styles compare? | Labour | The Guardian
description: From TikTok appearances to ‘sugar rush’ policies, new prime minister is taking different approach to predecessor
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: From TikTok appearances to ‘sugar rush’ policies, new prime minister is taking different approach to predecessor
Content: Andy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer after being crowned as Labour leader unopposed.Composite: Shutterstock/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer after being crowned as Labour leader unopposed.Composite: Shutterstock/PALabourBurnham v Starmer: one week in, how do their leadership styles compare?From TikTok appearances to ‘sugar rush’ policies, new prime minister is taking different approach to predecessorPippa CrerarandAlexandra ToppingSun 26 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSix weeks ago Andy Burnham was not even an MP; now the former mayor of Greater Manchester is the most important political figure in Britain. After orchestrating a bloodless coup againstKeir Starmer, in which he was crowned as Labour leader unopposed, the new prime minister has started his tenure in Downing Street with some eye-catching policies and a radically different approach to communication. A week into the job, how do their leadership styles compare?Freewheeling v traditional mediaEver since his first big speech at the People’s History Museum in Manchester, at which he took no questions but made all the headlines anyway, Burnham has resisted media scrutiny. He did just three interviews as an MP before becoming prime minister – and since entering No 10 has had a brief huddle with political editors and several broadcast pool clips. Instead, his early focus seems to be on social media, answering softball questions on Reddit, appearing alongside viral TikTok starsBus AuntyandMax Klymenko, and replying to X posts by members of the public.While Keir Starmer has upped his social media game in recent weeks, his Downing Street operation recognised that “traditional” media still had power to drive the narrative and – while he didn’t much like it – he regularly subjected himself to scrutiny. Burnham’s team say he will take more questions, but it hasn’t happened yet.Relaxed style v sticking to the scriptView image in fullscreenOne of Andy Burnham’s big selling points with Labour MPs was his ability to connect with the public.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersBefore he became prime minister, Burnham promised to do politics differently, and he didn’t just mean wearing T-shirts and jeans. “I want to answer questions honestly in this job … I’m determined to keep working in that way.” One of his big selling points withLabourMPs was that he could connect more naturally with the public than Starmer, who was often criticised for sticking to the script and coming across as wooden.But, as Burnham has already found, his words now carry greater weight. He has already been accused of performing U-turns over issues including raising the income tax threshold – when he was really just speaking openly about his ideas before they were fully formed. “It’s funny, these days you can’t answer a question honestly without then people reading everything else into it,” he said. His critics may call him naive, but his more relaxed style may go down well with the public.Sugar rush v long-term changeGrabbing public attention has been one of the big ambitions for Burnham’s first week in office – partly so voters know he’s there, but also to show that he’s different from Starmer, and will shout about what his government is doing. As a result, there have been a series of “sugar rush” cost of living announcements designed to give the public some much-needed breathing space – a VAT cut on electricity bills, a £2 bus fare cap and a 20% business rate cut for pubs.In contrast, Starmer wanted to focus on long-term solutions over what he called “short-term sticking plasters”. Burnham’s energy bills announcement – the equivalent of reducing electricity bills by £45 a year on average – crystallised their different approaches. It is to be paid for by scrapping the digital ID system, which advocates argue could have saved the government tens of billions in the long term by making public services more efficient. The question remains: what happens when the sugar hit wears off?Whitehall break-up v managed declineBurnham’s first big announcement on returning to Westminster was that he was going to set up No 10 North as the “nerve centre of a rewired Britain” to oversee a devolution of power and resources across the UK. While opposition parties have dismissed this as a gimmick, the new PM says he is determined to oversee a genuine shift of power from Whitehall to local communities via his Manchester operation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet he has also created a powerful new PM’s department taking in both No 10s, parts of the Cabinet Office, Treasury and housing ministry – all overseen by his close ally Louise Haigh, to become the “dominant driver of the UK’s economy”. Antonia Romeo, the United Kingdom’s most senior civil servant, has reportedly been given a seat in the coveted space of No 10’s outer office just outside the prime minister’s study.Starmer also promised to kickstart anew era of devolution, passing a bill allowing mayors to ask for new powers at the end of April – just before the local election trouncing that precipitated his downfall. He also pledged to reverse what he called“the tepid bath of managed decline”in Whitehall, putting his chief secretary, Darren Jones, in charge of its “rewiring” in January this year. Jones said civil servants who did not meet expectations would be “shown the door” – in the end, he followed his boss through it six months later.Labour love-in v painful neglectBurnham, who first became an MP in 2001 before resigning to become mayor of Greater Manchester in 2017, is steeped in the party’s lores and traditions. Back in 2009 he told the Guardian that the three most important things in his life, aside from family, were “Everton FC, the Labour party and the Catholic church – in that order”. After becoming a candidate to lead the party at his third time of asking, he insisted in a letter to the parliamentary Labour party that he wouldnever use party discipline to “stifle debate”and wanted to create a “different culture where everyone has a part to play”.View image in fullscreenKeir Starmer promised to kickstart a new era of devolution, only to step down months later.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APMPs, apart from angry Starmer loyalists, lapped it up. Not least because of the contrast to the hard line against dissent that Starmer and his team showed in the early days of his tenure, when many were suspended for defying the party line. But there are already thosequestioningBurnham’s pledge toend factional infightingafter heremoved or demotedmore than half of the outgoing prime minister’s cabinet in his first reshuffle.Explore more on these topicsLabourAndy BurnhamKeir StarmernewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for Modi | India | The Guardian
description: Ally forced to resign, with opposition parties reinvigorated and strongman leader’s grip over media channels rocked
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Ally forced to resign, with opposition parties reinvigorated and strongman leader’s grip over media channels rocked
Content: Cockroach Janta party supporters in New Delhi on Saturday. Their core demand, for Dharmendra Pradhan to resign, has been achieved.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersView image in fullscreenCockroach Janta party supporters in New Delhi on Saturday. Their core demand, for Dharmendra Pradhan to resign, has been achieved.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersIndiaAnalysisIndia’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for ModiHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiAlly forced to resign, with opposition parties reinvigorated and strongman leader’s grip over media channels rockedSun 26 Jul 2026 12.42 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 12.09 EDTShareEven the night beforeNarendra Modiaccepted the resignation of his education minister, India’s prime minister appeared confident that the largest mass uprising to take place in his 12 years in power would do little to rattle his government.‘I will die for this cause’: how India’s cockroach meme became the biggest challenge to Modi’s grip on powerRead moreAddressing his “young friends” in a late-night Instagram selfie reel on Friday, he thanked the people – who weremobilised en masse across the country, shouting anti-government slogans – for their “thoughtful suggestions”.Less than 24 hours later, Modi, who has fiercely cultivated his strongman image for years, had bowed to public pressure and accepted theresignationofDharmendraPradhan. It was, say analysts, the remarkable humbling of a government that has ruled with almost untouchable impunity since 2014.Over that past week, a gen Z movement that called itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) mobilised unprecedented protests in the name of justice for millions of young people, after the leaking of a crucial exam paper forced 2 million students to resit the test and was blamed for more than a dozen suicides.The resignation of Pradhan, Modi’s loyal political ally, remained their first and foremost demand for accountability, even as the protests expanded into a wider fight for democracy. Yet Pradhan went unmentioned by Modi in his Instagram address.0:51‘Cockroach’ movement: thousands march in anti-government protest in New DelhiOn Saturday morning, more people than ever were pouring into Delhi’s historic Jantar Mantar site – the centre of the protests – and unrest was spreading fast to other cities, including states ruled by Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).It was not only physical space that had been captured by the cockroach movement. Since coming to power, the BJP has proved enormously effective at capturing the online narrative, deploying its powerful, highly organised IT cell to mobilise and attack any perceived criticism of the government, whether it came from citizens, politicians or journalists.But this proved no match for the millions of gen Z memes and reels that began to flood Instagram over this past week, fearlessly insulting Modi and pillorying the government, each more creative and incendiary than the next. Modi’s last-ditch attempts to speak directly to the youth on Instagram were simply met with more ridicule and spin-off memes.View image in fullscreenCockroach Janta party supporters were in a jubilant mood in Mumbai on Sunday after Pradhan’s departure from government.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPAModi had also lost another medium critical to the BJP’s domination over the national narrative – the mainstream TV news channels widely acknowledged to have been co-opted by the BJP government over the past 12 years and turned into mouthpieces for its rightwing Hindu nationalist ideology.Initially, the channels ignored the protests, and when they did cover them it was to suggest the protesters were being bankrolled by sinister foreign forces and Pakistani terror groups. In response, the protesters turned on the channels, using social media to expose their “lies”. When the protests escalated, Modi remained conspicuously absent from the airwaves.Pradhan’s resignation came as it appeared that all other options for the government had gone. The option of a ruthless crackdown appeared untenable given the mass outcry to the police violence that had hit protesters on Monday.“The online space was totally conquered by the protesters and regime-loving media was seriously delegitimised,” said Ashutosh Varshney, a professor of international studies at Brown University in Rhode Island. “The anger was so comprehensive there was no option left but for Pradhan to go.”View image in fullscreenMany CJP supporters brought placards and signs openly criticising Modi.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPABut this was more than the loss of a minister, Varshney said, it was also the first time in 12 years that the Modi government had lost control of the political narrative. “This is a repressive government,” he said. “It wants obedience, it wants no critical discussion and it generates fear. But now the climate of fear has collapsed.”Analysts say the resignation of Pradhan could also have implications for Modi’s power over his own cabinet. Pradhan was one of Modi’s most loyal ministers and ideological footsoldiers, and had implemented policies exactly as senior party figures had wanted. He had also helped the BJP win Odisha state for the first time in the general election, bringing in crucial seats.“Modi knows once you start firing your most loyal ministers, it sets up the incentives for defections in other ministers as well,” said the political columnist Pratap Bhanu Mehta. “If your own cabinet starts to hedge for a future where they may not be backed by your own government, that’s when you are in trouble.”View image in fullscreenAbhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP, celebrated with his fellow protesters in New Delhi on Saturday.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersPrior to this week’s unrest, Modi had been riding high on a string of important state electoral victories, in particular the BJP’s first triumph in West Bengal, a politically important state that had long pushed back against its Hindu nationalist politics.The BJP appeared to have fully bounced back from the blow in the 2024 elections, when theparty failed to win an outright parliamentary majorityand had to scramble together a large enough alliance to take power. At the same time, the much-beleaguered opposition had continued to lose countless state elections and their allegations of voting impropriety by the BJP fell mostly on deaf ears.Yet the emergence of the cockroaches has reinvigorated not only India’s youth, but its political opposition parties as well. Jumping on the bandwagon, the opposition Congress party has had its best week in years as it mobilised protests and shut down parliament. The party’s leader, Rahul Gandhi, was dramatically dragged away by police outside Modi’s house in support of students.Analysts say that dissent, which had been systematically crushed over the past 12 years, has now been re-galvanised as an effective tool to hold the government – and in particular the prime minister – to account.“After a long time, there’s an assertion of political agency across different sections of society,” said Mehta. “And the minute you see that agency out in the street, it empowers lots of other agents.”The next big test of the electoral implications of the CJP movement will come early next year, when India’s largest and most politically important state holds its state elections. Holding on to power in Uttar Pradesh, the BJP’s political heartland, is seen as crucial for the party and would have major implications for the next general election in 2029.The grievances of India’s newly-politicised youth are extensive, including a chronic lack of graduate jobs and stagnant wages. Just how the CJP intends to politically mobilise after its striking victory on Saturday remains to be seen. Leaders and supporters insist this is just the “beginning”, particularly in their push for education reform. Their founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has some past experience as a political party organiser, but has not made his own ambitions known.Yet analysts said that one of the most crucial impacts of the CJP had been to reopen a rapidly closing democratic space and make it seem possible that a new kind of political opposition could emerge, one reflective of the voices heard on the streets of India this week.Saurav Das, a CJP spokesperson, said it was encouraging people involved in the movement to go into politics. “This is one of our goals,” he said. “We need to increase youth participation in politics, because right now it’s controlled by uncles and aunties who are only interested in looking after their own lifestyles and don’t understand the needs of our generation. The answer also has to be political.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaNarendra ModiSouth and central AsiaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Exfoliate, use ice and conceal eyebags wisely – makeup artists on how to look fabulous, at every age | Makeup | The Guardian
description: Are you stuck in a makeup rut? Or maybe just beginning to wear cosmetics? Here, experts reveal how to to find the right products for you
Author: Sarah Phillips
Headline: Are you stuck in a makeup rut? Or maybe just beginning to wear cosmetics? Here, experts reveal how to to find the right products for you
Content: Composite: Guardian Design; David  Espejo; yacobchuk/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design; David  Espejo; yacobchuk/Getty ImagesThe expertsMakeupExfoliate, use ice and conceal eyebags wisely – makeup artists on how to look fabulous, at every ageAre you stuck in a makeup rut? Or maybe just beginning to wear cosmetics? Here, experts reveal how to to find the right products for youSarah PhillipsSun 26 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMakeup trends change over time – and so does our skin. How can you enhance what you have and refresh your look? Here, makeup artists share the fundamentals of applying cosmetics, at every age.Commit to a good skincare routineView image in fullscreenKate Hughes, who specialises in midlife beauty.Photograph: Louise RoseWhatever your age, “first and foremost is skincare,” saysKate Hughes, who works as a freelance makeup artist in London and Ibiza. “No good skincare, no good makeup. Full stop. I’m a big advocate of this.”Hughes, who specialises in midlife beauty, explains that as we age, the turnover of our cells slows down. “The dead skin cells stay on top of the skin, giving you that dull look, and we want to look fresh – dewy is the buzzword.” People often say her skin is glowing and ask how she manages this at 56. “It is because I exfoliate three to four times a week, sometimes every day.” If you are starting from scratch, Hughes suggests exfoliating once a week at first, then slowly building up. “You could start off with exfoliating pads, anything from Boots’ own to First AidBeauty, and then go on to a liquid exfoliant, like Paula’s Choice 2% BHA Liquid Exfoliant.”If you are starting young, keep makeup minimalView image in fullscreen‘There isn’t a “right” age to start wearing makeup,’ says Bobbi Brown.Photograph: Posed by models; Maskot/Getty ImagesChildren are getting into cosmetics younger than ever before. “I don’t think there is a ‘right’ age to start wearing makeup,” says makeup artistBobbi Brown, founder of Jones Road Beauty and Bobbi Brown cosmetics, who lives in New Jersey. “It depends on the child, their maturity and, honestly, their interest.”Brown advises keeping it simple: “A little lip gloss, a tinted moisturiser, maybe a touch of blush or mascara when they’re older. The goal isn’t to look like someone else. It is to look like yourself, just a little more polished. Too much makeup is when it starts to feel like you’re covering yourself up instead of enhancing what is already there. Confidence will always be the best thing you can wear.”Don’t focus on covering blemishesView image in fullscreen‘Spot conceal only where you need it,’ says Bobbi Brown.Photograph: Posed by model; Samantha Pierre/Getty Images/500pxFrom adolescence on, hiding spots is often the focus. “The biggest mistake I see is people trying to cover every blemish with a thick layer of makeup,” says Brown. “It usually ends up drawing more attention to it. Use a lightweight complexion product if you want to even out your skin, but don’t feel you need full coverage everywhere. Spot conceal only where you need it, using a concealer that matches your skin tone, then blend the edges so it disappears into your skin. Less is almost always more.”“Pinpoint concealingis one of my most-asked-about techniques,” says Lisa Eldridge, a New Zealand-born, London-based makeup artist who received an MBE for her work in 2025. “My philosophy involves resisting the urge to apply a thick layer of blanket coverage to the skin, and precisely concealing only the areas you feel are absolutely necessary to disguise, moving focus to the skin in between your problem areas.”In the heat, go for a makeup sandwichView image in fullscreenLayered makeup will last longer during a heatwave.Photograph: Posed by models; Klaus Vedfelt/Getty ImagesHughes is spending the summer working in Ibiza, where it is 80% humidity and 30C at 9am. How can you prevent makeup from melting off? “Use a grippy primer –Maybelline do a fabulous one– then spray your face with a setting spray, put your makeup on and spray again. If you layer makeup, you get more longevity in the heat. The sandwich method, we call it.” But this is more for special occasions than every day, Hughes adds.Hughes also stresses the importance of wearing a high SPF and staying out of the sun: “If I sit outside, I’m in the shade. I wear a baseball cap and glasses all the time. I wear SPF on my body and my face religiously. The face factor 50s are brilliant now: Nivea has brought out a couple that are like primers. You don’t feel like you’ve got suntan lotion underneath your makeup, which can feel claustrophobic. A dermatologist said to me you can either have good skin or a suntan. You can’t have both.”Don’t try to disguise eye bagsEye bags are a common issue from middle age onwards, thanks to ageing skin and exhaustion levels. It can be tempting to want to hide them. “As we get older, the skin under our eyes becomes thinner and drier, so heavy concealer tends to settle into fine lines and emphasise texture,” says Brown. “Instead, focus on hydration first. A good eye cream and moisturiser will make any makeup you apply look better.”View image in fullscreen‘The more skincare you do, the less makeup you will need’ … Antonio Cruz.Photograph: Courtesy of Antonio Cruz“If you have bags, it’s all about finding the right eye cream for you,” agreesAntonio Cruz, a Venezuelan makeup artist in Manchester. “Eye creams with caffeine are fantastic. You have to be consistent, because a lot of people buy a cream, use it once, they are not sure [if it works], put it away” – and it definitely won’t work then. “You need to wear it for at least for 28 days,” says Cruz. “It doesn’t need to be expensive. What matters is how consistent you are in applying that eye cream, moisturiser, retinol. The more skincare you do, the less makeup you will need.”“You’ve got to regulate sleep,” says Hughes, which can be easier said than done. “Eye bags come from within, not from outside. If I’ve had a bad night’s sleep, I’ve got some ice rollers in my freezer – they take down the puffiness and really tighten the skin.”View image in fullscreenTired eyes can be refreshed with ice cubes, says one expert.Photograph: Posed by model; Tatiana/Getty Images“One of my favourite remedies for refreshing tired eyes are homemade green tea ice cubes,” says Eldridge. “They are great for boosting circulation and for draining the fluid under the eyes. Make a cup of strong green tea, allow it to cool, then pour into an ice-cube tray. Once frozen, wrap a single cube in a piece of muslin or gauze and use the cube to gently massage and press under and around the eyes for a few minutes.”“Then you need to be quite creative with your concealer,” says Hughes. “Find a really hydrating concealer with good pigment. Again, layer it. Apply a little bit, blend, then apply more. I probably put four to five coats of concealer on my face. If you didn’t blend that correctly in between, it would look awful. I can use Rimmel or Chanel – I’m still going to get the same finish. Application is king.”Apply foundation with a brushView image in fullscreen‘A really good finish.’Photograph: Posed by model; Halfpoint Images/Getty Images“A lot of people are happy to apply foundation by hand,” says Cruz, “but the bristles of a brush would be better at blending the foundation into the skin,” to give a smoother effect. A sponge like a Beauty Blender can work well, says Hughes, but on the whole she has more of a “whatever works for you” approach – although she does stress that if you use your hands, quite a lot of makeup will get lost on them. “Some days I’ll put my concealer on with my fingers because I’m in a rush. I use brushes if I want to get a really good finish.”Don’t feel you have to cover wrinklesView image in fullscreen‘As skin changes, less makeup usually looks better.’Photograph: Posed by model; Maria Korneeva/Getty Images“Your goal shouldn’t be to erase every line or wrinkle,” says Brown. “As skin changes, I find that less makeup usually looks better. Focus on skincare, hydration and lightweight formulas that let your skin show through. Heavy foundation and too much powder can make skin look older.”If you are worried about signs of ageing, focus on your favourite features, says Hughes. “So many people say to me: ‘I really don’t like this about myself.’ Well, then put a bright lip on, or do a really soft, smoky eye, and that will take away the focus on the thing that you don’t like.”Keep up to dateView image in fullscreenMaking makeup fun again … Linasha Kotalawala.Photograph: Courtesy of Pave CreatorsCruz used to work for YSL at the Trafford Centre in Manchester and saw customers who “probably learned how to do their makeup in the 70s and 80s and just carried on with those techniques”. To update your look, he advises chatting to beauty counter makeup artists and possibly having a makeup lesson (top tip: bring along what you already have rather than buying all new stuff), or look online for inspiration.Hughes recommends recreating the actorZendaya’s recent eye makeupthat went viral – “eyeshadow in the corner of the eyes that gives you a fresh and glowy look”. For more mature skin, rather than a shimmery shadow go for “a lighter concealer, blended right in, which can really open up the eyes”.Linasha Kotalawala, a makeup artist and beauty content creator in west London, loves the trend for brightly coloured liner and mascara: “I am obsessed with an NYX liner in a metallic, bluish mermaid colour – it is so beautiful on the skin – and then I apply Marc Jacobs’ blue mascara on top.” She says after the post-Covidclean girl aesthetic, renewed attention on colour is “making makeup fun again”.View image in fullscreenThe actor Zendaya’s eye makeup recently went viral.Photograph: Scott A Garfitt/APThose who came of age in the early 00s may be fixated oncat-eye flicks, which can look dated. How can you wean yourself off them?“Small adjustments can make a big difference,” says Eldridge. “The black eyeliner you may have loved for decades can start to close the eye slightly, whereas softening the tone or lifting the placement can create a fresher, more wide awake look. Or you could apply a powder shadow over liquid liner to soften it while keeping impact – a trick I use for the red carpet because it photographs beautifully.”Makeup is for men, tooView image in fullscreenMakeup boosts men’s confidence, says Antonio Cruz.Photograph: Courtesy of Antonio Cruz“You will be surprised how many men love it, or secretly love it,” says Cruz, who personally likes to go “full glam”, to show off his credentials. “I normally joke to men: ‘Don’t worry, you won’t look like me.’”Cruz did prime minister Andy Burnham’s makeup for a BBC interview three years ago: “He had been on that TV show a few times, so he knew the deal. You would be surprised by the amount of men who, after we do a little bit of powder or something, they notice a difference, and it gives them a boost of confidence.”Eldridge says: “One of the most popular products for men is concealer. We all need help sometimes to conceal a late night or a temporary blemish. As with everyone, the main thing to avoid is anything that’s too light-reflective. Men’s skin tends to be thicker than women’s, so anything thick or drying will be too visible. If it’s undetectable coverage you’re going for, look for sheer textures.”Practice makes perfectWhen you get new makeup, make sure you practise putting it on at home, and don’t just apply it for the first time when you are about to go out, advises Cruz. Often, “people only do their makeup when their friends are waiting for them or they have to take a train, and it’s very rushed, like it’s an afterthought.”Meet your matchView image in fullscreenLinasha Kotalawala says finding the right foundation takes time.Photograph: Courtesy of Pave CreatorsMatching a foundation correctly is one of the hardest things to do, says Kotalawala, who recommends Fenty, Mac and Estée Lauder for their range of shades.Cruz says: “You don’t have to apply the product to your skin – hold the packaging close to your face to see which one speaks to you. He also recommends putting on the outfit you will be wearing to see the final effect of a certain shade.View image in fullscreen‘Look for a lip balm that’s close to your natural colour.’Photograph: Posed by model; Liliya Krueger/Getty ImagesTo find your perfect lip colour, says Brown, “the easiest trick is to bite your lips and look at the colour they naturally turn,” says Brown. “That’s usually the most flattering lip shade for you. From there, look for a lipstick or balm that’s close to that natural flush. It will enhance your features without overpowering them.”If you have one thing in your makeup kit, make it …“Blusher,” says Cruz. “If you’re feeling ill, just put on a little extra blusher. If you’re having a sad day, put on a little blusher. I do that myself. Blusher makes you look a bit more awake.”“Find a cream multi-use product that you can put on your cheeks and lips,” says Hughes. “MUA does a blush balm in lots of different colours. You can put that on your cheeks to give you an instant pop, and can press it into your lips for a colour freshness.”“A ‘blonzer’ – in between a blusher and a bronzer,” says Kotalawala, and in particular one that gives a burnt-red warmth, which “looks incredible on deeper skin tones”.Explore more on these topicsMakeupThe expertsSkincareWomenBeautyShareReuse this content

title: Force of Nature review – this nature show turns the climate crisis into a pompom-shaking spectacle | Television | The Guardian
description: Cheetahs forced to cross roiling rivers, owls battered by storms … the tone of this look at how extreme weather affects animals is all a bit disaster movie. Subtle, it is not
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: Cheetahs forced to cross roiling rivers, owls battered by storms … the tone of this look at how extreme weather affects animals is all a bit disaster movie. Subtle, it is not
Content: Like a pair of sulky teens … sibling cheetahs in the flood-struck Maasai Mara national reserve in ITV1’s Force of Nature.Photograph: Plimsoll Productions/ITVView image in fullscreenLike a pair of sulky teens … sibling cheetahs in the flood-struck Maasai Mara national reserve in ITV1’s Force of Nature.Photograph: Plimsoll Productions/ITVTV reviewTelevisionReviewForce of Nature review – this nature show turns the climate crisis into a pompom-shaking spectacleCheetahs forced to cross roiling rivers, owls battered by storms … the tone of this look at how extreme weather affects animals is all a bit disaster movie. Subtle, it is notSarah DempsterSun 26 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou have a thick neck and poorly defined calf muscles and you live in South Dakota with your feckless partner and your five expressionless children. You are an owl. Your days consist of lengthy stretches of nothing, punctuated by sudden bursts of unimaginable terror. Coyotes, badgers and snakes are all bent on reducing your beak to marmalade.But it’s the weather that poses the biggest threat. Specifically, shouts Force of Nature, it’s the “MONSTER STORMS” that rumble ominously across the prairies, each of which forces you and your family to scurry into your burrow, whereupon you will stand with your trembling backs to the wall, legs wide apart and fluffy britches a-flap, like anxious viscounts in the court of Charles II. Will you survive? Or will you be eviscerated by the “cluster bombs of tornadoes” that churn with increasing frequency through the midwest?Three years in the making, this six-part documentary focuses on the impact of such “extreme weather events” on the planet’s animals. The gist? They’re stuffed. Or are at the very least in terrible trouble. What to do?“When nature turns against them,” declaims narrator Andrew Lincoln, “they’re not just enduring … they arefighting back. These animals are,” he adds, Zeus-like in what one imagines are a particularly large pair of chinos, “… a FORCE OF NATURE!” Cue a dramatic montage of climate-battered creatures, each of which has presumably been captured in the moments before it rolled up its sleeves and invited the weather to step outside “for a word”.View image in fullscreenThreatened by climate change … a family of owls pictured in South Dakota.Photograph: Plimsoll Productions/ITVThere are elephants up to their trunks in churning storm water. There is a lizard clinging to a plant stalk as it’s blown sideways by a gale. There is, inevitably, a polar bear – long established as the poster-beast for the climate crisis – floating mournfully into the distance on a small disc of ice. These scenes are accompanied by disembodied snippets from global news reports – each a ghostly transmission from Doom FM. “West Africa’s worst heatwave in living memory,” rumbles one. “Arctic is warming at around three times faster than the rest of the globe,” booms another.It’s all a bit late-90s Hollywood disaster movie, a bit Earth Song; the thunderous soundtrack and shots of crashing waves and sorrowing elephants adds up to a vision of catastrophe that offers little room for subtlety.
