Instead, we get a closeup of chimps holding hands and Lincoln doing this … andthis… and sometimes …THISto the final three words of every sentence, a maddening quirk that makes it doubly difficult to take lines such as “When water is hard to come by, peace …turns to violence” seriously.Still, the photography is tremendous, so let’s do our best to focus on that.Emergencies on planet Earth: images from the climate crisis – in picturesRead moreOff we go, then, to Kenya, where cameras capture the dreadful majesty of the skies as they wreak record-breaking havoc on a pair of cheetah siblings in the flood-struck Maasai Mara national reserve. It’s quite something. There are clouds that look like fists and the sort of clouds that cock their leg over cricket grounds and run away laughing as spectators scramble for their building-society umbrellas.Cheetahs, alas, don’t have umbrellas. Plus, they are terrible at cricket. And so they just stand there looking drenched and miserable, like sulky teens at a bus stop. But the flood waters continue to rise, and so the brothers are forced to cross a roiling river to reach lunch (antelopes). It’s a poignant sight, the swimming-averse cats bobbing and lurching through the water like chickens through wallpaper paste.“The bigger the storm, the greater the heroes,” weeps Lincoln as the cheetahs eventually reach the other side. Heroes? “Fighting back”? Or just everyday victims of a human-made disaster, forced to struggle for survival as the world hems, haws and makes documentaries that, however well-meaning, turn it all into a pompom-shaking spectacle?Back in South Dakota, the owls emerge from their storm-burrow, wobbly but alive. Phew. Whether they can endure another five episodes of Lincoln’s italics, however, remains …TO BE SEEN.Force of Nature aired on ITV1 and is on ITVX now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The kindness of strangers: When Mum was hospitalised on a family holiday, our hotel’s owners were heaven-sent | Family | The Guardian
description: I was just 10 at the time but my siblings and I will never forget the sense of safety, comfort and warmth they offered
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: I was just 10 at the time but my siblings and I will never forget the sense of safety, comfort and warmth they offered
Content: ‘We had been staying in a gîte but moved to a small hotel closer to the hospital. It was a terrifying and stressful time.’Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreen‘We had been staying in a gîte but moved to a small hotel closer to the hospital. It was a terrifying and stressful time.’Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian DesignKindness of strangersFamilyThe kindness of strangers: When Mum was hospitalised on a family holiday, our hotel’s owners were heaven-sentI was just 10 at the time but my siblings and I will never forget the sense of safety, comfort and warmth they offeredRead more inthe kindness of strangers seriesMelanie Brock, as told toKatie CunninghamSun 26 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 20.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe were doing the groceries when a blood vessel burst in my mother’s brain. I was 10 years old and on a family holiday to France that very suddenly changed its tenor. In the following weeks Mum went through brain surgery, suffered a stroke and was placed in intensive care.We had beenstaying in a gîtebut moved to a small hotel closer to the hospital. It was a terrifying and stressful time, even as a young kid who knew things were serious – but didn’t understand quitehowserious.The kindness of strangers: After losing my wife and son, I ate alone one Father’s Day – and another diner paid my billRead moreSo it was an unexpected blessing that the owners of our new hotel, Jean-Claude and Therese, were heaven-sent. Jean-Claude, a fabulous chef, would cook us kids whatever we wanted for dinner (most often spaghetti bolognese, much to our father’s embarrassment). When Therese caught me hand washing our clothes in the sink, she intervened and began doing our laundry for us. Both dished out hugs as required. And they introduced our father to English-speaking locals who were able to help him navigate the French medical system.One weekend the entire hotel had been pre-booked for a wedding, meaning there was no room for us. Rather than allowing us to find another hotel for a couple of nights, Jean-Claude arranged for his mother to take us in. She was a lovely, non-English speaking octogenarian with a pet canary, kind enough to open her doors to a family she’d never met and could not communicate with.Many decades have passed and we’ve since lost both Mum and Dad but my siblings and I will never forget Jean-Claude and Therese. At a time when we needed it most, they not only helped my dad with the practical matters that accompany a critically ill wife overseas but offered my siblings and me a priceless sense of safety, comfort and warmth.I hope I can show half as much kindness for a stranger in need, should I ever have the opportunity.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: This is how we do it: ‘I could have sex every day, but he says no about 80% of the time’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Will’s lack of self-worth is creating a barrier between him and Fi, but talking more could help them adjust to their mismatched libidos
Author: Olivia Ladanyi
Headline: Will’s lack of self-worth is creating a barrier between him and Fi, but talking more could help them adjust to their mismatched libidos
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘I could have sex every day, but he says no about 80% of the time’Will’s lack of self-worth is creating a barrier between him and Fi, but talking more could help them adjust to their mismatched libidosHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toOlivia LadanyiSun 26 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFi, 42double quotation markI worry that Will sees me more as a mother figure than a sexual beingThe other morning, I woke up horny and suggested a quickie, but Will said he was too tired – it was too early. When I found him masturbating in bed the next day, I felt so rejected. I drove to work in floods of tears. I knew my feelings weren’t rational – there’s nothing wrong with masturbating – but they were real. All I could think was: couldn’t we have had those two minutes of intimacy yesterday?I love sex and the connection it brings. I could have sex every day, but Will says no about 80% of the time. For me, sex creates closeness. For Will, the opposite is true: he has to feel close before having sex – and his depression, performance anxiety and low confidence mean his libido is lower than mine.Until a couple of weeks ago, we hadn’t had sex in more than six months. My previous relationship was sexless for five years, and I don’t want to end up living with a friend again. But I’ve realised I played a part in that too. I find being vulnerable difficult, so instead of talking honestly about sex and how important it is to me, I put up a wall.double quotation markFinding Will masturbating led to the healthiest conversation I’ve had in a relationshipIt’s hard to know how to drive sex when you have mismatched libidos. I usually initiate with a joke like, “Do you want to put your stick in my hole?” When he says no, I assume it’s my failure, that I asked in the wrong way. I worry that I desire him more than he desires me.I also worry that Will sees me more as a mother figure than a sexual being. When we moved in together last autumn, our differences became more obvious. I was the fixer, the one who gets things done; Will was out of work and in bed for four months with a broken back. He felt worthless.Finding Will masturbating led to the healthiest conversation I’ve had in a relationship. He understood that hearing how attracted he is to me isn’t enough – I need to feel desired through his actions. We’re back to having sex about once a week, which is enough for me to get the validation and reassurance I need. He’s teaching me how to slow down and open up more.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreWill, 42double quotation markThere’s a disconnect between my brain and my penis. I’d rather say no than feel as if I’m letting Fi downI often ask Fi why she’s with me. She’s got everything sorted, whereas a lot of the time I see myself as nothing. Low self-worth and antidepressants mean there’s a disconnect between my brain and my penis. I overthink everything. What if I ejaculate too quickly? What if I can’t come at all? I’d rather say no than feel as if I’m letting Fi down.We met on Hinge 18 months ago, at a time when I’d almost given up on dating. We went for a walk and I just knew she was right for me. My last partner was emotionally and physically abusive, so I really need to be able to trust that someone is honest and kind, and I felt that with Fi immediately. So did my daughter – and kids are very good judges of character.double quotation markBecause I don’t think I’m worth anything, being with someone amazing is overwhelmingThings changed after we moved in together. Life became more about house admin than sex, and I injured my back, which completely killed intimacy. I could barely walk; I couldn’t roll over in bed or reach my arm across Fi without excruciating pain; I wasn’t even allowed to pick up a bag of shopping. Fi kept telling me I was doing brilliantly, but I felt physically and mentally useless.This is how we do it: ‘I fell in love with my lover’s husband – and now we’re a trio’Read moreWhen Fi found me masturbating after I’d turned down sex, it wasn’t about choosing masturbation over her. I was doing it to try to get back to sleep.Sexwith Fi is completely different – I need to be emotionally present because I care so much about whether she’s enjoying it too.Even though we seem to be out of the rut now, Fi says she doesn’t want to initiate any more so she doesn’t get rejected. She worries it’s about her, but it isn’t at all – I think she’s amazing. But that’s part of the problem – because I don’t think I’m worth anything, being with someone amazing is overwhelming. I try to reassure her how incredibly sexy I find her, that I love her. And when we do have sex, it’s dynamite.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From the strait of Hormuz to the North Sea, a global maritime war rages around us – and more than the price of oil is at stake | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: The collapse of the rules-based order is not confined to the land: we’re imperilled as centuries of maritime cooperation sink beneath the waves, says foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: The collapse of the rules-based order is not confined to the land: we’re imperilled as centuries of maritime cooperation sink beneath the waves, says foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: The Russian frigate Admiral Grigorovich off the coast of Tartus, Syria, September 2024.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenThe Russian frigate Admiral Grigorovich off the coast of Tartus, Syria, September 2024.Photograph: APOpinionStrait of HormuzFrom the strait of Hormuz to the North Sea, a global maritime war rages around us – and more than the price of oil is at stakeSimon TisdallThe collapse of the rules-based order is not confined to the land: we’re imperilled as centuries of maritime cooperation sink beneath the wavesSun 26 Jul 2026 07.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 12.47 EDTShareThe US military campaign to protect merchant shipping from Iranian attacks by asserting direct maritime control in the strait of Hormuz is not an idea unique to Donald Trump’s administration. Almost exactly 200 years ago, in the period 1825-27, a powerful US naval squadron led by Commodore John Rodgers was sent to the Mediterraneanto defend American shipsfrom the depredations of Greek corsairs and pirates.For all the new-minted republic’s brave talk of liberty, the US squadron did not assist Greece’s ongoing “regime change” struggle for independence from the Ottoman empire. Its sole, self-serving purpose was to defend US trade, markets and business interests. After abandoning his call for apeople’s revolution in Tehran, this, too, is what Trump’s reckless war with Iran has now boiled down to.Although the US has not ratified the 1982 UN convention on the law of the sea, which establishes a legal right of freedom of passage without interference by littoral states, it has historically upheld the principle of freedom of navigation ormare liberum(the free sea) developed by Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist. Rejecting Iran’s claims, Marco Rubio, US secretary of state,declared in Junethat “no country is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway”.Yet Trump has since suggested the US itself may yet do exactly that and impose tolls. Although helater rowed back, last month’s “memorandum of understanding” with Iran accepts that it has a right, with Oman, to monetise transit through the strait of Hormuz. Despite the resumption of US attacks and Trump’sincreasingly hysterical threats, the MOU currently remains the only basis for a future peace deal.Two-faced Trump’s equivocal stance reflects a wider breakdown in the “free sea” consensus underpinning maritime law – and hastens the overall degradation of the international rules-based order. Trump believes nation states (or at least the US) have an absolute right to act unilaterally in their own interests, unconstrained by laws, treaties or regard for the “global commons” of the high seas.The destabilising ramifications of this approach, emulated by other countries,grow clearer by the day. This new 21st-century war of the sea does not involve titanic clashes between Bismarck-class battleships or huge naval showdowns such as Jutland and Midway. But its frontlines are the same as ever: defence, security, borders, free trade, money, power.Today’s war of the sea has many aspects. One is the spreading impact of precedents set by the Hormuz standoff. In Yemen, Iran-aligned Houthi militias have begun a copycat blockade of the Bab al-Mandab strait, at the mouth of the Red Sea, in reprisal, they claim, for attacks by Saudi Arabia. Two oil tankerswere struck this week, further spooking energy markets and presaging wider escalation.Also potentially fatal for international norms is the post-Hormuz debate in Indonesia about imposingtolls in the strait of Malacca, through which 22% of global maritime shipping passes. Might Turkey adopt the US-Iran approach and charge for passage through the Bosphorus? Or Spain in the strait of Gibraltar? The dire implications for global trade and supply chains are obvious. About80% of goodstraded worldwide by volume go by sea.Friction over seaborne trade aside, overt maritime clashes between regional rivals are increasing, particularly in theSouth China Seaand the waters around Taiwan. Expansionist China’s creation of artificial, militarised islands on obscure reefs and sporadic confrontations with neighbours such as the Philippines are the root cause. Like the US, Beijing rejects international law when it doesn’t suit it – notably the 2016 ruling by the permanent court of arbitration, which found its claim to sovereignty over most of the South China Sealacked a legal basis.China crossed another red line last week when one of its missile destroyersundertook a live-fire drillinside Japan’s exclusive economic zone, about 180km (110 miles) from Okinotori, Japan’s southernmost island. Tokyo and Beijing have longstanding maritime disputes. But tensions rose sharply after Japan’s new prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, suggested a Chinese bid to seize Taiwan could trigger a Japanese military response. Few weeks go by without reports of Chinese air and sea exercises in preparation for a not-so-hypothetical amphibious assault on Taiwan.The fact a Russian frigate accompanied the offending Chinese warship off Japan points to another major actor in the global war of the sea. Vladimir Putin’s once-vaunted Black Sea fleet hassuffered severe losses, caused by Ukraine’s missiles and drones, since 2022. Its ships no longer control the Black Sea, mostly cowering in port. As if to compensate, hybrid “grey zone” Russian military maritime operations against Ukraine’s European alliesare expanding. Baltic undersea pipelines and communications cables have proven vulnerable targets.Russia has also stepped up surface fleet and submarine activities in the North Atlantic approaches, the North Sea and the Channel, where it is suspected of mapping underwater infrastructure with a view to future sabotage. Last Monday, one of its warshipswent a step further, marking Andy Burnham’s first day as UK prime minister with a rare live-fire drill 70kn (45 miles) south of Plymouth, home of the Royal Navy.It was the latest in a string of hostile actions designed to provoke, intimidate and test British and European defences. Last month, a Russian frigatefired warning shotsnear a private yacht off the Isle of Wight. The incident seems trivial until it is set in the wider context of a rapidly building Nato-Russia at-sea confrontation. Then it begins to look scary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe sense of increasing inter-state maritime lawlessness is fed by numerous other recent incidents, such as the unlawful USsinking of an Iranian warshipoff Sri Lanka in March, last week’sbitter clashbetween Chinese and Philippine ships, Trump’s revived threats to forcibly annex the Danish-owned island of Greenland and his bombing of civilian boats off Venezuela. A Chinese nuclear submarine test-fired along-range ballistic missilein the South Pacific this month to the outrage of Australia, which is itselfacquiring nuclear-powered subs.US submarine sinks Iranian warship near coast of Sri Lanka – videoAll this instability is fuelling anaccelerating global arms race. Little wonder Burnham’s revamped government faces pressure togreatly increase defence spending, especially on the badly depleted Royal Navy. Current UK plans include upgrades to the Trident at-sea nuclear deterrent.This many-fronted war of the sea tells a bigger story still: of how centuries-old, hard-won maritime cooperation and collaboration protocols are breaking down, of how international legal norms and rules – whether the issue is free trade, offshore defence, sovereignty, borders, fisheries, deep-sea mining or environmental pollution – are sinking beneath the waves.It’s a story about a world where one country can impose its will on others less powerful and less wealthy, rather than seeking their agreement; where the fundamental concept of global commons or shared space is shot to hell. It’s about Lord Palmerston-style gunboat diplomacy writ large. It’s about a world all at sea.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzOpinionChinaRussiaMilitaryAsia PacificDonald TrumpRoyal NavycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Burnham bounce’ risks deflating unless focus remains on struggling households | Richard Partington | The Guardian
description: UK’s inequalities expose splits in consumer economy, with spending suffering and a decline in savings among the poorest
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: UK’s inequalities expose splits in consumer economy, with spending suffering and a decline in savings among the poorest
Content: Andy Burnham has been credited with helping to lift UK consumer confidence but will the political honeymoon last?Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has been credited with helping to lift UK consumer confidence but will the political honeymoon last?Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersEconomics viewpointAndy Burnham‘Burnham bounce’ risks deflating unless focus remains on struggling householdsRichard PartingtonUK’s inequalities expose splits in consumer economy, with spending suffering and a decline in savings among the poorestSun 26 Jul 2026 07.34 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareA“Burnham bounce”, sunshine and a strong World Cup run for the England men’s football team. Could this be a turnaround moment for Britain’s struggling consumer economy or yet another false start for the UK’s spluttering growth engine?Last week the data company GfK credited Andy Burnham’s return to Westminster politics for lifting UK consumer confidence at its fastest monthly pace for almost three years in June.The lion’s share of the improvement was driven by how consumers viewed the prospects for the British economy, with a 10-point advance in how they felt about the past year, and an eight-point gain for the next 12 months.“The sense of a fresh start following the appointment of a new prime minister surely accounts for some of this bounce,” GfK said.For the economy at large, keeping the tills ringing is important: household consumption accounts for about 60% of the total economy, providing the lifeblood for high streets, service providers, builders and makers nationwide.Burnham’s decision to introduce a temporaryVAT cut for electricity billsin Great Britain from October, capbus faresat £2 across England, and a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues, is designed to help. In a further boost, the headline rate of inflation fell by more than expected, to 2.6%.However, when it comes to the British consumer there is more going on than immediately meets the eye.View image in fullscreenYouth unemployment is at the highest level in a decade.Photograph: Philip Toscano/PADrill down into the GfK data, and some revealing trends emerge: older Britons, aged 65 and over, are among the gloomiest. By contrast, 16- to 29-year-olds are more optimistic – despite the challenges facing the younger generation from an AI-disrupted jobs market and sky-high rents and house prices.Youth unemployment is at the highest level in a decade. But over-65s are more likely than the under-30s to predict a rise in joblessness. They also worry more about the economic outlook, their own financial situation and the property market.Some of this will be down to data quality. Consumers can be unreliable readers of economic conditions. Their mood on survey day can play a role, as can the news agenda.There are real splits in the consumer perception of the economy, too – exposed by the UK’s deep inequalities. Time and again the poorest, unsurprisingly, have the gloomiest outlook. And it is not hard to see why.Official figures show UK households spend£676.60 a week on average,with housing, fuel and power accounting for about a fifth of the total. Transport is the next most consumed category, followed by other spending including package holidays, leisure, communications and food and drink. Health and education make up just 3% of weekly spending on average.There are worrying signs the wealthiest are pulling ahead. The latest official figures for the year to March 2025 show weekly spending by the richest fifth of households increased at twice the rate of the poorest fifth’s, rising by £98.10 (10%) to £1,083.60 compared with £18.10 (5%) to £407.30.Since the onset of the cost of living crisis in late 2021, the average consumer price level has risen by more than a quarter. But in some categories – including for food and energy – it has risen by significantly more.On top of this, the Bank of England has driven interest rates to elevated levels to combat the inflationary splurge – heaping pressure on borrowers. But a large group of older Britons are mortgage-free, and so have been more insulated.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith these headwinds it is hardly surprising consumer spending has suffered: official figures showconsumer-facing servicesoutput remains about 6% below its pre-pandemic level. Travel agents, food and drink, and hoteliers are among the hardest hit.Threadneedle Street predicts real incomes will have fallen by about 0.5% in the year to the end of June. And with the volatile Middle East conflict expected to stoke inflation over the coming months, the belt-tightening for the British consumer is only likely to continue.The counterpoint to the spending weakness has been a highhousehold saving ratio, which measures the proportion of disposable income left unspent. At 8.9%, it is currently among the highest levels in a decade.double quotation markSavings were concentrated among affluent people in richer southern English neighbourhoodsHouseholds pushed the ratio to 27.5% during the pandemic lockdowns, when they were unable to spend much of their income. Billions of pounds were banked – helping to power the consumption boom, and inflationary burst, after the easing of restrictions.However, not everyone was in a position to squirrel away money. Bank research shows thehighest 40% of earners and retireessaved the most, while the poorest fifth of households suffered a decline in savings.Reflecting regional divisions, savings wereconcentrated among affluent peoplein richer southern English neighbourhoods, where the Centre for Cities thinktank found households banked £12 for every £1 saved in poorer areas – mostly in northern English cities and towns.For the “Burnham bounce” to be sustainable, it will require a continued turnaround in consumer confidence. That will need a laser-like focus on the households struggling the most.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamEconomics viewpointConsumer spendingUK cost of living crisisInequalityEconomicsEconomic growth (GDP)commentShareReuse this content

title: I was a terrible teen. Now my son is turning into one, karma is coming for me | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: My mum loves to remind me how sullen, furious and monosyllabic I was. Now she can’t wait to see how I’ll handle parenting an adolescent, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: My mum loves to remind me how sullen, furious and monosyllabic I was. Now she can’t wait to see how I’ll handle parenting an adolescent, writes Polly Hudson
Content: Soak up every second … the terrible teens are coming.Photograph: Jordi Salas/Getty Images (Posed by models)View image in fullscreenSoak up every second … the terrible teens are coming.Photograph: Jordi Salas/Getty Images (Posed by models)OpinionYoung peopleI was a terrible teen. Now my son is turning into one, karma is coming for mePolly HudsonMy mum loves to remind me how sullen, furious and monosyllabic I was. Now she can’t wait to see how I’ll handle parenting an adolescentSun 26 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 15.55 EDTShareThe “Baader-Meinhof phenomenon” is a more satisfying name for frequency illusion – noticing a concept, word or product more often just after becoming aware of it. And after readinga fascinating articleby a professor who insists that when a teenager makes “the stupid choice”, their brain is actually “working exactly as designed”, I’m suddenly seeing teens everywhere. Not just literally, because it’s the school holidays – hanging about in groups, being scarily tall and all dressed identically – but also in news stories, adverts for adolescent skincare, old clips of Harry Enfield’s Kevin and Perry sketches. Not unrelated: my son’s 12th birthday is fast approaching. This is the very last year my little boy will be nice and preteen, and I’m being reminded from all angles, by all algorithms. Soak up every second while there’s still time! Tick tock, tick tock! Thanks, Baader-Meinhof.Teenage minds function “in a way that has been shaped by evolution for a unique and uniquely challenging time of life,” according toDr Evelyn Svingen, assistant professor of criminology at the University of Birmingham. This is reassuring and concerning in equal measures – in the future my son’s going to make dumb decisions, but it’s OK, because that’s what he’s meant to do. Sheesh.However, the most awful part of preparing to parent a teen is that I’m certain karma is coming for me. My mum physically rubs her hands together with glee whenever the subject arises, already snuggling into her front row seat, ready to enjoy the show. I was the most terrible teenager who has ever stomped across the earth, then slammed the door while screaming “I hate you!” And I’m worried that what goes around will come around. The way my mum tells it – and boy does she still tell it now, decades later – I went up to bed on the eve of my 13th birthday a delightful angel, sunshine personified, cartoon birds landing on my finger. The next morning, I had transformed into the princess of darkness. The sky went black, there was an ominous clap of thunder, and sullen, furious and monosyllabic, I appeared at the breakfast table.Over the next few years I made every stupid choice going (although, look Mum, it turns out my brain was working exactly as designed). But to be honest, what haunts me most now isn’t the risks I took, the dangerous situations I blundered into, or the mistakes I made, it’s how embarrassed I was by my parents, simply because they existed.I remember walking into the town where I grew up with my dad once, purposely dawdling to ensure I was five paces behind him, so no one would see us together. Some of this was because he was wearing a deeply unfashionable anorak, but mostly it was because being out in public with either parent was horrific. I didn’t consider for a millisecond what that experience was like for him. The irony that now, 14 years after his death, I would give almost anything to walk down a road with him is not lost on me.But it’s astonishing how quickly that switch flicked; one day I was happily holding my dad’s hand, chatting away, thrilled to spend as much time with him as possible, the next lagging behind him and eye-rolling likeTrinny and Susannah. I can recall that feeling so vividly, and while of course I want my son to be safe through his teen years, it’s humbling to acknowledge that I also really want him to still like his parents, even if only behind closed doors, when nobody’s looking.His descent into teenagerdom has already started. Driving with him last week I realised I needed to pop into a supermarket, and he was mortified by the idea, in case any of his schoolfriends were around. I suggested he stay in the car, but waiting in the car for your mum is apparently a fate worse than being seen in Sainsbury’s with her, if you can imagine such a thing.This is an essential stage of growing up. I know we have to try to understand. I know we have to not take it too personally. I know we have to let him go … but not too far, hopefully. Tick tock, tick tock.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerExplore more on these topicsYoung peopleOpinionParents and parentingFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: An act of kindness, or mitzvah, teaches us to be part of something bigger than ourselves | Nomi Kaltmann | The Guardian
description: More than anything, I want my kids to grow into people who notice others and who care about the world around them
Author: Nomi Kaltmann
Headline: More than anything, I want my kids to grow into people who notice others and who care about the world around them
Content: Composite: Nenov/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Nenov/Getty ImagesMaking sense of itJudaismAn act of kindness, or mitzvah, teaches us to be part of something bigger than ourselvesNomi KaltmannMore than anything, I want my kids to grow into people who notice others and who care about the world around themMaking sense of itis a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday lifeSun 26 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 18.59 EDTShareSeveral times a week, I write small notes on pretty stationery for my three-year-old daughter to take to kinder the next day.Sometimes the note is about how she shared a toy with a sibling, other times it is about how she helped someone without being asked. Often it is praising her for saying thank you or please.In our family, we call themmitzvahnotes.The Hebrew word mitzvah is often translated as a good deed but perhaps the best way to describe a mitzvah is an intentional act of goodness and kindness.AI claims to have the answers to life’s big questions. But sometimes not knowing brings us closer to the truth | Amy GallifordRead moreMy daughter proudly takes her mitzvah notes to kinder, where her teacher reads them out loud to the whole class. The notes are then pinned to a wall filled with other children’s mitzvah notes, celebrating the good deeds of her three-year-old peers.So, while other children covet stickers or prizes, my daughter is thrilled when she gets a mitzvah note and loves it when she has one to take to school.As a parent, I spend a lot of time thinking about what values I want to pass on to my kids. Of course, I want my children to be capable and confident, and I want them to work hard and develop resilience. But more than anything, I want them to grow into people who notice others and who care about the world around them. I want them to understand that even the smallest acts of goodness and kindness can have a ripple effect far beyond what we can ever see.There is a verse in the Bible, in the Book of Proverbs, that says: “Train a child according to their path, and even when they are old, they will not depart from it.”I have always loved this quote, because to me it represents the idea that children grow into the identities we help them see in themselves.When I want my children to help clean up their rooms and they are feeling particularly reluctant, instead of focusing on what they are not doing, I usually try to say something like, “I love when you help Mummy clean up your room.”By framing the request like this, I am reminding them of who I think they are. That as their mum, I see them as someone who helps, someone who cares and someone who tries to do the right thing.This is what makes mitzvah notes so powerful. They are not just about praising a single action; they build a mindset where children want to be noticed for the good deeds that they do. They encourage children to look outward rather than inward and they teach every human that they are part of something bigger than themselves.After the Bondi terror attack, many people were left asking what they could do in the face of such darkness.This ancient Jewish tradition brings me closer to my faith and invites me to imagine a better worldRead moreOne response was a renewed focus on acts of kindness, and with consultation from the Jewish community, anational dayto performmitzvotwas announced for people of all faiths to try to bring more light into the world. Across Australia, people volunteered at soup kitchens, cleaned beaches, visited elderly people in nursing homes and found small ways to be kind to others.None of those acts could undo the tragedy that occurred but they reflected a belief that darkness spreads when people withdraw from one another, while goodness grows when people choose to do small acts of goodness and kindness for each other.And perhaps that is why I love mitzvah notes so much.They are small notes, jotted down in a minute or less, yet they carry a much bigger message. They tell a child, “I saw what you did, and I love that you are doing small acts of kindness,” and they encourage them to continue doing small acts of goodness and kindness.And if enough children grow up believing that being kind and thoughtful is part of who they are, then perhaps those small notes are doing far more than recognising a good deed. Perhaps they are helping raise the sort of people our world needs right now.Nomi Kaltmann is an Australian lawyer and journalist. She is a proud member of Melbourne’s Jewish communityExplore more on these topicsJudaismMaking sense of itReligionParents and parentingAustralian educationChildrenFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Pitt is powerful – but it’s the rawness of The Bear that truly portrays hospital work | Seema Jilani | The Guardian
description: Both restaurant work and medicine involve abusive training and relentless devotion to minutiae – and the joy of offering comfort
Author: Seema Jilani
Headline: Both restaurant work and medicine involve abusive training and relentless devotion to minutiae – and the joy of offering comfort
Content: ‘The Bear captures the intimacy of a shared language and bodily familiarity unspoken amongst both doctors and chefs.’Photograph: FXView image in fullscreen‘The Bear captures the intimacy of a shared language and bodily familiarity unspoken amongst both doctors and chefs.’Photograph: FXOpinionDoctorsThe Pitt is powerful – but it’s the rawness of The Bear that truly portrays hospital workSeema JilaniBoth restaurant work and medicine involve abusive training and relentless devotion to minutiae – and the joy of offering comfortSun 26 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.05 EDTShareIpass a mother heaving in grief while her son’s heart monitors flatline. It is the last time she will ever hold his hand. For me, this is another day on call in the intensive care unit as a pediatric physician. For her, this is the day her life shatters.Later that night, a striking, charismatic surgeon from work treats me to an exquisite meal. Served outside a trailer, humidity barreling through our scrubs, the food is neither extravagant nor decadent. It is, however, the most succulent Texas barbecue brisket I will ever taste. This is the night I rest my head on his shoulder and he doesn’t flinch. This is the night an “us” was born.A shared humanity links doctors and chefs. We both craft life’s most tender moments. Some will ricochet off your brain for years, dull with ache. Others will leave you heady, craving more. The television seriesThe Pitthas garnered well-deserved praise for its excellent depiction of an emergency room staff battling insurance companies, mass shootings and mental health crises. In fact, I was one of many healthcare providers who shared my insight for The Pitt, andconsulted to help craft narrativestrue to reality, so I deeply respect its advocacy for destigmatizing mental healthcare for physicians.And yet, I have never been more convinced thatThe Bearis actually the reigning television show for accuracy in its depiction of hospital medicine. From the delayed gratification of abusive, humiliating training to the chaotic intensity of its work-hard-play-hard ethos, training for chefs is, in many ways, comparable to physician pedagogy. Both professions spend infinite hours mastering minutiae no one will ever discern. Both lose themselves in the relentless pursuit of precision, and in their dedication to service, an art form few will appreciate.double quotation markBoth professions spend infinite hours mastering minutiae no one will ever discernWe inhabit two of the last true apprenticeships, marred by years of exploitation, insults and chronic sleep deprivation. It is the perfect recipe for both professions to suffer from disproportionately higher rates of depression, anxiety, addiction, and even suicide. OnThe Bear, Jeremy Allen White’s Carmy once described his former boss at an elite restaurant as: “Very, probably, mentally ill. Dead inside. Cold. Never turns it off. Accomplishes more by 10am than most people do in a lifetime. I don’t think he sleeps. I don’t think he eats. I don’t think he loves.” Ask any doctor about their most feared mentor in residency, and they’d sputter these words out with the same cadence.In one scene, this boss berates his employees for their slowness and orders them to repeat: “Chef, I’m so tough,” while he taunts: “You are not tough ... You are talentless … You should be dead.”It brought to mind the first day of gross anatomy class in medical school. One of our professors joked that if we were to attempt suicide, as many doctors do, that we should at least not shame the profession by surviving. They would gladly show us on a cadaver how to “do it right” so at least we weren’t total failures.We – doctors and chefs - dissolve into our professions chasing illusions of perfection. For me, it is the chance to save your life or to assuage your pain. For a chef, it is the hope that the couple who got engaged at his restaurant retells their proposal story breathlessly for years to come, that he enshrined that memory with the tenderness it deserves.WhileThe Pittis what you might desire from your ideal physician, it’s the frenetic back-of-the-house pulsing turbulence in The Bear that I recognize. The audience gets glimpses of the staff’s camaraderie, which, similar to hospitals, is airtight. These are the only people who truly comprehend the grueling mess it takes to make this look this easy.My patient’s near-death experience in hospital left me with worry and guilt. This is how vicarious trauma starts | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreI remember one night in the ER, a child had been brutally beaten and was dead on arrival. I meticulously washed matted blood from her hair, cloaked her in a hospital blanket and tried to restore some of her dignity. I gave her body, cradled, to her mother, where she lay one last time. And then I hurried along. My next patient was already angry about the wait. This is the raw reality that public-facing professions grapple with. Whether we are wearing scrubs or chef’s uniforms, we serve as punching bags; society has license to exorcise its demons onto us.But The Bear is not only an exacting look in the mirror – not just the mental health woes, not just life’s most dramatic days. It is also a celebration of the joy of the ordinary, luxuriating in the perfect bite. The Bear gets even the most cynical of us to revel in the purest of humanity: offering comfort to another human, hoping that our presence will make their pain more bearable in some way. We show up for life’s most gutting times, but also at its most promising: the moment a baby’s first cry reverberates, or just as the candlelight across the table flickers ever so gently. Food, when done right, offers healing too.The Bear also captures the intimacy of a shared language and bodily familiarity unspoken amongst both doctors and chefs. After working decades alongside one another at godforsaken hours of the night, we know each other’s eyebrow arch. We recognize a vocal tremor infinitesimally longer than it should be. We pick each other up when we fail. We have no choice. It’s a bond borne of collective fatigue, and one of sharing abject frustration and sacred silences in the same day.As for my handsome surgeon, he would later ask me to meet him at a Michelin starred restaurant. I would get my hair done and wear lace. An hour and two glasses into the evening, I would take off my heels as the waiter asked me if I wanted to call it a night. I don’t remember much about that relationship, unceremoniously pronounced dead when he stood me up that night. But I will never bid goodbye to the exquisite flavor of that Texas brisket, which remains a glimmer of magnificence in an otherwise harrowing day. My memories return far more to the taste of that barbecue than to the taste of his kiss, so all things considered? Worth it.Seema Jilani is a pediatric hospitalist who has treated critically ill children on medical evacuation flights. Her humanitarian work has taken her to Afghanistan, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Ukraine, Bosnia, Gaza and the West Bank, and on refugee rescue boats off the coast of Libya. Her radio documentary, Israel and Palestine: The Human Cost of the Occupation, was nominated for the Peabody AwardIn the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. title: How do we defeat authoritarianism? By building a sense of belonging | Julie Fernandes and Katrina Gamble | The Guardian
description: Eighty-five million Americans are disaffected and less likely to vote, our survey found. Our democratic revival depends on a sense of community
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Eighty-five million Americans are disaffected and less likely to vote, our survey found. Our democratic revival depends on a sense of community
Content: ‘They want to see progress on issues they care about. They just don’t see the connection between voting and making their lives better.’Photograph: Eric Risberg/APView image in fullscreen‘They want to see progress on issues they care about. They just don’t see the connection between voting and making their lives better.’Photograph: Eric Risberg/APOpinionActivismHow do we defeat authoritarianism? By building a sense of belongingJulie Fernandes and Katrina GambleEighty-five million Americans are disaffected and less likely to vote, our survey found. Our democratic revival depends on a sense of communitySun 26 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.37 EDTShareOur country is at a crossroads between democracy and authoritarianism. And the only antidote is an organized, engaged citizenry. But at this critical moment when we need people to lean into the fight for our future, we find that far too many people have given up.In acomprehensive, multiracial study, Sojourn Strategies, Ariel Research Partners and Richard Shafranekfoundthat 35% of the US electorate – 85 million people – are disaffected, characterized by high levels of disillusionment and low levels of trust in government and politics. Our democratic revival depends on solutions that transform people from disaffected bystanders into powerful civic agents.The desire for community is where we find hope. Almost six in 10 of the disaffected (58%) would like to feel more connected to other people. These feelings provide organizers with an opening to invite new people into community where they can build a sense of belonging and develop collective agency. The research also shows that the disaffected electorate is reachable: they are more likely to act when they feel like they belong and can see the tangible impact of their actions.Americans declared independence from a tyrant once. And we must do that again | Claire FinkelsteinRead moreThe disaffected electorate is the same as the overall population as far as race, ethnicity and gender – although disaffected people tend to be younger, have fewer resources and are less likely to be college educated. What surprised us in the research was the finding that the disaffected are as civically engaged as the general population, with the exception of voting. Disaffected people have almost the same likelihood to talk to a friend or a family member about a political issue (61% of the overall population and 60% of the disaffected electorate) or to search online for information about politics (both at 42%). Yet while 65% of the overall population would vote if the midterm elections were held today, only 56% of disaffected voters say the same.Most institutions, including the traditional political industry, write these folks off as apathetic. But the research shows something very different. They care a great deal about their families, neighbors and communities. They want to see progress on issues they care about. They just don’t see the connection between voting and making their lives better.So, what is going on? A common thread within this group of disaffected people is that they are extremely isolated with no or few friends or organizational affiliations. Almost half (49%) do not belong to an online community, church, mosque or synagogue or other religious groups, a community or political group, a labor union, or other community spaces. But collective spaces that we call“civic homes”are where people develop a sense of belonging and agency that is critical to their belief in the power of voting to drive change. Thus, investment in the organizing groups that operate as civic homes is a critical solution to our current democratic crisis.Civic homes are developed by organizers as places where people can meet each other, feel seen and heard, work together on issues that matter to them, experience concrete benefits and make life better for themselves and the people they care about. Our research shows that even small increases in feelings of belonging within a civic home are associated with significant increases in voting and taking other civic and political actions.Take Angeles in Nevada, for example. She was working long hours as a car wash supervisor, earning wages that never seemed to stretch far enough. Every month, she wondered whether her family would be able to cover rent. A few years ago, an organizer with Make the Road Nevada invited Angeles to a monthly membership meeting. During the discussion, Angeles heard her neighbors sharing similar struggles such as difficulties in making rent, stagnant wages, lack of affordable childcare and a feeling that those in power were not listening. This experience made Angeles feel seen and she began to develop a sense of belonging. She got connected to Make the Road Nevada’s Know Your Rights workshops, which helped her learn about the voting process and made her feel included. This year, Angeles will cast her first ballot as a US citizen. Not because a candidate’s campaign finally reached her. But because her people did.Shared culture creates a feeling of belonging. Familiar food, language, music and even games are what make people feel at home. For example, a non-profit called Power Interfaith is running an innovative Soul Food Dinners program in Pennsylvania. These are nonjudgmental spaces where young, disaffected Black people, especially young men, can have honest conversations about their lives and visions of the future over a meal. Part of the focus is on young Black men who are skeptical about civic engagement and voting, but guided by their faith – a group that is undiscovered and under-researched.The Soul Food Dinner project is similar to Georgia Alliance’s We the People initiative, which hosted intergenerational conversations among younger and older Black people as a strategy for rebuilding a sense of agency and belonging across differences. Older participants often arrived believing young people were disengaged or apathetic, while younger participants frequently viewed older generations as dismissive, out of touch or unwilling to share power. The series created opportunities for participants to ask deeper questions, listen to one another’s lived experiences and recognize shared values beneath different forms of expression. As participants moved beyond stereotypes, the emotional ground softened for collaboration, curiosity and mutual respect. Pre- and post-event feelings of power increased on both sides of the conversations, a measure that correlates to voter turnout in the Black community.In the state next door, game facilitators with North Carolina Asian Americans Together are hosting Mahjong nights with communal hotpot meals for people in their late teens and 20s. The young people who come feel disconnected from traditional politics, but care very much about the cost of living, immigration, healthcare and making life better for their communities. The blend of familiar foods, games and conversations create connections and make people feel comfortable before they are invited into civic engagement, such as registering to vote or attending an organizing meeting.Building trust and belonging that allows people to be transformed into civic agents is deep relational work. And it takes time. But the payoff is powerful. Transactional civic engagement aimed at a discrete outcome is a quick hit, like a sugar rush: it might feel great in the moment, but the long-term effect is weak and empty. Working to support people to become powerful civic actors through belonging and collective agency results in strong, durable architects of a hopeful future.What’s giving us hope nowThe stories of everyday people across the US standing up, getting organized and driving change to make life better for themselves, their families, and their communities is a tremendous source of hope. TakeElnora Gavin in Benton Harbor, Michigan. Working with a local civic organization, We the People Michigan, she organized a base of supporters and won $114m in school debt relief for majority-Black school districts in her state.And she is not alone. More and more people in communities are using organizing strategies to buildpowerful civic homesthat can be containers for people-driven collective action. In these turbulent times, people are choosing to lean into people-centered organizations and movements where they can find belonging, develop collective agency and make a better future possible.Julie Fernandes is managing director of the Democracy & Power Innovation Fund, a community of organizers, researchers and funders who are working together to strengthen state-based community organizing, and associate director of the Rockefeller Family FundKatrina Gamble, PhD, is founder and CEO of Sojourn Strategies, a Black woman-owned social impact consulting firm that brings a people-centered approach to advocacy campaigns, research and philanthropic advisingExplore more on these topicsActivismOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Always remember how Macquarie built its millionaires on outrageous tolls and charges  | John Quiggin | The Guardian
description: As Shemara Wikramanayake retires with shares worth hundreds of millions, the public is left counting the cost of high prices for utilities, roads and airports
Author: John Quiggin
Headline: As Shemara Wikramanayake retires with shares worth hundreds of millions, the public is left counting the cost of high prices for utilities, roads and airports
Content: Outgoing Macquarie boss Shemara Wikramanayake is leaving after nearly 40 years at the ‘millionaires’ factory’.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenOutgoing Macquarie boss Shemara Wikramanayake is leaving after nearly 40 years at the ‘millionaires’ factory’.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersOpinionBankingAlways remember how Macquarie built its millionaires on outrageous tolls and chargesJohn QuigginAs Shemara Wikramanayake retires with shares worth hundreds of millions, the public is left counting the cost of high prices for utilities, roads and airportsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSat 25 Jul 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 23.58 EDTShareThe recent retirement of the Macquarie Group CEO, Shemara Wikramanayake, marks the culmination of a highly successful career. She is leaving the company with shares worth hundreds of millions of dollars after nearly 40 years at the Sydney-based institution. Under her leadership, the “millionaires’ factory” has increased its annual revenue by about 80% and nearly doubled its profit.Wikramanayake has also overseen and consolidated the group’s transition from a firm specialising in privatised infrastructure to a global merchant bank earning profits from commodity trading, specialist asset finance and wealth management.Macquarie shareholders, who have tripled their money over the past eight years (with dividends and capital gains), have plenty of reason to be grateful.The public, in Australia and elsewhere, may take a slightly more jaundiced view. The foundations of the millionaires’ factory were laid through a string of private infrastructure deals that greatly enriched Macquarie while delivering expensive or substandard services.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe biggest disaster of all has been Thames Water,privatisedby the Thatcher government in the UK and acquired by a Macquarie-led consortium in 2006. After extractingbillions in dividendsforitself and other investors, and loading the company with debt, Macquarie sold out in 2017. By that time, the utility’s performance was so dire as to be unsalvageable. Nearly a decade later, the UK government is still grappling with the choice between an unpalatable renationalisation and a hybrid model that is likely to prove unworkable.In June, Andy Burnhamcalled forpublic ownership at Thames Water. As parts of Wales are in drought and the rest of the country is experiencing prolonged dry conditions, about 23 million people across the UKare undera hosepipe ban.Another example worth mentioning is the privatisation of Sydney airport to a Macquarie-led consortium, which promptly raised a wide range of fees and charges. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has repeatedly concluded that the airport is a monopoly and that price monitoring is ineffectual. The issue was predictable – and predicted.Macquarie was also a pioneer of the private toll road industry, which has left Australian cities saddled with costly transport systems, characterised in the words of areview of the Sydney toll-road systemas a “poorly-functioning patchwork”. International deals such asOntario’s Highway 407were even worse for the public, though highly successful for Macquarie’s millionaires.Macquarie Group is not the only corporate giant built on lucrative deals with the public. CSL, one of Australia’s most valuable companies, was created by the privatisation of the Commonwealth Serum Laboratories, which had produced a wide range of innovations. The privatised CSL was awarded a long-term contract to supply products derived from blood plasma at a far higher cost.The resulting cashflow was ploughed into aglobal acquisition programthat made CSL the giant it is today. Meanwhile, research on commercially less attractive products such as antivenoms and vaccines for tropical diseases was scaled down, abandoned or left to universities and public research institutes.Other privatisations have followed a similar pattern of rhetoric about private sector efficiency combined with continued public largesse. Qantas has enjoyed the favoured treatment of a national flag carrier while disclaiming their obligations to either the travelling public or its own employees, beyond those dictated by profit maximisation.Telstraforced us to buy back, at massive expense, the telephone network built under public ownership and sold only a few years previously.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf there is any consolation here, it is that (long after the public) policymakers have finally woken up to the damage done by these deals. Not so long ago, Infrastructure Australia was proclaiming the benefits of innovative finance and universities were offering courses in “financial engineering”. Today these terms are rightly viewed with suspicion. As the UK commentatorAnthony Hilton wroteafter the crash of Carillion (a major participant in private finance initiatives):double quotation markIts demise is also the consequence of the relentless application of a neo-liberal political philosophy that for years has elevated financial engineering above real engineering; off-balance-sheet finance above paying for things openly; and lauded the private sector above the public sector.Ordinary people can express respect for the achievements of Shemara Wikramanayake at Macquarie Group. But every time you pay a toll or an outrageous airport parking charge, remember that the millionaires’ factory was built from the proceeds of charges like these.John Quiggin is a professor at the University of Queensland’s School of EconomicsExplore more on these topicsBankingOpinionAustralian economyThames WaterQantasTelstracommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on a US-Saudi nuclear agreement: an offer that further erodes international safeguards | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Even if no reactors are built, Donald Trump’s announcement of a double-standards deal with Riyadh has wrought further damage in a new era of proliferation
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Even if no reactors are built, Donald Trump’s announcement of a double-standards deal with Riyadh has wrought further damage in a new era of proliferation
Content: Donald Trump and Mohammed bin Salman at the White House last November.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Mohammed bin Salman at the White House last November.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersOpinionUS foreign policyThe Guardian view on a US-Saudi nuclear agreement: an offer that further erodes international safeguardsEditorialEven if no reactors are built, Donald Trump’s announcement of a double-standards deal with Riyadh has wrought further damage in a new era of proliferationSun 26 Jul 2026 12.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareEven as he threatened to escalate an unlawful war sold in part as preventing Iran from gaining a nuclear weapon, Donald Trump opened the door to proliferation in the region on Wednesday. The US announced that it hadsigned a dealwith Saudi Arabia which would potentially allow the kingdom to enrich uranium in future and to avoid the fullest inspection rights for the international watchdog.Experts have long warned that a civilian nuclear programme could create a path towards a nuclear-armed Riyadh. Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince and de facto leader, hassaidthat if Tehran gets a nuclear weapon, “we will have to get one”. Concerns are magnified by the agreement’s terms. Washington previously argued that the “gold standard” was theUnited Arab Emirates’ agreementto permanently forgo enrichment and accept full monitoring by the UN’s International Atomic Energy Agency. Weakening it sets a precedent that Russia or China could also cite in nuclear deals in future.The turmoil that Mr Trump has created in the Middle East is encouraging governments both to hedge their bets and to tool up. The USpaused attackson Iran at the weekend, after 13 successive days of strikes, amid reports that it is concerned about declining interceptor stockpiles, but no exit is in sight. As António Guterres, the UN secretary general,saidon Thursday, the region “is teetering on the edge of [the] unimaginable … One crisis feeds another. One escalation triggers the next.”View image in fullscreenAntónio Guterres.Photograph: Omar Sanadiki/APGulf statespremised their securityon American-guaranteed order. But Benjamin Netanyahu’sstrike on Hamas leaders in Qatar last yearshowed that the US shield would not protect them from Israel (itself anundeclared nuclear power). The reckless war on Iran has made US military presence an invitation to damage. Washington may be looking to bind Riyadh closer with a reactor deal, though the billions of dollars involved is probably a bigger incentive for Mr Trump. The crumbling of the region’s internal architecture – most visibly with the UAE’s departure from Opec – adds to the dangers of proliferation. Players are acting less predictably.The US president threw the Saudi deal into doubt within hours by declaring it contingent on Riyadh recognisingIsrael. That had long been a precondition for an agreement, but Israel’s war of annihilation in Gaza has shored up the Saudi position that recognition cannot happen without a Palestinian state. Yet even if no reactors are built, the announcement itself acts as legitimation of and encouragement for the pursuit of nuclear capabilities by others. Negotiations produced an Obama-era nuclear deal with which Tehran complied – until Mr Trump trashed the agreement. His war appears to have produced a more aggressive, risk-taking Iranian regime, as foretold; further military action is more likely to spur than end nuclear threat. The prospect of Riyadh acquiring a bomb is further encouragement.Look further afield. The last US-Russia nuclear arms control treatyexpiredin February. China israpidly expandingits arsenal. Asian and European states which counted on the US nuclear umbrella prior to Mr Trump are discussing acquiring or enhancing their own capabilities. Most of them at least understand that diplomacy, multilateralism and global standards are a better choice than a race for the bomb. Mr Trump does not believe in international institutions. But upholding existing nuclear safeguards would be in US interests too as we enter a new age of proliferation.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyOpinionSaudi ArabiaDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsMiddle East and north AfricaIraneditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on a new director at Tate: an old institution must tackle fresh issues | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A decline in visitor numbers, staff strikes and budget cuts – Jessica Morgan faces many challenges as she takes on the biggest job in the British arts scene
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A decline in visitor numbers, staff strikes and budget cuts – Jessica Morgan faces many challenges as she takes on the biggest job in the British arts scene
Content: ‘With record-breaking shows currently at Tate Modern, suggestions that Jessica Morgan is inheriting an institution in a state of “existential crisis” seem exaggerated.’Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘With record-breaking shows currently at Tate Modern, suggestions that Jessica Morgan is inheriting an institution in a state of “existential crisis” seem exaggerated.’Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyOpinionTate ModernThe Guardian view on a new director at Tate: an old institution must tackle fresh issuesEditorialA decline in visitor numbers, staff strikes and budget cuts – Jessica Morgan faces many challenges as she takes on the biggest role in the British arts sceneSun 26 Jul 2026 12.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareAlack of clear vision, low morale, dwindling popularity and financial shortfalls – this may sound like a description of the previous Labour government, but these are also criticisms levelled at the UK’s most powerful arts institution, Tate.Maria Balshaw’stenure as the first female director of Tate – comprising Tate Modern, Tate Britain, Tate Liverpool and Tate St Ives – lasted nine years and saw as many culture secretaries. One of Sir Keir Starmer’s last acts as prime minister was to approve the appointment of her successor,Jessica Morgan, a former curator at Tate and head of the Dia Art Foundation in New York.With record-breakingFrida KahloandTracey Eminshows currently at Tate Modern, suggestions that Ms Morgan is inheriting an institution in a state of“existential crisis”seem exaggerated. Tate Britain, often overshadowed by its more fashionable younger sister, pulled in crowds for itsTurner & ConstableandLee Millerexhibitions. These blockbusters in the past year also rebutaccusationsthat Ms Balshaw focused on little-known artists instead of bankable stars. Her commitment to diversifying the collection will surely be taken up by Ms Morgan, who also has a strong track record in promoting marginalised artists. Ms Balshaw is leaving on a high.View image in fullscreenJessica Morgan.Photograph: Gabriella Herman/Tate/PABut after thedouble blow of Brexit and Covid, Tate has had a turbulent few years. Thenumber of London visitorslast year was still more than 2 million below pre-pandemic levels, with the number of 16- to 24-year-oldsfrom Europe nearly halved. Yet Tate Modern remains one of thetop 10 most visited museums in the world. The reopening of Tate Liverpool, which closed for refurbishment in 2023, has beendelayeduntil 2027 because of lack of funding. Last year’sredundancies and staff strikesacross the galleries showed an institution under pressure.It is a far cry from when Nicholas Serota spearheaded Tate Modern just over25 years agoon the crest of Cool Britannia and the rise of the Young British Artists.Olafur Eliasson’s The Weather Project, which filled the Turbine Hall with a giant sun and entranced over 2 million visitors in 2003, seemed to herald a bright future. But recent Turbine Hall commissions have lost their shine. Even the Turner prize looks tired, with the Guardian’s Jonathan Jones lamenting its retreat“into wilful obscurity”and some criticscallingfor it to be scrapped.Looming external challenges include the National Gallery’srecent announcementof plans to ditch its 1900 cut-off, thereby encroaching on Tate Modern’s territory, and the possibility ofan end to free museum access in the UK. Both raise fundamental questions for the direction of Tate. Then there is the increasingly problematic issue of funding. Ms Balshaw was right totake a standagainst arts donations from fossil fuel companies.According to a profile inThe Gentlewoman, Ms Morgan is not just “one of the great collection-builders of our time”, but is also (though British) “armed with an American unflappability about asking rich people for money”. Gavin Turk, one of the YBAs, compared the role to “the England football manager job now”; the director must be able to support artists and “convince the public with the shows they put on”. Like the new prime minister, Ms Morgan has been hailed as“an agent of change”. How to make lasting change, without alienating core supporters, while inspiring confidence at home and abroad – all when budgets are tight – is the momentous task facing both.Explore more on these topicsTate ModernOpinionTate BritainArtArts fundingExhibitionsLondonTate LiverpooleditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Blame privatised water firms for hosepipe bans | Water industry | The Guardian
description: Letters: Gillian Metheringham, Dr Gillian Austen and others respond to articles about water shortages in the UK and the high and rising pay of water industry bosses
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Gillian Metheringham, Dr Gillian Austen and others respond to articles about water shortages in the UK and the high and rising pay of water industry bosses
Content: An aerial view shows low water levels at the Walthamstow Wetlands, part of the Coppermills water treatment works, in east London.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenAn aerial view shows low water levels at the Walthamstow Wetlands, part of the Coppermills water treatment works, in east London.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAWater industryLettersBlame privatised water firms for hosepipe bansGillian Metheringham,Dr Gillian Austenand others respond to articles about water shortages in the UK and the high and rising pay of water industry bossesSun 26 Jul 2026 11.58 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.02 EDTShareI was dismayed, when reading your article about hosepipe bans leading to culture wars (‘People are scared their neighbours will call the police on them’: how the hosepipe ban got caught up in the culture wars, 23 July), by the part that said: “Why has the ban been put in place, anyway? The answer, as with so many things, is the climate crisis.”No, it’s not. The climate crisis is only part of the answer, and probably the smaller part. The privatised water companies have, over many years, privileged the lining of their own pockets over proper maintenance and improvement of the water systems, a fact which has been revealed again and again in your own pages.As a result, hosepipe bans are needed far more often than they would be if we were just looking at climate change as a cause. Indeed, the article goes on to reflect some of these sentiments, but they come from the gardeners who were interviewed.If we go on referencing climate change and “unusual conditions” to excuse the despicable behaviour of the water companies, we are colluding in their great fiction.Gillian MetheringhamStroud, GloucestershireThe key to the issue of hosepipe bans being needed is surely the privatisation of the water companies. They extract huge sums in dividends for their owners –largely investment funds not based in the UK– while failing to live up to their responsibility to maintain the water supply network. Ofwat has no effective powers of enforcement, it seems.The new prime minister should consider imposing a very large tax burden on water company shareholders to fund the replacement of old pipes and the building of new reservoirs. Our water bills are the highest they’ve ever been, our need for water is greater than ever, but leaky pipes are causing a water shortage.As for datacentres, they should never be allowed to take priority over such a fundamental human need. If artificial intelligence is so important, let the techies find another way to cool their servers.Dr Gillian AustenBathI was disappointed that your article on hosepipe bans did not mention the exemption forgolf courses and car washes. What madness allows hundreds of thousands of litres to be used to water barren areas of golf courses and keep a car clean?I want to keep my flowers and vegetables alive, for the insects and for food. Allotments should have exemptions, as should wildflower meadows and ponds for wildlife. Why should I be concerned about a golf course? I am seriously worried about the neglect of our natural world and those who live in it.Christine PedderSt AlbansIt was sad to read about disabled people taking flak for hosepipe rules that have been in place for decades, and people lamenting lost plants. But we gardeners have a big responsibility to reduce water use. Harvest rain – our many water butts lasted until last week; use a bowl to reuse washing up and rinsing water from your sinks; be selective in deciding which plants to water; mulch! And if a plant dies, replace it with a drought-resistant alternative.Graham JackHarrow, LondonIf water company bosses don’t adhere to the spirit as well as the letter of the ban on bonuses, don’t expect me to stick to the ban on hosepipes (Water bosses’ pay rises despite bonus ban and public fury over bills and pollution, 24 July).Toby WoodPeterboroughHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Arts and humanities have a role in understanding space exploration | Space | The Guardian
description: Letter: Prof Abbie Garrington reflects on an interview with the physicist Laura Grego about the battle for our skies
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Prof Abbie Garrington reflects on an interview with the physicist Laura Grego about the battle for our skies
Content: A satellite constellation launched by Elon Musk’s company SpaceX.Photograph: Stephen Chung/Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenA satellite constellation launched by Elon Musk’s company SpaceX.Photograph: Stephen Chung/Alamy Live NewsSpaceLettersArts and humanities have a role in understanding space explorationProf Abbie Garringtonreflects on an interview with the physicist Laura Grego about the battle for our skiesSun 26 Jul 2026 11.58 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.02 EDTShareWhere are the arts and humanities in current debates about space research? The physicist Laura Grego tells us we “have to be aware of what is happening in space”, that we should probe Elon Musk’s potential “appropriation” of space via satellite, and that our spacefaring era raises questions about our stewardship of the Earth for future generations, and the significance of human culture (‘Most people don’t know we’ve set up a doomsday system’: physicist Laura Grego on satellites, nuclear weapons and the battle for our skies, 20 July).Meanwhile, your interviewer Aida Edemariam notes both the Artemis mission’s potential to inspire, and the relegation of most of us to an audience agog, with no say in civilisational decisions about major space missions.The sciences cannot tackle these matters alone. Successive UK governments have prioritised Stem subjects, while our forthcoming national space strategy will focus on economic growth and national security, so major leaps in technologies of exploration and surveillance come to the fore in what is effectively a second space race. Yet listening to Grego, it’s clear we also need new collaborative structures, theories of jurisdiction and laws; new philosophies of the human, the unique status of human culture, and interplanetary environmental responsibility; and a sharp eye on the history of human hubris.Durham University’s Space Research Centre, and the new Leverhulme Centre for Humanity and Space at the University of Leicester, might show us the way. Addressing arts and humanities layoffs at our universities (at Exeter and Edinburgh most recently), we rightly worry about what the British Academy calls “cold spots” around the UK where students will miss out on enriching subjects.We should also be talking about these cuts as a national diminishment of subjects which, among many other functions, are essential to the UK’s flourishing in a new phase of space exploration.Prof Abbie GarringtonUniversity of DurhamHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
