title: Every day is a good-hair day with no shampoo | Men's hair | The Guardian
description: Letters: I would only shampoo now if I swam through something nasty in the sea or if a bird crapped on me, says Paddy Eason. But the ‘no poo’ method didn’t work for Kerri Thornton
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: I would only shampoo now if I swam through something nasty in the sea or if a bird crapped on me, says Paddy Eason. But the ‘no poo’ method didn’t work for Kerri Thornton
Content: George Francis Lee doesn’t use shampoo.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGeorge Francis Lee doesn’t use shampoo.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianMen's hairLettersEvery day is a good-hair day with no shampooI would only shampoo now if I swam through something nasty in the sea or if a bird crapped on me, saysPaddy Eason.But the ‘no poo’ method didn’t work forKerri ThorntonSun 26 Jul 2026 11.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.01 EDTShareI was fascinated by George Francis Lee’s account of getting off the shampoo bandwagon (I tried the ‘no poo’ method – and it transformed my hair, 20 July). Or should I say his “confession”, as the social power of the shampoo message is strong enough to make most of us “no pooers” keep a low profile.I’ve not used shampoo for at least five years. I rub my hair through in the shower every morning, and either towel or air-dry it. Every day is a now a good-hair day – mine is thick, glossy and easy to style, with a very slight waxy feel that comes with the natural oils that hair products are designed to strip away and then replace (badly). I would only shampoo my hair now if I swam through something nasty in the sea or if a bird crapped on me.Paddy EasonLondonI went through a “no poo” phase in 2012. It was a turbo-hippy phase where I learned about the method from a man who had the most beautiful, luscious long hair, and he’d been doing this for 10 years. He washed his hair with water. So, convinced, I tried it. I lasted nine months, waiting for my hair to get the same texture. It just remained greasy. But I discovered sulphate-free and paraben-free shampoo, and it changed my life.Kerri ThorntonGlasgowHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Ignore a call and enjoy a good night’s sleep | Sleep | The Guardian
description: Brief letters: Insomnia advice | Raging wildfires | Dinner or supper? | Simple meal plan | Best travelling attire
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Insomnia advice | Raging wildfires | Dinner or supper? | Simple meal plan | Best travelling attire
Content: Calling teachers at 10.30am isn’t advisable, says Colin Mann.Photograph: Posed by model/Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenCalling teachers at 10.30am isn’t advisable, says Colin Mann.Photograph: Posed by model/Getty/iStockphotoBrief lettersSleepLettersIgnore a call and enjoy a good night’s sleepInsomnia advice | Raging wildfires | Dinner or supper? | Simple meal plan | Best travelling attireSun 26 Jul 2026 11.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.01 EDTShareI noted with interest Dr Jemma King’s advice to aid sleeping by making a to-do list before going to bed (13 surprising reasons you’re always dog tired – and what to do about it, 24 July). One of the examples given was: “Call Sammy’s teachers at 10.30am”. As a teacher of 34 years of broken sleep, I am going to take Dr King’s advice by creating my own list. Item 1: ignore Sammy’s parent’s phone call at 10.30am as I will be too busy teaching. If it’s important, they will leave a message. I feel better already.Colin MannBarrhead, East Renfrewshire“Some say the world will end in fire, / Some say in ice”. Well, that’s thatargument settled, anyway (More than 200,000 people flee or lock down as wildfires sweep France and Spain, 24 July).Emeritus profGlyn TurtonBaildon, West YorkshireHannah Kaitlin-Boyerreckons everyone knows what she means by supper (Letters, 24 July). She’d be very welcome to have supper at our house, but she might become a little peckish: “supper” is a substantial meal taken just before bedtime. Sometimes the chipper is fired up, so it’s worth waiting.Mike JonesExeterLook, it’s perfectly simple. Breakfast, second breakfast, elevenses, lunch, afternoon tea, high tea, dinner, supper and a little something just before bed to ward off night starvation.Nigel SteelUxbridge, LondonA jumpsuit? For travelling? I can’t get the image of trying to negotiate a train loo out of my mind (School’s out for summer: what to wear when travelling, 24 July).Joan LewisSaint-Étienne-de-Gourgas, FranceHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Pleaseemailus your letter and it will be considered for publication in ourletterssection.Explore more on these topicsSleepBrief lettersFoodTeachinglettersShareReuse this content

title: Adam Ramsay-Peaty armed with ‘battle plan’ for golden revival in 50m breaststroke | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Briton is ready to bounce back after his 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games and he said: ‘The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind’
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The Briton is ready to bounce back after his 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games and he said: ‘The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind’
Content: Adam Ramsay-Peaty is looking for 50m gold after bronze in the 100m breaststroke.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenAdam Ramsay-Peaty is looking for 50m gold after bronze in the 100m breaststroke.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersCommonwealth Games 2026Adam Ramsay-Peaty armed with ‘battle plan’ for golden revival in 50m breaststrokeBriton ready to bounce back after 100m bronze‘The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind’Sean Ingleat the Tollcross International Swimming CentreSun 26 Jul 2026 15.54 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 10.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdam Ramsay-Peaty has never been one to hide his emotions. He wears them proudly on his sleeve, next to the striking tattoos of a huge lion and Poseidon, the Greek god of the sea.After his shock defeat in the 100m breaststroke final at theseCommonwealth Games, the 31-year-old was back pouring his heart out on Sunday – and insisting he had a “battle plan” to win gold in Monday’s 50m breaststroke final.Tearful Ramsay-Peaty tells critics ‘you can’t hurt me’ after shock Commonwealth bronzeRead moreRamsay-Peaty certainly looked smoother in qualifying third fastest from the semi-finals in 26.82sec. However, he still has a couple of tenths to find on the South African Michael Houlie, who was fastest in 26.61.The Australian Sam Williamson, who is hoping to add the 50m to his 100m crown, also looked good as he won his semi-final in 26.79. Yet Peaty pronounced himself happy with how he had bounced back from Saturday’s shock loss.“It felt much better,” he said. “The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind, but I’m really happy with that. We’re on a great trajectory for tomorrow.“For me, the best way to ever get anything out of my head is just to write it out. When I write down what’s going wrong, what’s going right, what kind of change? What can’t change? Then I’ve got a battle plan.”He added: “People forget that I haven’t done this for two years. And even I forget that. So as you go through heats, semis and finals, it’s quite difficult if you’re not used to it. So I think that perspective is a good thing.”Peaty has stood on the top of the podium 32 times in global championships across his glittering career. Yet he has not won a gold medal since the Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games. That record was extended on Saturday when he could take only bronze in the 100m breaststroke in 59.65, behind Williamson, who won in 59.3, and the brilliant 18-year-old Filip Nowicki from Jersey.Afterwards Ramsay-Peaty was strikingly honest about “all the shit I have been through” to get ready for the Commonwealth Games, including the 5.30am starts, missing family gatherings because of training, and also the amount of abuse he and his family has received on social media.On Sunday he added more context to his struggles, pointing out that he battled with burnout and a broken foot over the past four years, as well as hinting at the much-publicised estrangement with his family.“There have been a multitude of things at play over the last few years – burnout, breaking my foot, fighting against something that you love. It’s been hard,” he said. “Some of it has been quite painful, particularly from that foot injury onwards.“Coming back to where I am now and making the decision to go for LA, I think this is going to be the hardest climb I’ve ever faced and the hardest test. It’s really hard to see the summit because it’s so hard. I don’t think anyone understands.”What was perhaps most striking about that 59.65 was that it was nearly three seconds behind his world record – and slower even than he swam at the British trials in the spring.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I work a lot harder than a 59.6, really. It’s not a good time – we know that,” he said on Sunday. “When your world record is three seconds away, we’ve got to seriously ask what’s going wrong because that’s not me.View image in fullscreenHolly Ramsay-Peaty (centre) watches on as her husband, Adam, prepares for his 50m breaststroke heat.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA“We need to look at it, interrogate it, look at the data, and ask whether it was an issue with race pace, fitness, or something else. I don’t think it was fitness, but there are a lot of components that make us swim, so we really have to analyse it.”He added: “I was fitter in April with less training, which doesn’t really make sense, to be honest. I guess that’s the learning point. Maybe I’m on a plan that I don’t fully understand, and maybe it’ll take another two years to find the right way.”On Saturday, Ramsay-Peaty also took aim at social media and traditional media too, which has become fixated with him and his pregnant wife, Holly – the daughter of the celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay – and his estrangement with his mother.“You don’t know who I am,” he said. “And people who comment, people who see the story because you read a headline, they’ve got to look themselves in the mirror. You can’t hurt me.”He added: “That hasn’t played a part in the sense of what I’ve experienced, because I’m still happy with that result in some sense, but it has to stop. How many athletes, how many people, have to go through this until the media learn their lesson? You have to learn and do better.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Adam Ramsay-PeatyCommonwealth GamesSwimmingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Idi Amin’s boxing grandson vows to be ‘new king of Scotland’ at Commonwealth Games | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Aziz Abdul, known as ‘Ringo’, says the former Ugandan dictator is the inspiration behind his bid to become the ‘baddest man in the Commonwealth’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Aziz Abdul, known as ‘Ringo’, says the former Ugandan dictator is the inspiration behind his bid to become the ‘baddest man in the Commonwealth’
Content: Aziz Abdul says he will rely on his ‘Ringo punch’ to get the job done against England’s Damar Thomas.Photograph: Ckristu Mbabazi/Uganda Boxing Federation WebsiteView image in fullscreenAziz Abdul says he will rely on his ‘Ringo punch’ to get the job done against England’s Damar Thomas.Photograph: Ckristu Mbabazi/Uganda Boxing Federation WebsiteCommonwealth Games 2026Idi Amin’s boxing grandson vows to be ‘new king of Scotland’ at Commonwealth GamesAziz Abdul faces England’s Damar Thomas in Glasgow‘I will be the baddest man in the Commonwealth’PA MediaSun 26 Jul 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDamar Thomas, the English super-heavyweight, must overcome the grandson of Idi Amin, the former Ugandan dictator and self-proclaimed “King of Scotland”, if he is to progress into the medal rounds ofCommonwealth Gamesboxing competition in Glasgow on Wednesday.Aziz Abdul, known as “Ringo”, is not shy of his family connection to Amin, a brutal military dictator who seized power in 1971, killing up to 500,000 people and expelling Uganda’s entire Asian population before he was deposed and sent into exile eight years later.Commonwealth Games 2026 medal tableRead moreAmin was an accomplished boxer who held the Ugandan light-heavyweight title for nine consecutive years from 1951 to 1960. Having lost a bout to Peter Sseruwagi in 1958, he orchestrated a rematch after becoming president, delivering a staged knockout of his opponent while still wearing his suit jacket and tie.“My grandfather’s achievements inspired me,” the 25-year-old Abdul said. “He was a heavyweight boxer like myself, and I am so proud of him. Lions give back to lions. A lion cannot give back to a dog or a camel. A lion must resemble a lion. It is what it is. I am a real warrior. I am the son of the son.”Amin declared himself the “King of Scotland” in 1976, having developed a fascination with the country during his time serving in the King’s African Rifles regiment in his 20s. His remark inspired an Oscar-winning film, The Last King Of Scotland, starring the Glasgow-born actor James McAvoy.Abdul hails from the same remote West Nile region as his grandfather, who died in 2003, and displays the same bullish confidence despite a daunting draw. Thomas, a 21-year-old European youth champion, is aiming to become the fourth consecutive English winner of the +90kg title.Abdul said he will rely on his mysterious “Ringo punch” to get the job done before the judges get the chance to intervene, making good on the advice of Amin, who once advised that “the only way to defeat an enemy who is against the country is to win by knockout”.“I am very happy to be fighting the English fighter,” Abdul added. “I have waited for this moment for three years. But now we are not in Africa, we are in Europe. As my grandpa used to say, you need to win by knockout, so that’s what we have trained for and that’s what I hope to do.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I know the British heavyweights Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury, but my idol is Mike Tyson: the baddest man on the planet. If I win the gold medal, I will be the baddest man in the Commonwealth, the baddest man in Glasgow and the new king of Scotland.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesBoxingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia dispatch England with ease in Commonwealth Games netball clash | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Australia extended their fine netball record against England to seven wins in their last eight meetings with a convincing win in front of a lively crowd at the Hydro
Author: Yara El-Shaboury
Headline: Australia extended their fine netball record against England to seven wins in their last eight meetings with a convincing win in front of a lively crowd at the Hydro
Content: Australia players celebrate their confident performance in their Pool A match against England.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenAustralia players celebrate their confident performance in their Pool A match against England.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPCommonwealth Games 2026Australia dispatch England with ease in Commonwealth Games netball clashAustralia 66-47 EnglandSophie Garbin pours in 41 goals from 42 attemptsYara El-Shabouryat the HydroSun 26 Jul 2026 09.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEight years after England’s dramatic last-gasp triumph over Australia on the Gold Coast, netball’s greatest Commonwealth rivalry was renewed in Glasgow. But this time there was no fairytale finish for the Roses as the defending champions dismantled England 66-47 at the Hydro, theDiamondsextending their record against this opposition at the Games to seven wins from eight meetings.Ever since Helen Housby’slast-second winner stunned the Diamondsin the 2018 final, every meeting between these two heavyweights has carried extra edge. Australia gained a measure of revenge by beating England on the way to gold in Birmingham four years ago and Sunday’s Commonwealth Games pool clash was another marker of where the sport’s fiercest rivalry stands.Australia were quicker, sharper and more clinical from the opening whistle, with their star-studded attack of Sophie Garbin and Kiera Austin immediately exposing England’s defence.Commonwealth Games 2026 medal tableRead more“It was very physical out there, but that’s what we expected and that’s what we prepared for,” said Garbin. “Obviously it’s nice to get the win, but England put up a really good fight.“It’s really exciting, especially playing over here in Glasgow. We knew we had a lot of Scots barracking for us. I think everyone told us to go and smash the English girls, so we knew we’d have a lot of support here, but they would as well. It’s awesome. That’s what you want – to play these games in front of these crowds in this amazing arena. It was really exciting.”The Diamonds raced into an early 10-4 lead as Austin began dictating proceedings, while England struggled to live with Australia’s relentless pressure through the court. Sasha Glasgow was withdrawn before the end of the opening quarter as the interim head coach, Anna Stembridge, searched for answers, and Lois Pearson’s move into goal attack briefly stemmed the tide.England clawed back to 13-9, but every glimpse of momentum was extinguished by Australia’s ruthless efficiency. Garbin repeatedly found space on the baseline, finishing with 41 goals from 42 attempts, while Austin contributed 15 goals alongside 19 assists and 17 feeds.By the end of the opening quarter Australia led 18-11. England attempted to shake things up early in the second period, introducing Jayda Pechová into defence while shifting the captain Fran Williams into goal defence. The changes initially worked, with Pechová disrupting Australia’s rhythm as England opened the quarter with a 4-1 burst.Jamie-Lee Price and Austin restored Australia’s composure, while England’s frustration began to show. Liv Tchine remained the Roses’ brightest attacking outlet, using her height and movement to keep England competitive, but Courtney Bruce and Jo Weston continually forced difficult feeds and turnovers.View image in fullscreenEngland’s Liv Tchine scores through traffic against Australia on day three of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PABruce and Tchine exchanged plenty of contact in the circle, while the contest became increasingly feisty as England tried to unsettle Australia’s defensive unit. Tchine’s shove into Bruce’s back late in the second quarter summed up the growing frustration as the Diamonds stretched their advantage to 35-24 at half-time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf England harboured hopes of another famous fightback, Australia extinguished them in the third quarter. They outscored the Roses 21-11 in a devastating spell, capitalising on England’s errors with clinical precision. Turnovers, offensive contacts and loose passes repeatedly handed possession straight back to Australia, who punished every mistake. With a 21-goal cushion entering the final quarter, the contest was effectively over.“That’s definitely not the result that we came for but it’s also not the performance,” said Williams. “We were just far off our best and we never really got some momentum to get our teeth into the game, which is a shame. It’s really tough when a game blows out like that in the second half. You’ve got to make sure that you’re still going after those small wins and little fights.”England fan favourite Eleanor Cardwell entered to a huge reception from the Glasgow crowd and immediately injected fresh energy into the attack. Her battle with Sarah Klau added another flashpoint to an already bruising encounter, with Klau receiving an official warning after sending Cardwell tumbling to the floor. Cardwell refused Klau’s offer of assistance before dusting herself down and continuing.England marginally won the final quarter, but by then the damage had long been done.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026DiamondsEngland netball teamCommonwealth GamesNetballAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Relentless Tadej Pogacar wins fifth Tour de France to equal record | Tour de France 2026 | The Guardian
description: Tadej Pogacar joined the all-time greats as Mathieu van der Poel won a frantic final stage in Paris
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Tadej Pogacar joined the all-time greats as Mathieu van der Poel won a frantic final stage in Paris
Content: Tadej Pogacar passes Sacré-Coeur as the Tour de France finished with a thrilling final stage in Paris.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/EPAView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar passes Sacré-Coeur as the Tour de France finished with a thrilling final stage in Paris.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/EPATour de France 2026Relentless Tadej Pogacar wins fifth Tour de France to equal recordSlovene becomes fifth rider to win five ToursEddy Merckx: ‘He’ll soon break our record’Jeremy Whittlein ParisSun 26 Jul 2026 14.08 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar took a record-equalling fifth win in theTour de Franceon Sunday, joining Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Induráin in the canon of the Tour’s most successful cyclists. In a thrilling finale to the Tour, Mathieu van der Poel took his second stage win of the race on the Champs-Élysées, fending off the pursuing pack of sprinters by a tyre’s width, after breaking clear with Pogacar on the final climb of the Butte de Montmartre.Tadej Pogacar tells rivals he is ‘improving a lot’ after fifth Tour de France winRead moreMerckx, widely considered the greatest-ever cyclist because of the breadth of his achievements beyond the Tour itself, believes that Pogacar will now go on to win a sixth Tour. “I don’t think he’ll be content just to draw level with me and the other ­champions,” the 81-year-old Belgian said. “He’ll soon break our record for Tour victories.”From Montjuïc to Montmartre, Pogacar and the stifling temperatures suffocated the 2026 Tour. A race staged against the backdrop of heatwaves and wildfires, culminated in the inevitable – another win for the relentless Slovene.Pogacar had no equal in this Tour de France, breaking records on two of the most daunting climbs in cycling, the Col du Tourmalet and Alpe d’Huez, and shepherding his protege, Isaac del Toro, to third place in the final standings.In another life, the Olympic road race champion, Remco Evenepoel, would probably have won his first Tour, and the French debutant Paul Seixas climbed on to the podium. It is their misfortune, and that of Jonas Vingegaard – who crashed out of the Tour – to race in the era of Pogacar and his impregnable UAE Emirates XRG team.View image in fullscreenMathieu van der Poel celebrates his second stage win of this year’s race, on the Champs-Élysées.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersA leaner, meaner and more driven Evenepoel proved his doubters wrong, reasserting himself as a genuine contender for victory in Paris. But the Belgian knows too that Pogacar may have to retire before that happens.The statistics tell the story of one of the most dominant performances in the modern history of the Tour. Pogacar won the race overall by almost six and a half minutes, took five stages and set record times for legendary climbs in the Pyrenees and Alps. He might have won six stages, had it not been for his decision to allow Del Toro to win on stage two.“I did really good this Tour,” Pogacar said afterSaturday’s stage to Alpe d’Huez, while acknowledging the bad luck of rivals such as Vingegaard and Florian Lipowitz, both of whom finished on the podium in Paris last year and crashed out of this year’s race.“It’s the Tour, it’s three weeks,” Pogacar said. “A lot of shit can happen.”View image in fullscreenPogacar (left) helped his protege, Isaac del Toro, to third place in the general classification.Photograph: Mosa’ab Elshamy/APBut his unrelenting success comes with caveats. It would be naive to celebrate a five-time Tour winner without understanding the context. There is no doubt that Pogacar is a phenomenon, but his entourage has baggage from less happy times.His team manager, Mauro ­Gianetti, said: “Pogacar is so strong that no matter the team, there will be doubts concerning him.” But 24 hours before the peloton arrived in Paris, Gianetti said he was a “victim” of past scandals involving riders on his teams.The most infamous is the Saunier Duval scandal of 2008, when the Gianetti-managed team quit the Tour after their star rider, Riccardo Riccò, tested positive for a blood-doping agent. Riccò was fired, along with his teammate Leonardo Piepoli, and sponsors withdrew funding.“I made the mistake of taking them in my team,” Gianetti told L’Équipe.“I should have reacted differently, been clearer with the press, explained that I was a victim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You never know what your children do in their rooms, and you certainly don’t know what the riders do at home. Before signing Riccò, I asked him to go to the UCI [the sport’s governing body] to be tested. The UCI then sent me a document stating that he did indeed have a naturally occurring hematocrit level above 50%. I feel like a victim of this.”View image in fullscreenPogacar climbs the Galibier pass ahead of Remco Evenepoel and Paul Seixas on Saturday’s stage to Alpe d’Huez.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APThe old anxieties around Pogacar’s entourage resurfaced after the Slovene and Vingegaard were subjected to night-time tests by the ­Independent Testing Agency before stage 15. The tests were supported by the Tour de France director, ­Christian Prudhomme, and the UCI.In a statement released three days after the tests, which were authorised by a Paris judge, the UCI described the controls as “an exceptional measure, reserved for limited and justified circumstances”.Tour de France 2026: Pogacar seals fifth title as Van der Poel wins incredible sprint on the Champs-Élysées – as it happenedRead moreDespite the interrupted sleep, Pogacar was accepting of the tests. “If this is necessary to prove that we are riding clean,” he said, “then I totally accept it. I commit to it.”The ITA has reiterated to the Guardian that “no public communication is made regarding negative results” but also that “there is no date from which all tests can be considered definitively negative”.To some extent, this leaves the achievements of Pogacar and those of Vingegaard, his longstanding rival, in limbo. Regardless, the Slovene is expected to ride August’s Vuelta a España, in an attempt to claim the only Grand Tour title he has yet to win. Right now, the 27-year-old is at the peak of his powers and few would bet against him completing a Grand Tour grand slam.Next year, the Tour looks northwards, towards a Grand Départ in Scotland. Speaking to the Guardian last week, Prudhomme described Edinburgh as “a magical city”. “Every time the Tour has visited Great Britain, it has helped the Tour de France grow,” he said. “If the Tour can help bring major cycling events back to different parts of Britain, that would be fantastic. The UK has given the Tour an enormous amount.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France 2026Tour de FranceTadej PogacarCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pretty bad’: Lewis Hamilton hits out at Ferrari after dropping points in F1 title race | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton has questioned Ferrari’s strategy after he was fifth at the Hungarian GP, losing a place after a five-second penalty for pit-lane speeding
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton has questioned Ferrari’s strategy after he was fifth at the Hungarian GP, losing a place after a five-second penalty for pit-lane speeding
Content: Lewis Hamilton said he ‘definitely should not have taken the [pit] stop’ that cost him points at the Hungarian Grand Prix.Photograph: David Davies/PAView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton said he ‘definitely should not have taken the [pit] stop’ that cost him points at the Hungarian Grand Prix.Photograph: David Davies/PAFormula One 2026‘Pretty bad’: Lewis Hamilton hits out at Ferrari after dropping points in F1 title raceHamilton questions strategy after finishing fifthBriton lost place after penalty for speeding in pit laneGiles Richardsat the HungaroringSun 26 Jul 2026 15.51 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton expressed frustration with his Ferrari team after he dropped points in the title battle against Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli at the Hungarian Grand Prix, while Lando Norris returned to form with the defending world champion claiming hisfirst race victory of the season.Lando Norris wins F1 Hungarian GP for first victory of season as Piastri retiresRead moreHamilton finished in fourth place on the track at the Hungaroring but, with a five-second penalty imposed for speeding in the pit lane, he was classified as fifth in the race won by McLaren’s Norris, with Max Verstappen second for Red Bull and Antonelli third.Hamilton had been called into the pits late on for a stop under the virtual safety car, which gave him fresh tyres but cost him track position to Verstappen and Antonelli. He could not make the places back and this was the stop from which he received the penalty. The call left him questioning the strategy decisions by his team.“It was pretty bad. Pretty frustrating,” he said. “I definitely don’t think we should have taken the stop but the call came literally just before the pit-lane entry and I didn’t have time to debate.“I would never have stopped if it meant I was giving up track position. I may have been able to hold on to P2. He [Verstappen] was catching me but most likely it would have been P3 [in front of Antonelli] and it would have been much better. Instead, I lost a bunch of points.”Quick GuideF1 Hungarian GP resultsShow1Lando Norris🇬🇧McLaren1:39:56.180 –25pts2Max Verstappen🇳🇱Red Bull+15.080 –18pts3Kimi Antonelli🇮🇹Mercedes+18.728 –15pts4Charles Leclerc🇲🇨Ferrari+23.840 –12pts5Lewis Hamilton🇬🇧Ferrari+24.540 –10pts6Isack Hadjar🇫🇷Red Bull+55.488 –8pts7George Russell🇬🇧Mercedes+57.503 –6pts8Liam Lawson🇳🇿Racing Bulls+1 lap –4pts9Nico Hülkenberg🇩🇪Audi+1 lap –2pts10Arvid Lindblad🇬🇧Racing Bulls+1 lap–1pt11Gabriel Bortoleto🇧🇷Audi+1 lap12Pierre Gasly🇫🇷Alpine+1 lap13Lance Stroll🇨🇦Aston Martin+1 lap14Fernando Alonso🇪🇸Aston Martin+1 lap15Franco Colapinto🇦🇷Alpine+2 laps16Esteban Ocon🇫🇷Haas+2 laps17Alexander Albon🇹🇭Williams+2 laps18Carlos Sainz🇪🇸Williams+2 laps19Oliver Bearman🇬🇧Haas+2 lapsNCOscar Piastri🇦🇺McLarenDNFNCSergio Pérez🇲🇽CadillacDNFNCValtteri Bottas🇫🇮CadillacDNFWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Hamilton had been 45 points behind Antonelli but now trails the Italian by 50 points asFormula Oneenters its summer break. The Briton has also been on the receiving end of a swathe of penalties in recent races, including one at Silverstone, one at Spa, a three-place grid drop in Hungary for impeding in qualifying and then pit-lane speeding during the race. He feels that the annual shutdown has come at the right moment.“I’ll work hard to try and come back, reset,” Hamilton said. “There’s still a lot of places to take. I’m going to try and make sure I don’t give them any reason to give any penalties moving forwards.“It has been an amazing first half given I think we’ve been probably three or four-tenths down on the straights in pace and power for the first half of the season. We’ve got a bit more to come in the second half and we keep on pushing. The second half will be stronger, usually the second half is a stronger period for me. So I’ll really take this time to reset and try and come back stronger, fitter and better mentally prepared.”Norris, who took his and McLaren’s first win of the year, believes that he is driving at his very best, better even than when he won the title last season, despite being outpaced by what has been a dominant Mercedes over the opening 11 meetings.“Today I would probably say it was up there with one of my best performances, in terms of extracting performance out of the car and being so close to the limit every single lap,” he said. “So close that the team had to ask me to peg it back a little bit.View image in fullscreenLando Norris celebrates with the McLaren team after his Hungarian Grand Prix success.Photograph: David Davies/PA“So although it kind of hurts me saying it because it doesn’t mean that you just win, I feel I’m doing a better job this year than I was last year, and I have done for a little while.”The British driver is 91 points behind Antonelli in the championship with 12 races to come. It is a huge mountain to climb but, like Hamilton, Norris said there is still much to play for in the second half of the season, especially after the significant upgrades McLaren brought to Hungary had proved so effective, even if driving the current F1 cars is still not to his and many drivers’ taste.“What pleases me the most? The fact we were so quick, the fact the car was very strong today,” he said. “I was just very happy with a lot of things. I mean, the car was still horrible to drive at times but quick and I’d rather have a horrible but quick car than anything else.“I was convinced I could win the race today and we did. We were just on another level and I felt in a very good flow of things. When the car’s good and when I’m in a good flow, there’s no stopping.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportLewis HamiltonFerrariLando NorrisMcLarennewsShareReuse this content

title: Chiesa wants ‘new chapter’ with Iraola after frustrating time under Slot at Liverpool | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: The forward, who scored in Liverpool’s friendly win against Sunderland, had a frustrating two seasons under the former head coach Arne Slot
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: The forward, who scored in Liverpool’s friendly win against Sunderland, had a frustrating two seasons under the former head coach Arne Slot
Content: Federico Chiesa (left) celebrates with Dominik Szoboszlai after scoring Liverpool's third goal against Sunderland in Nashville.Photograph: George Walker IV/APView image in fullscreenFederico Chiesa (left) celebrates with Dominik Szoboszlai after scoring Liverpool's third goal against Sunderland in Nashville.Photograph: George Walker IV/APLiverpoolChiesa wants ‘new chapter’ with Iraola after frustrating time under Slot at LiverpoolForward scored in friendly win against SunderlandChiesa had frustrating two seasons under Arne SlotAndy Hunterin NashvilleSun 26 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederico Chiesa has said he wants “a new chapter” atLiverpoolwith Andoni Iraola following a frustrating time under Arne Slot and claimed the club were lucky to qualify for the Champions League last season.The Liverpool forward has been linked with a return to Italy this summer having struggled for minutes during his two years at Anfield. Chiesa made 36 appearances for Slot last season, a healthy return on paper, but only five were starts.Liverpool start Iraola era in style to beat Sunderland but Gomez injury deepens defensive worriesRead moreHe started one Premier League game last season despite the problems Liverpool had in attack because of injuries to Alexander Isak and Hugo Ekitiké, and his last start came in the FA Cup fourth-round winagainst Brighton on 14 February. A change of head coach, Chiesa hopes, will herald a change in fortune as a Liverpool player.“It is always a fresh start at the beginning of the year,” said the 28-year-old, who produced a fine finish inLiverpool’s 4-2 friendly defeat of Sunderlandin Nashville on Saturday. “Maybe there have been too many fresh starts [for him]. But I don’t care, I am trying to do my best for this new manager.“Last season under Arne Slot, I was trying to do my best. Last year I felt ready for a bigger role, then it depended on the coach whether he wanted me to play or not. Of course I wanted to play more but it is what it is. The gaffer had his gameplans, he took his decisions, I have nothing to say about that. It is football. This year, let us say it is a new chapter. There is a new manager and I have to focus on that.”Chiesa admits he has not discussed his future with Iraola since the Basque coachsucceeded Slot in June. “The only conversations I had were about pressing and tactics,” he said. “He put me striker against Sunderland and he wants me there.”But the Italy international, who has two years remaining on his Liverpool contract, claimed his priority is to prove himself to the head coach rather than seek a return to Serie A. Como and former club Juventus have been linked with a move for the forward.“Right now, at the moment, I am happy here at Liverpool,” said Chiesa. “I love the club, I love the fans, I love everything. I am doing the best I can to have a chance here. And then we will see. At the minute, the only thing I am thinking about is Liverpool.”View image in fullscreenFederico Chiesa scored for Liverpool against Sunderland in Nashville on Saturday.Photograph: George Walker IV/APLiverpool secured Champions League qualification on the final day of a troubled season in May in what proved to be Slot’s final game in charge. Chiesa insists that was no cause for celebration at a club of Liverpool’s stature and there must be improvement next term.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe forward said: “Liverpool deserves more. Two years ago, we were Premier League champions. Last year, we almost went out of the Champions League spots. We were battling for fifth, which was enough at the time but as we know usually only four go in. We were lucky.“It was a tough season last year and this season we need to do better, in the Champions League as well. We went out to PSG. We want to go further in that competition and then we want to do even better in the Premier League as well.”Chiesa also hopes to reclaim his place in the national team next season, having missed out on several squads recently. Italy are now searching for a new head coach, having failed to qualify for the World Cup under Gennaro Gattuso.Chiesa said: “The situation is that I spoke to the manager a few times, Gattuso, and I was not ready physically at the time. When I got back in March, unfortunately I got injured. But I am looking forward to playing for the national team. I have won with the national team [the European Championship]. It is always nice to play and win for your national team.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We want to win the league’: Arsenal’s new recruits ink in WSL success | Arsenal Women | The Guardian
description: Despite a busy transfer window with Beth Mead moving on and seven new signings, academy graduates such as Lotte Wubben-Moy remain key to trophies
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Despite a busy transfer window with Beth Mead moving on and seven new signings, academy graduates such as Lotte Wubben-Moy remain key to trophies
Content: Georgia Stanway gets ready to hit the new season running for Arsenal.Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorgia Stanway gets ready to hit the new season running for Arsenal.Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesArsenal Women‘We want to win the league’: Arsenal’s new recruits ink in WSL successDespite a busy transfer window with Beth Mead moving on and seven new signings, academy graduates such as Lotte Wubben-Moy remain key to trophiesSuzanne WrackSun 26 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorgia Stanway looks at her arms and then down at her legs on day one of Arsenal’s pre-season. “As you can see, I’m covered in tattoos,” she says. “I only see the bare skin, the space, so I need to keep collecting more.”Tattooing and being tattooed is her creative outlet, her way of expressing herself off the pitch. But seeing space is key to the 27‑year‑old England midfielder being exceptional on the pitch.From Popp to Diani: 10 women’s transfers you may have missed during the men’s World CupRead moreStanway’sunveiling video, after hermove from Bayern Munich, showed a delicate, cursive script reading “whatever the weather” tattooed on her arm. It was a bold statement to get the lyric from North London Forever, Arsenal’s anthem, etched into her skin before she has stepped on to the Emirates Stadium pitch in red and white. “It shows I’m going to give absolutely everything for this club. I want to hit the ground running, play my game, connect with my teammates, connect with the fans and look forward to an exciting future at the club.”Stanway is emblematic of Arsenal’s summer of change, one of seven signings so far. Meanwhile,Lotte Wubben-Moy, a lifelong fan who joined Arsenal’s academy at 13, represents the core and culture that is a point of focus at the club. It is a culture players want to be a part of, so much so it leads to getting a tattoo on day one of being there. “She has set a very high bar,” says Wubben-Moy, with a grin. “That’s Georgia. She goes all in and I like that.”Wubben-Moy is ready to stake a claim in Arsenal’s starting XI after struggling to nail down a position in defence despite having performed exceptionally well when covering for injured players. “I’ve always felt ready,” says the 27-year-old. “When I get my moment, I deliver. Historically, as a club, we’re built on defensive solidity. If we have a solid defence, it allows us to create and score. That should be the stepping stone towards victories. So I will continue to contribute to the defensive solidity in whatever way, shape or form that is. But I want my spot.”View image in fullscreenLotte Wubben-Moy lifts the Champions Cup trophy during the Arsenal trophy parade in May.Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesThere was widespread recognition that Arsenal’s squad needed a revamp, that the age needed to be lowered and changes made if they were going to take the next step. That meant big names leaving, most notablyBeth MeadandKatie McCabe. “They’re both absolute legends of the game and we have so much respect for them,” says Jodie Taylor, the former Arsenal striker who became the club’s technical director in January. “But we always knew this window was going to come with some changes.”“Change is inevitable in women’s football,” says Wubben-Moy. “If you speak to a player and they don’t say they’re nimble, you’ve got someone that’s not built for the game. We’ve become a nimble team, a team that can move with the ebb and flow of women’s football.View image in fullscreenBeth Mead left in a busy summer for Arsenal.Photograph: Rhianna Chadwick/PA“That’s not just within the playing group, it’s something replicated within the staff, the boardroom, the commercial team, the comms team. Everyone is so willing to move and to dictate what we want.“If you’d asked me about change four or five years ago, I’d have been a bit intimidated, but now I know what to do and I’m part of the driver of it. The opportunity we have and that I see for us as a team, as a collective, is something that really excites me.”Arsenal’s approach to Stanway’s recruitment was a contributing factor to her wanting to join the club. “Arsenal came in early doors,” she says. “I really enjoyed they were super loyal from the beginning and wanted me even when I wasn’t available. It’s a nice feeling being wanted.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArsenal continue squad revamp with signing of Spain keeper Misa RodríguezRead more“The last four years in Munich were unbelievable, but I knew I wanted to take the next step and I felt at Arsenal there was an opportunity for me to be able to progress, to make my game better and to play with world-class players.”Arsenal have done most of their business early, with Stanway joined by experienced internationalsSelina Cerci, Géraldine Reuteler,Ona BatlleandMisa Rodríguez, as well as young talents Lisa Baum and Isabella Damm. No major international tournament and seven signings in for day one of pre-season is a big boost for Renée Slegers and her coaching staff, particularly after two seasons of slow starts to domestic campaigns.“The market is not easy, though, it’s constantly changing and the pool of elite talent is small and several clubs are fishing from it,” says Taylor. “You try and plan as much as you can, but you also have to be reactive in the market. We’re always trying to keep an eye on the future, but we have to be quite agile.“We can talk about positional needs, qualities, ages and succession planning, but if a player’s not available or they just don’t exist, it can be like trying to fit square pegs and round holes. As well as looking at current needs and positional profiles, we talk a lot about our core style of play, but we also want to play with variety, be unpredictable and have different qualities in players too.”View image in fullscreenFormer Arsenal striker Jodie Taylor, now technical director, is leading the strong recruitment this summer.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyThe players who have come in have brought energy, says Wubben-Moy, who was on an emotional rollercoaster duringArsenal men’s Premier League and women’s Champions Cup-winning parade, with the bus looping past Highbury Corner, where she filmed her contract renewal video, and past Islington town hall, where she got married to cyclist Tao Geoghegan Hart a few weeks later.“I like to focus on what they’re entering,” says Wubben-Moy, “which is a culture that has been created by history, by players and staff that are the core of this team and who have all lived through the changes to different degrees: Kelly [Smith], Renée, myself, Leah [Williamson], Kim [Little], Jodie too. We’ve been privy to lots of different things but all of us are holding on to and releasing, in a healthy way, the things we know we need to. It’s efficient, we’re focused, we know what we do next.Missing a major football tournament? Fear not, Wafcon 2026 is about to startRead more“It’s like you’re cooking the most beautiful recipe and then you add the final small ingredients that make the marginal difference, that elevate, and you create something that’s beautiful and that you can relish and enjoy. That’s what we’re in the process of now with a beautiful long pre-season. I’m desperate to get it out of the way so we can then serve what we’re cooking to the fans and be like: ‘Let’s eat and we’ll all eat together for the whole year.’”The average attendance of more than 34,000 fans for WSL games at the Emirates last season and the club’s pioneering history in women’s football, as well as theChampions League win in 2025, are huge selling points, and all concerned at Arsenal want more, including a first Women’s Super League title since 2019.“We’re in a great place,” says Taylor. “But we would have liked to have won more trophies last season and that is our huge ambition coming into this year. I’ll flat out say it: we want to win the league. We are an ambitious club and with the signings we’ve made we feel like we’re in a great place to do that.”Explore more on these topicsArsenal WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Joshua emerges from Prenga fight with urgent questions while Fury is uninspiring | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Anthony Joshua’s lack of punch resistance is clear, which could place him in danger in the highly anticipated £150m fight with Tyson Fury
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Anthony Joshua’s lack of punch resistance is clear, which could place him in danger in the highly anticipated £150m fight with Tyson Fury
Content: Anthony Joshua was in good physical condition against Kristian Prenga but showed his obvious vulnerabilities.Photograph: Ali Issa/APView image in fullscreenAnthony Joshua was in good physical condition against Kristian Prenga but showed his obvious vulnerabilities.Photograph: Ali Issa/APBoxingJoshua emerges from Prenga fight with urgent questions while Fury is uninspiringJoshua’s lack of punch resistance is clear, which could place him in danger in the highly anticipated £150m fight with Tyson FuryDonald McRaeSun 26 Jul 2026 09.54 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bedlam and madnesslasted for just five minutes and 43 secondsand, after Anthony Joshua was back in the sanctuary of his dressing room, he claimed to have learned “a valuable lesson”.Joshua had been knocked down twiceby Kristian Prenga before he rescued himself in the second round with a brutal stoppage of the previously obscure Albanian.Joshua also looked ahead to the hugely anticipated fight withTyson Furyafter the two faded former world champions came through wildly contrasting bouts which were meant to be routine exhibitions this weekend. “I’m gonna come back stronger now,” Joshua claimed as he tried to clear the concussive fog from his brain after the worst round of his tumultuous career.Tim Tszyu eyes world title tilt after beating Errol Spence Jr in 12-round epicRead moreBut the sad truth had already risen up with piercing clarity after just 20 seconds of that first round. A sweeping right hand, which was the first meaningful punch of the fight, rocked Joshua and set him up for Prenga’s jolting uppercut. They were decent blows but it was disturbing to see how little punch resistance Joshua retains. He still cuts a sculpted figure of hard muscle but he looked lost and scrambled as he tumbled to the canvas. Joshua managed to roll over and, pressing his white gloves down on the blue canvas, he pushed himself up.His legs were rickety as a grimace of a smile crossed his confused face. After he took a count of eight, Joshua was soon in trouble again. A sharp right cross sent him reeling into the ropes and the referee could have given him another count. Every time Prenga landed the right hand, even without undue force, Joshua was vulnerable.Another uppercut sent him down again, even if this time his gloves only brushed the canvas before he was up again. Joshua’s courage was obvious but, in those desolate moments, the idea that he would survive another onslaught and face Fury in November seemed beyond fanciful.But then, inexplicably, everything changed. During the break between rounds it was almost as if a loaded message had been given to Prenga that he should pack away his artillery and stop ruining the $200m (£150m) showdown between Fury and Joshua. In reality it seemed more a case that Prenga had shocked himself by dragging Joshua to the brink of a shattering defeat.View image in fullscreenKristian Prenga gave Anthony Joshua a scare in the first round in Jeddah.Photograph: Ali Issa/APRather than coming out to close the show, Prenga backed away. He allowed his dazed victim to seize control and start unloading punches. The Albanian was pinned in a corner and, throwing nothing of consequence in return, he was suddenly under immense pressure. Successive combinations made him sag before a ferocious right hand poleaxed Prenga.Joshua deserves praise for his fortitude and finishing power. But even that clinical knockout could not wipe away the images of him weaving like a battered old tree about to crash to the ground whenever he was tagged by blows he would have once shrugged aside.Having beeninjured seven months ago in the car accidentwhich killed Sina Ghami and Latif “Latz” Ayodele, his close friends and key members of his camp, Joshua paid tribute to them: “It’s more than punch power. That was spirit. That was Latz, that was Sina, that was their families. It hurts to even talk about it. It has been tough. It’s my brothers.”Joshua was close to tears. His distress was understandable but it was more worrying when he suggested that personal tragedy had given him higher powers of recovery. “You know what I learned? I can’t be stopped, man – I can’t be denied.”His family, friends and promoters should all pause and, in the coming days, take great care of him. It would be best if they advised Joshua he is no longer equipped to absorb heavy punishment from even a merely competent heavyweight. Younger fighters such as Moses Itauma and Daniel Dubois, who administered acrushing knockout of Joshua in 2024, would have hurt him badly had they, rather than Prenga, been in the ring.It’s trueFury was uninspiring when beating Mariusz Wach, a mediocre 46-year-old Polish heavyweight, after seven one-sided rounds in Thailand on Friday night.Wach still managed to tag Fury a couple of times as the old Gypsy King is no longer an elusive ring technician. But Fury remains a fighter to his core and he could cause serious damage against such a reduced version of Joshua.“We’ve signed the contract,” Joshua’s promoter, Eddie Hearn, said after his fighter’s lucky escape. “Everything is done. But tonight wasn’t about Tyson Fury. It was about the strengthAnthony Joshuahas shown to be here. No one knows what he’s been through the last seven months. When he went down in the first round, I thought he’d come back too soon.”View image in fullscreenTyson Fury laboured to victory against Mariusz Wach in Thailand.Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/ReutersYet, as Hearn conceded later, the signed contracts stipulate that Fury and Joshua will fight in the UK in November. It is now widely expected that the contest will take place in the US instead and so a new set of contracts could delay the circus yet again.Reflecting on his near nightmare against Prenga, Joshua added: “It was a tough moment but I learned a valuable lesson. Start faster. Come out, fuck this boxing, and be ready. You can do it in 20 seconds. If Prenga had a bit more luck on his side, he could have had me out of there.”He also suggested that “today was a real good eye-opener.” It was, in the sense that his lack of punch resistance was stripped bare for all to see. In a business more sensible and compassionate than boxing, those close to Joshua would try to persuade him that the time has come for him to walk away with his riches and senses still intact.Instead, he will be enticed back into the ring to fight Fury – in a contest between two old heavyweights which now seems freighted as much with danger and potential calamity as colossal amounts of money.Explore more on these topicsBoxingTyson FuryAnthony JoshuafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Water supply restored to Gatwick airport after hours without working toilets | Gatwick airport | The Guardian
description: Airport’s bars and restaurants were also unable to serve drinks to passengers because of lack of running water
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Airport’s bars and restaurants were also unable to serve drinks to passengers because of lack of running water
Content: Passengers at the airport had no access to working toilets or bars and restaurants because of a water supply failure.Photograph: Tom Jeffreys/PAView image in fullscreenPassengers at the airport had no access to working toilets or bars and restaurants because of a water supply failure.Photograph: Tom Jeffreys/PAGatwick airportWater supply restored to Gatwick airport after hours without working toiletsAirport’s bars and restaurants were also unable to serve drinks to passengers because of lack of running waterJamie GriersonSun 26 Jul 2026 18.01 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWater supply has been restored to most ofGatwick airportafter passengers spent hours without access to working toilets, and bars and restaurants were closed.Most toilets had reopened across both terminals on Sunday evening, with the remaining facilities, including bars and restaurants, expected to return to normal for the first of Monday’s flights.Although flights were unaffected, toilets in both terminals were out of use, cafes, restaurants and bars were shut, and taps were either not running at all or running with low pressure since Sunday morning.Announcing that the water, supplied by SES Water, had been restored, Gatwick airport said: “Following an issue at the Bough Beech water treatment works which impacted the local area today, we are pleased to report that the water supply has now returned to the vast majority of theLondonGatwick campus.“Most toilet facilities are now open and we expect all toilets – as well as food and beverage outlets – to be open for tomorrow’s first flights. Since becoming aware of the issue, we have been working closely with @SESWater and our airport partners to help minimise the impact, and ensure all today’s flights departed as scheduled.”Earlier on Sunday, passengers posted online that they were unable to get hot drinks, wash their hands or fill water bottles at the airport in Sussex.The problem also had an impact in the wider Sussex andKentarea, water suppliers said.View image in fullscreenAn empty restaurant at Gatwick on Sunday.Photograph: Roger Wood/PASES Water said there had been interruptions to water supplies in parts of the TN11, RH1, RH6 and RH10 postcode areas.At 2pm the company had said its Bough Beech water treatment works were running again but the water needed to be treated before services could return to normal.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve never seen Wetherspoons empty,’ said one traveller who was heading to New York.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAOn Facebook, one user posted: “Gasping for a drink & crossing my legs right now. This is ridiculous! Gatwick airport has shut all restaurants and most toilets due to a water outage. Not a great start to the holiday.”The former MP and recently appointed government “music champion” Michael Dugher wrote on social media: “At least allow people to use the chairs in all the closed restaurants and bars. No water is one thing, but depriving people of somewhere to sit is another … Families are having to sit on the floor.”Roger Wood, from Tunbridge Wells, Kent, arrived at Gatwick’s south terminal at about 11am on Sunday to fly to New York. He told reporters: “There was no communication. We arrived at 11ish and it had only started recently.“We met friends at the bar but they couldn’t serve us as they were unable to wash their hands. I’ve never seen Wetherspoons empty. No idea when it’ll be resolved. The toilets also lacked water to wash hands.”Explore more on these topicsGatwick airportAir transportTransportLondonWest SussexWater industryEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Restricted eating hours may reduce cognitive decline in older age, researchers find | Ageing | The Guardian
description: Preliminary study shows older people who avoided food four hours before bed did better in problem solving tests
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Preliminary study shows older people who avoided food four hours before bed did better in problem solving tests
Content: The small clinical trial run by academics at Rutgers University in New Jersey found ‘additional benefits’ beyond weight loss to restricted eating.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe small clinical trial run by academics at Rutgers University in New Jersey found ‘additional benefits’ beyond weight loss to restricted eating.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianAgeingRestricted eating hours may reduce cognitive decline in older age, researchers findPreliminary study shows older people who avoided food four hours before bed did better in problem solving testsIan SampleScience editorSun 26 Jul 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConfining mealtimes and snacks to a nine-hour window and avoiding food for four hours before bed may help stave off cognitive decline in older age, researchers say.A pilot study of older women living with overweight or obesity found hints of improvement in mental skills among those who ate within the restricted period compared with those who spread their meals over a longer time.The finding is preliminary given the numbers in the trial, but if confirmed in larger studies, the work suggests people could help to protect their cognitive abilities byeating within a relatively narrow windowand not eating late into the night.Losing weight alone can help slow cognitive decline in older age, said Prof Sue Shapses, a nutritional scientist at Rutgers University in New Jersey, US, but there may be “additional benefits” for people who do not eat outside an eight to nine-hour window, and stop eating four hours before going to sleep.Dementia is the leading cause of death in the UK and the seventh worldwide, leading to nearly 2 million deaths globally each year. Some risk factors are unavoidable, such as age and genetics, butexperts believenearly half of cases could be prevented or delayed through changes to lifestyle. Obesity in middle age can raise the risk of dementia in later life by 30%.Shapses ran a small clinical trial in which 47 women aged 50 to 79, who were living with overweight or obesity, were encouraged to cut 500 calories from their daily diet for six months. Within the group, 26 were advised to eat only within a nine-hour window. Typically, this meant eating between 10am and 6pm, while the rest of the volunteers spread their meals over about 12 hours.At the end of the trial, both groups had similar weight loss averaging about 7kg (15lbs). But cognitive tests revealed that those who confined their eating to the narrow window performed better than the others on spatial planning and problem solving tests. There were also hints that they made fewer errors on memory and learning tests, though on some multitasking and reaction time tests both groups performed the same.NHS staff battling wave of food supplement disinformationRead moreShapses called the effects “modest” but said they suggested time-restricted eating may improve people’s ability to remember information for everyday tasks and reduce mistakes linked to memory, attention and problem solving. Details werepresentedat Nutrition 2026, the annual meeting of the American Society for Nutrition in Maryland.The researchers now plan to investigate why it may be important to consider when we eat as well as what we eat. The benefitscould be drivenby a complex interplay of circadian rhythms, metabolism and inflammation.In many countries, the UK and US included, it is common to eat over a 14-hour period, leaving only 10 hours overnight without food. But research points to clear health benefits from extending overnight fasting. Areviewpublished in January found that finishing eating before 7pm was associated with significant improvements in body weight, BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure and markers of metabolic health.Prof Wendy Hall, the head of nutritional sciences at King’s College London, who was not involved in the study, said confining mealtimes to a narrow window may have benefits for the brain.“Time-restricted eating is a plausible approach to supporting cognitive health in midlife and older adults with overweight, not only because it may help with weight management but also because avoiding large meals late in the evening may improve blood sugar control, vascular function and inflammation,” she said.Hall cautioned that the findings were preliminary and that it was important to see the full peer-reviewed study to determine whether any improvements were clinically meaningful.Explore more on these topicsAgeingObesityDementiaHealthDiets and dietingnewsShareReuse this content

title: England’s north-south life expectancy gap grows despite record longevity | Health | The Guardian
description: King’s Fund report finds men and women live, on average, for 80 years and nearly 84 years, but gains are in south
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: King’s Fund report finds men and women live, on average, for 80 years and nearly 84 years, but gains are in south
Content: The half of England’s population who live in five northern regions have experienced little or no rise in life expectancy.Photograph: John Stillwell/PAView image in fullscreenThe half of England’s population who live in five northern regions have experienced little or no rise in life expectancy.Photograph: John Stillwell/PAHealthEngland’s north-south life expectancy gap grows despite record longevityKing’s Fund report finds men and women live, on average, for 80 years and nearly 84 years, but gains are in southIan SampleScience editorSun 26 Jul 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe north-south divide in life expectancy inEnglandhas grown over the past decade, with people in northern regions facing more illnesses such as heart disease and cancer, but also suicides and deaths related to alcohol and drug misuse.Provisionalfiguresshow life expectancy reached an all-time high in 2025, with men and women in England living, on average, for 80 years and nearly 84 years respectively, but the gains were overwhelmingly in the south, the King’s Fund said.Despite suffering the sharpest fall in lifespan during the Covid pandemic, life expectancy in London rose by nearly a year in the decade to 2023-25. The south-east, south-west and east of England also recorded gains.But the half of England’s population who live in five northern regions, namely the north-west, the north-east, Yorkshire and the Humber, West Midlands and East Midlands, experienced little or no rise in life expectancy over the same period, reflecting greater levels of deprivation.According to the health charity, people in London can now expect to live three years longer than those in the north-east. Even starker disparities emerged at the local level, with life expectancy in Blackpool, Lancashire, being 10 years shorter for men and eight years shorter for women than in Hart, Hampshire.“In the most deprived 30% of areas, life expectancy either fell or didn’t improve over the past decade and that’s a disturbing story,” said Veena Raleigh, a senior fellow at the King’s Fund. “Meanwhile, it went up by half a year in the least deprived 30% of areas.”“Over the past decade, the north has fallen further behind, and the plans for levelling up and the regeneration of the north haven’t materialised,” Raleigh added. “This isn’t just a question of fixing the health service. It requires a cross-government drive to also address the wider, underlying determinants of health, for example, ensuring people have secure jobs, fair pay, adequate housing, clean air, accessible transport and affordable access to healthy diets.”The government’s10-year plan for the NHSaims to increase healthy life expectancy – the number of years people spend in good health – for everyone in England, while halving the gap between the richest and poorest. But the King’s Fund called the goal “unrealistic”, requiring improvements in population health on a scale not seen in decades.Healthy life expectancy fell in all regions of England in the decade to 2022-24, with people now spending on average about 2.5 years longer in poor health, the charity found. The regional divide has remained unchanged at about six to seven years, but can reach 20 years between the most and least deprived regions. The figures mean those in the most deprived parts of England have shorter lives and spend more years in poor health.“Although thegovernment’s 10-year health planpromises a shift from sickness to prevention, the focus is mainly on reducing waiting lists and waiting times,” Raleigh said. “Public health and prevention of ill health need to be much higher up the policy agenda, for example, to tackle the rising prevalence of obesity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘It was like something was crawling over me’ – the worrying rise of shingles among millennial womenRead more“The increasing prevalence of ill health in adults of working age, in particular, is deeply concerning because it risks jeopardising the life course of some young people with, additionally, the high costs of rising economic inactivity.”A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said the government’s aim to halve the gap in healthy life expectancy reflected the “scale and complexity of the challenge”. They said £2.2bn was being repurposed for critical resources such as medicines and medical equipment in deprived areas.“Someone’s postcode should never dictate how long they live, and this government is determined to tackle the stark inequalities that still exist across Britain,” the spokesperson said. “We’re already taking action, from allocating GP funding more fairly to delivering pioneering neighbourhood health centres in the areas that need them most. But we will now go further in devolving power to local communities, putting decision-making into the hands of those who know their areas best and driving lasting change across the country.”Explore more on these topicsHealthLife expectancyNHSEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Industry star David Jonsson to play Black Panther in Marvel sequel | Black Panther | The Guardian
description: Director Ryan Coogler announces British actor in lead role alongside co-stars Letitia Wright and Winston Duke
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Director Ryan Coogler announces British actor in lead role alongside co-stars Letitia Wright and Winston Duke
Content: From left to right, Letitia Wright, Winston Duke, Ryan Coogler, David Jonsson and Kevin Feige on stage at Marvel Studios’ Comic-Con International.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APView image in fullscreenFrom left to right, Letitia Wright, Winston Duke, Ryan Coogler, David Jonsson and Kevin Feige on stage at Marvel Studios’ Comic-Con International.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APBlack PantherIndustry star David Jonsson to play Black Panther in Marvel sequelDirector Ryan Coogler announces British actor in lead role alongside co-stars Letitia Wright and Winston DukeNadeem Badshahand agenciesSun 26 Jul 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British actorDavid Jonssonhas been unveiled as the new Black Panther by the film’s director, Ryan Coogler.Jonsson, 32, known for roles in Industry, The Long Walk and Alien: Romulus, will play the son of Chadwick Boseman’s T’Challa in the thirdBlack Panthermovie.He joined Coogler on stage atMarvelStudios’ Comic-Con International presentation to announce the news on Saturday, alongside co-stars Letitia Wright and Winston Duke.Coogler, who won the Oscar for best original screenplay for his vampire film Sinners earlier this year, said: “The last time we got to make a movie, we introduced a character who is the son of the character that the great Chadwick Boseman played – our T’Challa – in that film.“And today, I want to tell you that in this next film, he grows up, he comes of age.”Born in London, Jonsson began his career in the West End. He made his screen debut in 2018 in two episodes of the British detective drama Endeavour before being cast as Augustus “Gus” Sackey in the first two series of Industry from 2020 to 2022.He appeared in the 2025 adaptation of Stephen King’s thriller The Long Walk and in the same year won the Bafta rising star award.Jonsson, who also has roles in the upcoming films The Chaperones, Benn/Eubank and Scandalous, said: “Thank you to this family that I have the honour and the blessing to join. I don’t want to say too much, because I want to let the screen do the talking.”Black Panther III will be released in US cinemas on 15 December 2028. A UK release date yet to be confirmed.Boseman died in 2020 aged 43, four years after being diagnosed with colon cancer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBlack Panther: Wakanda Forever, released in 2022, revealed that Boseman’s character, T’Challa, had a son. It followed Wright’s character, Shuri, as she takes on the role of the protagonist after the death of T’Challa.The first film, released in 2018, was set in the mythical country of Wakanda, a hidden African kingdom with innovative technology thanks to its reserves of the world’s most useful precious metal. It won three Oscars.Coogler, who directed the first two Black Panther movies, also co-produced the 2025 series Ironheart and Eyes of Wakanda.Explore more on these topicsBlack PantherDavid JonssonRyan CooglerMarvelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump ‘border czar’ says ICE officer in Maine killing should not have cleared vetting | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Tom Homan comments on officer’s eligibility to serve after reports that agent’s two ex-wives had accused him of abuse
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Tom Homan comments on officer’s eligibility to serve after reports that agent’s two ex-wives had accused him of abuse
Content: White House ‘border czar’ Tom Homan speaks with reporters outside the White House, on 20 July 2026.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreenWhite House ‘border czar’ Tom Homan speaks with reporters outside the White House, on 20 July 2026.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump ‘border czar’ says ICE officer in Maine killing should not have cleared vettingTom Homan comments on officer’s eligibility to serve after reports that agent’s two ex-wives had accused him of abuseMaya YangSun 26 Jul 2026 14.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Homan, the Trump administration “border czar”, on Sunday said he did not believe the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer at the center of a recent fatal shooting in Maine “should have ever cleared vetting”.Speaking to CNN’s State of the Union, Homan was asked by host Dana Bash about the officer’s eligibility to serve followingreportsthat two of his ex-wives hadaccusedhim of abuse.“Should someone with those issues be an ICE agent?” Bash asked.“No, if those … are facts … I don’t think he should ever have cleared vetting,” Homan replied.Homan also said part of an ongoing investigation into the 13 July shooting deathJoan Sebastián Durán Guerrerois determining “how … did the vetting process fail”.“When they hire somebody, they put them through a vetting process and look at all that stuff. So I know, based on that information – that’s part of the ongoing investigation,” Homan said. “How … did the vetting process fail? Was that information not available? Did they not know?”He added: “So there’s a separate administrative investigation on what happened here. Did we have that information? Did we not have that information? But the vetting process … if that was factual, he would have an almost impossible time to pass vetting.”The officer involved in the killing of Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian man in Biddeford,Maine, has since been identified by news outlets as David Brouillette. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, has not publicly confirmed Brouillette’s identity.Since the shooting, two of Brouillette’s ex-wives have publicly described alleged abuse during their relationships with him. One, Lucinda Brouillette,allegedher ex-husband engaged in a “persistent pattern of abuse, intimidation, manipulation, fear and control”.“If you were to ask me whether I believe David Brouillette is capable of this level of violence, my answer is unequivocally yes,” she said in a statement to NPR.Although Homan declined to comment directly on this particular case, describing it as “a rare instance”, he said: “If this person had that type of history, it would have been a vetting issue, and it should have been brought to the attention of those who make those decisions.”He added, in part: “We will see. It’s all being reviewed. We will see where it lies.”The shooting has prompted renewed scrutiny of ICE’s hiring practices.Democrats have called for reviews of the agency’s vetting process. For instance, Mississippi congressman Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the US House homeland security committee,saidthat Brouillette’s alleged abusive past “directly call[s] into question the supposed vetting and training ICE does of its recruits”.Neither the fatal shooting in Maine noranother oneinvolving an ICE officer in Texas earlier in July yielded body camera footage from officers. That prompted Homan toannouncethat the agency would require officers to wear body cameras during vehicle stops.In the Texas case, which resulted in the killing of Mexican nationalLorenzo Salgado Araujo, the Harris county district attorney Sean Tearesaidin a statement that lab results of a white substance found in a van at the center of a case tested negative for narcotics or illicit drugs – despite an FBI search warrant application that maintained a bag with substance in question was consistent with methamphetamine.Salgado’s family had said the substance was a salt mixture that he and his construction crew colleagues used as electrolytes to stay hydrated in extremely hot temperatures.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationUS immigrationMaineUS politicsTexasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Every new UK home should have air conditioning, say Liberal Democrats | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Party says housing stock ‘woefully unprepared’ for extreme heat and new rules for builders must be set
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Exclusive: Party says housing stock ‘woefully unprepared’ for extreme heat and new rules for builders must be set
