Content: The Liberal Democrats want developers to be made to build homes able to cope with increasing heat.Photograph: Unai Huici/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Liberal Democrats want developers to be made to build homes able to cope with increasing heat.Photograph: Unai Huici/AlamyClimate crisisEvery new UK home should have air conditioning, say Liberal DemocratsExclusive: Party says housing stock ‘woefully unprepared’ for extreme heat and new rules for builders must be setPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentSun 26 Jul 2026 13.34 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll new UK homes should be built with air conditioning to cope with the effects of the climate crisis, according to theLiberal Democrats.The party says British homes are dangerously unsuited to rising temperatures, meaning passive cooling measures such as planting more trees in residential areas are necessary.The Lib Dems also want air conditioning to be mandatory in essential public buildings such as schools and health facilities.The problem of overwarm homes has been highlighted by a UK Health Protection Agency yellow alert for high temperatures to run from Tuesday morning until Friday morning for the south-east, south-west and east of England, the Midlands, and Yorkshire and the Humber.Temperatures in London are forecast to reach 32C (90F) on Wednesday, before cooling. Some other parts of the UK will be wet with notably lower temperatures.As well as being hot, much of the summer has been exceptionally dry. In July so far, there has been just 5% of the average rainfall across England, falling to 1% in the south, bringing droughts and severe risk of wildfires.My homemade air-con unit does the trick | Brief lettersRead moreThe Lib Dems’ “climate ready” programme would make it a legal requirement for new homes to have either air conditioning or another cooling system. They say this is especially important for older people or those in poor health.The number of UK homes with air conditioninghas doubledin the past three years amid rising temperatures, according to industry estimates. However, this still comes to only about 4m of the estimated 30m-plus homes in the country.According to polling commissioned by the Lib Dems, 28% of people said they had bought a fan or an air conditioning unit during the recent heatwaves, with 26% of respondents saying the conditions had left them feeling unwell or faint.Tim Farron, the party’s environment spokesperson, said: “This latest set of relentless heatwaves has taught us that Britain is woefully unprepared for extreme heat, and families across Britain are paying for the cost of inaction.“With another heatwave on the horizon, the government must step in with a new plan that takes the onus off already-struggling Brits and commits developers to build homes fit for the future – insulated properly and equipped with air conditioning.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGideon Amos, the party’s housing spokesperson, said: “Air conditioning is becoming essential in UK homes, which are now among the smallest and hottest in Europe after previous Conservatives governments swept away minimum space standards.“Andy Burnham must see sense and enable the country to adapt fast – looking at how we build well for the future so that we give our society the security needed during these devastating heatwaves.”The heatwaves of May and June, during which there were an unprecedented three successive days of red warnings for extreme heat,killed about 2,700 people, with a peak fatality rate of about 440 people a day, according toan analysisled by Imperial College London.The statistics illustrate the increased risk from extreme heat exacerbated by human-created global heating. More than 40% of the people affected would not have died without the 1.4C of human-caused heating to date, according to the analysis.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisLiberal DemocratsExtreme heatConstruction industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: V&A workers hold ballot to strike over pay and heatwave conditions | V&A | The Guardian
description: Union calls for museum to become accredited London living wage employer and let staff carry water during shifts
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Union calls for museum to become accredited London living wage employer and let staff carry water during shifts
Content: V&A East in Stratford officially opened in April, having been conceived as a legacy development for the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park area of east London.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenV&A East in Stratford officially opened in April, having been conceived as a legacy development for the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park area of east London.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyV&AV&A workers hold ballot to strike over pay and heatwave conditionsUnion calls for museum to become accredited London living wage employer and let staff carry water during shiftsDiane TaylorSun 26 Jul 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorkers at one of the world’s leading art and design museums are balloting for “heatwave” strike action.The ballot atV&Ais taking place because of concerns about soaring temperatures and access to drinking water, along with pay and conditions.More than 300 workers at four V&A sites inLondon– the museum in South Kensington, V&A East Museum and V&A East Storehouse in Stratford, and Young V&A in Bethnal Green – are taking part in the ballot.The V&A, founded in 1852 after theGreat Exhibition, is described as “a family of museums dedicated to the power of creativity”. Its mission is to “promote art and design for all”.View image in fullscreenV&A East Storehouse in Stratford, east London, a collections and research building, opened in May last year.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe ballot has been launched during a summer ofextraordinarily high temperaturesand is thought to be one of the first to raise concerns about workplace conditions during a heatwave.The Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS) launched the strike ballot on 23 July owing to “serious and unresolved concerns affecting staff across the museum”.While pay rates are an issue, with calls for a minimum 4% pay increase, the union has also raised concerns about heat exposure and access to drinking water.It is calling for management to implement a policy of closing public areas across all four sites when temperatures exceed 30C, introduce heat mitigation measures for back of house workers, and allow staff at V&A East Storehouse to carry and drink water while working in areas where exhibits are on display, rather than waiting for another worker to come and relieve them while they go for a drink.The union is also calling on V&A to become anaccredited living wage employerin London. The current London living wage is£14.80 an hour. The V&A has confirmed that all its staff are paid at least this rate. However, some of the museum’s outsourced contractors arenot in receiptof the living wage and V&A has not so far become an accredited living wage employer, although it says this will be reviewed later this year.V&A Dundee, which is not part of the strike ballot, is an accredited living wage employer.View image in fullscreenPart of the PCS complaint concerns access to drinking water during shifts at museum sites such as V&A East Storehouse (pictured).Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianNick Marro, the culture secretary at PCS, said: “PCS members at the V&A are balloting for strike action because enough is enough. Management refuses to let staff carry or drink water while they work, refuses to become a London living wage accredited employer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom leftwing voters to unions: can Burnham win back Labour bases lost by Starmer? – visualisedRead more“At the same time, it claims it cannot afford a decent pay rise for staff. This is an employer that is failing the very people who keep one of Britain’s most prestigious museums running. It’s unfair, it’s unsafe and our members are prepared to fight back.”The Prospect trade union is alsoballotingmembers for strike action at the V&A over concerns about pay and conditions. Its ballot closes on 29 July.A spokesperson for the V&A said: “The V&A has been in negotiations with the trade union side since February and those negotiations are ongoing. Our offer sees a 3.6% increase in the overall pay bill, an above-inflation pay award as a minimum and 6.9% increase for our lowest-paid colleagues. As always, we have maintained our longstanding commitment to paying at least the London living wage.“The safety and wellbeing of our staff is of utmost importance to the V&A – all our staff have access to water and toilet facilities and regular breaks while at work. Extensive measures were implemented to support our staff during the heatwave, ranging from additional rest breaks, increasing staff rotations across gallery spaces, closing several galleries at V&A South Kensington and closing Young V&A altogether on 11 days during the peak of the heatwave.“To ensure the safety and security of national collections, duringOrder an Objectappointments at V&A East Storehouse, food and drink are not permitted and visitors are accompanied by V&A staff during their appointment.”Explore more on these topicsV&AIndustrial actionLondonMuseumsTrade unionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK journalists ‘self-censoring stories about Trump and the right over safety fears’ | Journalist safety | The Guardian
description: Government-backed investigation finds risks are normalised amid ‘a narrowing of the public conversation’
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Government-backed investigation finds risks are normalised amid ‘a narrowing of the public conversation’
Content: Investigators found a widespread belief that abuse linked to reporting had increased, especially online.Composite: PA Images/Guardian Design / AlamyView image in fullscreenInvestigators found a widespread belief that abuse linked to reporting had increased, especially online.Composite: PA Images/Guardian Design / AlamyJournalist safetyUK journalists ‘self-censoring stories about Trump and the right over safety fears’Government-backed investigation finds risks are normalised amid ‘a narrowing of the public conversation’Michael SavageMedia editorSun 26 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJournalists are self-censoring their reporting on rightwing protests, Donald Trump’s administration and trans issues because of growing concerns about their personal safety, with newsrooms accused of “normalising” the risks they face.Hundreds of journalists from across the UK have anonymously disclosed increasing nervousness over their security. Some have reported avoiding or altering coverage on certain topics due to intimidation, leading to self-censorship and “a narrowing of the public conversation”.The findings are revealed in a government-backed investigation into the safety of journalists, ordered amid growing hostility to traditional media across the west.“There have definitely been times where there’s been a story that’s maybe in the public interest, maybe worth reporting on, where we have had frank discussions about whether it’s ‘worth it’,” said one journalist.Another said: “I was definitely looking over my shoulder and making sure I wasn’t being followed and making sure that people weren’t going to start shouting things at me.”Investigators found a widespread belief that abuse linked to reporting has increased, especially online. They also reported newsroom cultures that treated the increase as inevitable given the polarised political environment – with journalists expected to be “thick-skinned”.Female journalists faced the brunt of abuse, describing gendered and sexualised harassment, explicit threats, inappropriate messages and online comments focused on appearance.Common topics raised by journalists as causing safety concerns were rightwing anti-immigration protests, the Trump administration, including protests against US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), as well as trans issues.“Anti-immigration protests were most widely referenced by journalists, both regarding the in-person risks of attending the marches and the backlash to any subsequent reporting,” the investigation found.Similar findings have been recorded in the US, where the International Women’s Media Foundation found journalists wereworking in heightened political polarisation, declining public trust in the media and increasing exposure to physical and psychological risks.We can’t talk about press freedom without talking about misogynyRead moreThere are numerous accounts of journalists in Northern Ireland facing intimidation from masked men while coveringanti-immigration riots, disclosed to the UK’s National Union of Journalists.In another case, footage of a journalist covering an anti-immigration protest was circulated in a Facebook group, with people working together to identify and locate them.One respondent described seeing a female journalist subjected to misogynistic heckling at a “unite the kingdom” rally, with the footage later uploaded to social media.With debates about the personal safety of reporters now a regular discussion point in newsrooms, ministers ordered an investigation by Alma Economics. It amounts to one of the most comprehensive assessments of journalist safety ever produced in the UK, surveying 531 journalists, alongside 55 in-depth interviews.Almost half of those surveyed said safety concerns influenced their willingness to report on certain stories, while about a third had changed how or what they covered.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe investigation found the shift to online and video journalism had made journalists more identifiable.“Journalists used to be much more anonymous,” said one reporter. “Now, you’re expected to be live, presenting TikToks all the time … People talk about all sorts of things about like: ‘What’s the future of journalism?’ and ‘How can we adapt?’ But very rarely is it discussed, ‘What does that take from us?’ And especially from female journalists.”Participants acknowledged that the UK still remained a safe place to work as a journalist compared with other parts of the world.However, reporters said the risks had intensified over time, driven by “declining public trust, narratives portraying the media as ‘fake news’, and blurred boundaries between journalists and the public” – meaning the rise of “citizen journalists” who have no journalistic training but have access to large online audiences.“The research findings make for grim reading,” said Laura Davison, the NUJ’s general secretary. “Abuse should never be viewed as part of a journalist’s job. Not only does this behaviour have a hugely detrimental impact on people’s lives, it also has a chilling effect on journalists’ ability to do their jobs and freedom of the press.“It’s also time for social media companies to finally recognise their responsibility in preventing the abuse and harassment.”A Department for Culture, Media and Sport spokesperson said the government was working with the National Committee for the Safety of Journalists to tackle harassment and threats.“It is crucial tocreate the conditions in which reporters feel supported and protected so that they can focus on telling the stories that matter most,” they said.Explore more on these topicsJournalist safetyPress freedomNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Birmingham council accused of giving ‘free rein’ to group erecting England flags | Birmingham | The Guardian
description: Campaigners call for injunction against Raise the Colours, which is accused of spreading anti-immigration rhetoric
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Campaigners call for injunction against Raise the Colours, which is accused of spreading anti-immigration rhetoric
Content: Raise the Colours describes itself as a grassroots movement ‘covering Britain in symbols of unity and patriotism’.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRaise the Colours describes itself as a grassroots movement ‘covering Britain in symbols of unity and patriotism’.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianBirminghamBirmingham council accused of giving ‘free rein’ to group erecting England flagsCampaigners call for injunction against Raise the Colours, which is accused of spreading anti-immigration rhetoricNeha GohilMidlands correspondentSun 26 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBirmingham residents have accused the local council and police of “dragging their heels” and giving “free rein” to a group responsible for erecting flags across the city.Raise the Colours, which describes itself as a grassroots movement, has been placing union jack and St George’s cross flags on lamp-posts, roundabouts and other public infrastructure since last summer.Although its website states it is a “campaign to cover Britain in symbols of unity and patriotism”, others have accused the group of racism and spreading anti-immigration rhetoric – claims it has denied.The Guardian spoke to residents in Birmingham who said they had met the city council and the West Midlands police and crime commissioner (PCC) several times in six months, highlighting concerns about the conduct of Raise the Colours and its activities.Sara*, a member of the Brummies United Against Racism group, said she wants the council to seek an injunction against the group. “We’ve been lobbying the council continuously to remove the flags and they’ve been really dragging their heels about it,” she said.During the meetings, Sara said the council and the PCC, Simon Foster, had been presented with a compilation of evidence with brief statements, videos and images, from residents of incidents and confrontations involving Raise the Colours and others.“Action needs to be taken against this group,” Sara said. “People are being intimidated, people are being threatened, people are being doxed [having personal information, such as home address, published online].“We’re hearing now that [the council] is weeks away from getting an injunction but for us, it’s a little too late.”Duncan Ali, a Green party councillor, said the council was in a “quagmire” over the issue but his party was committed to ensuring action would be taken. The Greens are in a minority administration with the Liberal Democrats and Better Birmingham Independent Group.View image in fullscreenDuncan Ali, a Green councillor, talks to the Guardian journalist Neha Gohil (right) about the behaviour of Raise The Flags.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The Guardian“There’s a huge amount of evidence of the aggressive, intimidating, violent behaviour of Raise the Colours and that is being used to request an injunction against that organisation,” Ali said. “As Green party councillors, I’m not going to sit back and let this continue. It will be stopped. It may take time, and it may cost money, but it will be stopped.”Oxfordshire county council successfully secured a high court injunction preventing the unauthorised hanging of flags, including St George’s cross and union flags, on or near public highways, specifically naming four individuals, including the Raise the Colours co-founder, Ryan Bridge.In itsclaim to the high court, the Lib Dem council in Oxford said contractors removing flags had been met “with hostility and obstruction”. The claim also acknowledged Bridge was arrested in Oxford on suspicion of causing religiously and racially aggravated harassment in April.View image in fullscreenRyan Bridge speaks during a protest in East Sussex.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Separately, he has been charged with common assault by Sussex police after an incident in Brighton in June.After Oxfordshire secured the injunction, Bridge, along with the others named, agreed to stop hoistingEnglandflags on lampposts in the region and to not encourage others to do so.Birmingham residents informed local authorities about an incident in May when a man was seriously injured in a hit-and-run after a group of people had gathered to remove flags. Two men have since been arrested in relation to the incident and released on bail, West Midlands police said.Adam*, a resident in Birmingham who took down flags that day, said: “It strikes me that there are set scripts that in any confrontation you have with Raise the Colours. First it’s, ‘Why do you hate the flag? You’re not patriotic’… Then it quickly leads to, ‘We’re against the boats coming in, stop the boats.’Oxfordshire council seeks injunction over flags tied to lamp-posts across countyRead more“I don’t think any boat has ever been stopped by a flag in a lamp-post,” he added.Sara said local officials in Birmingham were also told about the 10-year France travel ban against Bridge and others after the French interior ministry said “far-right” activists had attempted to stop migrants from crossing the Channel in small boats.In an interview with GB News in February, Bridge said he hadn’t committed a crime in France and he went to “document what’s not happening and its weak government and weak borders”.Sara said such incidents, as well as Oxford’s high court injunction, further validated the demands of Birmingham residents that the council could and should take action.“We compare Oxford’s response to Birmingham, where they have acted much more quickly,” she said. “Raise the Colours have been given a free rein of our city to put up flags.”West Midlands police said the decision to remove flags from public infrastructure was a “matter for the local authority or relevant highways agency”.“Our role is to ensure those authorities can carry out their work without incident, intimidation, or breach of the peace,” a spokesperson for the force said. “We understand the strength of feeling around the issue of flags and will continue to listen to the concerns of local communities.”Foster, the the West Midlands PCC, said: “I have consistently and repeatedly encouraged Birmingham city council and West Midlands police to take proactive and robust action to prevent and tackle any and all harassment, alarm, distress or other criminal behaviour associated with the illegal erection of flags and that includes an application for a civil injunction.“I trust that proactive and robust action will be taken to resolve this matter at the earliest possible opportunity.”A Birmingham city council said attaching unauthorised items, such as flags, to public infrastructure was “not permitted, and any such items will be removed”.They added: “We are aware that recent flag related activity has contributed to increased tensions in some areas, and we encourage all residents to act responsibly and respectfully to help maintain calm, reduce the risk of intimidation, and support community cohesion during this period.”Raise the Colours has been contacted for comment.*Names have been changed.Explore more on these topicsBirminghamEnglandLocal governmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: How the Met police spent £2.5m hiding spycop from former partner | Police | The Guardian
description: Spycops inquiry has revealed how Helen Steel was secretly monitored in her search for undercover officer who deceived her into relationship
Author: Rob Evans
Headline: Spycops inquiry has revealed how Helen Steel was secretly monitored in her search for undercover officer who deceived her into relationship
Content: Helen Steel with John Dines, who started a two-year relationship with her in 1990 before disappearing.Photograph: Courtesy of Helen SteelHelen Steel with John Dines, who started a two-year relationship with her in 1990 before disappearing.Photograph: Courtesy of Helen SteelSpycops scandalPoliceHow the Met police spent £2.5m hiding spycop from former partnerSpycops inquiry has revealed how Helen Steel was secretly monitored in her search for undercover officer who deceived her into relationshipRob EvansSat 25 Jul 2026 23.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 2pm on 14 December 2002, Helen Steel, a well-known leftwing campaigner, and her parents landed at Auckland airport for a family holiday. It had been a tiring journey, so they were irritated when they were delayed leaving the airport for an hour.What they did not know until recently is the reason for that delay. Their arrival had triggered a secret warning on Steel that had been put in place by police three weeks earlier. It prompted customs to carry out a discreet search of her luggage.Steel’s sister collected the family and drove them to her home 90 minutes away. Again, none of them knew surveillance officers employed by New Zealand police were tailing them.Nor did they know that over the next few weeks, police officers tracked their movements and took photographs of them. One picture was of them leaving her sister’s home.Details of this extraordinary operation came in yet another damning disclosure to the spycops public inquiry, which is examining the conduct of undercover police officers who spied on more than 1,000 political groupsbetween 1968 and at least 2010.The inquiry has heard in recent weeks how senior Scotland Yard officers arranged for the police force of a country 11,000 miles away to covertly monitor Steel on two of her trips there as part of a calculated plan to protect a secret.They feared that Steel was about to expose one of their undercover officers. The spy, John Dines, had had a sexual relationship with Steel for two years without disclosing his real identity to her. When he mysteriously vanished from her life, she set about tracking him down.View image in fullscreenJohn Dines seen operating undercover at a Greenpeace stall in the 1990s at an anti-McDonald’s event.Photograph: Spycops inquiryAs well as the surveillance, the senior officers authorised the expenditure of £2.5m of public funds to relocate Dines to ensure that Steel did not find him. This included helping him buy a new house.On Friday, Steel, giving evidence to the inquiry, said the surveillance and use of taxpayers’ money was an abuse of state powers to prevent her discovering how a police officer had “deceived and sexually exploited” her.She was “really angry” that theMetropolitan policehad put her and her family under surveillance, adding the police also wanted to protect an “illegitimate and undemocratic” operation, in which undercover officers such as Dines spied on tens of thousands of political campaigners across four decades.On Tuesday, Paul Condon, the former Met commissioner, admitted at the inquiry that Scotland Yard hadfailed to control the officersand their managers who committed “horrendous abuses”.These included monitoring grieving familiessuch as the parents of murdered teenager Stephen Lawrence, who were campaigning about police wrongdoing, stealing theidentities of dead children, andlying in court.When Dines started the relationship with Steel in 1990, she believed she had fallen in love with an ideal man in what felt like an “idyllic” relationship. He told her he wanted to have six children and spend the rest of his life with her.Who were the undercover cops who deceived women into sexual relations?Read moreBut in 1992, he disappeared from her life after claiming that he was having a mental breakdown. It was a lie to enable him to end his deployment.Steel has described how Dines had subjected her to a “sadistic and callous psychological torture over a prolonged period”. For six months, he had given her contradictory signals – repeatedly going missing, claiming that he could not handle their relationship and life, before returning and proclaiming his love for her.After he finally disappeared, Steel was devastated and also fearful that her missing partner might have been suicidal. She started to investigate who he really was as “none of it made any sense”.It took Steel nearly two decades to establish, by fitting together disparate clues and visiting many archives, that he had been an undercover spy.Documents before the inquiry now show that, while Steel was trying to trace Dines, Scotland Yard was secretly tracking her progress, logging, for example, how she had visited people who turned out to his relatives and who she was phoning.At one point, in 1995, police recorded that “an examination of telephone calls from Steel’s home also shows her to have been in contact” with the chambers of Keir Starmer, then a barrister supporting progressive causes.He was giving her legal advice as she had become a defendant in the celebrated McLibel case. Inthe longest trial in English history, she and another campaigner were sued by the fast food chain, McDonald’s, in a David and Goliath battle.The inquiry has previously heard howDines spied on Starmerand accessed the confidential details of his legal advice. In December 2002, Steel flew to New Zealand with her parents to visit her sister and friends for about two months.View image in fullscreenDave Morris and Helen Steel outside the high court in London at an appeal hearing in the McLibel case, which became the longest trial in English history.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyAt the behest of Scotland Yard, New Zealand police put them under surveillance and reported back. One police report set out the measures that would be put in place to “monitor Steel’s movements whilst in New Zealand … Thus far Steel has done little other than local shopping with her sister.” It added “urgent inquiries are in place to fully identify” her sister and family.Steel said that, although it was not the primary purpose of her visit, she also contacted people she believed could have been relatives of her former boyfriend to see if they would tell her where he now was.Revealed: at least 25 UK ‘spy cops’ had sex with deceived members of publicRead moreAs part of his fake identity while he worked undercover, Dines had said he had previously lived in New Zealand for part of his life.What Steel did not know at the time was that Dines was nearby – he had moved to New Zealand in 1995 after quitting the Metropolitan police and was working as a barrister in Auckland.Fearing that she would locate Dines, the senior police officers agreed to fund the costs of moving him and his family to Australia quickly.The £2.5m bill included the cost of subsidising the purchase of a house in Sydney, which was four times more expensive than his New Zealand home, and compensating him for his lost income as a barrister.The senior officers justified the expenditure on the grounds that Steel posed a threat to Dines. She rejected this claim as “malicious lies”, adding that the real reason was to protect Dines from bad publicity.The officers claim they did not know that Dines had had a sexual relationship with Steel, and did not question why she was so intent on finding him. It is a claim that has been dismissed as implausible by campaigners and lawyers at the inquiry, who point out that the undercover officers routinely formed sexual relationships with women they were spying on.Explore more on these topicsPoliceSpycops scandalUndercover police and policingUK civil libertiesHuman rightsMetropolitan policefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Joy in Greece as Mount Olympus joins Unesco list of world heritage sites | Unesco | The Guardian
description: Mythical home of the ancient Greek gods designated alongside the D-day landing beaches in Normandy
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Mythical home of the ancient Greek gods designated alongside the D-day landing beaches in Normandy
Content: A statue of Alexander the Great holding Nike, the Greek goddess of victory, with Mount Olympus in the background.Photograph: Petros Giannakouris/APView image in fullscreenA statue of Alexander the Great holding Nike, the Greek goddess of victory, with Mount Olympus in the background.Photograph: Petros Giannakouris/APUnescoJoy in Greece as Mount Olympus joins Unesco list of world heritage sitesMythical home of the ancient Greek gods designated alongside the D-day landing beaches in NormandyHelena Smithin AthensSun 26 Jul 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 15.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a 12-year wait, Mount Olympus, the mythical home of the ancient Greek gods, has been inducted into a hall of more modern fame asUnescoannounced it would be added to its world heritage list.Greece’s highest mountain made the list alongside the second world war D-day landing beaches in northernFranceand the ancient Japanese capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara. South Sudan’s Boma-Badingilo landscape, host to one of the world’s largest land mammal migrations, also won a designation – a first for the east African country.The nominations were among dozens reviewed at a Unesco committee meeting in Busan, South Korea, on Sunday.In the case of Olympus, inscribed as a mixed world heritage site in recognition of its cultural and natural significance, the news was met with near euphoria inGreece.Immortalised as the seat of Zeus, king of the 12 Olympian deities, the mountain rising 2,918 metres from a base near sea level had been on a tentative list of sites since 2014.View image in fullscreenA conservator prepares an ancient sculpture of the head of Zeus for exhibition in Melbourne, AustraliaPhotograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianThe head of Greece’s Unesco delegation in Busan, Georgios Koumoutsakos, hailed the decision as one that would ensure the site’s preservation.“It reaffirms our unwavering commitment to safeguarding Mount Olympus for the benefit of present and future generations,” he said. “As Greek mythology wisely reminds us, it is always best to remain on good terms with the gods.”The region’s mayor, Evangelos Geroliolios,said before the announcementthat the site’s induction would “place greater responsibility on our part to protect the [local] environment”, not least its extraordinary biodiversity.The committee’s annual meeting, which ends on Wednesday, is expected to examine about 30 nominations. Those successful will join 1,248 sites across 170 countries admitted to the world heritage list for their “outstanding value to humanity”.Inscribed monuments can provide a vital boost for their preservation under an international convention overseen by Unesco, which also gives advice and financial support. Other world heritage sites include the Acropolis in Athens, the Great Wall of China, the pyramids of Giza in Egypt and the Taj Mahal in India.As with Mount Olympus, efforts to get the D-day beaches in Normandy inscribed had gone back years.View image in fullscreenTourists visit Les Braves monument on Omaha beach in Normandy.Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPAIncluded in the French bid were all five of the beaches – Omaha, Utah, Sword, Gold and Juno – where more than 150,000 allied troops came ashore on 6 June 1944, and the Pointe du Hoc cliff that was also a focal point of the assault.The largest amphibious operation ever mounted, in which 4,000 soldiers died, was decisive in the battle to liberateEuropefrom Nazi occupation.France first nominated the 50-mile (80km) stretch of coastline in 2008. Reacting to the decision, the country’s permanent delegate to Unesco, Ahlem Gharbi, said the designation carried particular weight at a time of such international tensions.The president of the Normandy region, Hervé Morin, who had championed the cause, maintained that inclusion on the list would represent “immense recognition” for the soldiers who had sacrificed so much to defeat Nazism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEchoing Greek officials, he said: “This decision places a responsibility upon us. It compels us to preserve this site, to protect it, to cherish it even more, and to promote its value.”View image in fullscreenAllied troops come ashore near Vierville sur Mer on 6 June 1944.Photograph: ReutersThe international council on monuments and sites, one of the bodies that recommends additions to the Unesco list, had previously warned of the threat posed to the Normandy sites by tourism, climate change, rising sea levels and nearby windfarm development, and had called for stronger monitoring and preservation.The coastline is covered with extensive remnants of the time of the landings, including concrete German bunkers and gun positions, sunken vessels and allied installations.Unesco said in a statement that the beaches formed an “exceptional cultural landscape shaped both by the events of 1944 and by their enduring remembrance”, all of which justified further protection. As with Mount Olympus, the landing points have attracted record numbers of tourists in recent years.The agency’s move to include places associated with conflict has fuelled controversial debate over whether “sites of memory” are befitting of world heritage status and Unesco’s stated mission to “foster a world of greater equality and peace”.Three sites used by Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge regime for torture and execution were inscribed last year.After so many years of campaigning, Greek officials said Sunday’s decision had been made all the sweeter given signs of further delays.In the draft agenda of this week’s meeting, Unesco had signalled the Mount Olympus file would be referred back to the country for further details, spurring fears that proved to be baseless when the nomination won unanimous support.Explore more on these topicsUnescoGreeceFranceSecond world warHeritageEuropeUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Romania summons Russia’s ambassador after downing third drone since Friday | Romania | The Guardian
description: F-16 fighter jet intercepted drone in Romanian airspace over Black Sea, defence minister says
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: F-16 fighter jet intercepted drone in Romanian airspace over Black Sea, defence minister says
Content: Romanian F-16s. The country’s president said Friday’s drone was a ‘Shahed model used by the Russian Federation in its war of aggression against Ukraine’.Photograph: Andreea Alexandru/APView image in fullscreenRomanian F-16s. The country’s president said Friday’s drone was a ‘Shahed model used by the Russian Federation in its war of aggression against Ukraine’.Photograph: Andreea Alexandru/APRomaniaRomania summons Russia’s ambassador after downing third drone since FridayF-16 fighter jet intercepted drone in Romanian airspace over Black Sea, defence minister saysAgence France-Presse in BucharestSun 26 Jul 2026 10.44 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRomania has said it is summoning Russia’s ambassador after the Nato member’s military shot down a third drone in as many days.Romania has experienced frequentdrone incursionssince Russia launched its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, but had not shot down any until Friday.On Sunday, a Romanian F-16 fighter jet shot down a drone over the Black Sea, five minutes after it entered the country’s airspace, Romania’s defence minister, Radu Miruță, said on Facebook.The foreign minister, Oana Țoiu, said Romania was summoning Russia’s ambassador after “repeated violations”.The Romanian president, Nicușor Dan, said that according to an investigation, a drone shot down on Friday was a “Shahed model used by the Russian Federation in its war of aggression against Ukraine”.Investigations into drones shot down on Saturday and Sunday continued, he said.“It is unacceptable and intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania’s airspace, which is also the airspace of Nato and the European Union,” Dan said on X.The drone shot down on Sunday also appeared to be of “Russian origin”, Martin O’Donnell, a senior Nato military spokesperson, said.He said the downing of the drones came as Romania and other Nato countries were actively acquiring “ground-based interceptors” to increase their air defences.Romania integrated the US-made Merops counter-drone system into its defences at the end of June. AI-powered, the mobile system is designed to intercept small targets flying at low altitudes.The country has reported dozens of drone incursions since the start of the Ukraine war. One smashed into a residential building in Galați on the border with Ukraine in May, wounding two people.Romania’s parliament adopted a law in 2025 allowing drones that breach its airspace to be shot down.Several countries near the Ukraine conflict have shot down drones since the war started.Explore more on these topicsRomaniaRussiaDrones (military)UkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: He’s a doctor and a progressive. Will he win a key US Senate race in Michigan? | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Abdul El-Sayed may be buoyed by a younger, anti-establishment coalition as he runs against an establishment candidate
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Abdul El-Sayed may be buoyed by a younger, anti-establishment coalition as he runs against an establishment candidate
Content: Abdul El-Sayed in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on 21 February 22026.Illustration: Evan Cobb/The Washington Post/Getty Images/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenAbdul El-Sayed in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on 21 February 22026.Illustration: Evan Cobb/The Washington Post/Getty Images/Guardian DesignUS midterm elections 2026He’s a doctor and a progressive. Will he win a key US Senate race in Michigan?Abdul El-Sayed may be buoyed by a younger, anti-establishment coalition as he runs against an establishment candidateJoseph Gedeonin Detroit, MichiganSun 26 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTShareAbdul El-Sayed spends a fair amount of his day not taking himself so seriously. He jokes about his haircut, films selfie videos with supporters and has taken – more than once – to cringey dancing and lip-syncing on camera.But ask him after a long day on the campaign trail to explain the difference between a virus and a bacterium, and the epidemiologist takes over from the entertainer.El-Sayed, running inMichiganto be the Democratic candidate for US Senate this November, is trying to strike a delicate balance between policy wonk and performer – capable of detailing the mechanics of the proposed Medicare for All system of universal healthcare one minute and delivering a punchline the next.At a moment when American politics has become conspicuously humorless, he is an unusual political persona. And in a matter of days, on 4 August, MichiganDemocratswill decide whether he’s their type to send him to the United States Senate.El-Sayed faces the more moderate representative Haley Stevens, who has the backing of the Democratic party establishment. The duo are virtually neck-and-neck at the polls – raising the prospect of the party’s grassroots voters again defying the wishes of its leaders.While astring of socialist victoriesacross Democratic primaries in recent months has boosted the left of the party, El-Sayed rejects the label. He just wants capitalism that works.El-Sayed, 41, has tried, and failed, to win office before: in 2018, he lost the Democratic gubernatorial race in Michigan. Has the younger, anti-establishment coalition he now represents grown larger than the one that rejected him eight years ago? El-Sayed believes it has.“I think people are sick and tired of the establishments on both sides of that, and I think we are having success because we’re speaking to that frustration,” he said. “And politics doesn’t have to suck, and you can build a politics that doesn’t suck.”Matt Grossman, director of Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research, points to a broader realignment inside the Democratic party. Voters in Michigan are united more by frustration with Democratic leadership, he suggested, than by agreement on every policy question.“In the previous campaign, El-Sayed was more the Bernie candidate – affiliated with a particular faction of the Democratic party,” Grossman said, referring to the progressive US senator Bernie Sanders. “Now, he’s more representative of a broader group of voters on the left side of the Democratic primary, who are anti-institutional or newly grassroots.”View image in fullscreenFrom left, Bernie Sanders, Abdul El-Sayed and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the People v the Powerful rally in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on 19 July 2026.Photograph: Chris duMond/ShutterstockNext month’s Michigan primary will test whether that coalition is now large enough to nominate one of its own as a Democratic candidate for Washington.El-Sayed insists he didn’t plan to run in this year’s US midterm elections. Heading into 2025, he said, “I thought I was going to keep doing what I was doing” – running Wayne county’s public health department, trying to keep key programs and health centers afloat as Donald Trump’s administration wielded the axe.“The straw that broke the camel’s back was when they froze federal funds,” El-Sayed recalled in an interview. “I’m sitting here trying to figure out how to flow programs like [nutrition support initiative] Wic and federally qualified health centers and vaccines, and meanwhile we’re watching our tax dollars get sent abroad to drop bombs on other people’s kids.”Throughout his campaign, El-Sayed has frequently tied the Israel-Gaza war, which he unflinchingly calls a genocide, and other conflicts involving the US to affordability at home. “Every time you want to put glasses on kids, people ask you: ‘Doctor, how are you going to pay for that?’” he said. “Nobody asks the general how he’s going to pay for the next war.”The roots of this worldview long predate this campaign, and run through Egypt, where El-Sayed spent childhood summers with his father’s family.He describes the country as both “glorious”, because of the fullness of family and social life, and “painful”, because of the strict political order surrounding it, and the role that decades of US military support helped play in sustaining it.“There’s no world in which, had I been born in Egypt, like I was supposed to, I would ever be able to run for office,” said El-Sayed. “That’s the thing I got to do, because I’m an American.”El-Sayed credits his grandmother, whom he calls the smartest person he ever knew, for teaching him that, while talent is distributed widely, opportunity is not.“I’m playing with house money, man,” he said. “Put all the chips back on the table and try and do something new. I was supposed to be a cab driver in Egypt. That’s not my life.”Instead, as a student, he was a starting defenseman on the University of Michigan lacrosse team, vice-president of its Muslim Students Association and, in 2007, the university’s first Rhodes scholar in years. He studied at Oxford, attended Columbia medical school and eventually entered public health,rather than private practice.“He was always the smartest guy, the awesome guy who can work the room,” said Mohamad Issa, a head and neck cancer surgeon in Ohio who knew El-Sayed during his college years. “The first person there. The last person to leave.”Issa remembers approaching El-Sayed after a game of basketball as a nervous freshman, having earned disappointing grades in his first science classes. He had been told by an adviser that medicine might not be for him.El-Sayed, then a student athlete, spent months mentoring him, offering study strategies that Issa says transformed his academic career. Two decades later, Issa says, he still teaches those same techniques to students he mentors today.“He’s a bro,” Issa said. “That’s all you gotta know.”After years of research and being an instructor, El-Sayed led Detroit’s health department after the city’s bankruptcy, then took over Wayne county’s, where he helped cancel roughly $700m in medical debt affecting 300,000 Michiganders.“He almost has an idealistic pressure in his mind about wanting to live fully, in a way that is admirable,” said Dr Sandro Galea, dean of public health at Washington University, who has known El-Sayed for more than 20 years. “It comes from a sense of wanting to do right by people, wanting to help in a better world for people.”El-Sayed sees government service, and elected office, “as an important pathway to doing that”, suggested Galea.In part, that is why he pushes back when the socialist label is used to describe his platform. “I’m a scientist,” he said. “I want to solve problems.”His critique of the economy is not that markets can never work, but that concentrated corporate power has prevented them from working as advertised. “If the markets actually worked the way they’re supposed to, you might have some efficient movement of money,” he said. “The problem is, we don’t live in capitalism, we live in oligopoly.”El-Sayed points to universal healthcare. Private insurers make money from people when they are younger and healthier, he says, before handing them to the government at 65, when their care becomes more expensive. A rational system would spread those costs across a lifetime, according to him, rather than privatize the profitable years and socialize the costly ones.For El-Sayed, the question is ultimately the same one he absorbed in Egypt, at school, in his research and from his grandmother: who is permitted to benefit from the institutions around them–and who is expected merely to endure them?With that message, he has gained ground inside the Democratic electorate, with rallies attended by hundreds of eager Michiganders from across the political spectrum, though the party establishment has been considerably slower to follow.Chuck Schumer, the US Senate minority leader, and retiring senator Gary Peters have backed Stevens, reflecting the party leadership’s preference for the more conventional candidate. El-Sayed, meanwhile, has assembled a different coalition, winning recent endorsements from the likes of progressive representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders.The divide reflects a broader disagreement inside the party over what will help it win.Grossman, at Michigan State University, does not believe the concern driving figures at the top of the Democratic party to oppose El-Sayed is primarily ideological. It is, he said, more about what a victory by someone to Stevens’s left would signal nationally.“The concern from Washington is more about the long-term image of the Democratic party and whether someone closer to El-Sayed’s politics would make it harder to hold the seat in future elections,” said Grossman. “I don’t think Abdul will suffer a major penalty for ideology in this election.”El-Sayed has faced unusually determined resistance.Not everyone inside the party embraces his offering. Lon Johnson, a former chair of the Michigan Democratic party who supports Stevens, argued El-Sayed’s politics could ultimately cost Democrats one of their best opportunities to retake control of the US Senate. “There is real concern that Abdul would not be able to beat [Republican Mike] Rogers and then potentially lose us a majority possibility in the Senate,” Johnson said.Outside groups, led by the pro-Israel lobbying network Aipac and its affiliated political funds and committees, have poured roughly $30m into the race on behalf of Stevens, making Michigan one of the most expensive Democratic primaries in the country.While El-Sayed continues to speak out about Israel’s destruction of Gaza, ads have leaned heavily on domestic issues, highlighting Stevens’s experience working with the Obama administration’s auto rescue in 2008.An uncertain raceThe race remains unusually difficult to read.Stevens, a four-term representative who has repeatedly won competitive districts, has cast herself as the Democrat with the proven record against Republicans, and sometimes aligning with them – and warned that national Republicans would rather face El-Sayed in November.A Detroit News/WDIV poll in mid-July showed Stevens ahead by seven points. Roughly 10 days later, another tracking poll showed El-Sayed ahead by the same margin.He will face one of his biggest challenges in Detroit, particularly in winning over the city’s Black voters, who have decided most competitive Democratic primaries in Michigan.Asked directly whether he’s done enough outreach, El-Sayed did not argue with the premise. “We’ve never done enough in politics,” he said. “There’s always more that could be done.”Republicans have already begun preparing for a potential El-Sayed nomination. The National Republican Senatorial Committee hasbranded him“the most radical Democrat Senate nominee of the cycle”, highlighting his support for Medicare for All, abolishing ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) and his criticism of Israel as evidence he is out of step with a battleground state like Michigan.Waiting in November for whomever emerges from the Democratic primary is their party’s candidate, Mike Rogers.El-Sayed dismisses the man he may face in November as a beneficiary of the same political system he argues has rewarded corporations while leaving ordinary Americans behind.When it comes to the tens of millions of dollars from pro-Israel organizations spent against him, he remains similarly unfazed. “If your product sucks, don’t be surprised if people don’t buy it,” he said.That the race remains uncertain despite support for Stevens from powerful figures in the Democratic party shows how far El-Sayed has come since 2018.Eight years ago, he represented a faction. Today, he represents a coalition the party establishment is no longer certain it can stop.This broader voter base is younger, more skeptical of party institutions and increasingly unwilling to separate economic inequality from US foreign policy, particularly on Israel. El-Sayed says he’d rather lose than win and compromise on these beliefs.“The paradox here is that the way to win is to actually have values, because people at least know what you’re for,” he said. “The hope is that people with more power than me fear that I’ll step up to them, and people with less power than me never think I’m arrogant.”

title: Venezuelan men sue aviation firms who flew them to notorious Salvadorian jail | US news | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: CSI Aviation and GlobalX accused of violating civil rights as part of Trump immigration crackdown
Author: José Olivares
Headline: Exclusive: CSI Aviation and GlobalX accused of violating civil rights as part of Trump immigration crackdown
Content: The Cecot prison in Tecoluca, El Salvador, where the Venezuelans deported from the US were imprisoned.Photograph: John Moore/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Cecot prison in Tecoluca, El Salvador, where the Venezuelans deported from the US were imprisoned.Photograph: John Moore/Getty ImagesUS newsVenezuelan men sue aviation firms who flew them to notorious Salvadorian jailExclusive: CSI Aviation and GlobalX accused of violating civil rights as part of Trump immigration crackdownJosé Olivaresin New YorkSun 26 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 08.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVenezuelan men sent last year to a notorious Salvadorian terrorism prison by the Trump administration are suing the US aviation companies that transported them there.Alawsuitfiled this week in federal court in Washington DC accuses the companies CSI Aviation and GlobalX of violating the Venezuelans’ civil rights, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence and other violations, for their role in flying the three planes that took the men to El Salvador.CSI and GlobalX “went to great lengths” to undertake the “rendition flights” toEl Salvador, “in concert with the US government, in flagrant violation of US and international law”, the lawsuit reads.Last year, in March, the Trump administration expelled more than 230 Venezuelan men held in US immigration custody to El Salvador, where they were detained for four months in a maximum security terrorism prison andtortured.The lawsuit accuses CSI and GlobalX of deliberately transporting the men to El Salvador, despite a federal judge ordering the flights to return and despite knowing they would probably be tortured inside the country’s Terrorism Confinement Center (known as “Cecot” by its acronym in Spanish).Without CSI and GlobalX’s complicity, “neither Plaintiffs nor the Class would have been rendered to CECOT”, the lawsuit reads.The suit was filed by a team of human rights attorneys on 17 July and is being reported first by the Guardian. It is one of the latest attempts by rights groups to hold private contractors accountable for their role in alleged abuses stemming from theadministration’s aggressiveanti-immigrant crackdown.Venezuelans deported by Trump to El Salvador describe ‘horror movie’ mega-prisonRead more“Many people might not be aware of the degree to which private companies are intertwined with the human rights abuses occurring under the Trump administration through the detention and unlawful deportation schemes that are occurring,” said Anthony Enriquez, the vice-president of advocacy and litigation for the Kennedy Human Rights Center, in an interview with the Guardian. Enriquez is one of the attorneys representing the Venezuelan men.CSI and GlobalX, which were hired by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), have “enjoyed unprecedented financial profits from the scheme”, while the Venezuelans “continue to experience severe emotional suffering from the humiliation, terror, and cruelty that they endured”, the lawsuit says.The DHS did not respond to specific claims in the lawsuit and instead referred all questions to the Salvadorian government. CSI and GlobalX did not respond to a detailed request for comment by time of publication.El Salvador’s government does not make efforts to publicly rebut allegations of brutal treatment inside Cecot. Online influencers areinvited into make videos of the harsh conditions.CSI Aviation Inc is incorporated in Texas and GlobalX is headquartered in Florida, with both companies playing a significant role in the administration’s mass deportation campaign. The lawsuit says that the American companies were hired by the US government to conduct the El Salvador-bound deportation flights.CSI has helped broker “nearly all” deportation flights, the lawsuit says, via a multimillion-dollar contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the main agency within the DHS carrying out deportations. CSI is the single highest-value recipient of ICE contracts, the lawsuit adds, with revenue from ICE in 2025 totaling $1.23bn.For the three flights to El Salvador, CSI sub-contracted with GlobalX, with CSI working as the “intermediary” between ICE and GlobalX, according to the lawsuit.On 15 March last year, Donald Trump stepped outside government norms toinvokethe Alien Enemies Act as a strategy to expel hundreds of Venezuelan immigrants from the US. The US president accused the Venezuelan government, at the time run byNicolás Maduro, who is nowfacing trialin the US, of instructing members of the South American gangTren de Araguato “invade” the US.After invoking the Alien Enemies Act, the administration rounded up 252 Venezuelan and Salvadorian men in ICE detention and expelled them to El Salvador. This came after the US and El Salvador struck acontroversialandopaquedeal, in which the US would paymillions of dollarsto El Salvador to detain deportees from the US in Cecot. The administration never proved, and has still not proved, the Venezuelan men were members of Tren de Aragua.The same day that the Alien Enemies Act was invoked, GlobalX, “working at the behest of CSI”, positioned three planes at an airport in Texas in preparation for the expulsion, the lawsuit says.After the flights hadtaken offto Central America, a federal judge in Washington DCorderedthey return to the US. The administration and airline companiesignoredthe court order and eventually arrived in El Salvador.“Despite knowing that El Salvador’s Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo (‘CECOT’) mega-prison was a notorious blacksite, from which no detainee had ever left alive, Defendants went to great lengths to transport Plaintiffs and Class Members there, in concert with the US government, in flagrant violation of U.S. and international law,” the lawsuit reads. “Defendants evaded or ignored judicial oversight and the foreseeable risk of torture and successfully delivered Plaintiffs and the Class to El Salvador for imprisonment at CECOT.”The real horror began for the men once they landed in El Salvador, with many thinking they had at least arrived home to Venezuela. Salvadorian security forces boarded the planes, beat the deportees, manylater said, and transported them to Cecot.According to a November 2025reportfrom Human Rights Watch, the men were “subjected to what amounts to arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance under international human rights law”.The HRW report and lawsuit also detail brutal conditions and torture inside Cecot, accusing guards of beating, pepper-spraying, firing rubber bullets and sexually assaulting detainees.Lawmakers, families and members of the public protested against the immigrants’ detention in Cecot. News reportsrevealedthe identities of some of the men, showing that some were falsely accused of being gang members.Four months later, in July 2025, the group of Venezuelans were returned to their home country after a prisoner exchange deal involving the three countries. The group of Salvadorians, also sent to Cecot in those flights, are still presumably detained there. To this date, the US government has not released the entire list of deportees sent to Cecot.The Venezuelan men continue tostrugglewith long-lasting health effects and mental healthtrauma, the lawsuit says. The three main plaintiffs in the case experience daily headaches, difficulty sleeping and emotional distress from the experience.CSI and GlobalX “have enjoyed unprecedented financial profits from the scheme and their relationship with the Administration”, the lawsuit says, while the Venezuelan men “continue to experience severe emotional suffering from the humiliation, terror, and cruelty that they endured”.The companies have not yet responded to the lawsuit. Federal judge James Boasberg, who is presiding over the original Cecot deportation case, will be overseeing the lawsuit’s proceedings and determine whether the entire class of Venezuelans can sue.Explore more on these topicsUS newsEl SalvadorAmericasVenezuelaUS immigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Weekday games were amazing’: pubs toast extra £150m in World Cup sales | Hospitality industry | The Guardian
description: England’s progress provides best football-related uplift of recent years, with one pub too packed to host its Dolly Parton tribute
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: England’s progress provides best football-related uplift of recent years, with one pub too packed to host its Dolly Parton tribute
Content: Pub sales over the course of the tournament were 16% higher than normal, said the payments provider Dojo.Photograph: Scott Heppell/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenPub sales over the course of the tournament were 16% higher than normal, said the payments provider Dojo.Photograph: Scott Heppell/AFP/GettyHospitality industry‘Weekday games were amazing’: pubs toast extra £150m in World Cup salesEngland’s progress provides best football-related uplift of recent years, with one pub too packed to host its Dolly Parton tributeRob DaviesSun 26 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLate opening hours and England’s progress to the semi-final of an expanded World Cup helped provide the best football-related uplift of recent years for pubs, figures suggest.Pubs poured 30m extra pints over the course of the tournament compared with a normal trading period, with busy pumps delivering £150m in added sales, according to the British Beer &PubsAssociation (BBPA).The World Cup-related increase in sales, as fans followed England and Scotland games, also appears to have outstripped that seen during previous competitions, including England’s run to the final of Euro 2024.The standout day over the course of the last three tournaments, in terms of sales uplift relative to a normal shift, was England’s game against Mexico in the early hours of the morning, according to data from the payment systems provider Epos Now.Sales nearly doubled on that day compared with the same period pre-tournament, as pubs were permitted to open through the night and could trade in regular hours as well.View image in fullscreenSales nearly doubled on the day of England’s game against Mexico.Photograph: Scott Heppell/AFP/GettyThree other games delivered a two-thirds increase in the number of transactions, according to the data.By contrast, only two games at each of Qatar 2022 and Euro 2024 led to an increase of more than 50%.Another payments provider, Dojo, said sales over the entire course of the tournament were 16% higher than normal, while the overall World Cup-related boost was 9% better than in Euro 2024.The rise in sales was swiftly followed by a £100m aid package for pubs from Andy Burnham, who announced a 20% cut in business rates for the sector on Thursday. While the government policy wascriticised for a lack of ambition, the dual benefits of the tax cut and the football brought rare respite for the hard-pressed industry, which recordedone pub a day closing last year, in England and Wales.View image in fullscreenThe combination of the World Cup and Andy Burnham’s £100m aid package brought rare respite for the pub industry.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma/ShutterstockDawn Slater, who runs the Garrick’s Head pub in Greater Manchester, said she and her staff had more than doubled their sales compared with previous tournaments after expanding capacity outside and installing giant screens.“It’s been really busy, fully booked every game. We stopped entry two hours before each game.“People definitely spent more money on this tournament but it was also more expensive to put it on. We had extra TVs, an outside bar. Plastic cups and pitchers alone cost us £8,700. But the take was good.“I’ve had to be here from 10am staying open till 2am most games and getting in bed at 5am. It was worth every minute, I wouldn’t change anything.”However, busy match days were often followed by quieter periods, offsetting some of the gains, with trading dependent on England’s progress.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The weekday games were amazing,” said Amy Williams, who runs the George in Witham with her husband, Tom. “We had a 300-400% increase in sales on our tills compared to the previous week.“For the Norway game we had a Dolly Parton tribute act but we cancelled her because there was no way she would have had space to perform.”View image in fullscreenMany pubs extended capacity outside or put up big screens for the World Cup.Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian“Sunday, for the final, we had a few people turn up. Had England got through it would have been a fantastic week but a lot of people didn’t come out that weekend. We’re normally busy but it was the quietest.“There was definitely a drop in sales the day before and the day after. The next day [after England’s loss to Argentina] was like a ghost town.”The World Cup benefit was not equally felt across the hospitality sector, with restaurants struggling in the hot weather.Mitchells & Butlers, the UK’s largest hospitality chain, reported flat sales in the third quarter of the year, as improvement in its pubs division during the World Cup was offset by the hot weather deterring customers from brands such as Toby Carvery.Restaurant groups that reported sales to the data analysis firm NIQ said sales were down by 0.7% year on year in June, making it the second worst month of 2026.Explore more on these topicsHospitality industryPubsWorld Cup 2026featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘Andy Burnham can grow a moustache!’: SNL UK’s Paddy Young on breakout stardom – and impersonating the new PM | Saturday Night Live | The Guardian
description: Not even a grisly hand injury could halt the rise of the Saturday Night Live UK comedian. And soon he’ll get to parody the prime minister every week. So why can’t he enjoy the good times?
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: Not even a grisly hand injury could halt the rise of the Saturday Night Live UK comedian. And soon he’ll get to parody the prime minister every week. So why can’t he enjoy the good times?
Content: Paddy Young … ‘I sort of feel like a 68-year-old bloke – like it’s all gone to pot’.Photograph: Sophie GiddonsView image in fullscreenPaddy Young … ‘I sort of feel like a 68-year-old bloke – like it’s all gone to pot’.Photograph: Sophie GiddonsSaturday Night LiveInterview‘Andy Burnham can grow a moustache!’: SNL UK’s Paddy Young on breakout stardom – and impersonating the new PMRachel AroestiNot even a grisly hand injury could halt the rise of the Saturday Night Live UK comedian. And soon he’ll get to parody the prime minister every week. So why can’t he enjoy the good times?Sun 26 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe day before I’m supposed to watch Paddy Young perform a work-in-progress version of his new show Will Sir Be Laughing Alone?, I’m told the gig has been cancelled; the standup has sliced his hand open and is about to have surgery. Soon after, Young shares aphoto of himself on Instagramin a hospital gown, thanking the Australian comedian Sam Campbell for “bringing the sword to my home” – a post quickly rehashed by the tabloids (The Mirror: “SNL UK star Paddy Young hospitalised after samurai sword accident”). When I finally see him on stage a fortnight later, he’s dosed up on codeine, his arm is in a sling and he’s in the uncertain early stages of refashioning this bizarre anecdote into a routine.“You’re getting an exclusive on the hand,” he tells me in an east London coffee shop the next day, after I’ve opened a bottle of water for him. Young and Campbell, who recently collaborated on the winningly madcap Channel 4 series Make That Movie, were preparing to host their occasional comedy night Floggers, which involves them dressing up as old men (fat suits, wigs, prosthetics) and helming a real daytime TV-style auction. Campbell had ordered the sword online as a prop, and when the pair’s Uber arrived Young hurriedly picked up the bag it was in. “Blood splattered up the wall like Kill Bill – we all laughed initially.” When his housemates removed the tea towel they’d wrapped around his hand “they could see yellow, which I think is tendon or muscle. Then I fainted.” He went to A&E for stitches but still did the show afterwards – “I cringe thinking about it because I was basically juggling [in the show]” – returning to hospital later to learn that one tendon was 90% lacerated and required an operation. Just before surgery, Young passed out again.View image in fullscreenHave they got news for you … Paddy with his Weekend Update co-anchor Ania Magliano.Photograph: Sky UKRiding high on the triumph ofSaturday Night LiveUK’s critically acclaimed first series – he co-anchors Weekend Update, the show’s satirical news segment, alongside Ania Magliano – Young was already about to embark on the busiest summer of his life: the Edinburgh fringe, an acting job, a new podcast, numerous Floggers shows. Now he’s cramming various medical appointments into his overstuffed diary, his recovery complicated by his inability to stay conscious. This is partly due to a severe phobia of needles, something that’s making him feel “truly pathetic”. As a veteran fainter myself, I tell him something I only recently discovered; it’s one of the five trauma responses: fight, flight, freeze, fawn and, in this case, flop. The term could describe “how I respond to a lot of things”, nods the 34-year-old. “I’m such a flop it’s unbelievable.”If you’ve only ever seen Young behind his desk at SNL – dapper, puckish, impossibly telegenic and armed with an arsenal of edgy current affairs zingers (plus a faintly worrying fixation with K-pop boyband BTS) – you might struggle to picture him as a failure. But in his sublimely funny standup, he’s a different beast: an indignant northern underdog, a messy millennial manchild of the people, a mordant poster boy for Generation Rent hissing at home-owning audience members. In his 2023 Edinburgh newcomer award-nominated show Hungry, Horny, Scared, he mined comic gold from bleak houseshares (his flat may have been freezing but at least he had an overheating 2012 Lenovo laptop for warmth), interspersed with anecdotes about his medical-grade childhood bed-wetting. (He was eventually assigned a specialist nurse: “How much piss is that? The NHS is getting involved …”)double quotation markYou pat yourself on the back because your video gets 200,000 views but someone getting hit with a frying pan might get 30mI had imagined this low-status shtick was mostly an act, but in person Young really does seem preoccupied with his weaknesses and rotten luck. He possesses none of the himbo-ish mischievousness of his Weekend Update performance. Instead, he’s a fast-talking, winningly candid overthinker with an “incredible talent” for seeing himself as a loser and a compulsion for self-reproach that is both completely ridiculous and extremely relatable. “I feel like I’m constantly either wronging someone or being wronged. I leave most situations thinking I really fumbled and fucked it up – or I’ve been betrayed.” (Same.)Young’s living situation is the overarching theme of his standup; this new show sees him contemplate singledom and his “bachelor” lifestyle (he finds the term amusing). Although he no longer cohabits with strangers in misery – he lives with fellow comedians Horatio Gould and Bebe Cave – he has a grim fascination with “people that have never got out of flatshares. I’ve always thought that’s going to be me.” He’s so fixated on this fate that he often imagines it’s already a reality. “I sort of feel like a 68-year-old bloke – like it’s all gone to pot and it hasn’t at all.” While some of his anxieties stem from his precarious profession, Young’s jokes are ultimately rooted in a near-universal struggle: making ends meet in London if you don’t come “from insane wealth”.View image in fullscreen‘A messy millennial manchild of the people’ … Paddy Young on stage.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanYoung grew up in Scarborough, north Yorkshire. As a schoolboy he was “so small” with no sporting talent, finding a social circle and sense of direction through his drama lessons at the Stephen Joseph theatre. It was helmed at the time by Alan Ayckbourn, one of Britain’s most prolific and popular playwrights, who cast a 10-year-old Young in one of his productions, his first professional acting gig. Ayckbourn even gave Young financial support after he won a placeat Manchester School of Theatre. He was an inconsistent student, he claims; revelling in small comic turns yet performing poorly when cast as a serious lead.After graduating, he tentatively tried standup. He was a comedy obsessive: Laurel and Hardy, Derek and Clive, Blue Jam, his dad’s collection of Viz comics, which “looked like the Beano but they were saying terrible things – that literally changed my brain chemistry”. His “extremely funny” mum was also an inspiration. Yet his early years on the circuit were awful; “going to these rubbish nights and being truly, truly depressed, then bombing and running away”. He has since realised his shtick doesn’t work at the open-mic nights that are a rite of passage for most fledgling comedians because of how he “plays with status” on stage. “I love the game of pretending it’s all falling apart, even though it actually isn’t. That doesn’t work at a gig that is actually bad.” What made him stick with comedy through the tough times? “I’m really fascinated by it – there is nothing else I think about.” He felt “mad” but had a deep-seated conviction he “could be good”.double quotation markShave off my moustache? I don’t know where my career would be without it. It’s like scaffoldingYoung’s career first began gaining traction in 2022, partly as a result of his Instagram sketches with the comedian Ed Night (“The love of my life”), which I return to repeatedly like favourite songs. The pair often parody content creators – conspiracy-minded podcasters, board game influencers and whatever people who make day-in-the-life vlogs are called – whose output Young describes as “the end of culture, but I can’t take my eyes off it”.Yet virality is relative. “You might pat yourself on the back because 200,000 people watch your video but then you scroll down and someone’s getting hit with a frying pan and it’s got 30m.” He doesn’t particularly like social media and thinks he’s “probably doing it completely wrong. It’s geared to be all about consistency” – posting “all the time” – whereas he and Night have a backlog of sketches they’ve never uploaded because they don’t think they’re up to scratch. He also feels slightly unsettled by how little work this kind of content requires compared with crafting an hour of standup. It’s a similar story with his new agony uncle podcast, Paddy Will Help (working tagline: “Oprah for blokes”). When we speak he’s in the process of workshopping the format, but knows he won’t be winging it with the kind of free-flowing parasocial banter his peers churn out. He likes finessing his material. “I couldn’t just be sat on the sofa chatting.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSounds to me as if he’s got integrity, yet Young also sees this as a failure to capitalise on his success (he has learned from friends that standups who pivot to podcasting “earn more than TV comedians”). While his peers discuss their five-year plans and audition strategies, “I’m fumbling in the dark. Everything I do, genuinely, there is no plan.”In the end he didn’t need one. Last year, he was cast in SNL UK: a huge opportunity he knew he was perfectly suited for (when he was told about the British version, his first thought was: “I have to do this. There’s less being made than ever and it just feels like you’re not quite right [for most TV projects],” hetold me in February). The show has offered him unexpected job security, the chance to break out of his own social media bubble – after just one month its sketches had amassed more than 86m online views – and a dose of surreal glamour. “You’re running down the corridor to get a wig fitted and then you pass Louis Theroux chatting to a beefeater. It really does feel like showbusiness, which nothing else does.” That said, being recognised in public isn’t the panacea he imagined. “You feel like someone’s got something on you – they know me and I don’t know them.”Young may need to prepare for more fan encounters: his SNL star is rising.
