Weekend Update has featured some surprisingly bracing satire and some genuinely great comic writing (“This week, former entertainer and entertainer of sixth-formers, Russell Brand …”). The more I watched, however, the more I became convinced of Young’s ability to sell literally any gag with a choice look or inflection. Initially, he begs to differ: “If it’s a joke I don’t like, I can’t say it – it pains me.” Yet trapped behind his desk, he is gradually finding “a way to pretend” if he’s not fully on board. Although he’s allowed to veto any quips he really doesn’t like – he tries to steer away from poking fun at voters of specific political parties, for example – he thinks it’s important to take this rare chance to really push the envelope. “There are people on set that are 30 years older than me that tell me they’ve never got away with this on TV.”‘How could this be anything other than funny?!’ Behind the scenes of Saturday Night Live UKRead moreOne slightly disappointing thing about the first series of SNL UK was how underutilised Young was as a comic actor. No longer: in the final episode of last season, he played Andy Burnham in a sketch about politicians jostling to become the next prime minister. Given the former mayor of Manchester ascent to the top job, Young looks set to reprise the role regularly next season. His Burnham isn’t a million miles away from his standup persona – they both use “shagger” as a term of endearment and hold southern extravagance in theatrical contempt – but the icing on the cake would be if Burnham “could grow a moustache over the summer”. Couldn’t Young shave his off? Nope – apparently it has talismanic properties. “I don’t know where my career would be without it. It’s like scaffolding.”SNL UK will be back in September and then again in January. In between, Young will tour the UK. It’s a strange sensation, having a full schedule until March. “I’m 34 and I’ve never known what I’m doing for more than six months.” Yet his success still hasn’t sunk in – besides, what if this good fortune is merely a flash in the pan? He’s so haunted by an encounter with an older comic who outlined his rapidly declining income after a career peak (“It’s always those stories that stick with me – any time I hear about someone who earns £5m a year, I forget”) that he’s considering drastic measures in the hope of turning what he fears could be a brief moment in the sun into a lifelong safety net.“I’m not a gambler, but I have thought: do I put all of my pay on red? Insane thoughts like that.” Young may not believe he’s made the big time yet, but I’d still bet against him being in that flatshare at 68.Paddy Youngtours the UKfrom 17 September to 12 December; tour starts Plymouth.Explore more on these topicsSaturday Night LiveTV comedyComedyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Keith David on his incredible career: ‘I want you to understand Black men as full-scope human beings’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The hard-working character actor has over 400 screen credits, from The Thing to Platoon to Rick and Morty, and he isn’t slowing down any time soon
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: The hard-working character actor has over 400 screen credits, from The Thing to Platoon to Rick and Morty, and he isn’t slowing down any time soon
Content: ‘One thing I always say is: Don’t quit before the blessing. You never know what it’s gonna take, or what’s in front of you’ … Keith David in The Lowdown.Photograph: FXView image in fullscreen‘One thing I always say is: Don’t quit before the blessing. You never know what it’s gonna take, or what’s in front of you’ … Keith David in The Lowdown.Photograph: FXMoviesInterviewKeith David on his incredible career: ‘I want you to understand Black men as full-scope human beings’Andrew LawrenceThe hard-working character actor has over 400 screen credits, from The Thing to Platoon to Rick and Morty, and he isn’t slowing down any time soonSun 26 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeith David’s voice precedes him. Deep and resonant, with mellifluous notes that hark back to his boys’ choir days, it has spent decades inhabiting warriors, gods, rogues, fathers and a welter of cartoon oddballs. Before David appears in a Zoom window from his Los Angeles home office, his voice reverberates through my tinny laptop speakers like a foghorn. “Can you see me now?” he booms once our connection is established after fits and starts. “OK. Outside of technology, you know I’m … OK.”‘Everything I know about evil I learned in that small town’: John Carpenter on terrifying the world with Halloween, The Thing and The FogRead moreHe fizzes about the project he just wrapped: a dark buddy comedy called My Friend Jim, in which he stars opposite Rob Lowe. It’s the latest entry in a seemingly unstinting slew of productions that have kept him booked and busy since the late 1970s, from The Thing to Platoon to There’s Something About Mary to Nope.“I went to see it last night,” says David, who generally avoids watching his on-screen performances once he’s given them. “I’ll go to a cast and crew screening, and that’s usually the first and last time I’ll see something. Every once in a while if I do something that comes on television that I haven’t seen in a long time, I’ll watch it. Sometimes I’ll look back on a choice I made in a particular scene and go, What the hell was I thinking …?”In an era that venerates stardom, David has made a life’s work of being more recognizable than famous, a character actor nonpareil. The past five decades have seen him amass more than 400 credits – enough to make him a ubiquitous presence in popular culture, even if many people couldn’t place the name behind the voice or the familiar profile – the glasses, the stately bearing and that mischievous grin. His résumé stretches from action movies to animation, Shakespeare to sitcoms; from Ken Burns documentaries to Call of Duty video games.At 70, David remains as in demand as ever, popping up in live-action series like the Ethan Hawke-led noir The Lowdown and Will Ferrell golf comedy The Hawk while his velvet baritone echoes everywhere from the Rick and Morty universe to a straight-to-streaming documentary on the Gettysburg Address. He caught up with the Guardian just before bolting off to San Diego Comic-Con to promote President Curtis, the Rick and Morty spinoff that marks the first standalone lead role of his remarkable career.View image in fullscreenKeith David at The Hawk premiere event.Photograph: Matt Baron/BEI/ShutterstockHe’s in no mood to slow down either, despite recent evidence to the contrary. At his Hollywood Walk of Fame induction in June – on his birthday, incidentally – David was photographed with his right arm in a sling, the result of a workout gone sideways. “I was in the gym fighting with a Bosu ball,” he says of the muscle injury – a line that could have been lifted from one of his animation scripts. “But I’m on the mend. I’m starting some light exercises right now. I keep in shape for whatever role happens to come along.”Work is what keeps him leaping out of bed every morning, thankful that he’s managed to stay in the game this long. If family history is a guide, he reckons he has a fair few productive years still ahead of him. “My grandmothers lived into their 80s and 90s,” he says. “My father is about to be 90. I feel like I’m in good company. There was a time in my life when the men in my family did not live that long. I had some fear of that in the back of my mind – but, you know, you wind up shortening your life, worrying about how long it’s going to be rather than how well you’re going to live.”David knew he wanted to captivate an audience before he knew how or where. The Harlem native might have become a preacher if he hadn’t taken so quickly to a citywide boys’ choir, where that voice first set him apart. By the time the 1970s rolled around and he got started at the High School of Performing Arts – a veritableXavier Institutefor New York City theater kids, where David overlapped with Ben Vereen, Glynn Turman and others – a life in the arts felt more like an inevitability.From there it was on to Juilliard, where he turned a school production of Romeo and Juliet into full-contact sport, tussling with future Tony winner Boyd Gaines. The duel wasn’t quite as drawn out as David’smuch-memed back-alley brawlwith Rowdy Roddy Piper in the 1988 cult classic They Live – but it did earn him and Gaines fight certifications. Two years after barnstorming the country with John Houseman for productions of A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Waiting for Godot, David found himself up for his first ever film part – a sci-fi horror starring Kurt Russell.The role was between David and another Black actor named Roger Mosley, who wound up booking Magnum, PI. The Thing, of course, is sci-fi canon now, a film that has only become more influential over time. But when the John Carpenter film arrived in 1982, David recalls, “it didn’t get the popular vote. It was overshadowed by ET and Poltergeist. Critics didn’t like it. I thought, well, I got an honorable mention [in the reviews]. Maybe I’m not going to have a life in the movies.”View image in fullscreenKurt Russell and Keith David in The Thing.Photograph: Ronald GrantFour years passed before Hollywood called on David again. In between auditions, acting company gigs and a side hustle as a speech teacher, he worked as a shiatsu masseur, charging fellow ensemble members $30 for a session. “The thing with putting out a shingle is that you have to work for anybody who’s got 30 bucks,” he says. “And I didn’t necessarily want to do that. It took me a long time to learn how to work on people’s energy without absorbing it myself. I did it for a while, but I was real selective.”In hindsight, those lean years were teaching David the very discipline that has served him so well over the course of his staggering career: selectiveness.It’s why David has pulled off the ultimate Hollywood sleight of hand: a body of work defined by both quantity and quality. As a young Black actor navigating Hollywood in the 80s and 90s, David understood how easily he could be pigeonholed – into the thug, the soldier, the sidekick, the stereotype. His solution wasn’t to avoid those roles, but to find the humanity within them. “I’ve played hustlers and pimps and all that,” he says. “My criteria is, I need to know why he made those choices so the audience understands the man. I want you to understand Black men as full-scope human beings. I try to go for that as much as possible.”David has a way of lending every character a measure of gravitas, as if the protagonists are interrupting his story. It doesn’t matter if he’s playing the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff in Armageddon, a shady DC alderman in the Chris Rock comedy Head of State or the world-weary Vietnam soldier King in Platoon – the Oliver Stone film that broke David’s four-year slump and set him on a path of near-constant work. But even Platoon could have nearly left him a footnote in a much bigger story.Charlie Sheen credits David withsaving his lifeduring a helicopter scene that nearly turned deadly. It’s the rare story David refuses to embellish. “We were circling back to the set-up point,” he says, “and the chopper tilted at a slightly different angle than before. I just sort of noticed, imperceptibly, he was sliding toward the open door. He didn’t seem to notice it himself, but I’m watching him inch toward that door and I just grabbed him instinctually – or maybe selfishly, because the truth of the matter is I didn’t want to think about what I should have done for the rest of my life. How close did it actually come? I don’t know. We’ll never know. But, praise God, it didn’t happen, and we live to tell the tale.”View image in fullscreenKeith David behind the scenes of Platoon.Photograph: Film PR handoutInterviewing David is a bit like trying to tour the Smithsonian during a lunch break. There’s no getting to everything, let alone all the highlights. But who could skip Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood? After The Thing, David booked a nine-episode arc on the children’s program as Keith, the neighborhood carpenter. The experience – a masterclass in captivating an audience, delivered by a Presbyterian minister no less – is one David still recalls with obvious affection.“One of the ladies in the cast, I believe, now you would say her son had autism,” David says. “He was a wonderful kid, but, you know, he could be all over the place. On set, they had a living room space where the TV was. And when Mr Rogers came on, Brian would sit in front of that television, riveted. He would shush you if you came into the room and made noise. It was really something to see the effect he had on children, on people. It was moving. It was a lesson.”Not every stop in the journey leaves a lasting mark. The Big House – the ill-fated 2004 sitcom that flipped The Fresh Prince’s rags-to-riches conceit and featured Kevin Hart and Leslie Odom Jr in their first on-screen roles – barely registers any more. David doesn’t spend much time dwelling on the misses. The best he can remember is telling himself, “Something else will come along.” And that something else was the 2000 sci-fi sleeper hit Pitch Black.His show business role models were people like Orson Welles, James Earl Jones and Ossie Davis – actors whose voices were instruments unto themselves. “What they were able to do in the realm of voiceover was just fascinating to me,” David says. “I wanted to be able to do that too, just by the voice, take you on a journey.”David had little sense of where that journey would take him when he booked a job on the ensemble sitcom Community. Dan Harmon, the creator and showrunner, called him in to narrate an episode in the elevated style of his Ken Burns collaborations and was blown away by the comedic potential in David’s gravitas and his ability to give fully committed, dead-serious performances in one take. “We had big fun with it,” he says.David was just as game to play around on camera as Elroy Patashnik, Community’s resident IT guy. When that job ended, David quickly found another on Greenleaf, a prestige drama about a Black church in Memphis. More than a starring role as Bishop James Greenleaf, his first true dramatic showcase at the center of a series, it was a prime opportunity on Oprah Winfrey’s young OWN network where he would share the screen with Winfrey, who played his barmaid sister.Did he feel the pressure? “You know, you always have some kind of awareness that that’s true,” David says. “But while she’s sitting at the table read or we’re in the episode, she’s not my boss. There’s no intimidation factor.”But Harmon wasn’t finished with David. Duringa much-publicized hiatus from Community, Harmon developed Rick and Morty, an animated series about a mad scientist and his grandson tearing through space-time and alternate realities. He brought David on almost immediately – first for a one-off role as a parasite giraffe; then as President Curtis, whose access to the government’s deepest secrets puts him on equal footing with Rick Sanchez himself.Together, Harmon and David found a singularity in Rick and Morty’s cosmic playground, where pop culture and chaos theory collide: a genuine breakout character. “The one thing about working with Dan is it can be wacky and crazy, but it’s alwayssmart. It’s the kind of stuff you can laugh at for days after you’ve seen it. Every time you think about a particular moment, you can just break out laughing. It resonates on more than one level.”President Curtis doesn’t just extend the joke. It unleashes the full range of David’s voice: speechifying through White House press room addresses, singing in the shower, one-lining through fight scenes. It’s a first lead role, one where he gets to bring pieces of every bit part he’s played along the way into a single character. Most of all, it’s a handsome reward for sticking it out, for trusting his voice. “You never know in this business. It’s a very funny business. But you gotta be in it. One thing I always say is: don’t quit before the blessing. You never know what it’s gonna take, or what’s in front of you.”President Curtis airs on Adult Swim on Sundays and will be available on HBO MaxExplore more on these topicsFilmUS televisionTelevisioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Curse of Love Island review – the deaths are more complex than this documentary can handle | Television | The Guardian
description: This show tries to grapple with the fact that three people associated with the reality juggernaut have killed themselves. But it forgets that the dating series doesn’t exist in a vacuum
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: This show tries to grapple with the fact that three people associated with the reality juggernaut have killed themselves. But it forgets that the dating series doesn’t exist in a vacuum
Content: The show feels ‘quite toxic’ … former Love Islander Malin Andersson.Photograph: AmazonView image in fullscreenThe show feels ‘quite toxic’ … former Love Islander Malin Andersson.Photograph: AmazonTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Curse of Love Island review – the deaths are more complex than this documentary can handleThis show tries to grapple with the fact that three people associated with the reality juggernaut have killed themselves. But it forgets that the dating series doesn’t exist in a vacuumHannah J DaviesSun 26 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn summer 2015, ITV revived its 00s reality format Celebrity Love Island, a show that was remembered mostly as a drunken, downmarket rival to Big Brother. Its new, slick, civilian Love Island was a slow-burn at first, but by 2017 it was one of British TV’s biggest hits. While it remains among ITV’s hottest properties, viewing figures are now more modest, with 600,000 people tuning in for its 2026 launch. Tastes have changed, but the fact that three people associated with the show – former contestants Mike Thalassitis and Sophie Gradon, and Caroline Flack, the presenter for five series – took their lives, may also have made viewers wary.Timed to coincide with the finale of the latest series of Love Island on Monday, Prime Video has released this two-parter about the apparent “curse” that stalks the programme. It opens with former contestant Anton Danyluk, who appeared on the show in 2019, declaring that there is “no higher high than the summer you’re preparing for Love Island”. But a stint in the show’s Mallorcan villa proved less of a high for some. Luis Morrison – a 2015 Islander – says it feels “disgusting” and “embarrassing” to watch the show back. “Everyone was having sex and stuff,” he says. Malin Andersson, a 2016 contestant, says, looking back, the show feels “quite toxic … so superficial and artificial”. Watching footage of herself coming into the villa for a post-elimination row with her partner, Terry, Andersson alleges there was much meddling on the part of the programme-makers: “The producers are fucking with people who can feel deep things!”View image in fullscreen‘Embarrassing to watch the show back’ … Luis Morrison.Photograph: AmazonSo far, so not shocking; these are all criticisms that could have been levelled at Celebrity Love Island in 2005, or pretty much any other reality dating show. But towards the end of the first episode and into the second, things get darker. Steven Douglass – a close friend of Gradon’s – speaks about her “zest for life” before the show, and the “spark” that faded once she was in the public eye and a victim of relentless trolling. Thalassitis was given the nickname “Muggy Mike” for his apparently sneaky behaviour. Former Big Brother psychologist Linda Papadopoulos says here it was a label that was reductive: “You’re distilling down a multidimensional human being into a catchphrase.” Gradon died in 2018, Thalassitis in 2019. There was, says journalist Caroline Frost, “a pattern forming” around Love Island.The problem, of course, is that such deaths are incredibly complex, and more complicated than The Curse of Love Island is equipped to deal with. Papadopoulos says: “This isn’t about trying to point at a show, or a company, or a person.” Yet much of the documentary concentrates on the programme rather than the online vitriol, financial pressures, family problems, existing mental health conditions, relationship problems, rolling media coverage, or the mind-bending reality of instant renown. Marcel Somerville, who appeared in the 2017 series, says: “If the care that is currently being offered to contestants was being offered back then, it might have had a better bearing for Mike.” Except that the increase in care for Love Island’s contestants – therapy, contact for 14 months, plus advice on finances, social media and adjusting to their new lives – only came about because of those tragedies. We can ask whether more could have been done earlier, but we will never know whether it would have made a difference. Dave Read, who has managed many former Islanders, including Thalassitis, says the media have got it “so wrong” when it comes to plotting a straight line between the show and his death.View image in fullscreenThe show’s saving grace … Anton Danyluk.Photograph: AmazonDanyluk’s frank testimony, rooted in two experiences on the show, is the programme’s saving grace. As reported in the press in 2024, he became a heavy drinker and drug user after Love Island, and tried to take his own life. Incredibly, he would later return for Love Island: All Stars in 2024, unable to shake the feeling that he had more reality mileage left in him, and wanting “to close that chapter of my life”. It was an experience which, he says, felt “a lot more produced” than it had the first time around. There was more support for contestants the second time, but that increased duty of care was, as he tells it, undercut by the producers provoking situations that were “causing a spiral effect online”. “I wouldn’t do reality TV ever again,” he says.Read says: “You need skin like a rhinoceros to be able to deal with this industry. That’s not a Love Island thing, that’s the whole industry. It’s savage.” Indeed, the Curse of Love Island makes many valid points about the difficulties of the reality world, but it seems to forget that Love Island doesn’t exist in a vacuum. The philosopher Mark Fisher wrote in Capitalist Realism in 2009: “Reality TV is continually haunted by questions about fiction and illusion.” In the years since, the massive expansion of social media has only intensified that uncanny boundary between real life and entertainment, performance and documentary, pathos and bathos. Surely the problem here is not so much the Curse of Love Island, but the well-worn curse of overnight fame.The Curse of Love Island is on Prime Video now.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123.In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. title: Shania Twain’s honest playlist: ‘If Dancing Queen comes on, you rush out’ | Shania Twain | The Guardian
description: The country-pop superstar loves Abba and secretly listens to Lloyd Webber, but which British heartthrob’s single gets her out of bed in the morning?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The country-pop superstar loves Abba and secretly listens to Lloyd Webber, but which British heartthrob’s single gets her out of bed in the morning?
Content: ‘I didn’t realise how powerful music could be until that moment’ … Shania Twain.Photograph: Timothy WhiteView image in fullscreen‘I didn’t realise how powerful music could be until that moment’ … Shania Twain.Photograph: Timothy WhiteHonest playlistShania TwainShania Twain’s honest playlist: ‘If Dancing Queen comes on, you rush out’The country-pop superstar loves Abba and secretly listens to Lloyd Webber, but which British heartthrob’s single gets her out of bed in the morning?As told to Hannah NewtonSun 26 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe song that changed my lifeThere’s many critical songs on The Mission soundtrack, but Gabriel’s Oboe [by Ennio Morricone] hit me hard. I had to pull off the road, I cried like a baby. I didn’t realise how powerful music could be until that moment. I was 22.The first single I boughtAt Seventeen by Janis Ian. I reference it in my album Little Miss Twain and it says so much about the emotions of a teenage misfit. I felt like her, I related – but I was also thinking: “Wow, I have to some day write this well.” It gave me a goal; I was so in awe. I made very little money, babysitting, taking care of my neighbour’s horse, singing in bars. I would get like 20 bucks, that I would mostly give to my family, but I got that record for myself.The best song to play at a partyIf Dancing Queen by Abba comes on and you’re in the bathroom, you rush to get out, you can’t miss a second of it.The song I secretly like, but tell everybody I hateNobody ever wants to listen to The Phantom of the Opera, but I nerd out and listen to the whole album. I have to do it by myself – it’s sort of a secret.The song that gets me up in the morningWhen it comes to getting out of bed, pop always brings me somewhere new, like Harry Styles’s Sign of the Times. I love it.The song that makes me cryMichael Jackson’s Ben used to make me cry as a kid.The song I do at karaokeI was always the kid singing in bars, the last thing I wanted to do was get up and pretend. I was really purist about it. But I realised I’m missing out on all the fun. My favourite is Killing Me Softly by Roberta Flack.The song I want played at my funeralI’ve been through a lot of grief in my life and there are intimate moments where you need to bawl your eyes out. As the dead person, I want to say: this is a moment you cannot control, life goes to shit sometimes. So I would choose Don’t Worry, Be Happy by Bobby McFerrin; some things you can’t change.Shania Twain’s Little Miss Twain is out now.Explore more on these topicsShania TwainHonest playlistCountryPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From author to anime hero: the unlikely revival of a Japanese literary star  | Fiction in translation | The Guardian
description: More than seven decades after they were first released, the dark novels of Osamu Dazai have become a publishing sensation, as a new generation of readers engage with his bleakness, humour and brilliance
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: More than seven decades after they were first released, the dark novels of Osamu Dazai have become a publishing sensation, as a new generation of readers engage with his bleakness, humour and brilliance
Content: Heartfelt desperation … Osamu Dazai.Photograph: Tadahiko HayashiView image in fullscreenHeartfelt desperation … Osamu Dazai.Photograph: Tadahiko HayashiFiction in translationFrom author to anime hero: the unlikely revival of a Japanese literary starMore than seven decades after they were first released, the dark novels of Osamu Dazai have become a publishing sensation, as a new generation of readers engage with his bleakness, humour and brillianceJohn SelfSun 26 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s no question that Japanese literature has been one of the outstanding successes for British bookshops in recent years: in 2024 close to half of the bestselling translated fiction titles were fromJapan. Much of the Japanese fiction translated into English fits into broad categories – cats, crime, coffee shops – but one surprise bestseller stands alone.Sales of books by Osamu Dazai, who killed himself in 1948 aged 38, have rocketed in the last few years. His best-known novel, No Longer Human (1948), has sold more than 75,000 copies in the UK alone. An intense semi-autobiographical account of one man’s alienation, it was the last work of fiction completed before Dazai’s death.Born in the north of Japan in 1909 to a wealthy family, Dazai was a brilliant student, but showed early signs of mental ill health, making two suicide attempts by the age of 21. He lived what his translator Donald Keene called a “life of wild dissipation”, including morphine addiction and a number of relationships.Until recently, Dazai’s work has been available only in imported editions from the US publisher New Directions. But this month, Penguin Classics capitalises on his unexpected popularity by publishing the first UK edition of Dazai’s work in almost 70 years: a collection of short stories from a female perspective, titled Schoolgirl.Polly Barton, who selected and translated the stories into English, tells me that, although Dazai may be relatively new to English-speaking readers, in Japan, he is “one of the big three, along with Yukio Mishima and Ryūnosuke Akutagawa, that everyone talks about as the fathers of modern Japanese literature”.In recent years, Barton adds, he has been discovered by a new generation of younger readers. “The sense I get is that he’s particularly popular with young men – the demographic that we’re constantly told is not reading books.” This is even more surprising, since Dazai’s novels are not traditional bestseller material. They are bleak, nihilistic and riddled with their narrators’ self-loathing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markDazai’s novels are not traditional bestseller material – they are nihilistic and riddled with self‑loathingNo Longer Human comprises a series of notebooks by a formerly “handsome young man”, who declares his incompatibility with the human race. For him, the world is “a place of bottomless horror”; he concludes that “living itself is the source of sin”. The narrator of the title story of Schoolgirl takes a similar view: “the problem is that I’m corrupt. I’m a bad girl.”The relentless pessimism in Dazai’s work risks seeming overwhelming or indulgent but, as Barton puts it, Dazai “leans into [the self-loathing] with a kind of exuberance”. Indeed, his appeal in part lies in this “unashamed emotional quality, but also tempered with enormous intelligence”.Tynan Kogane, the editor-in-chief at New York-based New Directions, agrees. “I think a lot of young readers see themselves in Dazai’s works.” He adds that “there’s a lot of nihilism and despair in Dazai’s work, and it’s unfortunate for our country at the moment, but there’s a lot of nihilism and despair [here too]. The unhappy man in postwar Japan really resonates with a lot of readers.”View image in fullscreenOsamu Dazai in  the 2016 Japanese anime TV series Bungo Stray DogsDazai’s popularity among younger readers may have spread online – on Reddit and TikTok, where commenters praise him as the only person that understands me”. But his renaissance also has unexpected roots in a 2016 Japanese anime TV series called Bungo Stray Dogs, which has fictionalised versions of real writers as its central characters.This bizarre series, featuring a “swashbuckling” version of Osamu Dazai, has been a godsend for book sales, says Chris Wait, an editor at New Directions. Soon after the TV series was released in America in 2018, New Directions noticed sales of Dazai’s books growing.“Before that we were selling dozens or hundreds of copies [a year],” Kogane says. As Bungo Stray Dogs fever grew, Dazai’s sales went stratospheric. “At the height of it,” Wait adds, “the annual figure was something like 150,000 copies, which for us is pretty rare.” Is it true that sales of No Longer Human bought New Directions a new office floor? “Yes,” replies Wait. “And our previous carpeting was very much in need of an update.”But the appeal of Dazai’s work goes much further than this cartoon cameo. His books have both style and substance. There’s “a natural gregariousness to his storytelling,” Wait says, “this raconteurship that keeps you reading no matter what he’s talking about”.Beyond the heartfelt despair of No Longer Human, novellas such as The Flowers of Buffoonery (1935) and The Beggar Student (1940) are frequently playful and funny; self-referential and self-mocking. “Why do I bother writing novels?” the narrator of The Beggar Student asks. “Am I lured by the glory of literary celebrity? Or do I simply want to write bestsellers and cash huge cheques? Let me spare you the theatrics. I want both. So bad it hurts.”Similarly, Schoolgirl, with its exclusively female viewpoints, presents a different side to Dazai. The authenticity of the voice may be in part because the title story, as Barton tells me, “was heavily based on the diary of a real 19-year-old schoolgirl that Dazai was sent in the post”.But Dazai’s most famous book remains inextricably linked with his own life – and death. In No Longer Human, the narrator has survived a suicide pact in which his girlfriend died. Soon after finishing the book, Dazai completed his own suicide pact with his lover Tomie Yamazaki. Their bodies were recovered six days later, on what would have been his 39th birthday. But his work – now more than ever – lives on.Schoolgirl by Osamu Dazai, translated by Polly Barton, is published by Penguin Classics.To order a copy go toguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. title: Three Choirs festival review – impressive opening salvo full of crackling energy and exuberant fireworks | Classical music | The Guardian
description: A packed crowd greeted this year’s curtain raiser for a delightfully Tiggerish premiere of Gavin Higgins’ Fanfare Americana, an exhilarating Elgar’s First and a joyful rendition of Walton’s Belshazzar’s Feast
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: A packed crowd greeted this year’s curtain raiser for a delightfully Tiggerish premiere of Gavin Higgins’ Fanfare Americana, an exhilarating Elgar’s First and a joyful rendition of Walton’s Belshazzar’s Feast
Content: Discipline, diction and considerable clarity of intent … the Festival Chorus and conductor Adrian Partington at Gloucester Cathedral.Photograph: James O'DriscollView image in fullscreenDiscipline, diction and considerable clarity of intent … the Festival Chorus and conductor Adrian Partington at Gloucester Cathedral.Photograph: James O'DriscollClassical musicReviewThree Choirs festival review – impressive opening salvo full of crackling energy and exuberant fireworksGloucester CathedralA packed crowd greeted this year’s curtain raiser for a delightfully Tiggerish premiere of Gavin Higgins’ Fanfare Americana, an exhilarating Elgar’s First and a joyful rendition of Walton’s Belshazzar’s FeastClive PagetSun 26 Jul 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSo shocked were the worthies of the venerableThree Choirs festivalby the eunuchs and concubines littering William Walton’s Belshazzar’s Feast that they banned the work for 26 years (the powers that be finally unpursed their lips sufficiently to allow it to be performed in 1957). These days it’s a hot ticket judging by the enthusiastic crowd packing out Gloucester Cathedral for this opening concert. It’s also a significant test of any group of singers, and one that this year’s Festival Chorus passed with flying colours.The UK premiere of Gavin Higgins’ Fanfare Americana opened proceedings, a likable work celebrating the can do attitude prevalent in the US. Whooping brass and tubular bells propelled vast wodges of sound into the resonant cathedral acoustic that exploded like exuberant fireworks. Adrian Partington led the Philharmonia Orchestra in a delightfully Tiggerish account.View image in fullscreenTheatricality and humanity … David Stout.Photograph: James O'DriscollThe noble tread of Elgar’s First Symphony brought matters down to earth, though the music took a little time to settle. The opening movement might have benefited from greater elasticity, and tempo changes needed more time to breathe. It was exhilarating nonetheless, as was the scherzo, which ran the gamut from elfin filigree to Darth Vader-ish menace. A warm, yet unsentimental Adagio preceded a brisk finale with plenty of Edwardian fire in its belly.The evening, however, belonged to the 141-strong Festival Chorus who delivered Walton’s cantata with discipline, diction and considerable clarity of intent. Blend and balance were highly impressive for what is essentially three choirs thrown together as one with inner parts and intricate intertwining lines invariably distinct. The male voices aced it in their forceful opening salvo, with female voices joining to pour their hearts out by the waters of Babylon.David Stout injected theatricality and a rare humanity into the baritone solos, his stentorian tones leading choir and orchestra into a “Praise ye the Gods” section that built to a terrific percussion-riddled hullabaloo. Partington adopted an ideally flexible approach here, drawing out the grinding dissonances in “Thou, O King, art King of Kings” and bringing a crackling energy to the concluding hymn of praise. As noises go, this one was joyful indeed.Three Choirs festival continues until 1 AugustExplore more on these topicsClassical musicChoral musicGloucestershireFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Oona Doherty: Leather Jacket review – dancers delight in their hard sweaty work  | Stage | The Guardian
description: Slaps, beats and bounces underscore the unified collective pleasure of sharing a rhythm in this world premiere of the singular choreographer’s latest piece
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Slaps, beats and bounces underscore the unified collective pleasure of sharing a rhythm in this world premiere of the singular choreographer’s latest piece
Content: A thrill to be up close … Leather Jacket by Oona Doherty at Bold Tendencies.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA thrill to be up close … Leather Jacket by Oona Doherty at Bold Tendencies.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianStageReviewOona Doherty: Leather Jacket review – dancers delight in their hard sweaty workBold Tendencies, LondonSlaps, beats and bounces underscore the unified collective pleasure of sharing a rhythm in this world premiere of the singular choreographer’s latest pieceLyndsey WinshipSun 26 Jul 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 11.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan it be a bit of a curse for an artist to knock it out of the park right at the start of their career? Choreographer Oona Doherty’s astonishing early works,Hope HuntandHard to be Soft, marked her as an unique (urgent, unfiltered) voice moving in uncharted territory. Her output since has been more variable, although she’s always utterly her own woman.Doherty’s last major piece,Specky Clark, was high concept. This new world premiere, Leather Jacket, feels the opposite, not quite enough concept. (I know, you can’t win.) The leather jackets of the title are being worn by eight dancers. Under bright fluorescent lights in the concrete space of Bold Tendencies – the Peckham multi-storey car park turned theatre – the dancers all slap one foot to the ground in a heavy thud, and again, and again, keeping a determined rhythm. It’s a thrill to be up close as foot slaps turn to thigh slaps, then bounces, then into Doherty’s own skewed kind of Irish step dance, matching the shift from electronic score to Cormac Begley’s experimental Irish folk music. (The dancers have shed the jackets by now; they’re just in their underwear.)View image in fullscreenExhausting … Leather Jacket by Oona Doherty.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHere is the collective pleasure of sharing a rhythm and a common dance. The unison is exacting, but always with a sense of being flesh-and-blood people, not a regiment. There’s something very honest about it, the dancers exhaust themselves, and between sections they pant, sweat, swig water, laugh with each other (in a way that says: “Can you believe we got through that!”). Their presence is real. And this is really what Doherty wants to show us: the pushing, the perspiring, the getting on with it. The dance is a means to an end, and the jackets only make it harder, sweatier work.The movement itself is not hugely interesting. There’s the odd wry theatrical flourish – one dancer, stripped to his pants, dons sunglasses and smokes a cigarette, a comical uniform of cool. There’s a slight sinister undercurrent when the dancers slap the heavy jackets on the floor, echoing the rhythm of the opening with thudding violence. You wonder if the mood is suddenly going to turn, open up another world. But at a tight 45-minutes, this isn’t that piece. It’s another unpredictable step in Doherty’s singular journey.Explore more on these topicsStageOona DohertyDanceTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sinfonia of London/Wilson review – night of Technicolor masterpieces from one of the finest orchestras on the planet | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Verdi’s La Forza del Destino felt vital, cellist Jonathan Aasgaard was immaculate in Walton’s Concerto but it was John Wilson’s wizardly conducting through Respighi’s Roman Trilogy that brought the audience to their feet
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Verdi’s La Forza del Destino felt vital, cellist Jonathan Aasgaard was immaculate in Walton’s Concerto but it was John Wilson’s wizardly conducting through Respighi’s Roman Trilogy that brought the audience to their feet
Content: Playing the Albert Hall acoustic like a fiddle … John Wilson with the Sinfonia of London at the Royal Albert Hall, London.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCView image in fullscreenPlaying the Albert Hall acoustic like a fiddle … John Wilson with the Sinfonia of London at the Royal Albert Hall, London.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCClassical musicReviewSinfonia of London/Wilson review – night of Technicolor masterpieces from one of the finest orchestras on the planetRoyal Albert Hall, LondonVerdi’s La Forza del Destino felt vital, cellist Jonathan Aasgaard was immaculate in Walton’s Concerto but it was John Wilson’s wizardly conducting through Respighi’s Roman Trilogy that brought the audience to their feetClive PagetSun 26 Jul 2026 07.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 10.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnother Sinfonia of London Prom, another five-star concert. Admittedly this programme of Technicolor masterpieces played into the wizardly hands of John Wilson, a conductor whose respect and enthusiasm for the golden age of MGM is legendary. None of this was movie music, however, and Hollywood panache is only a part of what makes this hand-picked ensemble one of the finest orchestras on the planet.View image in fullscreenDelight in the music making  … John Wilson and Jonathan Aasgaard with the Sinfonia of London.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCFirst, there’s that full-fat sound, where every musician is a potential soloist, yet the blend is to die for. Then there’s the parade ground discipline and a willingness to follow Wilson – who seldom lingers – into the very fires of Mordor. The spirit, too, is palpable. Whole sections sway as one, occasionally with broad grins on their faces, such is their delight in the music making.If the conductor has a superpower, it’s an instinct for homing in on tiny details, not just drawing them out but making them reallymeansomething. Take the beautifully articulated rustle of strings underpinning the poignant clarinet melody in the overture to Verdi’s La Forza del Destino. You may have already known it was there, but seldom has it felt so vital or so troubling.A blistering account of the Verdi was curtain raiser to Walton’s Cello Concerto, a golden Mediterranean canvas undercut with sinister ticks and jittery cross-rhythms that feel as if they’ve wandered in from a Hitchcock movie. Principal cellist Jonathan Aasgaard was the generous-toned soloist, articulate and technically immaculate, yet refreshingly undemonstrative.The second half was given over to Respighi’s Roman Trilogy, music with a reputation for cinematic excess, yet works that were embraced by Toscanini who was certainly no vulgarian. Wilson played the Albert Hall acoustic like a fiddle, whether depicting the brazen pomp of the Circus Maximus, Neptune’s chariot emerging from the Trevi Fountain, or nocturnal whisperings on the Janiculum hill, recorded nightingale and all. As the Roman army swept inexorably down the Via Appia, brass bands ricocheting across the balcony, the audience rose as one. All that remained to make the evening complete was a rip-roaring William Tell chaser by way of an encore and cue credits.The Prom is on BBC Four, 26 July at 8pm and available onBBC iPlayerandBBC Sounds(until 12 October). The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicProms 2026Royal Albert HallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Luke Combs review – regular Joe megastar brings the arena-sized party home | Country | The Guardian
description: Despite his humble persona, the highest-selling country artist of all time has the vocal firepower and heavyweight hits to deliver two hours of crowd-pleasin’ pyrotechnics
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Despite his humble persona, the highest-selling country artist of all time has the vocal firepower and heavyweight hits to deliver two hours of crowd-pleasin’ pyrotechnics
Content: Demanding a sing-along … Luke Combs Live at Murrayfield stadium, Edinburgh.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDemanding a sing-along … Luke Combs Live at Murrayfield stadium, Edinburgh.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The GuardianCountryReviewLuke Combs review – regular Joe megastar brings the arena-sized party homeMurrayfield Stadium, EdinburghDespite his humble persona, the highest-selling country artist of all time has the vocal firepower and heavyweight hits to deliver two hours of crowd-pleasin’ pyrotechnicsKatie HawthorneSun 26 Jul 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first we see of Luke Combs, the North Carolina-born megastar is walking through the stadium crowd. Cap pulled low, with a bashful look on his face, the stunt is less pap walk, more regular Joe dodging a flashmob on his way to work. Combs is now the highest-selling country artist of all time, but he wears his success with humility: when he finally reaches his saloon-themed stage, with near-70,000 screaming fans before him, he keeps that unassuming presence. “Normally I’d ask how you’re feeling tonight, but Iknowhow you’re feeling tonight,” he smiles.This week, Combs will perform to more than half a million fans across just seven dates in England, Scotland and Ireland: a remarkable coronation for an artist yet to have a Top 10 single here. Not that you’d know it, from the way the crowd screams every word to his 2016 hit Hurricane, a soft-rock heartacher about running into your ex in a bar, elevated by a cinematic chorus (“moon went hidin’, stars quit shinin’”) that’s closer to early-doors Taylor than any country-bro machismo.View image in fullscreenA whole lot of show … Luke Combs at Murrayfield stadium, Edinburgh.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The GuardianNamed after recent single My Kinda Saturday Night, this short tour promises – and delivers – a party. Combs brings us three opening acts, lashings of pyro, celebrity cameos, and packs almost 30 songs into two hours. It’s a whole lot of show, but its biggest moments, such as the nostalgic-before-it’s-even-over Tell ’Em About Tonight, deserved more breathing room.It’s a real shame that echoing sound makes it almost impossible to pick out words when Combs speaks, and muddies his more intimate songs, such as the fiddle-laced 5 Leaf Clover. But Combs has one of contemporary country’s most formidable voices, owning an almighty, torn-up roar as well as real tenderness and control, and his hardest-hitting tracks power through regardless.His exuberant band bring power-stance, arena-rock swagger to Back in the Saddle and Beer Never Broke My Heart, while the glittering, tragedy-struck Where the Wild Things Are demands a sing-along that endures as fans walk home. By storming closer Ain’t No Love in Oklahoma (from theTwisterssoundtrack), Combs is crackling with energy, his arms in the air, humbleness be damned – and deservedly so.AtWembley Stadium, London, from 31 July to 2 AugustExplore more on these topicsCountryPop and rockEdinburghreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not rocket science’: a day in the life of a Nasa behavioral health scientist | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Dr Suzanne Bell helps astronauts perform in a high-stress environment. To do that, she wakes up at 5am – without an alarm
Author: Jaya Saxena
Headline: Dr Suzanne Bell helps astronauts perform in a high-stress environment. To do that, she wakes up at 5am – without an alarm
Content: ‘We’re really focused on the moon, sustaining a presence there and going on to Mars.’Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/NASA, taken by James BlairView image in fullscreen‘We’re really focused on the moon, sustaining a presence there and going on to Mars.’Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/NASA, taken by James BlairA day in the lifeWell actually‘It’s not rocket science’: a day in the life of a Nasa behavioral health scientistDr Suzanne Bell helps astronauts perform in a high-stress environment. To do that, she wakes up at 5am – without an alarmTell us: what impact have GLP-1s had on your relationships?Jaya SaxenaSun 26 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDr Suzanne Bell, an organizational psychologist, leads the Behavioral Health and Performance Laboratory at Nasa’s JohnsonSpaceCenter.What’s your morning routine?My morning time is very important to me. I get up without an alarm by 5am every day, and from 5 to 7.15 I sit and have my morning latte. It’s a focused time where I do work or some longer reading, or respond to personal emails and do paperwork. Two hours of completely uninterrupted time every morning is just wonderful.What did work look like today?I am the principal investigator forArtemisresearch, for crew health and readiness. It’s the first time a crew’s gone beyondlow-Earth orbitin 50 years, and the first time they’ve flown in Orion.We collected data from the Artemis II crew, and finished our pre-mission data collection about a month ago. The human research program that funds the work wanted a briefing on a really quick turnaround. We briefed them on what we need to do and what we need to address before Artemis III.View image in fullscreenSuzanne Bell.Photograph: James Blair/NasaRight now, we’re working on sustained lunar presence andsetting up a moon base. We have data that can already inform some of the ways that should be built.When do you eat lunch?I actually didn’t have time for a lunch break, so I grabbed a salad on the way into a meeting. I’m a very healthy eater – Ifollow the daily dozen, which is a healthy longevity diet. I don’t eat flour or sugar unless it’s a special occasion.Was there anything especially challenging or exciting?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe know a lot about low-Earth orbit. We know a lot about what it’s like to work and live in the International Space Station. But we’re really focused on the moon, sustaining a presence there and going on to Mars. That research is so exciting because it is data from people who have gone into deep space, and that is the direction we’re heading.What time did you leave the office, and what did you do with your evening?I left at about 5. I tend not to work late. I have a 13-year-old and a 15-year-old, and they’re very busy in sports and activities, so in the evening I like to prioritize being available to them. My 15-year-old really likes to work out with me. So we go to the gym together and we lift weights. My other son is involved in a lot of sports, and we do indoor climbing. But I go to bed really early. I’m asleep by 9 or 9.30. I get my restorative time on a Saturday or Sunday – you need a break. It’s not rocket science.This interview has been edited and condensedExplore more on these topicsWell actuallyA day in the lifeNasaSpacefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to keep cool in a heatwave: 25 tips from the people who know best, from a Rio lifeguard to an Egyptian archaeologist | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: For some, scorching days and humid nights are just the norm. So how do they stay chilled and comfortable?
Author: Laura Potter
Headline: For some, scorching days and humid nights are just the norm. So how do they stay chilled and comfortable?
Content: Photograph: Franck Allais/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Franck Allais/The GuardianExtreme heatHow to keep cool in a heatwave: 25 tips from the people who know best, from a Rio lifeguard to an Egyptian archaeologistFor some, scorching days and humid nights are just the norm. So how do they stay chilled and comfortable?Laura PotterSun 26 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 14.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGet up and outLuis Pacherrez Antón is president of Agroperu Cooperative, a democratic collective of 102 small-scale farmers in the Chira River valley, Peru. He is based in Piura, known as “the city of eternal heat” because it stays hot and dry all year round. “The sun rays start to shine very early – from 9am,” he says. “So as people who work in cultivation, under a burning sun, we stay comfortable by starting much earlier and consuming the healthy foods that we produce, like bananas, oranges, lemons, grapes, papayas and avocados.”Obada Almaitah, a diving instructor and course director in Aqaba, Jordan, says that summer temperatures regularly reach 40C, and can exceed that during heatwaves. “The sun is very strong, humidity is generally low and UV levels are high for much of the year, so I schedule physically demanding tasks during the early morning whenever possible.” When temperatures soar, flip your schedule to do chores before work – and forgo that weekend lie-in; instead, mow the lawn or lug shopping home first thing.Tour guide Despina Savvidou has been leading visitors around the Acropolis of Athens for 48 years. She has witnessed first-hand the difference climate breakdown has made. “It’s like I’m in another country,” she says. “Thirty or 40 years ago, 32C was very hot; now 32C is normal. Two years ago, we had a heatwave that lasted two weeks.” Savvidou advises people to book on to her earliest tour – before the Acropolis even opens. “We have a tour that begins at 7.45am. We give a short introduction, and as soon as the doors open we go in. Between 8am and 10am – even if it’s 40C – it’s OK.”Don’t waituntil you’re thirsty to drinkThis is a common tip from people who work in the baking sun, like Egyptian archaeologist Dr Zahi Hawass, who has worked at sites in the Nile delta, the Western desert and the Upper Nile valley. “The weather in Egypt during the summer is extremely hot, especially at archaeological sites such as Saqqara,” he says. “I make sure to drink water regularly while working outdoors. In the heat, it’s important not to wait until you feel very thirsty, but to keep drinking throughout the day.”Sherene M El-Sioufi, a doctor in pulmonary and sleep medicine, lives and works in Jeddah, which experiences some of the hottest and most humid conditions in the world. She says: “In Saudi Arabia, many people drinklaban, a yoghurt-based drink that provides hydration and electrolytes. The key is to drink consistently.”Sip, don’t guzzle“We tell people to drink little by little: at 10am take two sips, at 10.15am two more,” says Savvidou. “I have at least 15 glasses of water a day, but slowly.” Luiz Eduardo Dos Santos Nascimento, a lifeguard in Rio de Janeiro, where temperatures can exceed 40C during heatwaves, says: “I always keep a water bottle nearby and stay constantly hydrated during my shift.” John Napolo, a wildlife protection services manager at Etosha Heights Wildlife Monitoring Unit in Namibia, where summer temperatures can exceed 40C, says: “Each ranger carries five litres of water for the day. We drink three or four and pour the remainder on our heads when the heat is too much.”Tip water on your headSpeaking of which, Prof Ollie Jay,director of the Heat and Health Research Centre at the University of Sydney, recommends this approach to cool down quickly: “When you apply water to the skin it evaporates, which cools you down, because it does the same job as sweating, but without the physiological stress of having to sweat. If you drink half your water and tip the other half over yourself, you get much more effective cooling.”Dr Youssouf Moussa of the International Organization for Migration in Obock, Djibouti oversees humanitarian operations in a region facing extreme heat – in the week we speak a heat alert warns that temperatures could reach 53C. He uses “practical methods such as lightly wetting clothes, which helps cooling through evaporation”. To quickly cool an adult or child so they are comfortable enough to sleep, El-Sioufi suggests “a cool damp cloth on the neck, wrists or forehead”.… Or ice your neckWondered why tennis players sit with ice towels around their necks? Jay and his team came up with an extreme heat policy for Tennis Australia. “Our studies showed that ice towels cool a relatively large area of the body in a small window, as a player spends just 80 seconds sitting in their chair.” Simply wrap crushed ice cubes in a rolled up wet towel and place it around your neck.Take warm showersFor a speedy refresh, Savvidou swears by “a warm shower – no Greek person has a cold shower and most of us get under the water two or three times a day. I shower at 10am, again at 4pm, just to refresh without soap, and again before bed.” El-Sioufi also advises taking a shower before bed – a lukewarm one. “Many people assume a cold shower is best, but a lukewarm shower allows the body to cool gradually.” Michael Haindongo, a guide at Etosha Heights, who patrols this Namibian wildlife reserve daily, walking up to 500km (311 miles) a month and living in a camp in the bush for three-month rotations, takes a bedtime lukewarm shower, and when the temperature soars: “I wet a large towel and lie on it, and keep windows and doors open if there’s no threat from animals.”He describes how houses in his village are naturally ventilated as they are thatched with grass and walls are made from wood, which is “semi open”. He also says “the Ovahimba people apply red ochre on their faces and any body parts exposed to the sun”. This natural cosmetic, made from butterfat and red ochre,providesprotection against UV rays, thanks to high iron oxide content.… Or play in a bucketThe village of Lytton in British Columbia became the hottest place ever in Canada for three days running in June 2021, reaching 49.6C. Dr Michael Schwandt is a medical health officer in the region.He says that to quickly cool small children, “one of the best things is immersion. It doesn’t need to be total, just getting their legs into a bathtub – or even a bucket. Similarly, placing cool, damp cloths on the body can help it to evaporate heat. That could be a flannel, a muslin or a lightly damp T-shirt – it shouldn’t have to be freezing cold, just cool.”Down tools at peak times“For humanitarian teams, rest is essential to stay safe and effective when working outside for extended periods in extreme heat,” says Moussa. “From noon until 3pm we limit movements to what is strictly necessary, although in case of an emergency, we remain fully available.” Haindongo isn’t “too sure if there’s such a thing as feeling comfortable working in the heat – we tolerate it, and would rather work early mornings and afternoons, or if necessary by moonlight.”Federica Salvo, who runs the Giardino della Kolymbethra garden in Sicily, notes a similar approach: “Sicily holds the record for the highest temperature ever recorded in continental Europe – 48.8C on 11 August 2021.” She describes how Sicilians felt “overwhelmed” during that heatwave. “It was hard to work, or to concentrate on anything.” Fortunately, there are rules in place to protect people. “Throughout summer, work is prohibited from 12.30pm to 4pm in the construction and agriculture sectors, and during working hours workers are encouraged to take long breaks in the shade.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Franck Allais/The GuardianEat light, a little later“If you have a big dinner, you suffer – you sweat and you don’t sleep,” says Savvidou. “On a hot day, for dinner I’ll have apricots, cherries and banana in yoghurt with raisins. For lunch, we cook vegetables – green beans, okra, peppers, aubergine – in olive oil with feta cheese and serve it with a big salad. In Greece, there is no meal without a salad. For lunch today, I grilled fish and served it with a salad of cucumber and tomatoes, and that’s it – no potatoes, no rice, no pasta.”Carmen Vallejo Carmona, a grandmother in Seville – known as the frying pan of Spain thanks to sweltering summer temperatures – says her hot weather diet is “based around salads and cold dishes. The gazpacho in our town is more liquid, drunk from a glass. We also eatsalmorejo(another chilled Andalucían soup),boquerones en vinagre(marinated anchovies), vegetables and the occasional ice-cream. Lunch is late – normally between 2pm and 3pm – and dinner is after 9pm, once the worst of the heat is gone.”Moussa says: “In extreme heat we avoid heavy meals, especially at midday. Instead, we focus on light, water-rich foods and drink plenty of fluids, including tea. A typical breakfast includeslahooh, a soft flatbread, with tea and water. On the coast near Obock, Red Sea fish grilled Yemeni-style is very common.”Eat to hydrate, tooDr Rashmi Sarkar is a dermatologist in New Delhi, where summer daytime temperatures commonly reach 42-45C. She says: “Traditional Indian diets include many foods considered to be cooling and hydrating: yoghurt,chaas[buttermilk], coconut water, fresh fruits such as watermelon and mangoes, and cucumbers. Drinks such as lemon water,jaljeera[a spiced beverage],aam pannamade from raw mango, [cordials such as]khusandsattuare popular because they help replace fluids and electrolytes.”Almaitah says: “During long diving days, I replace electrolytes naturally through foods such as melon, cucumbers, tomatoes and yoghurt.” Nascimento notes that “it’s common in Rio for people to consume coconut water, natural juices and chilled fruit”; while Napolo says: “Some rangers have traditional knowledge of plant roots and tubers that can give you extra water.” If you want a root veg with a high water content for salads,radish is 95% water, while celeriac, carrot and beetroot are all 88%.Remember, less isn’t always more“One of the biggest misconceptions is that less clothing is better,” says El-Sioufi. “Many traditional practices – including wearing loose, flowing garments – evolved for a reason. They provide excellent protection from direct sunlight while allowing air circulation.” Napolo agrees: “The best way to stay cool is to be completely covered – long sleeves and trousers, and something to cover your face. The key is to have light, loose layers that allow airflow as you move.” Savvidou opts for cotton trousers that “are so wide you don’t know where the leg is, a loose shirt, and no belts. People think they need everything open in the heat, but this isn’t wise because you get dehydrated.”Duong and Van, Vietnamese grandparents who live in Nam Dinh, where it’s very hot and humid, also cover up. “At home we wear shorts, loose dresses, vests, and men are topless, but when travelling by motorbike, people wear a full outfit on top of their normal clothes that covers their whole body, face and hands. It’s made of cotton.” Moussa also opts for light, loose, breathable clothing that protects the skin while allowing air to circulate. “In Djibouti, traditional clothing is well adapted to the heat. Women often wearpygama, a long, loose, lightweight dress, while men wear thefuta, a cotton wrap that allows airflow.”Don’t forget accessoriesSarkar wears sunglasses with UV protection, and when outdoors for longer periods a broad-brimmed hat, scarf ordupatta(long, shawl-like cloth), and she carries an umbrella. Savvidou would love to carry a parasol, “but it’s windy on the Acropolis, and we lose them. Hats make you sweat, so we wear visors, because they protect your face from the sun, but your head is in the air.”Duong and Van say battery-powered fans have taken off in Vietnamese cities but “people still use paper fans, and some use the traditional Vietnamese hat as a fan”. For Vallejo Carmona, her traditional hand fan “comes everywhere with me. It’s a verySevillanothing.” She also opts for “light footwear, preferably made of leather, so the foot can be naked and fresh”.Stop fantasising about air conIf you were guiltily Googling the cost of installing an air-conditioning unit mid-heatwave, Jayhas news for you: “There are many more sustainable ways to cool down. We have AC at home, but we haven’t turned it on in years. We installed ceiling fans, which work a treat. The more airflow you get across the skin the better, so if you’re lying on a bed, a ceiling fan is probably best; if you’re at a desk, a pedestal fan.” Salvo concurs: “When it’s very hot, I sleep with the fan on. I try to avoid the air con.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShutter upYou’ve heard all about closing the curtains, but here’s how it’s viewed where it has been a custom for generations. Salvo says: “In Italy, tradition has taught us to close the shutters during the day to keep the house dim and shield it from the sun, keeping it cooler. We then open the windows early in the morning and in the evening when the air cools down.”Romel Bernal, an architect in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, where recent temperatures have reached 38C, has a nifty tip: “Blackout curtains help a room retain its temperature when not in use during the day, while light-coloured linen materials offer a cooling effect – and if you mist them with water, the evaporation keeps them cool.”Get a thermometerSchwandt recommendsinvesting ina thermometer “to get an objective measure of when it’s OK to open windows”. Jay agrees, saying, “We’ve installed a temperature sensor inside and another outside so we can look at the difference. That way, we can keep the windows open when it’s cooler outside than in, and when that flips, we shut the windows.”Sit under a treeAs the climate heats up, nature can provide excellent relief. “The temperature on our forecast is measured in the shade, so if you’re out in the sun you’re exposed to 12 to 15 degrees higher heat load when you take into account the extra radiation,” says Jay. “Sitting under a tree is a nice way of getting shade. Grass also dampens the absorption of radiation, which is another moderating effect. Depending on the type of tree, you have the evapotranspiration effect, where water in the leaves evaporates and reduces ambient temperature by a couple more degrees celsius.” It’s why, says Haindongo, when the heat gets too much, “I lie under a tree, or climb to the hilltop for the breeze.”… Or create shade with canopies and drapes“You can achieve a microclimate in any home by taking  advantage of natural resources, like plants and trees that create shade and absorb the impact of the heat. Landscape design has gone from being a luxury to being essential,” Bernal says. Vallejo Carmona describes how internal patios in many houses in Seville are “covered by thick fabric to create shade and coolness, and the council covers some streets with awnings to avoid the direct sun and create shade”.Jay notes that while you can create shade in your garden, you must couple it with decent ventilation. “Some people create shade that blocks the prevailing wind, and then you get hot, because there’s no airflow.” Think sails or awnings, but choose heavy fabrics, as “some fabrics let radiation through because they’re not a tight enough weave,” he says.Use mulchSalvo says increasing temperatures are changing the way people garden. “Gardeners and farmers are increasingly using mulch to reduce evaporation. By practising this ancient method, we can increase soil water retention, protect roots from extreme heat and provide plants with more nutrients. We are also choosing more drought-resistant species, such as olive trees, lavender, rosemary, sage and Mediterranean native plants.”Start ’em youngAustralia has been incredibly successful at bringing skin cancer rates down among younger people, while here in the UK they arecontinuing to increase. It’s why starting some basic rules early is a great idea. “When Australian kids go to school, they have wide-brimmed hats and are not allowed to go out in the playground if they don’t have them on,” says Jay. “These very strong rules around sun safety start as early as five, and by the time you’re an adult, putting sunscreen on is like putting your underpants on – everybody does it every day.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Franck Allais/The GuardianStay safe in the waterHorribly, heatwaves are often coupled with drownings, so safety in the water is paramount. “Many people enter the sea unprepared after long periods in the sun, some after consuming alcohol, and end up ignoring the risks of currents, depth and sea conditions,” says Nascimento. “It’s important to respect lifeguard signals, swim in protected areas and never enter the sea alone.Extreme heatalso increases physical strain on the body, so it’s necessary to recognise its limits.”Almaitah says that “many people underestimate sun exposure because they feel cool in the water, but the combination of direct sunlight and reflection from the sea can cause severe sunburn, especially on boats, where exposure can be continuous”.Socialise later“We socialise as much as possible,” says Vallejo Carmona, “but during the hours of the worst heat, between 1pm and 6pm, most families are at home. After dinner, once it’s cool, neighbours gather with chairs to chat on the pavements outside, so by the time we go home to sleep, our houses are fresh.”Duong and Van “sit out in the evenings to havetrà đá,a traditional tea, but instead of having it hot in a cup, we dilute it in a big glass and put lots of ice in. It’s a lovely, traditional way of people having some cool air outdoors and socialising after a day of hiding from the heat.”Slow your pace“When I was doing my PhD, I did a field study in Seville in summer,” says Jay. “I immediately noticed that people moved more slowly and walked close to the side of a building to get shade.” Nascimento concurs: “Control your pace – it’s important to manage your energy throughout the day.” Almaitah says: “People often try to continue normal activities, but in very hot weather it’s important to slow down, stay hydrated, seek shade regularly and listen to the body’s warning signs.”Moussa has similar advice – “We adapt by working early in the morning or later in the day, and prioritising essential tasks” – but says there’s another side to it: “We work in extreme conditions, yet every day we also see hundreds of migrants crossing this same desert with access to nothing: no water, no shoes, no shelter. Some of our energy comes precisely from that, from the drive to help someone who has less than you do.”The 13 biggest myths about heatwaves – and how to bust themRead moreLower your expectations of sleep“The body naturally needs to cool slightly before sleep begins, so when temperatures remain above 40C, that becomes more difficult,” says El-Sioufi. “People often take longer to fall asleep, wake more frequently and spend less time in restorative deep sleep. Infants and young children are especially vulnerable, because their ability to regulate body temperature is less developed. Parents should be flexible and, rather than focusing on exact nap durations, ensure children remain hydrated, cool and comfortable.” Schwandt also says parents need “openness to changing schedules – because kids will go pretty close to flat out before they stop. Move playtimes to early morning and late evening, and recognise that oftentimes kids won’t fall asleep easily because of the heat, and that can transmit to fatigue the next day.”Adapt your homeRather than a total overhaul, Bernal recommends that you “reduce the impact of the heat in the areas of the home most used by its inhabitants”. Cross ventilation is crucial, so open windows and doors at opposite ends of your home and leave spaces clear to allow air to flow. “You can integrate technologies like windows with double and triple glazing, and windows with protective overhangs to minimise solar exposure. Outdoors, choose white for facades directly exposed to the sun and sand and beige tones for flooring, as they don’t cause glare or reflect heat.” Cement tiles, terracotta, light-coloured cantera stone and brushed-finish marble are excellent choices for preventing outside surfaces from overheating, and are suitable for walking barefoot.And finally … splash aboutPacherrez Antón shares that “in Piura, during the summer, we havecarnavales, where neighbours, tourists and the whole population gather, and water tanks and hoses are used to spray everyone as they dance and enjoy themselves”. Even if you are miles from Peru’s city of eternal heat, a local splash park or fountain should do the trick … just not at midday!Explore more on these topicsExtreme heatClimate scienceClimate crisisUnited KingdomHomesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lennox. Manchester: ‘A boot camp of flavours’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: You’ll leave fed, challenged and gastronomically punch-drunk
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: You’ll leave fed, challenged and gastronomically punch-drunk
Content: Lennox, Manchester: ‘Its pocket-friendly, six-course format gives a night out with friends a sense of occasion not available at Pizza Express.’Photograph: Shaw and Shaw/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenLennox, Manchester: ‘Its pocket-friendly, six-course format gives a night out with friends a sense of occasion not available at Pizza Express.’Photograph: Shaw and Shaw/The Guardian.Grace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewLennox. Manchester: ‘A boot camp of flavours’ – restaurant reviewYou’ll leave fed, challenged and gastronomically punch-drunkGrace DentSun 26 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 15.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNico Simeone is the Scottish-Italian chef behind theSix by Nicorestaurant empire, and Lennox, in Spring Gardens, Manchester, is his new baby. If you are unfamiliar with Six by Nico, it’s a fever-dream version of fine dining: Simeone conjured up themes such as “The Chippie”, “Italian Road Trip” and “Ancient Rome”, then served six courses in homage to them. Tokyo! Mad Hatters! Childhood! At one point, the Six empire was growing like knotweed, and by 2025 there were 17 restaurants. You had more chance of eating at a Six by Nico than finding an NHS dentist.Suffice to say, many adore the concept – overlooking its middling cooking skills – because it’s pocket-friendly, and the six-course format gives a night out with friends a sense of occasion not available at Pizza Express. Lennox, Simeone says, will be very different: à la carte, focused on dry-aged meat, but with the same playfulness and invention. There would be a fish finger with katsu curry and celeriac remoulade; a tempura oyster shell filled with dry-aged beef tartare and oyster emulsion; and gnocchi with deboned chicken wings and parmesan. Lennox would be personal, bespoke and absolutely unscalable. No rollout planned, no siree. But by August 2026, there will be three of them. Hang on, what? Yes, shortly after Manchester came Glasgow, and then Edinburgh. Simeone sleeps with one eye open; I salute his indefatigability.View image in fullscreenLennox’s gnocchi with chicken wings are ‘genuinely, strangely enticing. Does it work?’We arrive at lunchtime and survey the menu, which is puzzling and with definite moments of delicious intrigue: mussels, sourdough, ’nduja, pickled fennel; pork cheek, gochujang, cheese on toast; sole kiev, caesar salad, burnt lemon. And for pudding, hazelnut tiramisu with dulce de leche, and pavlova with extra-virgin olive oil. There’s an open kitchen, a Japanese barbecue and a plethora of visible dry-ageing fridges for both steak and fish, because chefs seem certain that what guests want is to watch meat rot first-hand, like a weirdSam Taylor-Johnsonart installation.First out of the kitchen, and ferried by a lovely server, was the dry-aged beef tartare with oyster emulsion – a chunky, oozy little bullet of beefy fishiness, styled to look like an oyster in a tempura batter shell. Tartare purists will hate it; oyster purists will hate it more. But Six by Nico, and now Lennox, have never been about stiff rules.View image in fullscreenThe fish finger with katsu curry is the ‘shining light’ on the menu at Manchester’s Lennox restaurant.In fact, the longer I’m in Lennox, the more difficult it is to know where one restaurant finishes and the other begins. A halloumi shawarma with baba ganoush and rosemary flatbread, for example, is really unappetising: dry, unseasoned, neither fine dining nor inventive. But then the gnocchi with chicken wings is genuinely, strangely enticing. Deboning chicken wings makes them small, but the gnocchi, on the other hand, is purposefully large, so what we have is a weird bowl of beige lumps with sheets of parmesan on top. Does it work? It’s comforting but lacks finesse. Still, it’s Friday lunchtime and Lennox is full of life, filling up with couples, groups of friends and Friday-night-out-earlies.For me, the shining light on the menu was the fish finger with katsu curry. A charming idea: think elevated McDonald’s Filet-O-Fish dipped in those tiny pots of curry sauce. Some aged ribeye was very good, although its red wine sauce was slightly thin and bitter.View image in fullscreenA ‘a chunky, oozy little bullet’ of aged beef tartare with parmesan game chips at Lennox Manchester.A plate of salmon gravlax in buttermilk, dill and grapefruit was highly pretty but underwhelming. Lennox feels like being bombarded with ideas from all sides; you’ll leave fed, challenged and ever so slightly gastronomically punch-drunk. We finished with a lemon tart, inexplicably served with a red wine sorbet and rosemary. Three very assertive flavours in a death fight to dominate. My heart cried out for a smidgen of chantilly cream, as a refuge from this bootcamp of flavours.On opening, Lennox was described as a highly personal venture, but there was no sign of Simeone when I visited, and oddly no other named chefs attached to the project.
