His omniscient powers and singular vision are not only running multiple Six by Nicos, but a brave new Lennox-shaped dawn, too. Hospitality would be far more boring without him, but next time, I’ll have the hazelnut tiramisu.LennoxManchester, 60 Spring Gardens, Manchester M2 2BQ, 0161 832 1815;lennoxrestaurant.co.uk. Open Tues-Sun noon-midnight (1am Fri & Sat, 9pm Sun). About £70 a head a la carte for three courses (set menus from £35) plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Electrolyte lemonade to probiotic pop: do the new generation of ‘functional drinks’ live up to the hype? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: They make grand claims about beauty benefits or extra energy – and even actor Gillian Anderson has her own brand. We investigate what they’re really doing – and put them to a taste test
Author: Rebecca Seal
Headline: They make grand claims about beauty benefits or extra energy – and even actor Gillian Anderson has her own brand. We investigate what they’re really doing – and put them to a taste test
Content: Photograph: Steven Joyce/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Steven Joyce/The GuardianLife and styleElectrolyte lemonade to probiotic pop: do the new generation of ‘functional drinks’ live up to the hype?They make grand claims about beauty benefits or extra energy – and even actor Gillian Anderson has her own brand. We investigate what they’re really doing – and put them to a taste testRebecca SealSun 26 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShow yourself some love. Fuel your focus. Life’s too good for bad energy. Find your calm in the everyday chaos. Live fit. No, not new-age slogans or something you’d find scribbled in neon on the wall of a cocktail bar, but marketing taglines slapped across cans of functional soft drinks. Walk into any supermarket or newsagent and there they are, bright and cheerful, right next to the Tango, promising everything from improved mental clarity and zen-like calm, to a blast of highly caffeinated energy as part of your sandwich-and-a-snack lunchtime meal deal. Influencers love them. Your favourite podcasters are sponsored by them. Even Gillian Anderson has a functional drinks brand (brilliantly, she’s called it G Spot).If you have not yet swigged an electrolyte-loaded lemonade or opened a can of probiotic fizzy pop, you might be wondering what functional drinks even are. Because they are marketed as having one or more of many possible physiological and cognitive benefits, it’s a big category. There are functional drinks for focus, productivity, relaxation, calm, protein, energy, gut health and perhaps most confusingly, for hydration – which is, after all, the core function of most potable liquids.Unsurprisingly, the branding of today’s functional drinks says a lot about each one’s intended market: high-caffeine products like Tenzing and Neutonic look as if they’re trying to lure club kids and gamers away from the Red Bull, while XOXO prebiotic drinks and Living Things probiotic drinks come in bright pink or lime green cans which could easily contain a hoppy lager microbrewed under a railway arch. Others are more pared back – Goodrays, Mushus, Mission and Water Junkie go for slim cans in a single colour – while Cadence Core Hydration and Celsius fruit-flavoured energy drinks come in minimal white, black and silver cans that look as if they’ve been designed to slot neatly into bro culture. (Celsius contains 200mg of caffeine per can, about three espressos’ worth, and is particularlypopular with bankers, traders and hedge funders).At £2-3 per bottle or can, functional drinks are readily available and often very sweet way into wellness – and the market is booming. Globally, functional drinks are now worth about £115bn a year and predicted to be worth twice that by 2030. In the UK, the market is generating £100m a year in sales, with aquarter of consumersnow saying that they want functional benefits from the drinks they buy, up from 13% in 2024. Functionality isn’t just limited to drinks: according to Mintel,one out of every four new food and drinklaunches now makes a functional benefit claim.Most functional drinks go hard on the idea that they can meaningfully improve not just your diet, but also your life. They offer everything from “multivitamin support” and “natural energy” to “the power of calm” and “beauty from within”. But can a canned drink really do all – or any – of this?Some functional drinks are made with added vitamins such as A, B12 or D, or minerals such as magnesium, chromium or molybdenum. Others contain so-called adaptogenic and nootropic botanical ingredients, such as ashwagandha, ginseng and reishi, chaga and lion’s mane mushrooms, or contain green tea, yerba mate, matcha, L-theanine, caffeine or CBD (the non-psychoactive ingredient in cannabis). Still more are enriched with collagen, protein, fibre or probiotics. And some contain a dizzying – and not always palatable – mixture of many of the above.double quotation markWhen I’m working with patients, sometimes functional drinks can help get them off less healthy things they already drink, like colasHaving taste-tested a bunch of them alongside drinks writer Aleesha Hansel, I cannot recommend Huel’s Daily Greens, a sparkling soft drink with 45 ingredients, including mushrooms and four green vegetables, and unexpected top notes of cooked broccoli and extremely well-boiled peas. And while many gym-goers swear by protein shakes, I’m going to give a hard pass to protein waters, which tasted not unlike cordial mixed with bone broth.Functional drinks can serve a useful purpose, says consultant dietitian Sophie Medlin, who works at City Dietitians. “They do offer more than other regular soft drinks do. But would I encourage people to start drinking them? No. When I’m working with patients, sometimes functional drinks can help get them off less healthy things they already drink, like colas.” She says three different groups of people consume functional drinks: people who drink a lot of soft drinks and want to swap to something less unhealthy; people looking for something to drink instead of alcohol; and people who previously didn’t buy soft drinks, but who think functional drinks are a worthwhile addition to their diets.Health claims on foods, drinks and supplements are tightly controlled in the UK, and some brands have already got into trouble with the Advertising Standards Authority. A2025 complaintagainst Trip was upheld after its ads suggested that the drink could reducelevels of the stress hormone cortisol and promote calm, while also in 2025, Myotawas censuredfor illegally suggesting a food product could have medicinal effects when promoting its metabolic booster drink.While you might assume that the health claims a brand makes refer to the sum total of all the ingredients in a product and their effects, food and drink producers can only legally make health and nutrition claims about certain ingredients, so vitamins C, D or B12 often do a lot of heavy lifting on the labels. For instance, as long as a product contains 15% of an adult’s recommended daily allowance (RDA) of B12 per 100ml (which costs manufacturers very little to add) a brand can say its drink reduces tiredness and fatigue, supports neurological functioning and helps the immune system. Whether it contains lion’s mane, ginseng or ashwagandha is irrelevant, because the health claim is only being made about the B12.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Steven Joyce/The GuardianIn some cases, the added vitamins aren’t doing much. “Some functional drinks add a long list of vitamins and minerals in small amounts to create a healthperception, even when those nutrients make little difference to overall intake,” says Gopi Chandratheva, a registered nutritionist who works in the NHS and privately.Huel’s Daily Greens drink is marketed as containing 41 vitamins, minerals and superfoods and although it has high levels of vitamins D and B9, each serving provides less than 20% of your daily phosphorus, iron, zinc, molybdenum and chromium requirements. Celsius, however, contains nearly 300% of the RDA for vitamin B7 and well over 100% of the adult RDA for B2, B3, B5, B6 and B12 – all of which we just wee out if taken to excess (although excess B6 can sometimes build up in the body and cause nerve damage). So it’s worth reading the label carefully, especially if you’re already taking other supplements. (Children’s requirements for vitamins and minerals are lower than adults: functional drinks are not designed for them. “ You can easily overdose a child on vitamins if they drink a lot of them,” says Medlin. Many cans do say they’re not suitable for children, or for pregnant or breastfeeding women.)While vitamins and minerals are listed with an RDA or nutrient reference level (NRV) on the label, it’s not always clear whether a functional drink contains clinically or nutritionally significant amounts of adaptogenic and nootropic ingredients, such as lion’s mane or reishi, because in most cases we don’t know what that amount would be. “Products often group together ingredients with very different mechanisms of action and levels of evidence,” says Chandratheva. Adaptogens are plant-based ingredients which are supposed to affect the way your body responds to stressors; nootropics are said to enhance mental functions like memory or function (some substances are both).“‘Clinically significant’ suggests that a product contains a dose which research has shown has a benefit,” says Medlin. “But there’s nowhere near enough research on that, and we don’t have long-term studies about people taking these products every day yet, either. It’s a growing area of research, but the problem with adaptogens and other ‘natural’ products is that things will be a bit different depending on where or how each ingredient, like a mushroom, is grown, so that also makes it difficult to be sure about what would cause a meaningful effect.”Chandratheva says mixing multiple adaptogens or nootropics whose effects we don’t totally understand with vitamins, minerals and stimulants, such as caffeine, or relaxants, such as CBD, might not be wise. “These drinks should be taken with caution, as they contain bioactive compounds and may interact with other medications. Often other ingredients are added to these drinks which can outweigh the benefits.” Some people find that rhodiola isn’t a good match with caffeine, say, and can make them feel jittery or restless.“It could be quite confusing, physiologically,” adds Medlin. “And if you do feel a benefit, it’s likely to be from ingredients like caffeine, rather than from the ingredients you’re paying a lot of money for.”But plenty of people love functional drinks and find them effective. “For me, it’s having them in specific moments of my day,” says Cem Yildiz, a business strategist. “Do I want an afternoon pickup or an evening wind-down; is it post-gym or pre-gym, or after a heavy night or a stressful day? They also taste so good that it’s a double whammy of feeling like you’re doing something good for yourself, but they’re also refreshing and tasty.”Today’s brightly packaged functional drinks feel novel, but they are not exactly new. Teas, coffee and alcohol are arguably the original functional drinks; probiotic fermented drinks, such as kefir, also have a long history. (It’s actually quite hard to think of any drink that doesn’t have some sort of function.) Coca Cola was marketed in the late 19th century as a medicinal temperance drink to rival alcoholic tonic wines, and was supposed to cure everything from addiction to indigestion. Energy drinks containing taurine and caffeine emerged in the 1960s, before Red Bull took them global in the 1990s. Sports drinks such as Lucozade and Gatorade are also functional drinks. But the new breed of mushroom-laden, herb-infused self-optimisation-obsessed functional drink really took off during the pandemic.double quotation markI haven’t drunk alcohol for six months and I lean very heavily on functional drinks as replacementsThe biggest of the new brands is Trip, which launched in 2019 but is now so widely available that it’s often part of the meal deal at my local Co-op. The wellness industry flourished in the aftermath of the pandemic, when many of us started to pay attention to our health in ways we never did before; functional drinks are a less expensive part of a larger trend that includes complex skincare regimes,red-light masks, health trackers and sleep monitors.Plus, as Laura Willoughby, alcohol-free drinks expert and founder of theClub Sodamindful drinking movement, says, “The number of people who don’t drink at all has plateaued in recent years, but the number of people who want to drink less is still rising.” She sees functional drinks as a great stand-in for alcohol, and so does Sian Fellowes (not her real name), who works in hospitality. “I haven’t drunk alcohol for six months and I lean very heavily on functional drinks as replacements.” (Not everyone who is sober agrees: “I gave up drink and drugs because I didn’t want to take anything mind-altering any more,” says my friend Tom. “Functional drinks have zero appeal to me.”)The Food Standards Agency in 2023 lowered its recommended daily intake limit for CBD, and some brands have since reformulated. It is now 10mg (down from 70mg) afternew evidence emergedthat long-term use might be connected to liver damage and thyroid disease.“CBD does have specific medical uses, and there is some evidence for anxiety reduction,” says Chandratheva. “But most consumer drinks contain relatively small doses and the evidence for meaningful effects from low doses remains limited.” Mosthuman trialslooking at CBD for anxiety have used doses from 150-600mg. A single can of a Goodrays CBD drink contains 10mg, as do Trip’s CBD drinks. Medahuman’s CBD drinks contain 20mg and a can of Hip Pop’s CBD kombucha has 15mg, so if you’re a regular consumer it wouldn’t be hard to take too much without necessarily getting any benefits.double quotation markI’ve tried a CBD drink a few times and always feel incredibly weird for an hour afterwards.Some people find they don’t react well to CBD on its own. Ceri Jones is a chef and food educator: “I’ve tried a CBD drink a few times and always feel incredibly weird for an hour afterwards. A kind of calm-but-spaced-out confusion. I had one on a train a few weeks back, then couldn’t find my way out of the station. So they definitely do something!”But for others, CBD is a gamechanger. “I use CBD drinks, often in the evening because they calm my brain,” says Dan Farr, a copywriter. “They work particularly well at the end of the week, or if I’ve been drinking the night before, and help my nervous system settle back into a ‘normal’ rhythm and calm my anxiety.”Electrolyte drinks are huge on social media (blame #watertok and heatwaves), and many wellness influencers sell or promote them. Historically, you probably only drank electrolytes if you’d had a stomach upset, and most electrolyte drinks contain a mixture of minerals, such as sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium, and perhaps sugar. Modern electrolyte drinks are marketed on the basis that none of us drinks enough water and that water alone isn’t fully hydrating. (Not true, says Medlin. “If you’re drinking enough water and you’re eating a normal diet, you don’t need electrolytes.”)The popularity of electrolyte drinks (and powders) may mean a lot of us are suddenly consuming too much salt. “Dietitians and public-health professionals have worked for decades to get people to reduce their salt intake, which has had a really positive impact on stroke incidents and cardiac problems,” says Medlin. “Now everybody’s taking electrolytes and potentially getting excess sodium. If it’s very hot, or you’re doing a lot of exercise and sweating a lot, if you’ve had diarrhoea or if you’ve got a medical condition that requires it, electrolytes are useful. But the rest of the time, nobody needs them.” (Electrolytes are handy if you have a hangover, a drinks writer friend tells me. “I do drinks trips where I feel woozy and generally dehydrated no matter how much water I drink, and electrolytes really save me,” she says.) The UK guidance states that adults should have no more than 6g of salt per day (the WHO says 5g). Cadence contains 1.25g of salt per 330ml can, as does a can of Na11.Medlin doesn’t think magnesium waters are particularly helpful, either. “ If you’ve got symptoms of magnesium deficiency, such as muscle cramps, or if you are struggling with sleep or mental energy levels or brain fog, it’s worth experimenting with a magnesium capsule,” she says. “It’s difficult to get enough magnesium into anything apart from a capsule, because you need quite a big dose for it to make a difference, which might mean drinking multiple of these drinks a day.” OHMG’s blackcurrant sparkling water contains 100mg of magnesium per can, about a quarter of a UK adult’s NRV; BetterYou’s citrus and botanical magnesium water contains about half the NRV per can.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Steven Joyce/The GuardianWhat about protein or collagen water? Many people may benefit from more protein in their diet, says Medlin. “But if you feel you need a bit more protein, eat a bit more protein rather than having a drink that has loads of additives in it. Ultimately, these drinks are all ultra-processed foods, and we need to see them in that light rather than as something beneficial.”There is still quite a large gap between what the makers of collagen products claim andwhat the research says– there is little high-quality, large-scale research to suggest that consuming extra collagen positively impacts joints, skin, hair or nails. When we eat collagen (or any protein or peptide) our bodies decide what to break it down into and where to use it – we can’t direct it specificallyat our wrinkles or aching knees. Many people don’t realise that bovine collagen is industrially extracted from the skin, connective tissue and bones leftover after cows are slaughtered for meat, or that marine collagen is made from fish bones and viscera. (Vegan collagen is in fact a selection of plant-based peptides mimicking those found in animal-based collagen.)Few functional drinks, such as Tenzing, contain sugar; most use artificial sweeteners, usually steviol glycosides or sucralose, acesulfame potassium, or erythritol. Steviol glycosides are 200-400 times sweeter than sugar and sucralose is about 600 times sweeter. “Most sweeteners are ultra-sweet,” says Medlin. “And that can make us more likely to look for sugary and sweet things elsewhere,” training our palates to want sweet flavours. “As a gut-health dietitian, I’m very careful with sweeteners, because we know they’re detrimental to gut bacteria.”Even caffeine, ubiquitous in modern life, needs a health warning. A cup of tea contains 30-50mg of caffeine and a cup of coffee 60-100mg, depending on size and strength, but some energy drinks contain 200mg per can.“Too much caffeine can affect our health negatively. It acts as a stimulant and can cause anxiety and poor sleep,” says Chandratheva. In rare cases,fatal heart arrhythmiacan result from drinking well above the NRV of 400mg a day ora large amount very quickly. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that children under 12 do not drink caffeine, and children aged 12-18 should have no more than 100mg a day. In the UK, the NHS says babies and young children should not drink it; the government is consulting on whether to ban the sale of caffeinated drinks to under 16s in England.Functional drinks with added fibre or live probiotics are perhaps the least problematic – and in some cases the least processed, too. “I don’t think adding fibre or probiotics to our diets is unreasonable,” says Medlin. “But I do worry about people who are doing it if they already have irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Most of the added-fibre drinks contain inulin, the most common source of which is chicory root, and that can trigger IBS symptoms.”Dr Daniel Lamport is a psychologist at the University of Reading who studies the impact of nutrition on cognition and mental health. He has researched probiotics, polyphenols and flavonoids (both beneficial chemicals found in fruits and vegetables) to see if they boost our brain power or our mood. “ There is a place for functional foods, but I’m not convinced there is currently a robust evidence base for many of the claims being made for wellbeing and cognition,” he tells me. “Ultimately, there is no substitute for a fibre-rich, fruit-and-vegetable-rich, whole-foods diet; on that front, the evidence is clear and compelling on the benefits for cognitive health.” So show yourself some love: “It’s just always better to eat the whole food.”‘If you love Red Bull, you’ll love this’: functional drinks, ratedView image in fullscreenWriter Rebecca Seal (left) and drinks writer Aleesha Hansel.Photograph: Steven Joyce/The GuardianKnowing that a tasting would involve a weird and wonderful range of flavours and ingredients, I recruited drinks writer and editor ofSlake magazine, Aleesha Hansel (pictured on right) to help. This wasn’t a blind tasting, as we wanted to know what the product was intended to do ahead of trying them, so looked at the ingredients before we began, and listed the key ones here. Though we both have good palates, picking out notes of yerba mate over those of chaga mushroom or broccoli juice is a challenge.Mission Lime+ Yuzu Natural Energy + HydrationView image in fullscreenWhat it costs£2/250mlWhat it promises“Functional, light energy and nothing else” and “science-led ingredients to fuel your extraordinary”.What it contains*Sparkling water, yerba mate extract, magnesium, natural flavourings, ginkgo biloba extract, Himalayan pink salt electrolytes, vitamins C, B3, B6, B7, B12 and D3, natural caffeine.How it tastes“You can really smell the citrus flavours just from opening the can,” says Hansel. “ It’s all in the front, though. You get the yuzu and lime on the front palate but then it goes to an almost sherbety, synthetic taste. There’s an earthy note underneath, probably the yerba mate. I think they’ve had to make the other flavours so intense to cover up that. Not for me, I’m afraid.”£25 for 12 at MissionG Spot ProtectView image in fullscreenWhat it costs£2/250mlWhat it promises“Daily defence for resilience and wellness” and “ this is where pleasure meets protection”.What it containsSparkling water, ginger juice, apple juice, lemon juice, erythritol, kombucha, meadowsweet, turmeric, peppercorn, chaga, natural flavours, vitamin C.How it tastesG Spot is actor Gillian Anderson’s functional drinks brand. “Oh Gillian, I wanted to love this,” says Hansel. Sadly, we don’t. “ It smells like baked-bean sauce – that’s not getting anyone in the mood. I was expecting ginger and peppercorn, but those flavours are not there.” Given that it’s made with apple and lemon juice plus kombucha, there isn’t much acidity, either. “It feels very limp, which is the opposite of what she’s trying to do.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£29.95 for 12 at AmazonFibe Fruit PunchView image in fullscreenWhat it costs£1.99/250mlWhat it promises“Happy gut, happy days” and 5g fibre per can.What it containsWater, chicory root inulin, calcium lactate, vitamin C, fructose, natural fruit flavours, citric acid, fruit colour extracts, steviol glycosides.How it tastes“On the can, it says it has pure party vibes, so I’m expecting a lot,” says Hansel. “The colour and the smell are definitely fruit punch, so they get a tick for that. It’s very nostalgic and it tastes exactly how I want a fruit punch to taste, and the sweetness is good. It’s not sophisticated, but it quite literally does what it says on the tin. I’m happy with that. Well done, Fibe.”£6.50 for 4 at Holland & BarrettWater Junkie Feel Alive, Chaga mushrooms, Coconut and LycheeView image in fullscreenWhat it costs£2.49/250mlWhat it promises“Energy and immunity support”.What it containsCarbonated water, grape juice, lychee juice, ginger extracts, chaga, turmeric, magnesium lactate, natural lychee and coconut flavourings, steviol glycosides, B6.How it tastes“ I don’t want this to taste of mushrooms,” says Hansel – and it doesn’t. “The coconut and lychee are giving suncream and pina colada, with a little bit of ginger and turmeric.” But not in a good way.£2.49 for 1 at Holland & BarrettVieve Strawberry& Rhubarb Protein WaterView image in fullscreenWhat it costs£2.59/250mlWhat it promises20g of protein, “a tasty, hydrating protein top-up.”What it containsWater, bovine collagen hydrolysate, phosphoric acid, carrot concentrate, natural strawberry and rhubarb flavouring, citric acid, sucralose.How it tastesAt first, the scent reminds us of strawberry bubble bath. “But there’s also a weird smell of animal hair and … animal’s feet?” says Hansel. The bovine collagen means it tastes as though someone has stirred beef stock into a glass of squash. “It’s excessively sweet. They’re trying to override the meatiness with the sweetness, trying to pretend it doesn’t exist. But it does exist. Oh, that’s horrible.”£11.10 for 6 at AmazonTrip Sicilian Lemon Mindful BlendView image in fullscreenWhat it costs£2/250mlWhat it promises“A drink that actually does something”.What it containsCarbonated water, grape and lemon juices from concentrate, magnesium, citric acid, extracts of lion’s mane, lemon balm and chamomile, ascorbic acid, steviol glycosides.How it tastes“I like how this one tastes,” says Hansel. “It’s got a very nice level of acidity, a nice zestiness – all the flavours feel integrated.” It doesn’t feel as if we are drinking something designed to include ingredients just because they are functional – it’s easy to see why Trip is such a successful brand.£6.50 for 4 at WaitroseNeutonic Natural Energy Orange Sunrise Productivity DrinkView image in fullscreenWhat it costs£2.75/330mlWhat it promises“Fuel your focus”, “research-backed nootropic ingredients” from the “world’s first productivity drink”.What it containsCarbonated water, green tea extract containing L-theanine, natural flavourings, Cognizin (citicoline), rhodiola rosea, panax ginseng, natural caffeine, sucralose, acesulfame potassium, B vitamins.How it tastesWe agree that coffee can probably make a better claim to be the world’s first productivity drink. It smells a little like Calpol. “This is so sweet, it’s almost syrupy,” says Hansel. “Wow, that’s intense – the orange flavour isn’t real oranges, it’s just like Berocca. If you love Red Bull, you’ll love this.”£29.99 for 12 at HealfGoodrays Raspberry& Guava CBD 30mgView image in fullscreenWhat it costs£7.50/4 x 250ml cansWhat it promises“A moment of calm for the curious, the creative, the bold and the brave”.What it containsCarbonated water, grape juice, raspberry juice, natural flavourings including guava, natural colourings, malic acid, lactic acid, acidity regulator, CBD isolate, vitamin D.How it tastes“I’m expecting this to be very zesty with lots of red fruit flavours and a bit of tartness from the guava.” The liquid is very pink “and it smells like squash,” says Hansel. “There’s a lavender or Parma Violet flavour to this, which I don’t like. It’s like I’ve eaten my grandmother’s pot-pourri – it’s so perfumed.”£11.25 for 6 at AmazonGrass & Co, Peach, Chamomile& Reishi Liquid RelaxView image in fullscreenWhat it costs£2.49 /250mlWhat it promises“Mental clarity, relaxation and natural energy”.What it containsWater, apple concentrate, magnesium, reishi extract, ashwagandha extract, citric acid, peach flavouring, chamomile flavouring, B vitamins.What it tastes like“There’s white-fruit fleshiness to the nose, from the apple and peach,” says Hansel. “ The flavours are muddy, whereas I want to be able to pick out what’s in this, so that’s disappointing. There’s a slightly savoury note, which I think would come from the mushroom and ashwagandha. It’s not the worst we’ve tasted, but I’m not in love. It’s very middling.”£9 for 4 at Holland & BarrettExplore more on these topicsLife and styleHealthMental healthFoodFood scienceFitnessShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect homemade viennetta – recipe | Dessert | The Guardian
description: Your rosy memories of the classic ice-cream dessert may not hold up to scrutiny today, but thanks to our resident perfectionist, you can make a delicious version of your own
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Your rosy memories of the classic ice-cream dessert may not hold up to scrutiny today, but thanks to our resident perfectionist, you can make a delicious version of your own
Content: Felicity Cloake's Viennetta.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake's Viennetta.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.How to cook the perfect ...DessertHow to make the perfect homemade viennetta – recipeYour rosy memories of the classic ice-cream dessert may not hold up to scrutiny today, but thanks to our resident perfectionist, you can make a delicious version of your ownFelicity CloakeSun 26 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was growing up,viennettawas something I had in other people’s houses – for some reason, my mum regarded these frilly blocks of ice-cream as a waste of money, which made them all the bigger treat on the rare occasion I did get a front-row seat at the cracking of the chocolate. Launched, like me, in 1982, when developers at Wall’s realised that pumping ice-cream on to the production line slightly faster than the speed of the conveyor belt created a concertina effect that, I think we can now, with the wisdom of age, agree, is more impressive to behold than to consume. No doubt diehard devotees will beg to differ, but even as a child I couldn’t help but notice that all that air made the viennetta distinctly light on flavour (no wonder one slice is never enough, as the old advertising campaign had it). Happily, you can recreate the magic at home with something that looks good and tastes great – and you don’t even need your own conveyor belt!The ice-creamView image in fullscreenThe Gladwins of London’s The Shed add egg yolks for a ‘paté à bombe’. Thumbnail pics direct from Felicity’s kitchen.You may be relieved to learn that this is not a recipe for which you’ll need an ice-cream maker – the real thing is an egg-free zone, though two of the recipes I try do use them. ForRichard, Oliver and Gregory Gladwinof Notting Hill’s The Shed, that’s in the form of yolks, which are whipped with sugar syrup to make apâte à bombe, which is then folded into whipped cream to produce something much like a frozen vanilla mousse. Delicious, but distinctly richer and denser than the authentic model. Pastry chef and award-winning author Nicola Lamb, however, who has trodden this particular obsessive path before me, and whose findings, published on her reliably excellentKitchen Projects Substack, I am indebted to, whisks a French (ie, uncooked) meringue into cream instead, with the aim of achieving maximum airiness without any other trace of the eggs themselves, because egg whites are “pretty much flavourless and colourless”.Her version is judged by my testers to be the closest to the original, but with a superior richness of flavour, rather than texture – it’s definitely lighter thanGabriella English’scondensed milk version in Red magazine, which is wonderfully creamy, but has the solidity of an old-fashioned brick of vanilla, orGeorgina Hayden’swhipped cream and mascarpone number in her new book MEDesque, which is positively velvety … unlike the OG. I’m also very keen on theslightly smoother version from the much-missed Delicious magazine, which combines whipping cream with glucose syrup and ice-cream, but, seeing as glucose syrup, which also features in the Wall’s version, is strictly speaking a UPF, I’ve decided to stick with the egg whites, which have the additional benefit of being easier to source in even the smallest of shops.“With double cream,” Lamb says, “we know that you need only 10-25% sugar to cream [by] weight to make a smooth and not-too-sweet final product. So, although it is tempting to add extra sugar to make a super-stiff meringue, we then have a potential issue of the dessert being over sweet.” I hold up my hands to our collective unsophisticated palate – my testing panel all wistfully say they wish it was a bit sweeter – so, though the credit must go to Lamb, I’ve tweaked the ratios.The chocolateView image in fullscreenGabriella English’s viennetta. English melts the chocolate and spreads it.The other signature characteristic of the actual Viennetta is its layers of crackly chocolate, which shatter satisfyingly under the knife. To get them to do this, they have to remain distinct from the ice-cream, and the recipes I try take a variety of approaches to this. Delicious magazine, English and Hayden all melt the chocolate, then add it in liquid form, though only the latter two advise leaving it to cool first, which is vital: molten chocolate has an inconvenient tendency to melt into whipped cream. Hayden drizzles it, which I find results in a somewhat patchy layer, English spreads it (which is impossible to do without some mixing of the cream and chocolate), while Delicious suggests piping or spraying it.Best I draw a line over my inept attempts to get molten chocolate through a spray bottle – suffice to say there was a fair bit of cleaning up to do afterwards – but having tried all these approaches, I would strongly recommend melting the chocolate in advance, then spreading it out into a thin layer that, once solid, can simply be slotted in between the layers of cream, as Lamb and the Gladwins do. You don’t need the marble slab the Gladwins mention for this purpose; in fact, I found it much easier on Lamb’s baking paper-lined tray than the clingfilm the brothers give as an alternative.You don’t even need to break the chocolate neatly – shards will do, though you might, as Lamb does, like to finish with a large piece on top. It doesn’t feature in the boxed sort, but it does snap very nicely.The flavouringView image in fullscreen‘Hayden goes brilliantly rogue by whizzing up basil leaves to create something that looks like a mint viennetta’.Wall’s Viennettas come in a reassuringly modest range of flavours – as well as the classic vanilla and chocolate, there’s a mint version (always my own favourite) and a salted caramel one that I haven’t yet tried, plus a few seasonal specials – but one of the great things about making your own is that you can make your childish dreams come true at the same time. Most of the recipes I try stick with vanilla (extract, paste or seeds, as you like, though the tell-tale black flecks of fresh seeds is always a suggestion of quality. I say “fresh”, because some commercial vanilla ice-creams get their speckles from “exhausted vanilla bean pieces”, which look good, but taste of very little). The Gladwins include a layer of homemade butterscotch sauce, English some little crunchy pieces of hazelnut, which remind us all pleasantly of another iconic Wall’s produce, the Cornetto, while Hayden goes brilliantly rogue by whizzing up basil leaves to create something that looks like a mint viennetta, but that has the sweet, anise-like, Mediterranean perfume of basil. I’ve stuck with the classic version, but I already have plans to get more adventurous: perhaps a fig leaf and almond caramel is in my future?The constructionAn ice-cream terrine is always a beautiful thing to eat, but, without suitable adornment, it can risk looking rather brick-like. Delicious pipes the mixture in pretty layers using a star-shaped nozzle, allowing each one to freeze before adding the next, which works well, but is an undeniable faff. A better solution, as far as I’m concerned, is to freeze the whole thing in a loaf tin, as everyone else recommends, then decorate it with sweetened whipped cream, as Lamb suggests (at this rate, her name should possibly be at the top of this column rather than mine). I’ve gone for whipping cream for this outer layer, to make it a little lighter, but if you’ve got double leftover from the ice-cream, feel free to use that instead, or go for a combination.View image in fullscreenNicola Lamb ‘s viennetta. Decorate with a single slab and ‘sweetened whipped cream’, as Lamb suggests.The top of the real deal is simply sprinkled with cocoa powder, but, depending how faithful you’d like to be to the original, you might like to add another layer of chocolate, some chopped nuts or perhaps (and I am very pro this idea) some cherries in syrup in a nod to another 1980s favourite,the black forest gateau.Once refrozen, this dessert should keep well in the freezer for up to a month.Perfect homemade viennettaPrep15 minFreeze3 hr 30 min +Cook5 minServes670g dark chocolateFlaky salt(optional)300g double cream3 medium egg whites1 pinch saltSeeds of 1 vanilla pod, or 1 tbsp vanilla bean paste or extract70g caster sugarTo decorate200g whipping or double cream40g caster sugarCocoa powder, to dustBreak the chocolate into pieces, then melt it in a heatproof bowl set over, but not touching, a pan of simmering water, or in the microwave. Meanwhile, line a baking tray with greaseproof paper, and stick the paper down at the corners with a little honey or jam.View image in fullscreenPour the melted chocolate on to the paper, spread it out as thinly as possible, then sprinkle with a little flaky salt, if using, and leave to set. Once set, break the chocolate sheet into shards.View image in fullscreenLine a roughly 19cm x 9cm x 6cm loaf tin (that is, a 450g or 1lb tin) with clingfilm, leaving enough overhang to fold over the top later (you may need to use two pieces of clingfilm set at right angles).Whip the cream for the ice-cream in a large bowl or food mixer until it just holds soft peaks, bearing in mind that you’ll be whipping it further in a minute.View image in fullscreenWhisk the egg whites (you should have about 105g) and a pinch of salt in a second bowl, until foamy, then beat in the vanilla. Gradually, and still whisking at a moderate speed, add the sugar and beat to soft peaks.View image in fullscreenAdd a spoonful of this meringue mix to the cream, whisk briefly to combine, then carefully fold in the remaining meringue until it’s thoroughly incorporated, and keeping as much air in the mixture as possible; don’t worry if it looks a little grainy.View image in fullscreenSpoon a third of the cream mixture into the lined tin and gently level the top (again, you don’t want to knock out the air), then scatter with half the chocolate shards.View image in fullscreenRepeat with another layer of cream and another layer of chocolate, then top with a final layer of cream. Fold the clingfilm over the top and freeze for at least three hours, until solid.View image in fullscreenWhisk the whipping or double cream with the caster sugar until it holds its shape, then spoon into a piping bag and cut a ½cm hole off the tip.View image in fullscreenLift the viennetta out of its tin and unwrap, then decorate the sides with alternating straight and frilly lines of whipped cream. If you’re feeling fancy, use a ribbon nozzle to decorate the top with wiggly parallel lines, or simply repeat the same pattern on top.View image in fullscreenReturn to the freezer for at least half an hour, until frozen. Sprinkle with cocoa powder before serving – a line down the centre looks authentic.Viennetta: is it still the fanciest dessert you can imagine, or have you grown out of this distinctly ultra-processed, if undeniably enjoyable treat? What’s your favourite memory of them, your favourite flavour, and what will you be putting in your homemade version?Explore more on these topicsDessertHow to cook the perfect ...FoodIce-cream and sorbetChocolateBritish food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I panic. It turns to rubber’: could I learn to make omurice, the ‘world’s hardest omelette’? | Japanese food and drink | The Guardian
description: These unctuous rice-filled Japanese egg dishes are all over social media. But what does it cost to make them? A lot of eggs and a whole lot of pans ...
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: These unctuous rice-filled Japanese egg dishes are all over social media. But what does it cost to make them? A lot of eggs and a whole lot of pans ...
Content: ‘If Bourdian wrote that omelette skills reveal your character, then I’m lacking integrity’ … Ammar Kalia tackles the classic omurice.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘If Bourdian wrote that omelette skills reveal your character, then I’m lacking integrity’ … Ammar Kalia tackles the classic omurice.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianJapanese food and drink‘I panic. It turns to rubber’: could I learn to make omurice, the ‘world’s hardest omelette’?These unctuous rice-filled Japanese egg dishes are all over social media. But what does it cost to make them? A lot of eggs and a whole lot of pans ...Ammar KaliaSun 26 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmong the endless videos of cute animals, influencer vlogs and celebrity content, something unusual has been going viral across social media recently: omelettes. A far cry from the usual solid egg slabs served in cafes, these bright yellow omelettes are a fluffy, oval-shaped treat filled with unctuous liquid curds, which are typically sliced open to unfurl across a mound of rice. Called omurice, the Japanese dish has been called “the world’s hardest omelette to make”.London-based software engineer Jeremy Ocampo, who goes by the social media tag OmuricePapi, has spent the past six months documenting his journey to perfect the art of the omurice online. In the process he has amassed 110,000 followers onYouTubeand more than 68,000 onInstagram. “I’m Filipino, so I grew up eating rice and eggs every day, but it took going to Japan for the first time in 2025 to have my mind blown by omurice,” he says. “I was hooked: the presentation of slicing it open over your rice makes it so alluring, while you can’t replicate that texture of egg in any other dish. It’s so unique that when I got home, I decided to teach myself how to do it.”Initially struggling to find the right nonstick pan that could allow the egg mixture to slide and fold easily, and then running into difficulties when it came to selecting the ideal temperature on his gas hob, Ocampo estimates it took him 50 tries until he finally came up with a passable attempt. “I’ve been making it three times a week and I was eating so many eggs I actually realised I was mildly allergic to them,” he laughs, adding that he now largely serves his omurice to friends. “I must have spent about £150 on 300 eggs and I’ve gone through at least five pans – but now I’m pretty consistent, and it takes me around a minute from start to finish,” he says. “You just have to keep a positive attitude if you want to keep trying and learn yourself eventually!”View image in fullscreenAn exemplary omurice at Kyuramen, Winchester, MA.Photograph: Boston Globe/Getty ImagesTheories differ as to the origins of omurice. Some believe it was invented at the turn of the 20th century in a western-style restaurant in Tokyo’s Ginza district; others say it emerged in Osaka in 1925, when a diner chef decided to pair an omelette with rice. Yet, it only became popular across Japan in the 1950s. “There was a period [of food] in Japan called Yōshoku, where we brought in lots of western cultural influences and it was very widespread after the second world war,” says Japanese chef and culinary expertYuki Gomi. “Things like yakisoba and katsu curry are all examples of this western mixing, while omurice has both French and American influences. I’m 50 now and I remember growing up in the 1970s with my mother making me omurice. It was a cute dish for children, where you would write their name or a smiley face on the egg with ketchup. I have made it lots for my own daughter, although my version is flatter than the ones going crazy on social media now.”A more traditional omurice is closer to a French-style omelette and always served over a seasoned tomato rice, with a squirt of ketchup the typical garnish. The buoyant, dome-like omurice that has gone viral over social media, however, originated in the late 1970s with omelette aficionado – and online personality in his own right – Motokichi Yukimura. Founding his restaurantKichi Kichi Omuricein Kyoto in 1978, in tribute to his favourite childhood dish, it was only a decade ago that Yukimura’sparticularly theatrical versionof the omurice began attracting international attention thanks to his penchant for singing and dancing while cooking the dish.“I spent years perfecting my version of the omurice. Then, I realised I wanted to create more than a delicious meal but a joyful experience too, so I started talking to my guests while cooking and creating a performance,” Yukimura says. “People would video my omurice and soon we began having customers queueing around the corner to get into the restaurant. Over the past decade I think I have made 100,000 omelettes. I just want to make the world happy through omurice!”Pairing his version with a glossy, umami-rich demi-glace glaze that takes nine hours to reduce, Yukimura’s renowned dish has since spawned alternative versions in the UK. Michelin-starred London restaurantMountainhas a spider crab omelette sprinkled with sea kelp on its menu, which, although not labelled as an omurice, still slices open to splay over the plate.Buy & Bite, which has three locations in London, serves omurice with everything from Thai green curry to Chinese sweet and sour sauce.View image in fullscreenAmmar begins his omurice by prepping the pan.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianWhen the time comes to make my own version, I decide to buy Yukimura’s branded nonstick skillet pan, which is one of Ocampo’s go-tos. I also choose to cook on a gas hob, to ensure I can manipulate the pan over the flame at different angles. Following Ocampo’s Instagramtutorial video, I heat the pan until a speck of egg mix sizzles, pour in three beaten eggs and immediately start whisking vigorously with chopsticks to develop curds. Once the edges look cooked, I peel them away from the pan with a spatula and try to fold the omelette into a dumpling shape. It immediately splits and the liquid filling pours back into the pan. Feeling as if I’m about to be shouted at by Gordon Ramsay, I panic and let it cook further to try to fold again but it simply hardens into rubber.View image in fullscreenThe eggs are set and it’s folding time for Ammar.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianI dump it out and start over, this time letting the base cook for a few seconds longer. Thankfully, it folds. I tilt the eggy mass to the front edge of the pan and angle into the flame so it can harden. Now for the method that both Ocampo and Japanese chefAkemi Yokoyamadescribe as the most difficult: performing a gentle pancake toss so that folded seam can land on the underside of the omelette. Of course, the entire thing breaks apart and I’m now left with two solid omelettes for my lunch.View image in fullscreenThe finished, successful, result.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianOver the course of the next week, I come to realise why omurice is described as “the world’s hardest omelette”, and why Ocampo cautioned patience and a positive attitude. The rice is simple and tasty enough – only requiring onion, Worcestershire sauce and ketchup to be mixed into a precooked portion – but my egg skills are left wanting. The several omelettes I make continually burst apart before I can roll them over my rice, and the experience of eating so many overcooked eggs is starting to make me think that I, too, may be allergic. On one miraculous occasion, I create a haphazard square version and get to taste the rich, almost sweet texture of the omurice innards. I can see why people might queue for Yukimura’s version, but if the late Anthony Bourdain thought that “the way you make an omelette reveals your character”, then I’m clearly lacking in integrity.I’m comforted by Ocampo’s 50 attempts to perfect his version; as well as Gomi and Yokoyama’s admissions that they are yet to make the social media version of the omelette without fault. “It requires a certain amount of muscle memory,” Yokoyama says. “In Japan, people just go to a restaurant to eat it cheaply now, rather than bother to make it at home.” I think I might have to do the same. Perhaps it’s best to leave the world’s hardest omelette to the experts.Explore more on these topicsJapanese food and drinkFoodFood and drinkChefsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My partner’s mother dominates him and it makes me feel helpless | Relationships | The Guardian
description: You are stepping into a family system with its own history and loyalties; try to consider how you might set boundaries without rejecting his mum
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: You are stepping into a family system with its own history and loyalties; try to consider how you might set boundaries without rejecting his mum
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignAsk Annalisa BarbieriRelationshipsMy partner’s mother dominates him and it makes me feel helplessYou are stepping into a family system with its own history and loyalties; try to consider how you might set boundaries without rejecting his mumAnnalisa BarbieriSun 26 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m in my 30s and have been living in Spain for a decade. My partneris Spanish and wehave lived together for a year.The bond he haswith his mumsometimes makes me feel angry, jealous and helpless. I’m aware that, culturally, Spanish people often have closer bonds with their families and I try toaccept that. He is an only child and his father left his family when he was a teenager and started another. I feel my partner has developed an unhealthy and codependent relationship with his mum.His mum often says thingssuch as “I never see you,”which feelsmanipulative.After he spends time withher, hewill sometimesbe more loving towards me, which makes me feel weird. I don’t know if we canbuild a life together because it seems heis still so emotionally attached toher.He doesn’tadmitthere is a dependencyand I find it hard to describe my feelings because hegets defensive. I end up feelinglike I’m making a big deal of it. Can you help me find some claritytohandle this?If something is causing you angst please don’t minimise it by thinking you are making it a big deal. I think most people would be upset by this. But you are right to say there is a strong cultural element.I went to the UKCP-accredited psychotherapist and social workerJason Maldonado-Page, who is from a southern European background, to help us unpick this.“You’re navigating this system from the outside, in a different country, with different cultural norms and without the fullness of their shared history,” he says. “Feeling unsure of your place as a couple is an understandable response.”It’s important to remember that all couples, regardless of background, compare familial upbringings and traditions and “try to decide what is normal”, says Maldonado-Page. Being Italian, I found quite a lot of differences and difficulties between me and my English husband in terms of our family dynamics.double quotation markIt may help to see this as a pattern all three of you are caught in“You are,” says Maldonado-Page, “stepping into a family system with its own history, losses and loyalties, while trying to build a partnership that feels anchored. As an only child whose father left during adolescence, he may have grown up feeling responsible for his mother’s emotional world. In many families that closeness is not only typical but expected. None of that makes your discomfort any less real, but it may explain why he becomes defensive – you’re touching a bond that has been central to his sense of safety for a long time.”In terms of becoming more affectionate after interacting with his mum, Maldonado-Page says this pattern can “develop when someone feels caught between two important relationships. It may be less about her influencing than him trying to regulate his anxiety or repair tension.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI ghosted a problematic friend. Now I feel terrible, but also relievedRead moreHe suggests “thinking together about the expectations and beliefs you grew up with around closeness and loyalty” – this can help you see each other’s differing points of view. How can you set boundaries without rejecting his mum? What parts of his relationship with her feel meaningful and which feel heavy? And also, if things get heated, “pre-empt the spiral, agree to pause and reflect later”.“It may help to see this as a pattern all three of you are caught in,” says Maldonado-Page. “The task is not to break his bond with his mother but to reshape it so that your couple relationship has space to grow.”He recommends trying to move away from viewing his mother as invasive and to think more about what strengthens you as a couple. Just don’t make him choose between you both – that rarely leads to harmony.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is availablehere.Comments on this piece are pre-moderated to ensure the discussion remains on the topics raised by the article. Please be aware that there may be a short delay in comments appearing on the site.Explore more on these topicsRelationshipsAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyParents and parentingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I never thought I’d fall for a scam’: the fake Spotify emails that put you at risk of fraud | Money | The Guardian
description: Criminals send victims to a cloned site that collects login, personal and payment details
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Criminals send victims to a cloned site that collects login, personal and payment details
Content: Spotify says it will never ask for personal information via email, including payment details.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSpotify says it will never ask for personal information via email, including payment details.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockScam watchMoney‘I never thought I’d fall for a scam’: the fake Spotify emails that put you at risk of fraudCriminals send victims to a cloned site that collects login, personal and payment detailsSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorSun 26 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou have had aSpotifyaccount for years and your credit card is linked for the monthly payments. When an email arrives telling you that your payment couldn’t be processed you are not surprised as the expiry date on the card is soon.“We encountered an issue while processing your recent payment,” it says. “To keep your access active and avoid interruption, please review and update your information.”All you need to do, according to the email, is click the button to “update payment method”. “This only takes a moment and helps ensure uninterrupted access to your account and services.”When you click the link you are taken to what you think is Spotify and you are asked to log in and then enter your new card details, your address and phone number.Unfortunately, the email is not from Spotify and the link takes you to a cloned scam site that collects your login, personal and payment details, which criminals then immediately try to use for online purchases.“I saw the email on my phone while I was having a conversation and watching the tennis so just tapped the link to update the card without thinking about it,” said Barry*, who contacted the Guardian after falling victim to the scam. “I was immediately hit with a suspicious credit card check for ‘Tm Connect’ followed by a Ticketmaster transaction in US$ for a sum equivalent to £469.22, which I declined.”“I never thought I would be the kind of person to fall for a scam and I am exactly the kind of person to judge those who do. Luckily I use virtual credit cards for online subscriptions, so I could quickly cancel the card and change my unique Spotify password to limit the damage.”What it looks likeView image in fullscreenThe scam email looks convincing at a glance, but look closely and you will spot inconsistencies that give the game away, such as an unknown sender and lower-case subject.Composite: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe fake emails are a convincing replica of Spotify’s email notifications, including the company’s logo, the correct colour scheme and MySpotify name on the email.Small telltale signs show the email is not legitimate, such as not including the tier of your Spotify subscription and using all lower-case letters for the email subject line.But the biggest give away is that the email does not come from an @spotify.com address and clicking the button takes you to a random site not using the spotify.com domain.View image in fullscreenThe site you end up at also looks convincing on first look, but the URL is not a Spotify.com domain.Composite: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianWhat to doIf you receive an email like this, even if you are expecting to change your payment details in the near future, do not click the links. Go direct to Spotify and log in on Spotify.com to make any changes when necessary.“Spotify takes the protection of users very seriously,” said a company spokesperson. “We will never ask for personal information via email, including payment details, passwords, or government-issued identification numbers. We will also never request payments through third-party services or ask users to download files or software from our emails.”Check the email headers and URL links toensure they are from the Spotify.comdomain. Report the fraudulent emails to your email provider and forward it to Spotify atspoof@spotify.com.“If anything about the message seems unusual, do not respond, click any links or download any attachments. Users who believe they may have already engaged with a suspicious email should immediately reset their Spotify password and review their account for any unauthorised changes,” Spotify said.If you believe your payment details have been compromised, contact your bank immediately.Spotify has various tools to recover accounts, lost playlists and other data. You can prove your ownership of the account with ascreenshot of a Spotify receipt or bank statement.* Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsMoneyScam watchSpotifyScamsConsumer affairsShareReuse this content

title: Gold dresses, flower markets and sitars: Pirelli’s 2027 calendar features all-Indian cast | India | The Guardian
description: Latest edition of one of world’s most influential fashion photography publications is also shot entirely in India
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Latest edition of one of world’s most influential fashion photography publications is also shot entirely in India
Content: Bhavitha Mandava is among the cast of Indian women who will be the face of the first Pirelli calendar to be entirely shot in India.Photograph: Alessandro ScottiView image in fullscreenBhavitha Mandava is among the cast of Indian women who will be the face of the first Pirelli calendar to be entirely shot in India.Photograph: Alessandro ScottiIndiaGold dresses, flower markets and sitars: Pirelli’s 2027 calendar features all-Indian castLatest edition of one of world’s most influential fashion photography publications is also shot entirely in IndiaHannah Ellis-Petersenin RajasthanSun 26 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 05.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgainst the ancient, weathered walls of Jaigarh fort, high on the hills above Jaipur, Bhavitha Mandava stood barefoot and draped in gold.Just a few months earlier, the Indian model had been catapulted from a life of obscurity as a student at New York University to become one of the most recognisable and celebrated new faces of fashion. This year, she became the first Indian woman to open the Chanel catwalk at their Métiers d’Art show and herdivisive Chanel outfit for the Met Gala,fashion’s most exclusive event, became an international talking point.Now Mandava, who grew up in the south Indian city of Hyderabad, is among the all-Indian cast of women who will feature in the first Pirelli calendar to be shot entirely inIndia.View image in fullscreenA shoot for the calendar in a flower market.Photograph: Alessandro ScottiLaunched in the 1960s as a marketing giveaway for the Italian tyre company, the Pirelli calendar is now seen as one of the most influential publications for fashion photography, and has featured almost every famous supermodel of the past six decades.Yet for decades it faced criticism for its lack of diversity, showcasing primarily thin, white models, and for its sexual objectification of women. The 1987 calendar included a topless 16-year-old Naomi Campbell among an all-black lineup. By 2016, fashion’s most famous photographer, Annie Leibovitz, shot a calendar celebrating a diverse roster of influential women, from Serena Williams to Yoko Ono.In 2018, Tim Walker returned to a cast of only black modelswith his Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland themed calendar.However,a return in 2025 to a focus on sensual and nude images, both female and male, drew criticism in the post-#MeToo era.The decision to shoot the Pirelli calendar in India this year comes amid a shifting landscape for south Asian representation in fashion, both in terms of talent but also in recognition and acknowledgment of the crucial role of Indian craft. While Indian craft, fabrics and embroidery have long influenced the designs of the top fashion houses, their contribution has rarely been acknowledged.View image in fullscreenRupi Kaur poses for a shot.Photograph: Alessandro ScottiIn March 2023, Dior staged a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India monument, the first major European luxury house to present a full runway show in India, with Indian embroidery workshops and artisans at the forefront.Less than two years later, Prada found itself engulfed in controversy after its runway show in June 2025 showcased models wearing leather sandals that were strikingly similar to traditional Kolhapuri chappals, a sandal originating in western India dating back centuries. After a backlash,the fashion house was forced to admit their Indian originsand sent a delegation to meet the artisans.Mandava, 26, said she initially had some hesitations prompted by the history of the Pirelli calendar and how it would work in India’s more modest culture.“I’ll be honest I wasn’t very enthusiastic about the past eroticism of the Pirelli calendar and those associations,” she said. “But I’m so glad, they have actively made an effort for me to feel like I belong.”She celebrated the decision by Pirelli to champion India’s “beauty and diversity”. But while she acknowledged a shift in the portrayal of Indian beauty in the west, she also cautioned against trying to make women such as herself “representations” of an entire country or race.“I like to think my race isn’t the most interesting thing about me,” said Mandava. “I’m happy that whatever I’m doing is providing representation but I also don’t think about how I’m representing India. That would just be too daunting.”View image in fullscreenPadma Lakshmi features in the calendar.Photograph: Alessandro ScottiThe project had initially been envisioned as a collaboration of two photographers, one of India’s most famous, Raghu Rai, and the Norwegian photographer Sølve Sundsbø. Rai was seen as the pioneer of photojournalism in India and his photographs remain some of the most vivid representations of the country.But after Rai’s death in April, his photographer daughter Avani Rai agreed to take on his part of the project. It was, she admitted, a difficult project to take on and follow in her father’s footsteps.“My father was always my audience,” said Rai. “And initially I thought: if he’s not going to see these photos, then why should I shoot? But then I started talking to him in my head and he started showing up in divine spaces.”View image in fullscreenFreida Pinto being photographed for the calendar by hanging pink blossom.Photograph: Alessandro ScottiRepresenting all of India’s vastness and diversity was impossible, said Rai, and instead she focused on capturing an essence, the contradictions and “multiple coexisting universes”. In homage to him, she decided to take the Pirelli calendar project back on to the streets, shooting scenes on the streets of Delhi’s crumbling old city, its flower market, gullies and old cinemas.For Anoushka Shankar, whose genre-bending music has revolutionised how the traditional Indian sitar is perceived – and was featured in Gorillaz’ latest album – India has “always been about beauty and grace and sensuality, but outside of the country, there was often a deeply ignorant understanding of the culture”.She will appear on the pages of Pirelli calendar with her sitar, something she said would have once felt unthinkable.“If I think of how it felt for me as a teenager growing up in the UK or in the States, as a south Asian, we weren’t thought of as the beautiful people,” she said, “I would feel a little bit self-conscious about being Indian when I walked into certain rooms. But watching the last decade or so, south Asian presence in mainstream global culture has really changed that.”View image in fullscreenAnoushka Shankar will appear on the pages of Pirelli calendar with her sitar, something she said would have once felt unthinkable.Photograph: Alessandro ScottiFor Padma Lakshmi, the model and chef who was born in Tamil Nadu, returning to shoot the calendar in India – her second time featuring in it – felt particularly poignant. “Coming back to India to shoot this makes it feel, in a way, a lot more feminine,” she said. “I was raised in a house of Indian women, and I associate my earliest talisman of femininity with those women.”At 55, she is among the oldest women who will feature in this year’s calendar, and she celebrated the recognition that “the world is a very big place with lots of beauty”.“For so long we saw only one kind of Indian beauty, manufactured to certain tastes or certain narrow stereotypes,” said Lakshmi. “But this shows the many faces of what it means to be an Indian woman globally.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaSouth and central AsiaFashion photographyPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s like bringing the kitchen into the piazza’: seven of the best Italian village food festivals | Italy holidays | The Guardian
description: Sagre – the historic local events that pop up in villages across the country in summer – are the perfect way to get a taste of regional cuisine and culture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sagre – the historic local events that pop up in villages across the country in summer – are the perfect way to get a taste of regional cuisine and culture
Content: Diners at the Sagra dei Canederli in Vipiteno, South Tyrol.Photograph: Vipiteno Tourist CooperativeView image in fullscreenDiners at the Sagra dei Canederli in Vipiteno, South Tyrol.Photograph: Vipiteno Tourist CooperativeItaly holidays‘It’s like bringing the kitchen into the piazza’: seven of the best Italian village food festivalsSagre – the historic local events that pop up in villages across the country in summer – are the perfect way to get a taste of regional cuisine and cultureGabriele PascaSun 26 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIcannot remember a summer when at least one evening hasn’t been spent following signs to a localsagra. Not quite a food market and not quite a village fete, asagrais like a village moving its kitchen outdoors for a few nights.When I think back to those nights from childhood, the first image that comes to mind is of a woman’s hand closed into a fist above a pan of hot oil. Through a tight circle formed between her thumb and forefinger, she would squeeze soft lumps of batter, one small ball at a time, into the oil. In a few seconds, each soft mass would become apittula, a small Salento fritter: swollen, uneven, golden, too hot to eat straight away but too good to wait for.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsI was born in Salento (Italy’s heel), in the south end of the Puglia region, and grew up in Taviano, a small town south of Lecce. Going away for the summer was something other people did. For my family, as with many local families, summer meant packing the car and moving from our main house in town to a smaller place by the sea, only a few miles away.That place was Mancaversa, the seaside part of Taviano, where theSagra tu Furese(mid August, dates to be finalised), which in Salentino dialect means the farmer’s festival, seemed to bring the whole village outdoors for dinner. From a small child’s perspective, it was a forest of legs and voices. I remember trying to pull my parents past the grown-up ritual of stopping every few yards to greet people they seemed to see only in summer, as we made our way towards the stalls near Piazza delle Rose, where men fanned embers with cardboard, sausages hissed on grills, horse-meat stew simmered in tomato sauce andgnummareddi(rolls of lamb offal) tempted the more adventurous.double quotation markThe village became an open-air sitting room, where people met over food that was ordinary for us, and almost incomprehensible to anyone who came to Salento for beachesMusic came from a small stage and the village became an open-air sitting room, where people met over food that was ordinary for us, and almost incomprehensible to anyone who came to Salento looking for beaches and white light. No one would have thought to call them experiences. They were simply the proper way to get through summer, and in a country where a meal can quickly become expensive, they still make dinner feel possible for about €15.Sometimes my parents, my brother and sister and I would go to Cannole. We would drive inland, passing through villages that all seemed to have a festival on. Only later did I understand that those roadside signs were a map of Italian summers, one I would go on to follow beyond Salento. Each led to a village gathered, for a few nights, around a dish of its own.Cannole itself – a small town of just over 1,500 people – lies on the other side of the province of Lecce, towards Otranto and the Alimini lakes, and since 1985 the localPro Loco Cercetovolunteer association has organised theFesta della Municeddha(10-14 Aug),dedicated to the small snail that has always been part of home cooking there.View image in fullscreenFesta della Municeddha celebrates the small snail that has long been part of home cooking in the Puglia region of Cannole.Themuniceddhais eaten in three main ways: in tomato sauce, cooked down with onion and oil, or roasted. But whichever the version, the method for consuming them is the same: you free it from the shell with a toothpick and eat it standing up. The festival today is large, with music, stalls and full tables, and is a far slicker operation than the one I remember.Around 400 miles up the Adriatic coast, in the Marche, is the small town of Campofilone, on the hills above the Aso valley. Since 1964, itsSagra dei Maccheroncini di Campofilone IGP(7-10 Aug) has taken an extremely thin local pasta (maccheroncini) and transformed it into the centrepiece of a public feast: cut even finer, made with semolina and eggs and cooked in one minute. As soon as it is drained, it is tossed through red mixed-meat ragù on large wooden boards, where these very fine strands, so delicate when dry, become a compact mass, glossy with sauce, ready to be sent out to the tables.View image in fullscreenFusillo is an egg pasta served at the Sagra del Fusillo Felittese in Felitto, south of Naples.For theSagra del Fusillo Felittese(13-23 Aug), set aside at least half a day. You leave the Cilento coast in the Campania region and climb inland, up to Felitto and the Gole del Calore (the Calore river gorge). The festival began in 1976 at Remolino, whenfusillo(literally, little spindle) was used to bring people to the village. The reason to go is still the pasta: made with fresh eggs, long and hollow, rolled by hand around a thin iron rod. It is served withcastrato ragù, traditionally made with goat from a castrated male animal, or with veal ragu.If you’ve spent any time around Modena or Bologna in northern Italy (I moved to Modena to study at 18 and have lived there since), Castelfranco Emilia is the sort of place you’ll have passed through. At first I thought of it as a drive-through kind of town, but today I’m drawn to such places as they tend to keep their traditions fuss-free.Thetortellino, claimed by both Modena and Bologna, finds a nice compromise in Castelfranco. Legend says it was born here, at Locanda Corona, when an innkeeper glimpsed Venus’s navel through a keyhole and took it as his model. In practice, it is thinly rolled egg pasta, folded by hand around a filling of pork loin, prosciutto di Modena, mortadella di Bologna, parmigiano reggiano, egg and nutmeg. Here it is served in hot capon broth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLocal customs are still going strong at Sagra del Tortellino Tradizionale between Modena and BolognaIn September, Castelfranco holds theSagra del Tortellino Tradizionalein Piazza Bergamini (4-14 Sept). What I remember is the square filling with long tables, people queueing at the cash desks and bowls of hot broth arriving one after another. Later, the parade leaves Corso Martiri like a small Renaissance pageant: women in brocade gowns and veils, men in caps and doublets, banners, music, and the innkeeper and noblewoman at the centre of the navel story that gave the tortellino its shape.I arrived in Vipiteno, in Alto Adige/South Tyrol, in September, when summer in north Italy was cooling down. TheSagra dei Canederli(13 Sept) takes place during the day, and what I remember most is the strange orderliness of it: a 400-metre table laid with a gingham tablecloth in the historic centre, people finding a place, menus changing from one section to the next, and plates of dumplings arriving. It feels less like a fair than an alpine dining room laid out in the street, with folk music in the square and the mountains close enough to seem part of the meal.Acanederlois a dumpling made from stale bread, eggs and milk – a way of using kitchen leftovers became one of the most recognisable dishes of these valleys. In Vipiteno, they come in broth, with speck, mushrooms, cheese and herbs; or sweet, with apricots or plums.View image in fullscreenGiarratana onions at the Sagra della Cipolla onion festival.Sicily is at the southern end of thesagremap. I came to know Giarratana through the onion that bears the name of this village, in the south-east of the island. In August, those onions fuel an open-air supper and a small seasonal economy, with visitors coming to taste them where they are grown.Salerno: the charming and affordable gateway to Italy’s Amalfi coastRead moreThe Giarratana onion is large, flat and particularly sweet. It has been recognised by theSlow Food Presidia,and during theSagra della Cipolla Giarratana(12-14 Aug), traditionally linked to the feast of San Bartolomeo, it fills markets, food stalls and tables along the village streets. It is served raw, finely sliced and dressed with olive oil, salt and cheese; baked whole or stuffed; or insidescaccia, a local speciality similar to a thin, folded focaccia. There are also hot dishes, preserves, local wine and music.Giarratana is small: it is worth arriving before dark, parking outside the centre and, if accommodation in the village is full, staying in Ragusa, Modica or Chiaramonte Gulfi.The Italy ofsagreis too wide to fit inside a dining room and, for every silver cloche lifted, somewhere else in Italy there is a ticket number being called over a microphone and a dinner being served from a pot larger than anything you’d find in a home kitchen.Explore more on these topicsItaly holidaysEurope holidaysFood and drinkItalian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: Some people want to break up the EU. Why not break up the US? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions looks at secessionary movements on both sides of the pond
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions looks at secessionary movements on both sides of the pond
Content: Photograph: GH Maps/AlamyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: GH Maps/AlamyNotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: Some people want to break up the EU. Why not break up the US?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions looks at secessionary movements on both sides of the pondAnswer the latest question:What is the true Breakfast of Champions?Sun 26 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf it’s wrong, as some would say, for European countries to come together as a fully federalEuropean Union, rather than individual states, why is it right for the US to be a federation rather than separate states? It always strikes me that the EU gets unfairly criticised for a system that was established over the Atlantic many years back. The US hasn’t looked back, but has become powerful as a result of being an umbrella for smaller entities. Just imagine if each state needed its own army, air force and currency, with its own customs and border controls not to mention trade tariffs! There’d be no White House and no Congress. Why is it so wrong for European countries to want similar strength, coming together as a union?Howard Phillips, LisbonSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyThere’s no nostalgic past for US states to hark back to. What the US achieved it did as a union. That’s the difference which prevents would-be secessionists from causing the harm they have done in Europe.John_Brown1955The US absolutely needs a secession amendment to the constitution. Based on the lessons of Brexit and limited to five states every 20 years.
