Each departing state should be able to take non-fixed assets in proportion to their net contribution to the federal budget over 20 years. That would mean the states that would like to leave – Alabama, Arkansas, Kansas, Oklahoma – would take nothing, while California and New York could take the cake. Politicians would be motivated to pander to the left.Elliot, by emailLanguage? English unites the US but divides the EU.jno50I’m very much in favour of collaboration between European countries and the integration of resources, but I’m also very much against the EU. After decades of staring into its navel and failing to resolve petty problems with its single market, continental Europe has found itself to be totally insignificant in the contemporary geopolitical turmoil. This despite having a larger population than the US and a greater GDP than China. Discussions on the future of Europe are characterised by two opposing teams of ignorant players hurling soundbites at each other. This lack of informed Europe-wide democratic debate is, perhaps, at the heart of the problem.Roger Irwin, ItalyIn a word: history. Too many wars over the centuries based on nationalism in Europe among the Indigenous populations mean that small differences can be exaggerated for political gain, which prior to the EU led to military conflict. In America, the main target of military intervention by Europeans was the Indigenous populations, while violence also had an outlet when taken out on those that they had transported there against their will. Although the latter in the guise of slavery led to a civil war, the former helped to bind the American states together.Dr Peter Davis, BristolThe US has had its share of growing pains. Can the EU become the US without its own civil war? Is abandoning the veto power, because pro-Russians and populists abuse it, so that we can finally have a unified defence force, a good idea, keeping that part of history to mind? I find that reforming veto power is needed, but let’s keep it for things where lack of unanimity threatens our existential principles. I wouldn’t want to see European troops marching in Budapest in 2056.Luca, by emailFirst, the US was put together 200 years ago. Second, they sort of speak one language, not 20 different ones. Last, no one has even bothered asking European citizens if a federal Europe is something they would like, mostly because they are afraid of the answer. We already have a situation where people in smaller countries have a disproportionate amount of say over EU laws.David Michaels, by emailI suppose you suggested the strongest answer yourself: “The US … has become powerful as a result of being an umbrella for smaller entities.” Vanished “customs and border controls, not to mention trade tariffs”. Who doesn’t want the EU strong? Economic competitors. Forces that see their global dominance waning. Separatists seeking salvation in the past. All that speaks for a strong EU. And for countries on the European continent to join, rather than to leave.Erik A Sevapiragasam, by emailThe US was born under a sense of honesty and togetherness. The founding fathers thought hard as how to serve the best interests of the people. The EU was born out of deceit and divisiveness. To hide the fact that its aim was always political union, populations were fed the “common market” ploy and not informed of its ultimate goal. The EU is fundamentally undemocratic. In the US, the president is elected by the eligible voters of the 50 states. In the EU, the president is elected by some 700 council members and, in many cases, not in a competitive ballot.Chris Zisimides, by emailI think the same forces that try to break the EU up are also trying to do the same to the US – they are just doing it more covertly. Regardless of whether these are state actors like Russia, large corporate entities or tech billionaires, they all would rather have smaller political units to deal with, if any at all. The only big difference is that there are now people inside the US government who want to break the EU up, while the reverse is not the case.anda_skoaIf you watch the TV show How the States Got Their Shapes, you will see that the US federal project was not predicted to work. Narrow necks of land join states to waterways or the sea. They didn’t trust their neighbours. Early consolidation was the result of conflict alliances for independence. Later it was federal colonisation of Native American land or conquest of Spanish territory. Why not break it up? It might still happen.WindydayAll empires fall eventually.GrannieSalThe civil war. There have always been movements to break up the US, and even today there are lots of Americans who like to talk about how the country can’t survive, or how it’s really made up of numerous different regions. But the civil war addressed that very question. The south said the states could leave at any time, the north said no you can’t, and the north won.CarnthebombersI’m surprised by the question. I’ve never considered the EU breaking up – well, not so much until Brexit. And why not break up the US? From my view over here is that the European Union has succeeded at so much that the United States has not, especially now with our wavering on those truths we hold to be self-evident.dallastxhollywoodBecause EU is more recent. Everyone is just used to US being one country, with some internal separations, more organisational than existential. Most of the states and territories became part of it long before anyone currently alive. But Europe has never been unified in any way. Except for geographical proximity, there’s virtually nothing European countries have in common. And unlike the US, the EU is still relatively new, making it achange. Change is something that terrifies many people, and is far easier to undo than something that no one remembers being any different.GrumpyMatAs a US citizen, I have no right to an opinion about the EU. As a student of history, I am profoundly grateful that the EU exists. Other than Russia’s horrible invasion of Ukraine, this is the longest period of peace among European nations since the Roman empire.AnneinMarylandRussia feels threatened by a united Europe, hence the need to encourage as much disunity as possible. It is less affected by a united US. It’s not just the US that offers a model of successful unification. Germany was only unified into one country in 1871.TobermoryNightlifeI think the US is already broken.eibhearWell, I sincerely hope that European states are discreetly stirring various secessionist pots in the US in response to the Trump administration’s blatant attempts to destabilise/break up the EU. Sauce for the goose. And I’m sure that Russia is.DaBishopIn reply:The stirring they do is a measurement of the fear felt of a cohesive EU. Onward towards unity increased, I say. Time for the UK to start the process to rejoin as a committed equal member. Also time to get serious and talk to the Canadians about some sort of associate membership.ErasmusVanBaltimoreIs the US truly unified? There have always been cultural and political differences between the states, and some of these seem only to be widening. Are there not real secessionist movements in California and Texas?kingscrosscowboyIn reply:I don’t know about Texas, but the California secession “movement” or “Calexit” is fake, the product of Russian meddling. There’s also the more popular “Cascadia” idea where California, Oregon, and Washington secede together, but that’s not going to happen either. You’re right about the illusion of “unity”. The only time the US was anything close to unified was during the second world war. Didn’t last.fantodA group of nations that have evolved over 2,000 or more years, frequently at war with each other, with differing governing systems, are coming together via trade and an understanding that war is futile. Negotiations are more careful and considerate as a result, and more often a compromise. The US, on the other hand, came together as a nation building its own, modern identity, and the first to do away with inherited monarchy. In what was felt to be an “empty” continent, this made sense. It sticks together today, through a shared sense of independence and “freedom”. It’s like comparing apples with elephants.GrasmereGardensSince many of the people investing money and effort in breaking up the EU are in the US, while no people in the EU have made corresponding efforts to break up the US, it might just be down to relative levels of malice.CharlieApplesIt’s a good question. I suspect one historical reason, in addition to what has anyway been mentioned, is language. The US white population is, of course 100% immigrant (which makes the current anti immigrant rhetoric all the more depressing). But the lingua franca is English (for now, at least). My understanding is that this wasn’t a given – there was a very significant German- speaking minority in the early days, and that could have changed things. But they voted to have a single, common language. I like the level of integration the EU has – I would not want to see everyone speaking a single language as their mother tongue – it enriches us all, and maintains cultural diversity (a good thing). I have no doubt there are state-level differences, beyond different political and religious preferences/biases in the US. But from the outside, the difference looks to be more pronounced at the individual person level than at the state level.scobie27I don’t think it’s an easy binary of “deeper integration good/bad”. Broadly speaking, deeper integration can give you efficiencies of scale, the more frictionless existence that comes with uniformity, and a more powerful whole, but it also (pretty much by definition) reduces the ability of the component parts to do their own thing even if they want to. The US is one level of integration (but states still have, say, their own laws, agencies and taxes); the EU is another, less integrated one. There are lots of possible levels, and people may favour different ones under different circumstances.One obvious reason people might be more in favour of doing things at the nation-state level in EU countries is they have been doing so for much longer – all but two states have been part of the US for over a century now, and many pre-joining were fairly new, low-population territories, rather than countries with centuries of acting as such.JebedeeExplore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘I worry the England flag is seen as racist – even at the World Cup’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A retired teacher and a resident doctor found common ground over the NHS, but how did they fare on pensions?
Author: Sam Wollaston
Headline: A retired teacher and a resident doctor found common ground over the NHS, but how did they fare on pensions?
Content: Saima (left) and Liz. Photographs: Andrew Fox/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSaima (left) and Liz. Photographs: Andrew Fox/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘I worry the England flag is seen as racist – even at the World Cup’A retired teacher and a resident doctor found common ground over the NHS, but how did they fare on pensions?Want to meet someone from across the divide? Clickhereto find out howSam WollastonSun 26 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenSaima, 25, BirminghamOccupationResident doctor and postgraduate researcherVoting recordLabour in two general elections. Describes herself as “socially left, economically slightly more conservative”Amuse boucheWhen her university works with researchers from overseas, Saima enjoys telling them about the Tudors. “They’ve got personal drama, worldwide navigation, it’s a nice part of history”View image in fullscreenLiz, 77, BirminghamOccupationRetired teacherVoting recordLiz lived in France for 30 years and was disenfranchised. Since returning six years ago, she has voted Labour and GreenAmuse boucheLiz’s twins were born at 10 to midnight and two minutes past. “The obstetrician asked if I wanted to cheat so they had the same birthday. I said, no way. It’s been great – one day we’d have a party, the next go to a restaurant”For startersLizWhen I saw Saima I thought: “We’re going to get on.” She was smiley and lovely. We talked about travelling: she’s done Europe, I’ve travelled a lot.SaimaI had an idea about the kind of person I was going to meet, and Liz fitted that in terms of age and race. We’re not so different politically; I think she’s more Green than I am. I was born in Dudley; my grandfather migrated to the UK from Pakistan in the 70s.LizThe restaurant was so welcoming. I had tacos and a glass of rosé. We both had passion fruit cheesecake.SaimaI had the barbecued lamb shank, which was gorgeous. And a zero-alcohol beer from a local brewery.View image in fullscreenThe big beefLizWe talked about all the England flags and union jacks going up. There’s a lot of this in south Birmingham. I don’t want them. I’ve spoken to people in shops around here, they’re concerned that it’s racist.SaimaThere’s one road where they had the St George’s cross, Scottish flag and Irish flag, and I quite like that – these are our flags, it feels inclusive. I’ve never felt anything against the union jack and St George’s cross. It’s a mark of our national identity as much as Buckingham Palace.LizWhere I live, someone was run over by people putting up flags with a cherrypicker. I spoke to some of the people doing it and said we don’t want them; they said that I didn’t support our nation, they were very aggressive. I said it would stop me putting an England flag in my window during the World Cup because everyone would see it as racist.SaimaWhen Rishi Sunak was PM, Starmer in opposition, we saw the union jack at every press conference – it was a bit on the nose. Everyone knew what they were both doing: it was about immigration, stop the boats. But during Covid, Boris Johnson or Chris Whitty had a union jack by the podium and it was quite nice. Covid was a time when the country united.View image in fullscreenSharing plateSaimaWe had a positive discussion about the NHS. It has its problems but we both think that a universal free-access healthcare service is a big plus.LizSaima works in hospitals – she’s used to old people, young people, everyone. I’ve got a big family and I’ve taught English. You get used to asking people questions and keeping conversations going.View image in fullscreenFor aftersLizI think the triple lock is great because it guarantees my pension. We lived in France, but because our children came to England for university we knew we would come back at some stage, so we paid the contributions to have a state pension here. It’s good for me, and a lot of people rely on that.SaimaI can understand why it’s not been touched, because pensioners are more likely to vote. I agree that if you work hard throughout your life, you deserve state support when you retire. But equally you have to recognise we have a declining birthrate, an increasing number of pensioners and a smaller working‑age population. In the future, it might become a difficult conversation.View image in fullscreenDining across the divide: ‘She’s fine with billionaires – I would call them hoarders’Read moreTakeawaysLizIt was a lovely evening. Saima gave me a lift home, and took a photo of us in the car. She lives in a suburb of Birmingham where there’s a really lovely Italian restaurant, and I told her if I went I’d give her a ring.SaimaAs a pensioner, Liz has a free bus pass but it was 10pm and we both live in south Birmingham – I wasn’t going to let her get the bus home.View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeLiz and Saima ate atThe Mayanin BirminghamWant to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How Trump could undermine the midterms | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: The president really has no power over elections – but that hasn’t stopped Trump from laying the groundwork to challenge results in November
Author: George Chidi
Headline: The president really has no power over elections – but that hasn’t stopped Trump from laying the groundwork to challenge results in November
Content: ‘It’s reckless that the president will continue to do what he’s doing, and that the folks around him will continue to let him do what he’s doing.’Photograph: Portland Press Herald/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s reckless that the president will continue to do what he’s doing, and that the folks around him will continue to let him do what he’s doing.’Photograph: Portland Press Herald/Getty ImagesThe Sunday readUS midterm elections 2026How Trump could undermine the midtermsThe president really has no power over elections – but that hasn’t stopped Trump from laying the groundwork to challenge results in NovemberGeorge ChidiSun 26 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 04.22 EDTShareWhenDonald Trumpcommandeered primetime US television last Friday, he delivered a familiar, but still extraordinary, message. The president argued once again that the results of the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden, were illegitimate.US elections are “vulnerable to being rigged and stolen”, Trump alleged, claiming that “the trust of the American people was lost” when he was defeated.Historically, incumbent parties underperform in midterm elections and with the president’s popularity sagging – he has an approval rating of just 37% –Republicansappear on course to lose seats in the US Senate and House of Representatives, as well as in state and local elections, in November.Trump’s latest intervention, in which he accused China of interfering with the 2020 election, is viewed by US voting rights activists as just the latest escalation of a bid by the White House to influence, and potentially alter, the results of the 2026 midterm elections.“The number one threat facing American elections is the continued lies coming out of the White House,” said the Arizona secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, the official responsible for overseeing the state’s elections.The president is fighting to persuade Congress to approve legislation, the Save Act, that would allow the US federal government greater control over elections. Trump has also called for the federal government to take direct control of elections in some states, falsely claiming that his defeats there in 2020 were illegitimate.View image in fullscreenA broadcast of Trump’s address on 16 July.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/EPAThere’s just one snag. “We have an election system that is not run by the federal government,” said Ben Berwick, who leads Protect Democracy’s election law and litigation team. “It’s run by states and local jurisdictions.”The president, he added, “really has no power over elections”. So what can Trump actually do?Republicans in a handful of states have already scrambled, at Trump’s urging, to redraw their congressional maps in the wake of alandmark decision by the US supreme court– controlled by a conservative supermajority – that effectively gutted a major section of the Voting Rights Act.Louisiana led the way,tearing up its old mapof four Republican and two Democratic districts in favor of a new one, which will probably give Republicans five of the state’s six congressional seats. Such efforts are designed to shift the outcome of future elections.And with threats to mail-in voting, sowing fears about voting machines, as well as a steady stream of unfounded allegations of election fraud, many fear Trump appears to be laying the groundwork to challenge results that don’t go his way in November.The memory of the deadly 6 January attack on the US Capitol in 2021, fueled by Trump’s denial of his election defeat, looms large.“It’s reckless that the president will continue to do what he’s doing, and that the folks around him will continue to let him do what he’s doing, and potentially trigger that sort of behavior that could cost lives,” added Fontes. “This is a powder keg out there, and there’s a lot of folks who just just want to get on with their lives, who just want to get on to solving their own problems.”Mail-in ballotsTrump has repeatedly tried to restrict voting by mail, and likened it to cheating, despitedoing so himself. It is a key focus of his administration’s efforts. In November, the administration could use the US Postal Service (USPS) to “control the flow of mail-in ballots, and potentially not send ballots to certain voters”, Berwick said.Democratic voters are deemed more likely to cast their ballots by mail than Republicans: about one in four registered Democrats did so in 2024,accordingto the States United Democracy Center, alongside 1 in 5 registered Republicans.Eight states and the District of Columbia rely almost exclusively on postal ballots. The USPS, at Trump’s direction, proposed a rule that would require states to turn over their voter roll information to the federal government, which would then tell states which voters were ineligible.View image in fullscreenVoting rights activists protest outside the US supreme court.Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesThat proposal, enforced by an executive order in March, faces a wall of legal challenges and was ruled unconstitutional by a judge. Cases pursued by the civil rights group NAACP in Washington DC and the League of Women’s Voters in Massachusetts have challenged the plan in court.Celina Stewart, CEO of the League of Women Voters, said the organization intervened to ensure the bid to restrict mail-in voting was “shut down” in time for state primary elections, taking place in the months ahead of November’s general election. “And so I think that was really important for us,” she said, “just to make sure that voters knew how that was going to work, and make sure that they understood what their rights were, and how they could execute their ballot effectively”.Voting machinesAt polling stations, Trump is also pointing to electronic voting machines, which he suggested in his 16 July TV address could be compromised by foreign actors. “China carried out what is believed to be the largest compromise of election data in history, resulting in China’s illicit acquisition of 220 million US voter files,” he said.Declassified files from US investigators show that China downloaded publicly-available election data in 2022. Those same investigators concluded that China did not interfere in the election.Voting rights advocates believe Trump may have been telegraphing his intent to try to block the use of some voting machines in a late-day election gambit, invoking national security as a rationale.View image in fullscreenA polling judge, right, helps guide a voter’s ballot into a voting machine during the Pennsylvania primary election in 2022.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/AP“The thing that maybe worries me the most is what we saw in Fulton county and elsewhere,” Berwick said, referring to an FBI raid in January that resulted in the seizure of 2020 ballots and election material in Georgia. The administration “may try to do something similar in the immediate post-election period under the sort of pretext of investigating ineligible voting, or votes cast by ineligible voters”, he suggested, “in a way that, if done in the immediate post-election period, would be designed to disrupt the ability of states to count votes and certify elections”.In the meantime, the White House has actively undermined safeguards to the election system. The Election Assistance Commission, a US federal agency designed to help states overcome technical challenges in election administration, which currently has nocommissioners. Trump fired the Democrat members, and allowed the Republicans to resign. More than a third of the staff of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency was meanwhile cut by Trump’s so-called “Department of Government Efficiency”, the cost-cutting drive fleetingly led by Elon Musk, including the entire team looking at cybersecurity threats in elections.“One cannot help but notice the irony of the administration’s purported interest in securing our election systems, and yet gutting the very agency responsible for that,” said Hannah Fried, co-founder and CEO of All Voting is Local.Save ActThe Save Act, which is stalled in Congress, would require voters to present their passport or birth certificate to register to vote, and then to provide photo ID from a narrow list of valid identifications to vote in person. Campaigners argue such restrictions would disproportionately impact Black, Native, elderly and student voters.The legislation would also sharply constrain voting by mail, too. And it would require states to turn over their voter rolls to the federal government.Absent that legislation – which is constitutionally questionable – federal agencies under Trump may still try to pressure states to purge voter rolls using unreliable or unverified federal data sets. Courts have consistently blocked attempts by the federal government to force unvetted voter purges.Some states – led by Republican officials – have already turned over voter rolls, when requested by the federal government.View image in fullscreenA voter works on his ballot at a polling station in Arlington, Virginia, in 2024.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesBerwick highlighted the prospect of federal agencies like the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security seeking voter lists from states, “presumably to then send to states lists of voters they believe are ineligible, which are very likely to be inaccurate”.While far-right figures like Steve Bannon, an ally and former adviser of Trump, have called for the deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents or federal law enforcement at voting sites, and the president himself has explicitly raised the prospect, it is considered remote because federal law plainly outlaws the presence of troops or federal agents at polling places.Voter intimidation has already manifested at early voting sites and drop boxes, said Stewart, of the League of Women Voters, who cited an incident in Arizona where armed contractors confronted voters. “The president in particular is pushing for increased ICE funding,” she said. “So you have to ask: for what?”Stewart highlighted how her organization successfully sued to stop armed drop-box intimidation in 2022, securing a court order within 24 hours. The incident was a demonstration of “how quickly things like that can happen” she said, “but equally as quickly … how we can shut that down”.Pins and needlesTrump’s increasingly inflammatory rhetoric is itself a threat to the integrity of the 2026 election, said Georgia state senator Saira Draper, a leading voting administration expert, who warned that narrative attacks are designed to undermine outcomes, regardless of who wins.“By sowing distrust in elections, no matter what the outcome is, he continues on the division, whether his party wins or not into the next term,” said Draper, who suggested that such constant rhetoric turns followers into “foot soldiers for the cause”.Some of those foot soldiers sit on county boards of elections, which are required to certify elections. And some are running for office, successfully winning the Republican nomination, likeAlex Kolodin, who helped lead failed legal efforts to overturn Arizona’s 2020 and 2022 election results, who is now the Republican candidate for Arizonan secretary of state: its top elections official.View image in fullscreenTrump addresses the US from the East Room of the White House on 16 July.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesAfter the 2020 election, some Republican elections board members refused to certify fair elections, threatening to disrupt the process. A mass refusal could cast doubt on the results in conservative states that have taken a Democratic turn in a swing year.“This federal interference led by the president isn’t helping anybody,” said Fontes. “It’s not good for, in my view, any circumstance across the country, and it’s got everybody on pins and needles for no really good reason.“I mean, what’s the really good reason why folks are afraid, that there’s something wrong with our elections? The only explanation is that Donald Trump can’t get over getting his butt kicked in 2020.”

title: ‘We count every litre’: how Cuba’s energy crisis sparked a daily struggle for water | Access to water | The Guardian
description: Power cuts not only leave people in the dark but leave taps dry, forcing millions of Cubans to spend their days fetching water any way they can
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Power cuts not only leave people in the dark but leave taps dry, forcing millions of Cubans to spend their days fetching water any way they can
Content: Carlos Sánchez and his nephew carry buckets of water up the stairs of an apartment building in Havana. All photographs by Lucien MignéPower cuts not only leave people in the dark but leave taps dry, forcing millions of Cubans to spend their days fetching water any way they canByLucien Migné in HavanaSupported byAbout this contentSun 26 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the cramped kitchen of her flat in Havana’s Chinatown, Mirella Martínez pushes an old metal trolley stacked with empty jerrycans. Wiping the sweat from her forehead, she fans herself gently. “It’s so hot!” she says, as the electric fans remain still due to another power outage that has left her flat sweltering in near darkness for hours.View image in fullscreenMirella Martínez’s flat in Havana has been without running water for nearly three yearsIn a few minutes, the 61-year-old former security guard will walk about half a mile to her daughter’s workplace, one of the few buildings nearby where water still flows regularly. For almost three years, the flat she shares with her three daughters and grandson has had no reliable running water.InCuba, power cuts do more than leave people in the dark: they also leave taps dry. As the country’senergy crisis deepens, electricity shortages prevent many pumping stations from operating, while an ageing distribution network and chronic fuel shortages leave millions struggling to access water.The country’s energy crisis, already severe, worsened further earlier this year afterthe capture of the Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro, by US forces. The suspension of oil exports from Venezuela, Cuba’s main fuel supplier,deepened fuel shortagesalready exacerbated by the US embargo and economic sanctions.View image in fullscreenA drinking water truck drives through Cotorro in HavanaAccording to Cuba’sNational Institute of Hydraulic Resources, nearly3 million Cubansare experiencing difficulties accessing water. The country’s water system is operating with just 37% of the fuel it requires, while up to70% of Havana’s water is lostthrough leaks before it can reach households.Wealthier families can afford private water trucks. Everyone else waits for deliveries, hauls water home themselves or pays informal water carriers to do it.Martínez boils and filters part of the water for drinking. The rest is rationed for cooking, washing and laundry.View image in fullscreenMartínez filters water for drinking after boiling it. ‘Everything is rationed,’ she says“This water is used for everything. We count every litre. I make this journey three times a day even though I’m retired. At my age, I shouldn’t be carrying these jerrycans, but I have no choice,” she says. “I often wonder how elderly people who live alone manage.”In Centro Habana, Dhayamis Hernández Díaz watches a thin stream of water slowly fill a plastic bucket. Cigarette in hand, she waits until it is full before emptying it into the rooftop tank serving her building. Nobody knows how long the water will keep flowing.View image in fullscreenDhayamis Hernández Díaz fills a bucket in her flat in Centro Habana to refill the tank on the roof“I’m exhausted. As soon as the electricity comes back – sometimes in the middle of the night – we get up to fill the tank, cook and charge our phones. Our whole lives depend on those few hours of electricity. This isn’t living.”Along with her sister, she earns a modest income operating an electric three-wheeled taxi. Hiring a private water truck is far beyond what they can afford.“So we fill the tank ourselves, bucket after bucket. At night, I barely sleep because of the heat. We just wait for the electricity to come back.”In Havana, life is organised around the few hours when electricity returns and water begins to flow. Water no longer arrives with the turn of a tap. It must be fetched, carried home and carefully rationed. As the public water system continues to fail, an informal water economy has emerged across the capital.View image in fullscreenAt the Escobar pumping station in Centro Habana, Juan de la Cruz Villalón, 66, and Juan Carlos Reyes, 55, fill containers with water to sellEarly each morning, Juan Miguel Reyes waits outside a state bakery with his ration book. After more than half an hour in the queue, he leaves with a few bread rolls to share with his brother and uncle.“Last night, the water came back for about two hours. We got up immediately to fill every bucket before going back to sleep. Sometimes, that saves us a trip to the pumping station.”By midday, the three men push a heavy cart through Los Sitios, a working-class neighbourhood of Havana. Its wheels rattle over broken pavements as they weave around piles of uncollected rubbish. After walking over a mile, they reach one of the few pumping stations still operating before hauling water to people whose taps have long run dry.View image in fullscreenJuan Miguel Reyes, 58, Juan de la Cruz Villalón and Juan Carlos Reyes push their water tank through the rubbish-strewn streets of HavanaFor 23 years, Reyes worked as an intensive care physician. “I never imagined I’d end up selling water. Now we spend hours walking under the blazing sun before carrying buckets up staircases,” he says. “It’s exhausting, but at least we always have something to eat.”Each 200-litre tank sells for 1,500 pesos (about £1.75 at the informal exchange rate). Reyes earns between 3,000 and 4,000 pesos a day.“Demand keeps growing. Every week we have to fetch water from further away, and we never know whether the pumping station will still be working tomorrow,” he says. “People often thank us because many are too old to collect water themselves. Here, without neighbours, nobody would make it.”View image in fullscreenCarlos Sánchez tops up the water tank in a flat in Centro HabanaA few miles away, near Havana’s ferry terminal, Carlos Sánchez collects water spilling from a broken pipeline. Bucket by bucket, he fills a 200-litre tank mounted on his bicycle.“The whole network is falling apart. All this water is being wasted while so many people need it. I collect it and sell it to people who don’t have the strength or the time to come here themselves.”‘History will tell’: as US pressure grows, Cuba edges closer to collapse amid mass exodusRead moreOnce the tank is full, he covers it with a tarpaulin and pushes his bicycle into Havana’s historic centre. Helped by his nephew, he carries buckets up the staircases of a crumbling building.“My back is starting to give out, but I have no choice. I earn more transporting water than I did working as a funeral technician,” he says. “My children have left the country. I stayed behind.”View image in fullscreenIn Cotorro, Havana, a man tries to repair a damaged water pipe to restore the supplyBy evening, Martínez is home again. The jerrycans line the walls of her living room. She carefully stores the day’s water, setting aside enough for drinking, cooking and washing over the days ahead. The television remains off. Without electricity, the family’s nightly telenovelas have become a rarity.“We never know when the power will come back. Water and electricity should be basic rights, but here they’ve become luxuries. I no longer go out after dark, and I don’t let my daughters go out either,” she says. “When the streets go dark, everything becomes more dangerous. I just hope that one day we’ll have a normal life again.”View image in fullscreenGuests enjoy the pool at a luxury hotel in Havana’s historic centre. Hotels and wealthy households often have water storage tanks, generators or solar panelsExplore more on these topicsSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanAccess to waterPovertyCubaUS foreign policyCaribbeanAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Venezuelan men sue aviation firms who flew them to notorious Salvadorian jail | US news | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: CSI Aviation and GlobalX accused of violating civil rights as part of Trump immigration crackdown
Author: José Olivares
Headline: Exclusive: CSI Aviation and GlobalX accused of violating civil rights as part of Trump immigration crackdown
Content: The Cecot prison in Tecoluca, El Salvador, where the Venezuelans deported from the US were imprisoned.Photograph: John Moore/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Cecot prison in Tecoluca, El Salvador, where the Venezuelans deported from the US were imprisoned.Photograph: John Moore/Getty ImagesUS newsVenezuelan men sue aviation firms who flew them to notorious Salvadorian jailExclusive: CSI Aviation and GlobalX accused of violating civil rights as part of Trump immigration crackdownJosé Olivaresin New YorkSun 26 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 08.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVenezuelan men sent last year to a notorious Salvadorian terrorism prison by the Trump administration are suing the US aviation companies that transported them there.Alawsuitfiled this week in federal court in Washington DC accuses the companies CSI Aviation and GlobalX of violating the Venezuelans’ civil rights, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence and other violations, for their role in flying the three planes that took the men to El Salvador.CSI and GlobalX “went to great lengths” to undertake the “rendition flights” toEl Salvador, “in concert with the US government, in flagrant violation of US and international law”, the lawsuit reads.Last year, in March, the Trump administration expelled more than 230 Venezuelan men held in US immigration custody to El Salvador, where they were detained for four months in a maximum security terrorism prison andtortured.The lawsuit accuses CSI and GlobalX of deliberately transporting the men to El Salvador, despite a federal judge ordering the flights to return and despite knowing they would probably be tortured inside the country’s Terrorism Confinement Center (known as “Cecot” by its acronym in Spanish).Without CSI and GlobalX’s complicity, “neither Plaintiffs nor the Class would have been rendered to CECOT”, the lawsuit reads.The suit was filed by a team of human rights attorneys on 17 July and is being reported first by the Guardian. It is one of the latest attempts by rights groups to hold private contractors accountable for their role in alleged abuses stemming from theadministration’s aggressiveanti-immigrant crackdown.Venezuelans deported by Trump to El Salvador describe ‘horror movie’ mega-prisonRead more“Many people might not be aware of the degree to which private companies are intertwined with the human rights abuses occurring under the Trump administration through the detention and unlawful deportation schemes that are occurring,” said Anthony Enriquez, the vice-president of advocacy and litigation for the Kennedy Human Rights Center, in an interview with the Guardian. Enriquez is one of the attorneys representing the Venezuelan men.CSI and GlobalX, which were hired by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), have “enjoyed unprecedented financial profits from the scheme”, while the Venezuelans “continue to experience severe emotional suffering from the humiliation, terror, and cruelty that they endured”, the lawsuit says.The DHS did not respond to specific claims in the lawsuit and instead referred all questions to the Salvadorian government. CSI and GlobalX did not respond to a detailed request for comment by time of publication.El Salvador’s government does not make efforts to publicly rebut allegations of brutal treatment inside Cecot. Online influencers areinvited into make videos of the harsh conditions.CSI Aviation Inc is incorporated in Texas and GlobalX is headquartered in Florida, with both companies playing a significant role in the administration’s mass deportation campaign. The lawsuit says that the American companies were hired by the US government to conduct the El Salvador-bound deportation flights.CSI has helped broker “nearly all” deportation flights, the lawsuit says, via a multimillion-dollar contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the main agency within the DHS carrying out deportations. CSI is the single highest-value recipient of ICE contracts, the lawsuit adds, with revenue from ICE in 2025 totaling $1.23bn.For the three flights to El Salvador, CSI sub-contracted with GlobalX, with CSI working as the “intermediary” between ICE and GlobalX, according to the lawsuit.On 15 March last year, Donald Trump stepped outside government norms toinvokethe Alien Enemies Act as a strategy to expel hundreds of Venezuelan immigrants from the US. The US president accused the Venezuelan government, at the time run byNicolás Maduro, who is nowfacing trialin the US, of instructing members of the South American gangTren de Araguato “invade” the US.After invoking the Alien Enemies Act, the administration rounded up 252 Venezuelan and Salvadorian men in ICE detention and expelled them to El Salvador. This came after the US and El Salvador struck acontroversialandopaquedeal, in which the US would paymillions of dollarsto El Salvador to detain deportees from the US in Cecot. The administration never proved, and has still not proved, the Venezuelan men were members of Tren de Aragua.The same day that the Alien Enemies Act was invoked, GlobalX, “working at the behest of CSI”, positioned three planes at an airport in Texas in preparation for the expulsion, the lawsuit says.After the flights hadtaken offto Central America, a federal judge in Washington DCorderedthey return to the US. The administration and airline companiesignoredthe court order and eventually arrived in El Salvador.“Despite knowing that El Salvador’s Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo (‘CECOT’) mega-prison was a notorious blacksite, from which no detainee had ever left alive, Defendants went to great lengths to transport Plaintiffs and Class Members there, in concert with the US government, in flagrant violation of U.S. and international law,” the lawsuit reads. “Defendants evaded or ignored judicial oversight and the foreseeable risk of torture and successfully delivered Plaintiffs and the Class to El Salvador for imprisonment at CECOT.”The real horror began for the men once they landed in El Salvador, with many thinking they had at least arrived home to Venezuela. Salvadorian security forces boarded the planes, beat the deportees, manylater said, and transported them to Cecot.According to a November 2025reportfrom Human Rights Watch, the men were “subjected to what amounts to arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance under international human rights law”.The HRW report and lawsuit also detail brutal conditions and torture inside Cecot, accusing guards of beating, pepper-spraying, firing rubber bullets and sexually assaulting detainees.Lawmakers, families and members of the public protested against the immigrants’ detention in Cecot. News reportsrevealedthe identities of some of the men, showing that some were falsely accused of being gang members.Four months later, in July 2025, the group of Venezuelans were returned to their home country after a prisoner exchange deal involving the three countries. The group of Salvadorians, also sent to Cecot in those flights, are still presumably detained there. To this date, the US government has not released the entire list of deportees sent to Cecot.The Venezuelan men continue tostrugglewith long-lasting health effects and mental healthtrauma, the lawsuit says. The three main plaintiffs in the case experience daily headaches, difficulty sleeping and emotional distress from the experience.CSI and GlobalX “have enjoyed unprecedented financial profits from the scheme and their relationship with the Administration”, the lawsuit says, while the Venezuelan men “continue to experience severe emotional suffering from the humiliation, terror, and cruelty that they endured”.The companies have not yet responded to the lawsuit. Federal judge James Boasberg, who is presiding over the original Cecot deportation case, will be overseeing the lawsuit’s proceedings and determine whether the entire class of Venezuelans can sue.Explore more on these topicsUS newsEl SalvadorAmericasVenezuelaUS immigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Get rid of them’: One Nation senator claims party will ‘remigrate’ illegal visa holders in resurfaced interview | One Nation | The Guardian
description: Malcolm Roberts uses white supremacist concept to describe the party’s plans for deporting 200,000 people from Australia
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Malcolm Roberts uses white supremacist concept to describe the party’s plans for deporting 200,000 people from Australia
Content: One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts with leader Pauline Hanson at a rally in Canberra.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenOne Nation senator Malcolm Roberts with leader Pauline Hanson at a rally in Canberra.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPOne Nation‘Get rid of them’: One Nation senator claims party will ‘remigrate’ illegal visa holders in resurfaced interviewExclusive:Malcolm Roberts uses white supremacist concept to describe the party’s plans for deporting 200,000 people from AustraliaFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerSun 26 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 18.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenatorMalcolm Robertsclaims One Nation wants to deport at least 200,000 people and has repeatedly referred to the far-right concept of “remigration” in podcast interviews and speeches to niche platforms.In two recent podcasts, Roberts saidOne Nationwanted to deport 100,000 temporary residents as well as 100,000 international students – a total much higher than the party’s published policy. The senator said after those people were removed, he wanted to “start working on the higher numbers of people we need to get rid of”.One Nation’s policy website states the party would seek to “deport 75,000 illegal migrants”, specifically noting “visa overstayers, illegal workers, and unlawful non-residents”. The website also pledges to “end the student visa loopholes that turn study into a backdoor to permanent residency or low-wage labour”.But Roberts, in an interview with the 2 Worlds Collide podcast in November 2025, suggested One Nation wanted to deport or “remigrate” a far higher number.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“We would also deport immediately anybody who’s here illegally, and that’s 100,000 people now … on contravention of their resident visas. That’s 100,000 we would deport, remigrate. Call it what you want. Get rid of them straight away,” he said.“Then we’ve got about an estimated 100,000 international students who are here illegally. They’ve either graduated and not gone home or they’ve breached their legal visa. So we would send them home.”In another interview with podcaster Brodie Buchal, published in June, Roberts repeated those sentiments.“We have 100,000 people here on temporary resident visas illegally. We would deport them, remigrate them, send them home,” he said.“We’ve got 100,000 students who are here illegally, and we suspect it’s much, much more. Send them home.”“We’d tighten the entry requirements, remigrate, deport, and then start working on the higher numbers of people we need to get rid of.”One Nation was contacted for comment and clarification of its deportation policy.One Nation’s hardline immigration policy has come under renewed scrutiny after Pauline Hanson’s appearance onChannel 7’s Spotlight program, where she met Rupert Lowe, leader of hard-right party Restore Britain. Lowe gave her a pamphlet titled “mass deportations” and Hanson replied they were “on the same page”.Barnaby Joyce backs One Nation’s ‘monocultural’ vision of Australia. But the reality in his NSW electorate is very differentRead moreSeven reporter Liam Bartlett asked Hanson whether she thought “this concept of mass deportation is a good one?” She replied: “I love it.”However One Nation has consistently declined to detail how it would enact such a policy. MP Barnaby Joyce on Mondaysaid people would be deported“as it becomes apparent that they’re not supposed to be here”, including “as people present themselves for medical issues”.Abul Rizvi, former deputy secretary of the immigration department, said it would be “eye-wateringly expensive” for a system to deport such numbers of people from Australia, or a Trump-style mass deportation operation like the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He said recent figures showed only about 2,000 people were apprehended, detained and deported from Australia last year, with another 6,000 voluntarily leaving.“It would cost a fortune and unless you did it carefully, it would result in massive errors and all sorts of problems,” Rizvi said.“There is a sensible policy in this space to be developed, but you need to do it in a careful, well-targeted way that doesn’t increase in huge errors, huge numbers of people detained and clogging up court systems.”Roberts’ recent comments have also repeatedly referenced “remigration”. The term has featured in Trump administration immigration policies, includingan “office of remigration” to oversee deportationsand “voluntary return of migrants” – Trump himself tweeted about his plan to return “illegal migrants to their home countries (also known as remigration)”.But remigration has also become abuzzword for the global far right. The Global Project Against Hate and Extremismdescribedremigration as “a white supremacist policy concept that calls for the forced removal of immigrants, refugees, and their descendants — including legal residents and citizens — based on race, ethnicity, culture, being perceived as ‘non-white,’ or a failure to ‘assimilate’.”One Nation was contacted for comment regarding Roberts’ understanding of the term.In addition to mentioning “remigration” on the 2 Worlds Collide and Brodie Buchal podcasts, Roberts also advocated for it during a speech to a conference organised by conservative campaign group Firebrand. Photos from that conference,posted to social media, show Hanson was also in attendance.The conference host, welcoming Roberts onto the stage, praised him as “one of the only MPs yet to mention the magical, unmentionable word ‘remigration’”.In his address, Roberts said: “Remigration is the second part of my my speech. Take the people who are not fitting in or that we don’t need and send them home.“We need to put Australia first. Stop immigration, deport people, remigrate.”In that speech, Roberts said he was “opposed to mass immigration, the swamping of our culture” but was “not opposed to immigrants”.Roberts’ speech was praised by a white supremacist news outlet, The Noticer. The outlet said “remigration” had been popularised by German and Austrian far-right parties and activists, who frame the term as meaning the mass removal of non-white citizens.Dr Kurt Sengul, a research fellow at Macquarie University who studies far-right ideology, called remigration “an extreme and dangerous” position.“It’s important to note that remigration refers to the forced repatriation of all non-white people, not just so-called illegal or undocumented migrants or reducing ‘mass migration’. It’s an extreme position rooted in ethnic cleansing and white supremacy,” he said.Asked if he thought there was any other way to interpret the term “remigration” in this context, Sengul said no.“I don’t think there is any other way to see it; there’s not a friendlier or more moderate version of remigration … it sends a powerful signal to far-right activists that One Nation are embracing the term,” he said.Explore more on these topicsOne NationMalcolm RobertsPauline HansonAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former NSW Liberal powerbroker at heart of Icac allegations now living in UK and not expected to appear | Independent Commission Against Corruption | The Guardian
description: Christian Ellis, a former registered lobbyist, is named in two Independent Commission Against Corruption allegations
Author: Penry Buckley
Headline: Christian Ellis, a former registered lobbyist, is named in two Independent Commission Against Corruption allegations
Content: The Independent Commission Against Corruption is examining some donations to the New South Wales Liberal party.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreenThe Independent Commission Against Corruption is examining some donations to the New South Wales Liberal party.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPIndependent Commission Against CorruptionFormer NSW Liberal powerbroker at heart of Icac allegations now living in UK and not expected to appearChristian Ellis, a former registered lobbyist, is named in two Independent Commission Against Corruption allegationsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPenry BuckleyandKrishani DhanjiSun 26 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 18.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA key figure at the centre of an anti-corruption inquiry involving theNew South WalesLiberal party has moved to the UK and is not expected to give evidence during eight weeks of public hearings.TheIndependent Commission Against Corruptionwill start its Operation Rosny hearings on Monday. The first witness will be a hotelier, Michael O’Hara, followed later in the week by a former Liberal staffer, Dylan Whitelaw, and a consultant, Robert Assaf.O’Hara and Assaf are among 10 individuals Icac has said it is investigating. Whitelaw is not named in the Icac allegations.Christian Ellis, a former registered lobbyist and Liberal powerbroker who once received a glowing endorsement from the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, is named in two Icac allegations but is not expected to appear.A 2023 parliamentary inquiry preceded Icac’s current examination of “possible offences under the Electoral Funding Act”. Since that parliamentary inquiry, Ellis has moved to the UK, Guardian Australia can reveal.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIcac is investigating several allegations, firstly that Liberal figures, including Ellis and Assaf, “solicited or accepted” donations, including from prohibited donors, in amounts which were undeclared or exceeded caps, to recruit or renew members to the party – a practice known as “branch stacking”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlleged illegal donations by Catholic Schools NSW to Liberals raise questions over use of taxpayer fundsRead moreThe corruption watchdog is examining a second allegation that between 2020 and 2023, the fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and his company, Toplace, made prohibited donations solicited or accepted by Liberals, including Ellis, “in exchange for the pursuit of outcomes sought by Mr Nassif”.The 2023 parliamentary inquiry was prompted by allegations made in a 2022 speech under parliamentary privilege by the Liberal MP Ray Williams that Nassif had met Ellis and other senior Liberals, who were paid significant funds to arrange for new councillors to be elected to the Hills Shire council.Ellis did not appear at the 2023 inquiry because he could not be served with summons after multiple attempts.The inquiry’s final report recommended that Ellis be called before any future inquiry to give evidence.Ellis, a director and shareholder of the former registered lobbying firm Beckington, whose clients included Toplace, was elected to the NSW Liberal state executive in 2019, following which he stepped down as director in favour of his wife.In 2022, Taylorwrote an endorsementof Ellis for a position on the NSW party’s state council, saying “our party will do well to have people like Christian elected to positions of state council”. Taylor, now the federal Liberal leader, is not accused of any wrongdoing.Ellis declined to comment when asked about the Icac allegations and his move overseas.Explore more on these topicsIndependent Commission Against CorruptionNew South Wales politicsNew South WalesLiberal partynewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to meet Zelenskyy at UK naval base in show of ‘unwavering’ support | Volodymyr Zelenskyy | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president will be first overseas visitor for new British prime minister
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Ukrainian president will be first overseas visitor for new British prime minister
Content: Volodymyr Zelenskyy was one of the first world leaders Burnham spoke to when he entered No 10 last week.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAView image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy was one of the first world leaders Burnham spoke to when he entered No 10 last week.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAVolodymyr ZelenskyyBurnham to meet Zelenskyy at UK naval base in show of ‘unwavering’ supportUkrainian president will be first overseas visitor for new British prime ministerPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentSun 26 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy will become Andy Burnham’s first overseas visitor as prime minister, in a visit that Burnham said underlined Britain’s “unwavering” backing for Ukraine.Less than two weeks after Keir Starmer travelled to Kyiv for the final foreign visit of his prime ministership, the Ukrainian president will on Monday join Burnham at a naval base where Ukrainian forces have been receiving training.Zelenskyy was one of the first world leaders Burnham spoke to when he entered No 10 last week, and the prime minister has promised to maintain Starmer’s strong support for the country in pushing back against Russia’s invasion.Andy Burnham says he will disagree with Trump in public if necessaryRead moreOn the visit to the base, the pair will speak to Ukrainian and British military personnel who have taken part in Exercise Sea Breeze, a 15-country training deployment based on mine exercises and other maritime operations in the Black Sea.The second part ofthis year’s exercise, which took place in Portland, Dorset, finished on Friday and involved more than 200 Ukrainian personnel.Burnham and Zelenskyy are also due to discuss joint projects including Stone Cloak, an electronic jammer for which the UK has shared the intellectual property, allowingUkraineto use the system immediately.Thousands of the jammers, each about the size of a tablet computer, have been sent to Ukraine to be fitted to drones, with the aim of stopping Russian air defence systems from tracking and targeting them.Ukraine is now able to mass produce the devices itself. After being initially used there, the jammers are due to be fitted to new UK weaponry, including cruise missiles.Burnham, in a comment released by Downing Street before the visit, said: “Britain stands with Ukraine, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering. Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve, and we will not back down until we achieve a long-lasting and just peace for Ukraine.“Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAccording to statistics released by No 10, since Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, total UK support for the country has totalled £25bn, including £16bn in military assistance.Starmer visited Ukraine a number of times, and hosted Zelenskyy regularly. In one of the most telling displays of UK support, after a March 2025 visit to the White Houseduring which the Ukrainian leader was publicly beratedby Donald Trump, he thentravelled to the UKand met not only Starmer but also King Charles at Sandringham, which is primarily a royal home and rarely used for official events.During Starmer’s final visit to Ukraine, Zelenskyy presented him with the country’s Order of Freedom, the most prestigious honour that can be given to an overseas national.During a press conference with Starmer, the Ukrainian president said he hoped to build a strong relationship with Burnham, and to arrange a meeting “as soon as possible”.Explore more on these topicsVolodymyr ZelenskyyForeign policyAndy BurnhamLabourMilitaryUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Police shoot dead Berlin Pride van and knife rampage suspect, officials say | Germany | The Guardian
description: Abdul Ballout, 21, reportedly shot in operation at allotment in Spandau district after fatal attack in Tiergarten park
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Abdul Ballout, 21, reportedly shot in operation at allotment in Spandau district after fatal attack in Tiergarten park
Content: Police officers secure the area at an allotment garden complex in the Berlin suburb of Spandau where the man suspected of the attack was shot and killed.Photograph: Christian Mang/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice officers secure the area at an allotment garden complex in the Berlin suburb of Spandau where the man suspected of the attack was shot and killed.Photograph: Christian Mang/ReutersGermanyPolice shoot dead Berlin Pride van and knife rampage suspect, officials sayAbdul Ballout, 21, reportedly shot in operation at allotment in Spandau district after fatal attack in Tiergarten parkDeborah Colein Berlin andJennifer RankinSun 26 Jul 2026 13.53 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by police, German officials have said.Police confirmed on Sunday evening that the chief suspect had been shot dead, reportedly during an operation at an allotment garden complex ⁠in the capital’s Spandau district.One woman was killed on Saturday evening and 29 others were injured after a man drove a rented minivan into a crowd of pedestrians, then attacked people with what appeared to be a machete. The attack took place in the Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate at about 10pm local time on Saturday, close to one of Europe’s biggest LGBTQ+ celebrations.The attack forced organisers to cut short one of Europe’s largest Pride events and came asGermanyremained on edge after a series of deadly vehicle and knife attacks.map showing the location of the attack in the Tiergarten and the park’s location within Berlin city centre.View image in fullscreenThe 21-year-old suspect was identified by police as Abdul Ballout, a German national with Lebanese roots.Photograph: Polizei Berlin/ReutersThe German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, named the chief suspect as 21-year-old Abdul Ballout. “We are dealing ​here with ‌a suspected ‌perpetrator, who had previously drawn attention ‌to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene,” he told ‌a press conference near the site of the attack. He said Ballout had a criminal conviction and had been sentenced as a juvenile to a year and 10 months in prison, but that the sentence had been suspended.German media reported that Ballout, a German national with Lebanese roots, was a supporter ofIslamic Stateand last year travelled to the Middle East in a failed attempt to join the group. He was then convicted in Germany of “preparing a serious act of subversive violence”, the news outlets Bild and Der Spiegel reported.Police and prosecutors had asked for help in finding Ballout, but warned the public to avoid “direct contact” with him, saying he may be armed and dangerous. Police searched an apartment in the Schöneberg district of Berlin near the scene of the attack in the early hours of Sunday, but said they had found no one there.View image in fullscreenPolice officers secure the scene where the suspect was killed.Photograph: Michael Kappeler/DPA/APBefore Ballout was shot,Der Spiegel spoke with his father, Tawfik,by telephone from Lebanon, where he was visiting relatives.Describing Ballout as “generous, emotional, loving”, he said his son had lived with his mother, from whom Tawfik is divorced, and two of his three sisters. Ballout attended school until 10th grade, then bounced from job to job, in security or as a driver.Tawfik described the family asShiabut “not extremely religious” and said it “does not support Islamic State”, an extremist Sunni group.He and Ballout had fought about his hair and beard. “I did not allow him to wear a long beard,” he told Spiegel, calling it a symbol of extremism. Asked about a possible motive for the attack, he said: “He was brainwashed.”Tawfik spoke with Ballout on Saturday, the day of the attack. “He called me and we spoke normally, like every day. He said he missed me and wished he was with us in Lebanon.”The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, urged Germany to avoid division and intimidation in the aftermath of the attack. “We ​will think ​about ​consequences, we ​will ‌defend ​our freedom,” he said in a news conference.Earlier, Merz vowed to punish those responsible, describing the “heinous act” as an “attack on our society” in a social media post. The flag at the German Bundestag was ordered to be lowered to half mast.Police said the vehicle had struck multiple ⁠people after being driven into the Tiergarten. Shortly before 10pm the driver of the white minivan swerved into the park, close to where the route of the Pride march had been earlier in the day, hitting people on a path and crashing into a tree.Bild cited a witness as saying that a man had emerged from the vehicle and fled on foot. A hunt involving helicopters and officers from several German states was under way across the capital on Sunday.View image in fullscreenEmergency personnel work near the scene where a group of people were injured.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAJulian Methig, who attended the event, described it as a nightmare come true. “It’s one of the worst days for the queer community and a day I personally hoped I’d never have to experience … I’m shocked,” he said.Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered in Berlin in warm summer sunshine to celebrate the Pride parade. It is known in Germany as Christopher Street Day (CSD), named after the site of the Stonewall Inn in New York City where riots against police raids touched off the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. CSD was first held in West Berlin in 1979.View image in fullscreenPeople attend the annual Christopher Street Day parade.Photograph: Maryam Majd/ReutersBerlin’s mayor, Kai Wegner, called the deadly assault “an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society”.“Following a peaceful and colourful CSD, the rally for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal manner,” he said on X. “Berlin is the city of freedom – and our freedom has today been attacked in the most appalling way. My thoughts are with the victims, their families and friends.”View image in fullscreenTwo people embrace as they stand near emergency personnel in Berlin.Photograph: Markus Schreiber/APFor the first time in its history, CSD began on Friday night this year with a pro-democracy political rally. Berlin will hold a regional election in September along with two other states.The parade on Saturday ran under the motto “taking a stand is hot”, which organisers said was “in response to increasing hostility” to LGBTQ+ people in Germany.More than 80 floats and 50 groups on foot joined the procession through the city centre past Potsdamer Platz and the Victory Column monument in the Tiergarten, culminating in a rally at the Brandenburg Gate.View image in fullscreenEmergency personnel and police gather in Berlin.Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/APEarlier in the day one person was arrested for resisting police orders at a far-right counterprotest.Before last year’s parade, Berlin LGBTQ+ organisationssounded the alarmthat attacks had become more frequent while hard-won rights were under threat. Campaigners said a rise in hostility had accompanied the surge in support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), now the most popular party in national opinion polls, as well as an increase in Islamist-inspired attacks.European leaders offered solidarity, including heads of government in Belgium, the Netherlands and Sweden. “Italy firmly condemns and opposes all forms of hate and extremism,” the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, wrote on X, adding: “We stand with Germany and the German people.” The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said: “Faced with hatred and violence, our response will always be unity, freedom, and resolve.”The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, a German centre-right politician allied with Merz, sent her deepest sympathy to the victims of the attack, describing the CSD parade as standing for “freedom, dignity and equality – the fundamental values of the EU”.View image in fullscreenThe vehicle used in the attack on the parade was removed from the scene in the Tiergarten park on Sunday.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersBritain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said he was “horrified by the appalling attack in Berlin” and had spoken to his counterpart, Johann Wadephul, “to convey the UK’s solidarity: we stand with Germany”.Far-right leaders were also quick to comment on the attacks. The co-leader of the AfD Tino Chrupalla wrote on X: “We will not allow religious extremists to divide our country with violence and intolerance!”The president of France’s far-right National Rally, Jordan Bardella, wrote: “The Islamist threat remains a major issue in Europe and continues to target what they hate most about our civilisation – and what we cherish so much – freedom.”Explore more on these topicsGermanyIslamic StateLGBTQ+ rightsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Joy in Greece as Mount Olympus joins Unesco list of world heritage sites | Unesco | The Guardian
description: Mythical home of the ancient Greek gods designated alongside the D-day landing beaches in Normandy
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Mythical home of the ancient Greek gods designated alongside the D-day landing beaches in Normandy
Content: A statue of Alexander the Great holding Nike, the Greek goddess of victory, with Mount Olympus in the background.Photograph: Petros Giannakouris/APView image in fullscreenA statue of Alexander the Great holding Nike, the Greek goddess of victory, with Mount Olympus in the background.Photograph: Petros Giannakouris/APUnescoJoy in Greece as Mount Olympus joins Unesco list of world heritage sitesMythical home of the ancient Greek gods designated alongside the D-day landing beaches in NormandyHelena Smithin AthensSun 26 Jul 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 15.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a 12-year wait, Mount Olympus, the mythical home of the ancient Greek gods, has been inducted into a hall of more modern fame asUnescoannounced it would be added to its world heritage list.Greece’s highest mountain made the list alongside the second world war D-day landing beaches in northernFranceand the ancient Japanese capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara. South Sudan’s Boma-Badingilo landscape, host to one of the world’s largest land mammal migrations, also won a designation – a first for the east African country.The nominations were among dozens reviewed at a Unesco committee meeting in Busan, South Korea, on Sunday.In the case of Olympus, inscribed as a mixed world heritage site in recognition of its cultural and natural significance, the news was met with near euphoria inGreece.Immortalised as the seat of Zeus, king of the 12 Olympian deities, the mountain rising 2,918 metres from a base near sea level had been on a tentative list of sites since 2014.View image in fullscreenA conservator prepares an ancient sculpture of the head of Zeus for exhibition in Melbourne, AustraliaPhotograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianThe head of Greece’s Unesco delegation in Busan, Georgios Koumoutsakos, hailed the decision as one that would ensure the site’s preservation.“It reaffirms our unwavering commitment to safeguarding Mount Olympus for the benefit of present and future generations,” he said. “As Greek mythology wisely reminds us, it is always best to remain on good terms with the gods.”The region’s mayor, Evangelos Geroliolios,said before the announcementthat the site’s induction would “place greater responsibility on our part to protect the [local] environment”, not least its extraordinary biodiversity.The committee’s annual meeting, which ends on Wednesday, is expected to examine about 30 nominations. Those successful will join 1,248 sites across 170 countries admitted to the world heritage list for their “outstanding value to humanity”.Inscribed monuments can provide a vital boost for their preservation under an international convention overseen by Unesco, which also gives advice and financial support. Other world heritage sites include the Acropolis in Athens, the Great Wall of China, the pyramids of Giza in Egypt and the Taj Mahal in India.As with Mount Olympus, efforts to get the D-day beaches in Normandy inscribed had gone back years.View image in fullscreenTourists visit Les Braves monument on Omaha beach in Normandy.Photograph: Christophe Petit-Tesson/EPAIncluded in the French bid were all five of the beaches – Omaha, Utah, Sword, Gold and Juno – where more than 150,000 allied troops came ashore on 6 June 1944, and the Pointe du Hoc cliff that was also a focal point of the assault.The largest amphibious operation ever mounted, in which 4,000 soldiers died, was decisive in the battle to liberateEuropefrom Nazi occupation.France first nominated the 50-mile (80km) stretch of coastline in 2008. Reacting to the decision, the country’s permanent delegate to Unesco, Ahlem Gharbi, said the designation carried particular weight at a time of such international tensions.The president of the Normandy region, Hervé Morin, who had championed the cause, maintained that inclusion on the list would represent “immense recognition” for the soldiers who had sacrificed so much to defeat Nazism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEchoing Greek officials, he said: “This decision places a responsibility upon us. It compels us to preserve this site, to protect it, to cherish it even more, and to promote its value.”View image in fullscreenAllied troops come ashore near Vierville sur Mer on 6 June 1944.Photograph: ReutersThe international council on monuments and sites, one of the bodies that recommends additions to the Unesco list, had previously warned of the threat posed to the Normandy sites by tourism, climate change, rising sea levels and nearby windfarm development, and had called for stronger monitoring and preservation.The coastline is covered with extensive remnants of the time of the landings, including concrete German bunkers and gun positions, sunken vessels and allied installations.Unesco said in a statement that the beaches formed an “exceptional cultural landscape shaped both by the events of 1944 and by their enduring remembrance”, all of which justified further protection. As with Mount Olympus, the landing points have attracted record numbers of tourists in recent years.The agency’s move to include places associated with conflict has fuelled controversial debate over whether “sites of memory” are befitting of world heritage status and Unesco’s stated mission to “foster a world of greater equality and peace”.Three sites used by Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge regime for torture and execution were inscribed last year.After so many years of campaigning, Greek officials said Sunday’s decision had been made all the sweeter given signs of further delays.In the draft agenda of this week’s meeting, Unesco had signalled the Mount Olympus file would be referred back to the country for further details, spurring fears that proved to be baseless when the nomination won unanimous support.Explore more on these topicsUnescoGreeceFranceSecond world warHeritageEuropeUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police hunt for suspect after one killed and 16 injured in attack at Berlin Pride | Germany | The Guardian
description: Authorities issue wanted notice for Abdul Ballout, 21, after deadly van ramming described as Islamist terrorism
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Authorities issue wanted notice for Abdul Ballout, 21, after deadly van ramming described as Islamist terrorism
Content: 0:51Emergency services respond after van hits people at Berlin Pride – videoGermanyPolice hunt for suspect after one killed and 16 injured in attack at Berlin PrideAuthorities issue wanted notice for Abdul Ballout, 21, after deadly van ramming described as Islamist terrorismDeborah Colein BerlinSun 26 Jul 2026 11.22 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 17.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGerman authorities have issued a wanted notice for a suspect in a deadly van ramming near Berlin’s Pride festival that has been described as an Islamist attack.The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, named the chief suspect as 21-year-old Abdul Ballout. German media reported he was a supporter of Islamic State with a criminal conviction in May.Dobrindt said all ​the evidence surrounding Saturday night’s attack, which left one person dead and at least 16 wounded, pointed to Islamist ⁠terrorism. “We are dealing ​here with ‌a suspected ‌perpetrator, who had previously drawn attention ‌to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene,” he told ‌a press conference near the site of the attack.Police and prosecutors have asked for help in finding Ballout, who is a German citizen. They said he was believed to have injured several people with a moving vehicle on Saturday night, and that one or more people apparently then left that vehicle. Several people were also apparently stabbed, they added.View image in fullscreenEmergency personnel work near the scene where a group of people were injured.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPASunday’s notice warned the public to avoid “direct contact” with the suspect, saying that he may be armed and dangerous.Police had said earlier that they had identified a suspect with ties to Islamist groups in the German capital.“The suspect is known to police.
