He is known to us as a member of Islamist circles here in Berlin, and our search for this person is proceeding at full speed,” police spokesperson Florian Nath said.Nath added that “we still have no information whatsoever regarding his specific motives, the exact sequence of events, or his role in the crime itself”.Map of the parade route and where the attack took place in BerlinGerman media reported on Sunday that the chief suspect last year travelled to the Middle East in a failed attempt to join Islamic State. He was then convicted inGermanyof “preparing a serious act of subversive violence,” Bild and Spiegel newspapers reported.The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, vowed to punish those responsible.The attack forced organisers to cut short one of Europe’s largest Pride events and comes as Germany remains on edge after a series of deadly vehicle and knife attacks.View image in fullscreenPeople attend the annual Christopher Street Day LGBT Pride demonstration.Photograph: Maryam Majd/ReutersHours after the apparent attack many details remained unclear, but police said the vehicle struck multiple ⁠people after charging into the city’s central Tiergarten park close to the Brandenburg Gate.Police said those hurt “included several with life-threatening injuries”.The driver of a white van had swerved shortly before 10pm into the Tiergarten, close to the route of the Pride march earlier in the day, hitting people on a path and crashing into a tree, police said.“[The vehicle] was empty, which is why we are currently working intensively to track ​down the perpetrator or perpetrators,” police said. Tabloid newspaper Bild cited a witness as saying that a man emerged from the vehicle and fled on foot.A manhunt involving helicopters and officers from several German states was under way across the capital on Sunday.A Berlin fire department spokesperson, Dominik Pretz, said one person died and at least 16 others were injured.Emergency workers set up a helicopter landing pad near the Reichstag parliament building to transport the injured to hospitals.Merz said in a statement that he and Dobrindt would “push to make sure this horrific act is fully investigated and punished”.Julian Methig, who attended the event, described it as a terrible day. “It’s one of the worst days for the queer community and a day I personally hoped I’d never have to experience … I’m shocked.”View image in fullscreenForensic investigators collect evidence from the white van involved at the crime scene.Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/ShutterstockHundreds of thousands of people had gathered in the German capital in warm summer sunshine to celebrate the pride parade.It is known in Germany as Christopher Street Day (CSD), named after the site of the Stonewall Inn in New York City where riots against police raids touched off the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. CSD was first held in West Berlin in 1979.Berlin’s mayor, Kai Wegner, called the deadly assault “an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society”.“Following a peaceful and colourful CSD, the rally for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal manner,” he said on X. “Berlin is the city of freedom – and our freedom has today been attacked in the most appalling way. My thoughts are with the victims, their families and friends.”For the first time in its history, CSD began on Friday night this year with a pro-democracy political rally. Berlin will hold a state election in September.The parade on Saturday ran under the motto “Taking a stand is hot” which organisers said was “in response to increasing hostility” to queer people in Germany.More than 80 floats and 50 groups on foot joined the procession through the city centre past Potsdamer Platz and the Victory Column monument in the Tiergarten, culminating in a rally at the Brandenburg Gate.Earlier in the day one person was arrested for resisting police orders at a far-right counterprotest.View image in fullscreenPolice officers work near the site where a vehicle drove into crowd in Berlin.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockBefore last year’s pride parade, Berlin LGBTQ+ organisationssounded the alarmthat attacks had become more frequent while hard-won rights were under threat.Campaigners said a rise in hostility has accompanied the surge in support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party, now the most popular party in national opinion polls, as well as an increase in Islamist-inspired attacks.European leaders offered solidarity. “Italy firmly condemns and opposes all forms of hate and extremism,” prime minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X, adding: “We stand with Germany and the German people”. French president Emmanuel Macron said: “Faced with hatred and violence, our response will always be unity, freedom, and resolve”.The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, a German centre-right politician allied with Merz, sent her deepest sympathy to the victims of the attack, describing the Christopher Street Day parade as standing for “freedom, dignity and equality – the fundamental values of the EU”.UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband said he was “horrified by the appalling attack in Berlin”, adding that he had spoken to his counterpart, Johann Wadephul, “to convey the UK’s solidarity: we stand with Germany”.Explore more on these topicsGermanyLGBTQ+ rightsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe wildfires: ‘Difficult hours lie ahead’ in battle to contain fires, says Pedro Sánchez as more than 300,000 flee homes in France and Spain – as it happened | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Fires displace people on massive scale and trigger one of the largest peacetime civilian evacuation operations ever carried out in France
Author: Yohannes Lowe
Headline: Fires displace people on massive scale and trigger one of the largest peacetime civilian evacuation operations ever carried out in France
Content: 10.52 EDTClosing summaryHundreds of thousands of people have been evacuated from their homes due to the risks posed by the wildfires in France and Spain.Nearly 260,000 people have been evacuated across France as a whole, while in Spain more than 90,000 were evacuated from regions around Madrid and Ávila.In positive developments this morning, fires west of Madrid were reportedly being brought under control, although the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, later spoke of “difficult hours” ahead.Sánchez also said there needed to be “a major public pact on the climate emergency” going forward.However, a new front opened up overnight near the Spanish coastal city of Valencia, where at least 15,000 people were evacuated.In France, which has been worst affected, authorities are battling to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux that has consumed an area of land four times the size of Paris, as my colleagues notein this story.About 55,000 people were ordered to leave villages around Bordeaux, in the Gironde region in the south-west of the country, overnight.Bordeaux’s mayor, Thomas Cazenave, described the Gironde blaze as being “at the gates of the metropolitan area”, between 15 and 20 miles (25 and 30km) from the city itself.A Bordeaux city council spokesperson said earlier that a total evacuation of the city was being considered butthe mayor subsequently downplayed this possibility.At least 240 homes in Gironde have been totally destroyed by the wildfire which is still raging in south-west France.You can read more on the wildfires in our latest storyhere. We are closing the blog now. Thanks for following along.Share

title: Netanyahu accuses Mamdani of ‘fomenting hate’ in calls for PM’s arrest | US news | The Guardian
description: Israeli prime minister says ICC’s war crime charges are ‘bogus’ and plans to be in New York for UN gathering this fall
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Israeli prime minister says ICC’s war crime charges are ‘bogus’ and plans to be in New York for UN gathering this fall
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu speaks in Jerusalem during a press conference, amid the US-Israel conflict with Iran, on 19 March 2026.Photograph: Ronen Zvulun/ReutersView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu speaks in Jerusalem during a press conference, amid the US-Israel conflict with Iran, on 19 March 2026.Photograph: Ronen Zvulun/ReutersUS newsNetanyahu accuses Mamdani of ‘fomenting hate’ in calls for PM’s arrestIsraeli prime minister says ICC’s war crime charges are ‘bogus’ and plans to be in New York for UN gathering this fallAssociated PressSun 26 Jul 2026 16.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenjamin Netanyahusaid on Sunday thatZohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, is “fomenting hate” by calling the Israeli prime minister a war criminal who should be arrested overIsrael’s war in Gaza if he visits the city for the United Nations general assembly.Netanyahu said he intends to be inNew Yorkin September to address the annual UN gathering of world leaders, despite the mayor’s suggestion that he is not welcome. Mamdanisaidon Wednesday that while New York City does not have legal authority to execute an arrest warrant issued by the world’s top war crimes court, he encouraged the federal government to do so.“He’s supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers – Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone,” Netanyahusaidon the Fox News channel’s Sunday Morning Futures with Maria Bartiromo. “But he’s trying to turn one group against the other.”Mamdani says he can’t arrest Netanyahu as mayor and urges US to enforce ICC warrantRead moreThe prime minister has become an increasingly polarizing figure over Israel’swar in Gaza, which was ignited by the 7 October 2023 deadly attack on southern Israel by Hamas militants. Israel also joined the US in starting thewar against Iranon 28 February before launching a ground invasion in southern Lebanon in response to fire from the Iranian-backed Hezbollah group.Netanyahu on Sunday dismissed the international criminal court (ICC)’swar crimes chargesagainst him as “bogus”. He pointed to sexual misconduct allegations against the ICC’s top prosecutor, who wasremovedfrom that post on Friday, and said the warrant was an attempt to divert attention.Mamdani’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Sunday.Netanyahu on Sunday also said he was concerned that once-bipartisan political support for Israel in the US isatrisk, particularly as progressive and far-left Democratsaligned withthe Mamdani wing of the party splinter.He also warned against rising antisemitism in the US and other western countries, saying that when he talks to people inNew YorkCity, home to the second-largest Jewish population in the world, “Jews feel very uncomfortable”.“And I think it’s wrong,” he said. “The whole thing is wrong.”Throughout his 2025 mayoral election campaign, Mamdanisaidhe would seek to order the city’s police to execute the ICC’s arrest warrant over Netanyahu’s role in the war in Gaza.Trump says Benjamin Netanyahu ‘will not be arrested’ if he visits the USRead more“I want to be equally clear, Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large,”he saidin his video message on Wednesday.He told New Yorkers that he understood their frustration and that expressions of protest is something the city would “always respect”.The Hague-based court has accused Netanyahu, his former defense minister and the late leader of Hamas of crimes against humanity. The Palestinian territory’s health ministry says more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s offensive – roughly half of them women and children. About 1,200 people, most of them civilians, were killed in the initial Hamas attack onIsrael.Trump on MondaytoldNetanyahu in a social media post that he “will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States of America”.Netanyahu is expected in Washington DC on Monday to meet with Trump and attend funeral services forLindsey Graham, the late Republican senator.Graham, a leading defense hawk and strong supporter of Israel,died suddenlyon 11 July of a likely torn aorta. Netanyahucalledhim a “great patriot” and one of Israel’s “greatest friends”.Explore more on these topicsUS newsBenjamin NetanyahuZohran MamdaniUS politicsIsraelNew YorkMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: US pauses Iran attacks for second night after Trump advised to halt bombing | Iran | The Guardian
description: Top military officials say campaign has reached its limit of effectiveness and warn of dwindling stocks of munitions
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Top military officials say campaign has reached its limit of effectiveness and warn of dwindling stocks of munitions
Content: US naval forces carry out an operation as part of their blockade on Iranian ports and ships.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUS naval forces carry out an operation as part of their blockade on Iranian ports and ships.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesIranUS pauses Iran attacks for second night after Trump advised to halt bombingTop military officials say campaign has reached its limit of effectiveness and warn of dwindling stocks of munitionsAndrew Rothin JerusalemSun 26 Jul 2026 14.45 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 07.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has paused strikes on Iran for a second night as top military officials advisedDonald Trumpto halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war.Trump is said to be weighing up diplomatic and military options in the nearly five-month-old conflict, withBenjamin Netanyahuexpected to visit the White House on Tuesday. The Israeli prime minister is a vocal critic of Washington’s negotiations with Iranian leaders and has pressed for the US to continue its strikes against Iran.Netanyahu is under considerable political pressure to show that his military campaigns againstIranand Hezbollah in Lebanon have yielded results before elections scheduled for October.Tehran said on Sunday it would pause what it called “retaliatory” attacks against US allies in the region. “These [US] attacks continued until two nights ago, but over the past two nights the Americans have stopped their attacks,” said the army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia. “Our strategy has essentially been retaliatory, we have also halted our retaliatory operations.”‘Shameful’: Pentagon accused of cover-up over US military casualties in Iran warRead moreSenior officials in the Trump administration are reported to have told the president about dwindling munitions stockpiles that could hamper a sustained military campaign in the region.Axios reported on Sunday that Adm Bradley Cooper, the top US military commander in the region, had told Trump the US military campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness.The message was said to affect Trump’s decision to hold strikes on Iran for the first time in nearly two weeks. Cooper told Trump the US had nearly exhausted the list of targets that it had developed to attack in Iran, and without a return to major combat operations there was little point in continuing the bombing campaign, the news website reported.Asked on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press whether Trump was ruling out additional strikes in Iran, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz said: “I wouldn’t go that far at all. The president is keeping all options on the table.”The lull in fighting, which began on Friday evening, follows nearly two weeks of strikes against Iran and the collapse of a ceasefire brokered by Trump. Washington blamed Iran for strikes on US forces and allies in the region and its closure of the strait of Hormuz, a conduit for an estimated 20% of the world’s oil and gas.Senior diplomats from Iran and Oman were said to be holding negotiations on Sunday on reopening the vital waterway and an official in Tehran confirmed colleagues had been in touch with US negotiators to prevent a return to war. Iran has demanded payment and control over which ships pass through the strait.“Mediators are working and trying to prevent tension from escalating,” the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, told a press conference on Sunday.But an Iranian army spokesperson signalled defiance, saying the US had no clear strategy and was “experiencing strategic decision-making fatigue”.Graph showing how fighting has stopped ships transiting HormuzThe US vice-president,JD Vance, and Dan Caine, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff, warned Trump of the risks of a renewed military campaign against Iran at an Oval Office meeting on Friday, according to media outlets. The president then ordered the military to call off new strikes, which he had warned could “knock out everything they have”.“We’re talking to [the Iranians] right now,” Trump told reporters on Friday. “I think they’re getting more and more serious as the days go by. We’re locked and loaded and ready to go, but we’re talking to them.”At a White House Correspondents’ Association dinner that evening he said he did not think Iran was ready to make a deal but he was ready to listen.View image in fullscreenIsraeli army units stage a raid near Nablus in the occupied West Bank after the deaths of four Palestinians and two Israelis when armed settlers entered a village.Photograph: Mohammed Torokman/ReutersCaine warned Trump about dwindling munitions stockpiles, which include Patriot missile interceptors and offensive weapons like Tomahawk cruise missiles. Vance campaigned on his opposition to US military interventions in the Middle East and has grown more vocal in his opposition to the war in Iran.Netanyahu’s office announced on Sunday that he would convene a meeting of his security cabinet before leaving for Washington on Monday. He played a crucial role in lobbying Trump to launch joint strikes against Iran in February and has said that US negotiators must take a strong line on Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programme. US negotiators have instead prioritised opening the strait of Hormuz.Netanyahu will travel to Washington amid some of the worst violence this year in the West Bank, where his military is launching an “extensive” operation after the deaths of four Palestinians and two Israelis when armed settlers entered a Palestinian village on Thursday.The US and the UK under its new prime minister, Andy Burnham, are discussing plans for a high-level meeting in London this week to discuss the potential for a coalition to protect ships in the strait of Hormuz and de-mine the waterway. The discussions will be an early test for Burnham’s administration. The Labour government has so far refused to allow Washington to use a British airbase for offensive operations against Iran.Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpUS foreign policyIsraelPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for Modi | India | The Guardian
description: Ally forced to resign, with opposition parties reinvigorated and strongman leader’s grip over media channels rocked
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Ally forced to resign, with opposition parties reinvigorated and strongman leader’s grip over media channels rocked
Content: Cockroach Janta party supporters in New Delhi on Saturday. Their core demand, for Dharmendra Pradhan to resign, has been achieved.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersView image in fullscreenCockroach Janta party supporters in New Delhi on Saturday. Their core demand, for Dharmendra Pradhan to resign, has been achieved.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersIndiaAnalysisIndia’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for ModiHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiAlly forced to resign, with opposition parties reinvigorated and strongman leader’s grip over media channels rockedSun 26 Jul 2026 12.42 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 12.09 EDTShareEven the night beforeNarendra Modiaccepted the resignation of his education minister, India’s prime minister appeared confident that the largest mass uprising to take place in his 12 years in power would do little to rattle his government.‘I will die for this cause’: how India’s cockroach meme became the biggest challenge to Modi’s grip on powerRead moreAddressing his “young friends” in a late-night Instagram selfie reel on Friday, he thanked the people – who weremobilised en masse across the country, shouting anti-government slogans – for their “thoughtful suggestions”.Less than 24 hours later, Modi, who has fiercely cultivated his strongman image for years, had bowed to public pressure and accepted theresignationofDharmendraPradhan. It was, say analysts, the remarkable humbling of a government that has ruled with almost untouchable impunity since 2014.Over that past week, a gen Z movement that called itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) mobilised unprecedented protests in the name of justice for millions of young people, after the leaking of a crucial exam paper forced 2 million students to resit the test and was blamed for more than a dozen suicides.The resignation of Pradhan, Modi’s loyal political ally, remained their first and foremost demand for accountability, even as the protests expanded into a wider fight for democracy. Yet Pradhan went unmentioned by Modi in his Instagram address.0:51‘Cockroach’ movement: thousands march in anti-government protest in New DelhiOn Saturday morning, more people than ever were pouring into Delhi’s historic Jantar Mantar site – the centre of the protests – and unrest was spreading fast to other cities, including states ruled by Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).It was not only physical space that had been captured by the cockroach movement. Since coming to power, the BJP has proved enormously effective at capturing the online narrative, deploying its powerful, highly organised IT cell to mobilise and attack any perceived criticism of the government, whether it came from citizens, politicians or journalists.But this proved no match for the millions of gen Z memes and reels that began to flood Instagram over this past week, fearlessly insulting Modi and pillorying the government, each more creative and incendiary than the next. Modi’s last-ditch attempts to speak directly to the youth on Instagram were simply met with more ridicule and spin-off memes.View image in fullscreenCockroach Janta party supporters were in a jubilant mood in Mumbai on Sunday after Pradhan’s departure from government.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPAModi had also lost another medium critical to the BJP’s domination over the national narrative – the mainstream TV news channels widely acknowledged to have been co-opted by the BJP government over the past 12 years and turned into mouthpieces for its rightwing Hindu nationalist ideology.Initially, the channels ignored the protests, and when they did cover them it was to suggest the protesters were being bankrolled by sinister foreign forces and Pakistani terror groups. In response, the protesters turned on the channels, using social media to expose their “lies”. When the protests escalated, Modi remained conspicuously absent from the airwaves.Pradhan’s resignation came as it appeared that all other options for the government had gone. The option of a ruthless crackdown appeared untenable given the mass outcry to the police violence that had hit protesters on Monday.“The online space was totally conquered by the protesters and regime-loving media was seriously delegitimised,” said Ashutosh Varshney, a professor of international studies at Brown University in Rhode Island. “The anger was so comprehensive there was no option left but for Pradhan to go.”View image in fullscreenMany CJP supporters brought placards and signs openly criticising Modi.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPABut this was more than the loss of a minister, Varshney said, it was also the first time in 12 years that the Modi government had lost control of the political narrative. “This is a repressive government,” he said. “It wants obedience, it wants no critical discussion and it generates fear. But now the climate of fear has collapsed.”Analysts say the resignation of Pradhan could also have implications for Modi’s power over his own cabinet. Pradhan was one of Modi’s most loyal ministers and ideological footsoldiers, and had implemented policies exactly as senior party figures had wanted. He had also helped the BJP win Odisha state for the first time in the general election, bringing in crucial seats.“Modi knows once you start firing your most loyal ministers, it sets up the incentives for defections in other ministers as well,” said the political columnist Pratap Bhanu Mehta. “If your own cabinet starts to hedge for a future where they may not be backed by your own government, that’s when you are in trouble.”View image in fullscreenAbhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP, celebrated with his fellow protesters in New Delhi on Saturday.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersPrior to this week’s unrest, Modi had been riding high on a string of important state electoral victories, in particular the BJP’s first triumph in West Bengal, a politically important state that had long pushed back against its Hindu nationalist politics.The BJP appeared to have fully bounced back from the blow in the 2024 elections, when theparty failed to win an outright parliamentary majorityand had to scramble together a large enough alliance to take power. At the same time, the much-beleaguered opposition had continued to lose countless state elections and their allegations of voting impropriety by the BJP fell mostly on deaf ears.Yet the emergence of the cockroaches has reinvigorated not only India’s youth, but its political opposition parties as well. Jumping on the bandwagon, the opposition Congress party has had its best week in years as it mobilised protests and shut down parliament. The party’s leader, Rahul Gandhi, was dramatically dragged away by police outside Modi’s house in support of students.Analysts say that dissent, which had been systematically crushed over the past 12 years, has now been re-galvanised as an effective tool to hold the government – and in particular the prime minister – to account.“After a long time, there’s an assertion of political agency across different sections of society,” said Mehta. “And the minute you see that agency out in the street, it empowers lots of other agents.”The next big test of the electoral implications of the CJP movement will come early next year, when India’s largest and most politically important state holds its state elections. Holding on to power in Uttar Pradesh, the BJP’s political heartland, is seen as crucial for the party and would have major implications for the next general election in 2029.The grievances of India’s newly-politicised youth are extensive, including a chronic lack of graduate jobs and stagnant wages. Just how the CJP intends to politically mobilise after its striking victory on Saturday remains to be seen. Leaders and supporters insist this is just the “beginning”, particularly in their push for education reform. Their founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has some past experience as a political party organiser, but has not made his own ambitions known.Yet analysts said that one of the most crucial impacts of the CJP had been to reopen a rapidly closing democratic space and make it seem possible that a new kind of political opposition could emerge, one reflective of the voices heard on the streets of India this week.Saurav Das, a CJP spokesperson, said it was encouraging people involved in the movement to go into politics. “This is one of our goals,” he said. “We need to increase youth participation in politics, because right now it’s controlled by uncles and aunties who are only interested in looking after their own lifestyles and don’t understand the needs of our generation. The answer also has to be political.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaNarendra ModiSouth and central AsiaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: RAF Chinook crash victims’ families ask Andy Burnham for review of disaster | Military | The Guardian
description: PM urged to end ‘cover-up culture’ and order independent review taking in evidence that has emerged on 1994 crash
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: PM urged to end ‘cover-up culture’ and order independent review taking in evidence that has emerged on 1994 crash
Content: The Chinook Justice Campaign, made up of more than 55 family members of 25 of the victims, delivering a letter to Andy Burnham.Photograph: Chinook Justice Campaign/PAView image in fullscreenThe Chinook Justice Campaign, made up of more than 55 family members of 25 of the victims, delivering a letter to Andy Burnham.Photograph: Chinook Justice Campaign/PAMilitaryRAF Chinook crash victims’ families ask Andy Burnham for review of disasterPM urged to end ‘cover-up culture’ and order independent review taking in evidence that has emerged on 1994 crashJosh HallidayNorth of England editorSun 26 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe families of those killed in an RAF Chinook crashin 1994have urged Andy Burnham to end Britain’s “cover-up culture” and order an independent review intothe disaster.Twenty-nine serving military personnel died when the Chinook HC2 helicopter crashed on the Mull of Kintyre in south-westScotlandduring a flight from Northern Ireland.The two pilotswere initially blamedfor the crash butexonerated after an inquiry in 2011, which did not determine its cause.Liam Fox, the former Conservative defence secretary who orderedthat official review, said last month there were now “deep concerns” that “vital information” could have been withheld.Fox, who is backing the calls for a fresh independent review, said there was now a “strong enough belief” that a deliberate cover-up had taken place. There were concerns, he said, that details provided by the Ministry of Defence (MoD) onthe airworthinessof the Chinook that crashed were “not correct”.View image in fullscreenAll 29 personnel on the Chinook HC2 were killed when it crashed on the Mull of Kintyre, south-west Scotland, in June 1994.Photograph: Chris Bacon/PAA high court judge ruled this month that the families of several victims of the crash could not bring a legal claim against the MoD over the incident because it had been brought too late.The Chinook Justice Campaign (CJC), which is made up of more than 55 family members of 25 of the victims, said it would take the case to theEuropean court of human rights.However, Matt Tobias, whose father, Lt Col John Tobias, was killed in the crash, said the families “do not want years of further litigation” and urged the prime minister to help by ordering a fresh independent review.He said: “We would urge Mr Burnham to meet us within his first 100 days in office so we can present the evidence that has emerged over recent years and explain why we believe a fresh review, independent of theMinistry of Defence, is now essential.Mull of Kintyre crash: The last flight of Zulu Delta 576Read more“Mr Burnham’s speech in the House of Commons, in which he spoke about ending Britain’s cover-up culture and strengthening the duty of candour, gave our families real hope.”In a letter delivered to Burnham, the Chinook families said it could be a “test case” forthe new Hillsborough law, which was unanimously backed by MPs this month and creates a legally enforceable duty of candour compelling public officials and authorities to act transparently during investigations.Tobias said: “We ask that he and his ministers give the Chinook families more respect than we received from his predecessor, who denied us a meeting and an inquiry – believing MoD lies instead. After 32 years, we are not asking for special treatment. We are simply asking for the truth.”The CJC group said it wanted Burnham to establish a fresh review, independent of the Ministry of Defence, withfull access to all relevant documentsrelating to the airworthiness of the Chinook helicopter and the circumstances leading up to the crash.An MoD spokesperson said: “Our thoughts and sympathies remain with the families, friends, and colleagues of all those who died in the Mull of Kintyre crash.“We understand the recent court judgment will be disappointing for those involved. Defence Ministers have previously met with the CJC and we will continue to engage to hear concerns and discuss this important matter.”Explore more on these topicsMilitaryMinistry of DefenceLiam FoxScotlandEuropean court of human rightsAndy BurnhamHelicopter crashesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rising oil prices could force up UK interest rates, say economists | Interest rates | The Guardian
description: Bank of England expected to keep rates on hold on Thursday but renewed Iran conflict casts shadow over energy costs
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Bank of England expected to keep rates on hold on Thursday but renewed Iran conflict casts shadow over energy costs
Content: A US warship stops a tanker under a blockade of Iranian ports and vessels. Renewed fighting has pushed up oil prices.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA US warship stops a tanker under a blockade of Iranian ports and vessels. Renewed fighting has pushed up oil prices.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesInterest ratesRising oil prices could force up UK interest rates, say economistsBank of England expected to keep rates on hold on Thursday but renewed Iran conflict casts shadow over energy costsPhillip InmanSun 26 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Bank of Englandcould be forced to tear up its economic forecasts and raise interest rates later this year if oil prices return to above $100 a barrel, according to City economists.Before a meeting of Bank officials on Thursday, economists said that while an interest rate hike would probably be avoided this week there could be some in the future because of conflict in the Middle East.The UK economy has remained relatively resilient since Donald Trump’s war on Iran began in March, but this could be at risk after fighting reignited last week, the economists added.The breakdown of the fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran sent oil prices back to the highs seen in April and May, sparking fears that higher prices at the pumps would send inflation soaring.A barrel of Brent crude jumped above $100 a barrel (£75) on Thursday before falling back to $96 on Friday, well above the $71 recorded earlier this month.Gas prices have soared before the crucial period when most European countries refill their storage facilities in time for winter heating demand.All the major central banks say they are concerned about the impact of the war in the Middle East and its influence on rising prices.The Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee is expected to vote on Thursday in favour of holding interest rates, and to continue maintaining them at 3.75% until at least December, by a margin of seven to two. This echoestheir last meeting in Junewhen two officials on the committee voted to increase rates to head off rising inflation.Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said that calculation might change if the intensity of airstrikes was maintained and the sea channels allowing tankers to enter and exit oil terminals remained blocked.He said: “We see upside risks to the interest rate outlook in the near term, with much dependent on the duration of the unfolding energy shock. A second energy wave will likely amplify uncertainty around the inflation path and the risk of second-round effects.”View image in fullscreenThe Bank of England’s monetary policy committee is expected to vote on Thursday in favour of holding interest rates.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/ReutersGeorge Buckley, the chief UK and euro area economist at Nomura, said financial markets were giving a clear signal that higher oil prices would translate into higher interest rates. “At $90 they would see the need for one and a half quarter-point hikes. At $100 there would be a need for two 25 basis point hikes,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK inflation falls by more than expected to 2.6% in lift for Andy BurnhamRead moreMohamed El-Erian, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania and a former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, suggested a sustained increase in oil prices to $90 a barrel could be enough to rewrite UK policymakers’ forecasts.He said: “Should oil prices remain above $90 a barrel, an important ‘if’, then headline inflation would face significant upward pressure. This, in turn, would heighten concerns over immediate indirect effects, including rising food prices driven by diesel transportation costs, and broader second-round effects over time.“The result would be heightened market expectation of aBank of Englandrate hike, even as higher energy prices act as a tax on economic activity.”Ruth Gregory, the deputy chief UK economist at CapitalEconomics, said a worst-case scenario showed that if inflation rose to 7% over the coming months in response to the Middle East conflict, UK interest rates would probably rise from 3.75% to 4.75%.Harvinder Kalirai, the chief global currency strategist at Alpine Macro, a division of Oxford Economics, said he expected the Bank to “look through the oil shock and political noise” to hold rates steady for now before resuming cuts next year.He said the UK was not strong enough to withstand a rise in the cost of fuel and higher interest rates: “Demand is not strong enough to sustain a pass-through from the energy shock, forcing firms to absorb higher input costs.”Kalirai said once volatile elements of the inflation basket – including fuel and food – were excluded, prices were growing slowly while pay packets were rising at a slower pace.Costas Milas, an economics professor at the University of Liverpool, said oil price shocks triggered long bouts of inflation and should be tackled quickly.He said: “This is too uncomfortable for the BoE to stay inactive not least because the public remainsdissatisfied with the BoE. Since dissatisfaction increases with inflation, the BoE should act soon by raising interest rates, possibly as early as September.”David Aikman, the head of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said: “The longer inflation remains above target, the greater the change inflation expectations shift and wages respond – and hence the Bank needing to hike rates.”Financial markets also anticipate a hike at the European Central Bank governing council’s next meeting on 10 September. It raised interest rates in June for the first time since 2023 in response to higher inflation caused by the war in Iran.Central banks have come under fire for considering a rise in the cost of borrowing, with critics arguing increases in interest rates will only make a bad situation worse.Explore more on these topicsInterest ratesBank of EnglandInflationUS-Israel war on IranEconomicsOilCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Boy, 16, charged with murder of teenager stabbed in Luton park | UK news | The Guardian
description: Four others arrested on suspicion of same murder in Luton after death of 17-year-old
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Four others arrested on suspicion of same murder in Luton after death of 17-year-old
Content: Bedfordshire police said officers were called to Kingsway recreation ground shortly after 6.30pm on Friday.Photograph: GoogleView image in fullscreenBedfordshire police said officers were called to Kingsway recreation ground shortly after 6.30pm on Friday.Photograph: GoogleUK newsBoy, 16, charged with murder of teenager stabbed in Luton parkFour others arrested on suspicion of same murder in Luton after death of 17-year-oldNadeem BadshahSun 26 Jul 2026 18.26 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 16-year-old boy has been charged with murdering a teenager who died from multiple stab wounds at a park in Luton, police said.Four other teenagers have been arrested on suspicion of the same murder.Bedfordshire police said officers were called to Kingsway recreation ground shortly after 6.30pm on Friday following reports that a number of teenagers were seen “carrying large knives”.The 17-year-old boy, who has yet to be identified, was taken to hospital but died a short time later.Police said two boys, aged 16 and 17, had been arrested on suspicion of murder on Saturday after they were initially arrested on suspicion of violent disorder.The younger male has since been charged with murder and remanded in custody, the force said.Another three 17-year-old boys have also been arrested, each on suspicion of murder, violent disorder and carrying a weapon, it added in its statement on Sunday.DCI Nick Gardener said: “We are progressing our investigation and we are continuing to appeal to anyone who was in the area, or witnessed the events leading up to the disorder, to please get in touch.“Our officers are continuing to carry out additional high-visibility patrols, and we are continuing to engage with local members of the public.“We would also like to remind the public not to share any distressing videos or images as this can be concerning for families involved, but also form a vital part of the police investigation.”Zanib Raja, a councillor in Luton, has also encouraged people not to share alleged videos of the incident online.Raja wrote on Facebook: “Like many of you, I became aware of this horrific attack through disturbing videos circulating online.“Let me say this clearly: Do not share them. They traumatise the family, fuel fear, & do nothing to help.”She added: “A tragic incident took place … in Kingsway Park, a place many of us grew up in, played in, & built memories in.“A place that should be safe for families, children, & every resident of our town. Instead, a man lost his life in broad daylight. A family has been shattered. Luton is hurting.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Water supply restored to Gatwick airport after hours without working toilets | Gatwick airport | The Guardian
description: Airport’s bars and restaurants were also unable to serve drinks to passengers because of lack of running water
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Airport’s bars and restaurants were also unable to serve drinks to passengers because of lack of running water
Content: Passengers at the airport had no access to working toilets or bars and restaurants because of a water supply failure.Photograph: Tom Jeffreys/PAView image in fullscreenPassengers at the airport had no access to working toilets or bars and restaurants because of a water supply failure.Photograph: Tom Jeffreys/PAGatwick airportWater supply restored to Gatwick airport after hours without working toiletsAirport’s bars and restaurants were also unable to serve drinks to passengers because of lack of running waterJamie GriersonSun 26 Jul 2026 18.01 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWater supply has been restored to most ofGatwick airportafter passengers spent hours without access to working toilets, and bars and restaurants were closed.Most toilets had reopened across both terminals on Sunday evening, with the remaining facilities, including bars and restaurants, expected to return to normal for the first of Monday’s flights.Although flights were unaffected, toilets in both terminals were out of use, cafes, restaurants and bars were shut, and taps were either not running at all or running with low pressure since Sunday morning.Announcing that the water, supplied by SES Water, had been restored, Gatwick airport said: “Following an issue at the Bough Beech water treatment works which impacted the local area today, we are pleased to report that the water supply has now returned to the vast majority of theLondonGatwick campus.“Most toilet facilities are now open and we expect all toilets – as well as food and beverage outlets – to be open for tomorrow’s first flights. Since becoming aware of the issue, we have been working closely with @SESWater and our airport partners to help minimise the impact, and ensure all today’s flights departed as scheduled.”Earlier on Sunday, passengers posted online that they were unable to get hot drinks, wash their hands or fill water bottles at the airport in Sussex.The problem also had an impact in the wider Sussex andKentarea, water suppliers said.View image in fullscreenAn empty restaurant at Gatwick on Sunday.Photograph: Roger Wood/PASES Water said there had been interruptions to water supplies in parts of the TN11, RH1, RH6 and RH10 postcode areas.At 2pm the company had said its Bough Beech water treatment works were running again but the water needed to be treated before services could return to normal.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve never seen Wetherspoons empty,’ said one traveller who was heading to New York.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAOn Facebook, one user posted: “Gasping for a drink & crossing my legs right now. This is ridiculous! Gatwick airport has shut all restaurants and most toilets due to a water outage. Not a great start to the holiday.”The former MP and recently appointed government “music champion” Michael Dugher wrote on social media: “At least allow people to use the chairs in all the closed restaurants and bars. No water is one thing, but depriving people of somewhere to sit is another … Families are having to sit on the floor.”Roger Wood, from Tunbridge Wells, Kent, arrived at Gatwick’s south terminal at about 11am on Sunday to fly to New York. He told reporters: “There was no communication. We arrived at 11ish and it had only started recently.“We met friends at the bar but they couldn’t serve us as they were unable to wash their hands. I’ve never seen Wetherspoons empty. No idea when it’ll be resolved. The toilets also lacked water to wash hands.”Explore more on these topicsGatwick airportAir transportTransportLondonWest SussexWater industryEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Industry star David Jonsson to play Black Panther in Marvel sequel | Black Panther | The Guardian
description: Director Ryan Coogler announces British actor in lead role alongside co-stars Letitia Wright and Winston Duke
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Director Ryan Coogler announces British actor in lead role alongside co-stars Letitia Wright and Winston Duke
Content: From left to right, Letitia Wright, Winston Duke, Ryan Coogler, David Jonsson and Kevin Feige on stage at Marvel Studios’ Comic-Con International.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APView image in fullscreenFrom left to right, Letitia Wright, Winston Duke, Ryan Coogler, David Jonsson and Kevin Feige on stage at Marvel Studios’ Comic-Con International.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APBlack PantherIndustry star David Jonsson to play Black Panther in Marvel sequelDirector Ryan Coogler announces British actor in lead role alongside co-stars Letitia Wright and Winston DukeNadeem Badshahand agenciesSun 26 Jul 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British actorDavid Jonssonhas been unveiled as the new Black Panther by the film’s director, Ryan Coogler.Jonsson, 32, known for roles in Industry, The Long Walk and Alien: Romulus, will play the son of Chadwick Boseman’s T’Challa in the thirdBlack Panthermovie.He joined Coogler on stage atMarvelStudios’ Comic-Con International presentation to announce the news on Saturday, alongside co-stars Letitia Wright and Winston Duke.Coogler, who won the Oscar for best original screenplay for his vampire film Sinners earlier this year, said: “The last time we got to make a movie, we introduced a character who is the son of the character that the great Chadwick Boseman played – our T’Challa – in that film.“And today, I want to tell you that in this next film, he grows up, he comes of age.”Born in London, Jonsson began his career in the West End. He made his screen debut in 2018 in two episodes of the British detective drama Endeavour before being cast as Augustus “Gus” Sackey in the first two series of Industry from 2020 to 2022.He appeared in the 2025 adaptation of Stephen King’s thriller The Long Walk and in the same year won the Bafta rising star award.Jonsson, who also has roles in the upcoming films The Chaperones, Benn/Eubank and Scandalous, said: “Thank you to this family that I have the honour and the blessing to join. I don’t want to say too much, because I want to let the screen do the talking.”Black Panther III will be released in US cinemas on 15 December 2028. A UK release date yet to be confirmed.Boseman died in 2020 aged 43, four years after being diagnosed with colon cancer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBlack Panther: Wakanda Forever, released in 2022, revealed that Boseman’s character, T’Challa, had a son. It followed Wright’s character, Shuri, as she takes on the role of the protagonist after the death of T’Challa.The first film, released in 2018, was set in the mythical country of Wakanda, a hidden African kingdom with innovative technology thanks to its reserves of the world’s most useful precious metal. It won three Oscars.Coogler, who directed the first two Black Panther movies, also co-produced the 2025 series Ironheart and Eyes of Wakanda.Explore more on these topicsBlack PantherDavid JonssonRyan CooglerMarvelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pentagon reports more than 600 Iran war casualties in quiet database update | US news | The Guardian
description: Figures are source of dispute as US defense department days ago reduced record of troops killed and wounded
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Figures are source of dispute as US defense department days ago reduced record of troops killed and wounded
Content: Donald Trump and others salute as a US army carry team moves a transfer case containing the remains of 1st Lt Tyler James Feehan, on 22 July at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and others salute as a US army carry team moves a transfer case containing the remains of 1st Lt Tyler James Feehan, on 22 July at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APUS newsPentagon reports more than 600 Iran war casualties in quiet database updateFigures are source of dispute as US defense department days ago reduced record of troops killed and woundedMarina DunbarSun 26 Jul 2026 18.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Pentagon updated its official war casualty database over the weekend, adding more than 140 wounded service members. The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) also introduced a new casualtycategorylabeled “Overseas Operations” for personnel killed and wounded “starting July 7”.According to the updateddatabase, the official toll for the earlier phase of theUS-Iran war, known as Operation Epic Fury, now stands at 14 service members killed and more than 400 wounded in action.These figures have been the point of contention after the Pentagonpreviously reducedthe totals from 18 deaths and 482 wounded that had been recorded just days earlier.Pentagon list of service members killed in Iran war removes most recent fourRead moreThe dispute comes after the collapse of the ceasefire with Iran and the resumption of near-daily airstrikes beginning on 6 July. Analysts and officials have questioned whether casualties from the renewed fighting should be counted separately from Operation Epic Fury, a move that would be unprecedented.TheTrump administrationis seeking to classify the renewed military campaign as separate from Operation Epic Fury, the US military’s official name for the Iran conflict.The change is tied to the War Powers Act of 1973, which requires the president to end military operations within 60 daysunless Congress authorizes an extension. The Trump administration has argued that the April ceasefire with Iran paused the clock on 1 May for the conflict’s initial period. The separate casualty count beginning on 7 July follows that interpretation.The shift became apparent earlier this week when the Pentagon’s official online list of service members killed in the ongoing Iran wardid not includethe four soldiers who died during renewed fighting over the weekend. Their names, however, were included in a Pentagon press release announcing the formal transfer of their remains back to the US on Wednesday.View image in fullscreenReporters raise their hands to ask questions during a briefing on the Iran war with Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon in Washington DC on 16 April.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersCombined with the updated Operation Epic Fury totals, the new Pentagon figures show that 18 US troops have been killed and 624 wounded since the USlaunchedits war against Iran on 28 February.Lawmakers from both partieshave challengedthe administration’s interpretation of the War Powers Act timeline.Thomas Massie, a Republican House member from Kentucky, responded to the updated numbers inan X post, writing: “Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire.“The reality: By going more than 90 days without congressional authorization,” the defense secretary,Pete Hegseth, “IS BREAKING THE LAW and must be held accountable”.Explore more on these topicsUS newsTrump administrationUS militaryUS-Israel war on IranPete HegsethUS politicsUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Not standard’ for Taylor Farms to ask White House to delay cyclospora recall, ex-FDA head says  | US news | The Guardian
description: Scott Gottlieb responds to report that company contacted the White House seeking to delay a recall announcement
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Scott Gottlieb responds to report that company contacted the White House seeking to delay a recall announcement
Content: Taylor Farms products are displayed for sale at a grocery store in Washington DC on 24 July.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreenTaylor Farms products are displayed for sale at a grocery store in Washington DC on 24 July.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersUS news‘Not standard’ for Taylor Farms to ask White House to delay cyclospora recall, ex-FDA head saysScott Gottlieb responds to report that company contacted the White House seeking to delay a recall announcementMarina DunbarSun 26 Jul 2026 16.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 16.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer Food and Drug Administration commissioner Dr Scott Gottlieb said on Sunday that it was “not standard operating procedure” for Taylor Farms to ask the White House to intervene as the company prepared to announce a recall tied to a massive cyclospora outbreak.Appearing on CBS’s Face the Nation, Gottlieb was asked about areportfrom the Wall Street Journal that Taylor Farms contacted the White House seeking to delay a recall announcement while federal investigators were preparing to publicly link the company to the multi-state outbreak.US cyclosporiasis outbreak expands to nine states as CDC investigates 7,400 casesRead more“It was not standard operating procedure,” Gottlieb said. “And it wasn’t standard operating procedure when I was at FDA.”“I dealt with outbreaks in romaine lettuce and spinach as well, E coli in spinach and romaine lettuce. I never heard from the White House on those things, other than to have discussions to inform them of what we were doing, so that they were properly briefed and could respond to questions that they were getting,” Gottlieb said. “So it’s unusual.”According to the Journal, representatives for Taylor Farms contacted the White House requesting more time before the government publicly linked the company to the outbreak. The report said the White House asked FDA officials to join the call, during which Taylor Farms argued that federal investigators lacked positive laboratory evidence connecting its products to the outbreak and expressed concerns that the government was overstating the company’s responsibility.The company sought the meeting after executives believed they had not received sufficient clarity from the FDA about the evidence supporting a potential recall and its scope, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by the Journal.The recall associated with the cyclospora outbreak has been fraught withconfusing messaging. The iceberg lettuce was initiallylinked to a single supplier, Taylor Farms de Mexico, which issued a voluntary recall.However, the FDA issued an update last week: lettuce that was not part of the recall had tested positive for cyclospora. But a day later, the FDA deleted that line and said the test was a false positive. The recall still existed, the FDA insisted, despite an enigmatic statement from the supplier.“Today, FDA apologized to us,” astatementon the Taylor Farms website read, despite no public information about an apology. The farm added that “at this moment, FDA has not identified a single positive product test result for Cyclospora.” A day after that, Taylor Farms clarified that the recall was still in effect and that they were no longer sourcing iceberg lettuce from central Mexico for this growing season.Federal health officials have spent weeks on oscillating responses to the cyclospora outbreak, which has sickened thousands and can cause severe gastrointestinal illness, while officials and experts have questioned both the administration’s handling of the investigation and Taylor Farms’s response.Explore more on these topicsUS newsTrump administrationFood safetyHealthUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump ‘border czar’ says ICE officer in Maine killing should not have cleared vetting | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Tom Homan comments on officer’s eligibility to serve after reports that agent’s two ex-wives had accused him of abuse
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Tom Homan comments on officer’s eligibility to serve after reports that agent’s two ex-wives had accused him of abuse
Content: White House ‘border czar’ Tom Homan speaks with reporters outside the White House, on 20 July 2026.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreenWhite House ‘border czar’ Tom Homan speaks with reporters outside the White House, on 20 July 2026.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump ‘border czar’ says ICE officer in Maine killing should not have cleared vettingTom Homan comments on officer’s eligibility to serve after reports that agent’s two ex-wives had accused him of abuseMaya YangSun 26 Jul 2026 14.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Homan, the Trump administration “border czar”, on Sunday said he did not believe the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer at the center of a recent fatal shooting in Maine “should have ever cleared vetting”.Speaking to CNN’s State of the Union, Homan was asked by host Dana Bash about the officer’s eligibility to serve followingreportsthat two of his ex-wives hadaccusedhim of abuse.“Should someone with those issues be an ICE agent?” Bash asked.“No, if those … are facts … I don’t think he should ever have cleared vetting,” Homan replied.Homan also said part of an ongoing investigation into the 13 July shooting deathJoan Sebastián Durán Guerrerois determining “how … did the vetting process fail”.“When they hire somebody, they put them through a vetting process and look at all that stuff. So I know, based on that information – that’s part of the ongoing investigation,” Homan said. “How … did the vetting process fail? Was that information not available? Did they not know?”He added: “So there’s a separate administrative investigation on what happened here. Did we have that information? Did we not have that information? But the vetting process … if that was factual, he would have an almost impossible time to pass vetting.”The officer involved in the killing of Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian man in Biddeford,Maine, has since been identified by news outlets as David Brouillette. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, has not publicly confirmed Brouillette’s identity.Since the shooting, two of Brouillette’s ex-wives have publicly described alleged abuse during their relationships with him. One, Lucinda Brouillette,allegedher ex-husband engaged in a “persistent pattern of abuse, intimidation, manipulation, fear and control”.“If you were to ask me whether I believe David Brouillette is capable of this level of violence, my answer is unequivocally yes,” she said in a statement to NPR.Although Homan declined to comment directly on this particular case, describing it as “a rare instance”, he said: “If this person had that type of history, it would have been a vetting issue, and it should have been brought to the attention of those who make those decisions.”He added, in part: “We will see. It’s all being reviewed. We will see where it lies.”The shooting has prompted renewed scrutiny of ICE’s hiring practices.Democrats have called for reviews of the agency’s vetting process. For instance, Mississippi congressman Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the US House homeland security committee,saidthat Brouillette’s alleged abusive past “directly call[s] into question the supposed vetting and training ICE does of its recruits”.Neither the fatal shooting in Maine noranother oneinvolving an ICE officer in Texas earlier in July yielded body camera footage from officers. That prompted Homan toannouncethat the agency would require officers to wear body cameras during vehicle stops.In the Texas case, which resulted in the killing of Mexican nationalLorenzo Salgado Araujo, the Harris county district attorney Sean Tearesaidin a statement that lab results of a white substance found in a van at the center of a case tested negative for narcotics or illicit drugs – despite an FBI search warrant application that maintained a bag with substance in question was consistent with methamphetamine.Salgado’s family had said the substance was a salt mixture that he and his construction crew colleagues used as electrolytes to stay hydrated in extremely hot temperatures.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationUS immigrationMaineUS politicsTexasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Katy Perry ‘deeply appalled’ over White House using her song in Iran war video | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Singer rebukes Trump administration after it uses her song Firework over footage of missile striking Iranian naval ship
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Singer rebukes Trump administration after it uses her song Firework over footage of missile striking Iranian naval ship
Content: Katy Perry performs during the 49th edition of the Paleo Festival in Nyon, Switzerland, on Saturday.Photograph: Salvatore Di Nolfi/EPAView image in fullscreenKaty Perry performs during the 49th edition of the Paleo Festival in Nyon, Switzerland, on Saturday.Photograph: Salvatore Di Nolfi/EPATrump administrationKaty Perry ‘deeply appalled’ over White House using her song in Iran war videoSinger rebukes Trump administration after it uses her song Firework over footage of missile striking Iranian naval shipMarina DunbarSun 26 Jul 2026 13.19 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePop starKaty Perryhas condemned the Trump White House after it used her hit song Firework in a TikTok video showing US military strikes on Iranian targets, saying she never approved the use of her music.The White Housevideo, which featured Firework playing over footage of a missile striking an Iranian naval ship, has amassed more than 6 million views. The post was captioned: “Iran has been warned.”Perry responded on Saturday with astatement on Xcriticizing what she called the unauthorized use of the song.“I am deeply appalled and angry to see ‘Firework’ used on the White House TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes,” the singer said. “I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it.”Perry continued: “I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments. To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponized to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for. My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare.”The White House launched its TikTok account in August 2025, when Donald Trump threatened to ban the platform months into his second presidency.Perry is among a number of artists to criticize the Trump administration over the unauthorized use of music in government social media posts, with the presidentpicking fightswith several – mostly female – pop singers.Olivia Rodrigo previouslycriticizedthe administration after one of her songs appeared in a government video promoting deportation efforts.Beyoncé alsoblockedTrump from using her song Freedom after it was featured in a campaign video on social media. The track had served as the central campaign song for former vice-president Kamala Harris, who lost the 2024 White House election to Trump.In March, Keshacondemnedthe White House’s use of her song Blow in a military-promotional TikTok video, calling it a “show of blatant disregard for human life”.Sabrina Carpenterspoke outafter her hit song Juno was used in a Trump-posted video showing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers making arrests. Carpenter called the video “evil and disgusting” and told the administration: “Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.”In June, Ariana Grande alsorebukedthe White House for using her song Bye in a social media post promoting US immigration arrests, describing the video as “barbaric”.Singer Jess Glynne alsoobjectedafter the White House used her song Hold My Hand in a post on X promoting ICE deportations. Glynne said she felt “sick” that her music was being used to spread “division and hate”.It wasrevealedin December that Perry is in a relationship with former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, who is familiar himself with Trump’s trolling. He has repeatedly been targeted by Trump, who has continuously threatened to impose tariffs on Canada and has even suggested theUS should annexthe country, referring to Trudeau as the “governor” of the “Great State of Canada”.The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) lists the official death toll for the US-Iran conflict at 14 service members, with 420 total personnel wounded in action.Those official metrics, however, have been subject toongoing controversydue to a sudden drop from the 18 deaths and 482 wounded recorded days earlier.The collapse of the ceasefire with Iran and the subsequent resumption of near-daily airstrikes starting on 6 July have sparked debate over how casualties are counted. Analysts and officials have questioned whether victims from the two weeks since should be tracked in a separate tally, a move that would be unprecedented.The Trump administration is attempting to have the latest resumed strikes in Iran be treated as a separate campaign from Operation Epic Fury, the US military’s official name for the Iran conflict. Theseparate casualty countbeginning 7 July stems from that.The US House member Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, responded to the updated numbers inan X post, writing, “Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire.“The reality: By going more than 90 days without congressional authorization,” the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, “IS BREAKING THE LAW and must be held accountable”.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationKaty PerryUS-Israel war on IranUS militaryUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tadej Pogacar tells rivals he is ‘improving a lot’ after fifth Tour de France win | Tour de France 2026 | The Guardian
description: Tadej Pogacar also hinted he is contemplating retirement while the runner-up, Remco Evenepoel, said he proved his critics wrong
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Tadej Pogacar also hinted he is contemplating retirement while the runner-up, Remco Evenepoel, said he proved his critics wrong
Content: Tadej Pogacar celebrates his fifth Tour de France victory.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar celebrates his fifth Tour de France victory.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersTour de France 2026Tadej Pogacar tells rivals he is ‘improving a lot’ after fifth Tour de France winPogacar also hints he is contemplating retirementRunner-up Evenepoel says he proved critics wrongJeremy Whittlein ParisSun 26 Jul 2026 15.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar joined the small club of five-timeTour de Francechampions in a final stage in Paris that was neutralised by concerns over safety due to the threat of rain on the cobbles of the Butte de Montmartre.Pogacar’s dominant success, his fifth win in seven years, left Remco Evenepoel of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe and the Slovene’s UAE Emirates XRG teammate Isaac del Toro as the only others to finish within 10 minutes of his winning time.Relentless Tadej Pogacar wins fifth Tour de France to equal recordRead morePogacar’s achievements now rank with those of Eddy Merckx, another of the five-time winners and widely accepted as cycling’s greatest champion. The 27-year-old’s record-equalling fifth win was celebrated in a specially designed all-yellow kit, featuring the number five.“You get more experience, you deal with things differently, there are small things that are improving,” Pogacar said, “but it’s the details that sometimes count, the mood and emotions. I think this is where I am improving a lot.”He paid tribute to the efforts of his teammates, several of whom spent the second half of the Tour fighting off sickness. “Massive respect for what all of the guys have been doing over the last three weeks. I already appreciated the work of my teammates but now it’s another level and I must say thank you to every single one of them.”Pogacar hinted that he was again contemplating retirement. “I will definitely not be doing this for a long time,” he said, suggesting that his teammate Del Toro was his natural successor. “He’s still young, he’s a quick learner, super smart and has a big talent and big engine so let’s see where the road takes us. I’m happy to be with him in the team and that we can ride like this together.”Evenepoel, the Olympic road and time trial champion, who had faced a lot of scepticism over his ability to challenge Pogacar, said he had come to the Tour to “make the podium”. The runner-up added: “I’m happiest with the performances I delivered over the last two weeks. I knew I wanted to step up, starting from the Vosges stage. I don’t think I had any weak moments from that point on. Overall, I’m very happy with my Tour.“I’m proving once again that all the comments and criticisms were wrong. I finished third two years ago. I finished second this year. I won the Vuelta. I think that’s not too bad for someone who supposedly isn’t a Grand Tour rider.”View image in fullscreenRemco Evenepoel (left), Tadej Pogacar and Isaac del Toro celebrate on the Champs-Élysées.Photograph: Bernard Papon/EPADel Toro, who won the best young rider classification, ahead of Paul Seixas, paid tribute to his team leader. “There was sickness in the team,” the Mexican said. “I tried to prevent people from noticing I was weaker, saying I was OK, but it wasn’t true. My teammates took care of me. I don’t know why they supported me this much. Tadej has shown how good a friend he is. I can’t feel more privileged than I feel today.“It’s beautiful to carry this white jersey to Paris. We were here to fight to try and win it, and I’m super happy I have been able to perform at the level they wanted me to be at. From now on, I just want to enjoy the moment. The suffering is past me.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France 2026Tour de FranceCyclingTadej PogacarnewsShareReuse this content

Content: Jackson Koivun played the final two rounds of the tournament without carding a bogey.Photograph: Bailey Hillesheim/APView image in fullscreenJackson Koivun played the final two rounds of the tournament without carding a bogey.Photograph: Bailey Hillesheim/APGolfJackson Koivun holds off Scheffler to win 3M Open in third professional startUS golfer, 21, finished at 25-under par for three-shot winScheffler closed with 63 to finish second in MinnesotaField Level Media ReutersSun 26 Jul 2026 18.22 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 18.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rookie Jackson Koivun shot a five-under-par 66 to stave off a chargingScottie Schefflerand win ⁠on the PGA Tour for the first time at the 3M Open on Sunday at Blaine, ⁠Minnesota.Koivun, 21, finished ⁠at ​25 under par for a three-shot victory over Scheffler, who closed with a 63 at TPC Twin ⁠Cities.
