title: ‘Pretty bad’: Lewis Hamilton hits out at Ferrari after dropping points in F1 title race | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton has questioned Ferrari’s strategy after he was fifth at the Hungarian GP, losing a place after a five-second penalty for pit-lane speeding
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton has questioned Ferrari’s strategy after he was fifth at the Hungarian GP, losing a place after a five-second penalty for pit-lane speeding
Content: Lewis Hamilton said he ‘definitely should not have taken the [pit] stop’ that cost him points at the Hungarian Grand Prix.Photograph: David Davies/PAView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton said he ‘definitely should not have taken the [pit] stop’ that cost him points at the Hungarian Grand Prix.Photograph: David Davies/PAFormula One 2026‘Pretty bad’: Lewis Hamilton hits out at Ferrari after dropping points in F1 title raceHamilton questions strategy after finishing fifthBriton lost place after penalty for speeding in pit laneGiles Richardsat the HungaroringSun 26 Jul 2026 15.51 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton expressed frustration with his Ferrari team after he dropped points in the title battle against Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli at the Hungarian Grand Prix, while Lando Norris returned to form with the defending world champion claiming hisfirst race victory of the season.Lando Norris wins F1 Hungarian GP for first victory of season as Piastri retiresRead moreHamilton finished in fourth place on the track at the Hungaroring but, with a five-second penalty imposed for speeding in the pit lane, he was classified as fifth in the race won by McLaren’s Norris, with Max Verstappen second for Red Bull and Antonelli third.Hamilton had been called into the pits late on for a stop under the virtual safety car, which gave him fresh tyres but cost him track position to Verstappen and Antonelli. He could not make the places back and this was the stop from which he received the penalty. The call left him questioning the strategy decisions by his team.“It was pretty bad. Pretty frustrating,” he said. “I definitely don’t think we should have taken the stop but the call came literally just before the pit-lane entry and I didn’t have time to debate.“I would never have stopped if it meant I was giving up track position. I may have been able to hold on to P2. He [Verstappen] was catching me but most likely it would have been P3 [in front of Antonelli] and it would have been much better. Instead, I lost a bunch of points.”Quick GuideF1 Hungarian GP resultsShow1Lando Norris🇬🇧McLaren1:39:56.180 –25pts2Max Verstappen🇳🇱Red Bull+15.080 –18pts3Kimi Antonelli🇮🇹Mercedes+18.728 –15pts4Charles Leclerc🇲🇨Ferrari+23.840 –12pts5Lewis Hamilton🇬🇧Ferrari+24.540 –10pts6Isack Hadjar🇫🇷Red Bull+55.488 –8pts7George Russell🇬🇧Mercedes+57.503 –6pts8Liam Lawson🇳🇿Racing Bulls+1 lap –4pts9Nico Hülkenberg🇩🇪Audi+1 lap –2pts10Arvid Lindblad🇬🇧Racing Bulls+1 lap–1pt11Gabriel Bortoleto🇧🇷Audi+1 lap12Pierre Gasly🇫🇷Alpine+1 lap13Lance Stroll🇨🇦Aston Martin+1 lap14Fernando Alonso🇪🇸Aston Martin+1 lap15Franco Colapinto🇦🇷Alpine+2 laps16Esteban Ocon🇫🇷Haas+2 laps17Alexander Albon🇹🇭Williams+2 laps18Carlos Sainz🇪🇸Williams+2 laps19Oliver Bearman🇬🇧Haas+2 lapsNCOscar Piastri🇦🇺McLarenDNFNCSergio Pérez🇲🇽CadillacDNFNCValtteri Bottas🇫🇮CadillacDNFWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Hamilton had been 45 points behind Antonelli but now trails the Italian by 50 points asFormula Oneenters its summer break. The Briton has also been on the receiving end of a swathe of penalties in recent races, including one at Silverstone, one at Spa, a three-place grid drop in Hungary for impeding in qualifying and then pit-lane speeding during the race. He feels that the annual shutdown has come at the right moment.“I’ll work hard to try and come back, reset,” Hamilton said. “There’s still a lot of places to take. I’m going to try and make sure I don’t give them any reason to give any penalties moving forwards.“It has been an amazing first half given I think we’ve been probably three or four-tenths down on the straights in pace and power for the first half of the season. We’ve got a bit more to come in the second half and we keep on pushing. The second half will be stronger, usually the second half is a stronger period for me. So I’ll really take this time to reset and try and come back stronger, fitter and better mentally prepared.”Norris, who took his and McLaren’s first win of the year, believes that he is driving at his very best, better even than when he won the title last season, despite being outpaced by what has been a dominant Mercedes over the opening 11 meetings.“Today I would probably say it was up there with one of my best performances, in terms of extracting performance out of the car and being so close to the limit every single lap,” he said. “So close that the team had to ask me to peg it back a little bit.View image in fullscreenLando Norris celebrates with the McLaren team after his Hungarian Grand Prix success.Photograph: David Davies/PA“So although it kind of hurts me saying it because it doesn’t mean that you just win, I feel I’m doing a better job this year than I was last year, and I have done for a little while.”The British driver is 91 points behind Antonelli in the championship with 12 races to come. It is a huge mountain to climb but, like Hamilton, Norris said there is still much to play for in the second half of the season, especially after the significant upgrades McLaren brought to Hungary had proved so effective, even if driving the current F1 cars is still not to his and many drivers’ taste.“What pleases me the most? The fact we were so quick, the fact the car was very strong today,” he said. “I was just very happy with a lot of things. I mean, the car was still horrible to drive at times but quick and I’d rather have a horrible but quick car than anything else.“I was convinced I could win the race today and we did. We were just on another level and I felt in a very good flow of things. When the car’s good and when I’m in a good flow, there’s no stopping.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportLewis HamiltonFerrariLando NorrisMcLarennewsShareReuse this content

title: Tim Tszyu wins a battle of broken soldiers, and Errol Spence Jr heads into the sunset | Boxing | The Guardian
description: In Sunday’s bout, two boxers past their primes were fighting for the win, yes, but moreso for the chance to break themselves anew
Author: Owen Lewis
Headline: In Sunday’s bout, two boxers past their primes were fighting for the win, yes, but moreso for the chance to break themselves anew
Content: Tim Tszyu made good on his pre-fight promise to take it to Errol Spence Jr in their Sunday bout in Sydney.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/EPAView image in fullscreenTim Tszyu made good on his pre-fight promise to take it to Errol Spence Jr in their Sunday bout in Sydney.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/EPABoxingTim Tszyu wins a battle of broken soldiers, and Errol Spence Jr heads into the sunsetIn Sunday’s bout, two boxers past their primes were fighting for the win, yes, but moreso for the chance to break themselves anewOwen LewisSun 26 Jul 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 09.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmatchup between post-prime boxers has endless narrative potential, often disguising the ickiness of an already-shot fighter taking a beating. Robbed of their most explosive physical attributes, they try to compensate with wisdom and capacity for suffering. With legs dulled, they’re forced into harsh exchanges they were too defensively sound to allow in their primes. Fans get to enjoy the last gasps of greatness from their favorite fighters, and sportswriters get an excuse to describe them as “weathered veterans”. Afterwards, maybe one or both of them walks into the sunset.Tim Tszyu eyes world title tilt after beating Errol Spence Jr in 12-round epicRead moreErrol Spence, one of the best boxers of his generation, claimed he’ll do just that afterlosing a unanimous decisionto Tim Tszyu on Sunday in Sydney. After winning the first 28 fights of his career and contributing to ear-splitting hype for a purportedly 50-50 welterweight fight with Terence Crawford, Spence absorbeda surgical, brutal beating from Crawfordthat showed the two were never really on the same level. As Crawford went on to win a title at junior middleweight and astonishingly defeat the legendary Saul “Canelo” Alvarez at super middleweight, Spence took three years off before returning to face Tszyu at age 36. Believe that he’s really retired at your peril; if the annihilation he suffered at Crawford’s hands wasn’t enough to deter him from boxing again, his initially competitive, eventually one-sided, relatively untraumatic loss to Tszyu may not move the needle either.Tszyu is one of a few men who might know how Spence felt after that Crawford fight. In 2024, a then-unbeaten Tszyu fought late replacement Sebastian Fundora for the chance to become a unified junior middleweight champion. Tszyu looked sharp and mean and broke Fundora’s nose inside two rounds. In a stroke of freak misfortune, he then sliced his forehead open on the end of one of Fundora’s angular elbows. Tszyu fought the remaining 10 rounds with a flowing sheet of blood often impairing his vision or blinding him entirely, and lost the fight.Next, Tszyu fought unheralded destroyer Bakhram Murtazaliev with such blind aggression he walked into a beating every bit as concussive as the one Crawford handed Spence, condensed into three rounds instead of nine. After a tune-up, Tszyu took a rematch with an improved Fundora and took another violent loss. Tszyu recently changed his nickname from “the Soul Taker” to “the Phoenix”, surely among the most obvious rebrands in history. He’d left no shortage of ashes to rise from. This fight was billed asUSA v AUS, sold alongside a barren undercard for an appalling $79.99 on DAZN and Prime Video, but was most magnetic as a battle of broken soldiers.Each man had his moments in the first five rounds, but the opening act evoked more of a vacance than a feeling. In his prime, Spence had boundless energy. He’d keep his jab pumping constantly in the opponent’s face, and when they had to pause their counterfire he’d step in with a big overhand left. Eventually, his opponents broke down under the steady onslaught. No one punch would do as much damage as hispresence.In Sydney, that pressure was gone. Spence mostly fought in retreat, cannily sneaking in straight lefts and body shots. Commentators Paulie Malignaggi and Shawn Porter – another former Spence opponent, who, like Crawford, arrived at retirement before Spence – identified Spence’s iffy balance seconds into the fight. He regularly overbalanced over his front foot, leaving his chin hanging in an ocean of space. It was too easy to picture Crawford hammering it with a precise, punishing counterpunch.Luckily for Spence, Tszyu was mostly too stiff and slow to emulate Crawford. His calling card in his prime was his bloodlust, strong enough to quiet any fear of bleeding himself. He once hit Brian Mendoza with three successive uppercuts so animalistic it’s a wonder Mendoza didn’t run out of the ring in fear. But that version of Tszyu was gone, too. He stalked Spence, throwing isolated right hands that caught and jolted Spence but little else. After five rounds, Spence began to fade. He committed more of his energy to moving than throwing his own, made more difficult by Tszyu beginning to dig vicious shots into his stomach.View image in fullscreenTim Tszyu strikes Errol Spence Jr during their bout.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPBuoyed up by a pep talk from coach and former boxer Jeff Fenech, Tszyu dominated a larger and larger share of the rounds. In the 12th, he hit Spence with a punch so forceful that the American caromed off the ropes and almost back to the center of the ring. But Tszyu didn’t seem especially interested in pressing his advantage. He had a safe lead, but it was hard not to see the ghosts of Murtazaliev.Spence looked so weary in the corner before the final round that he was recognizable even to somebody who will never throw a punch in their life as a man who wanted this night to be over. I thought of a moment from the end of an interview Spence did with Andre Ward last month. Ward asked Spence why he was still fighting.“Uh,” Spence said, scratching his head. “Let me see.” He didn’t pause for long, and eventually gave an answer, but even his momentary uncertainty felt telling. Tszyu fighting after Murtazaliev and Spence fighting after Crawford is illustrative of the dependent relationship many boxers have with this fatal sport; not being fully committed in that relationship only invites disaster.During fight week, Tszyu declared, “I’m coming for every limb … especially that retina,” referring to Spence injuring his eye in 2021. The comment irked Spence into not shaking hands with Tszyu before the fight. Afterwards, they shook hands, hugged, and posed for a picture together. There wasn’twarmth, exactly – Tszyu was blustery in his postfight interview, and didn’t show anything that figured to impress the once great Spence – but maybe some mutual understanding. What these broken soldiers were fighting for wasn’t so much the merits of a win over the other but the opportunity to break themselves anew against a superior opponent. If only both of them could have lost.Explore more on these topicsBoxingErrol SpencefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How the death of Jayden Adams shook a community: ‘Being on the pitch was his happy place’ | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Those who knew Jayden Adams, who died aged 25 not long after playing at the World Cup, describe a humble and hard-working man who cared about friends and family
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Those who knew Jayden Adams, who died aged 25 not long after playing at the World Cup, describe a humble and hard-working man who cared about friends and family
Content: A photograph of Jayden Adams, with messages from his teammates, on display during his memorial service in Stellenbosch.Photograph: Rodger Bosch/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA photograph of Jayden Adams, with messages from his teammates, on display during his memorial service in Stellenbosch.Photograph: Rodger Bosch/AFP/Getty ImagesSoccerHow the death of Jayden Adams shook a community: ‘Being on the pitch was his happy place’Those who knew the South African, who died aged 25 not long after playing at the World Cup, describe a humble and hard-working man who cared about friends and familyFirdose Moonda in Cape TownSun 26 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor Jayden Adams,the South Africa midfielder who died this month at the age of 25, football was a “safe space”. Those words, used by Adams’s junior coach Steve Barker at his memorial service 10 days ago, tell you everything you need to know about his life beyond the pitch.Adams’s battles were bestowed on him almost from birth. Though he was born into newly democratic South Africa, by the early 2000s the revolution was well on its way to being betrayed. The vote was extended to all, but few could make full use of the freedoms available to them because socioeconomic circumstances in the country had barely changed. Stellenbosch, where the Adams family were based, is a perfect example.South Africa World Cup midfielder Jayden Adams dies aged 25Read moreIts facade is a tourist dream: a university town nestled among vineyards, Cape Dutch architecture and indie boutiques. Most visitors never venture beyond the town centre or into its suburbs, which are home to the far less privileged and are havens of neglect. Those areas are classic apartheid hangovers, where the wealth has been preserved for a historically advantaged elite and those on the margins, working-class communities of people of colour, are all but invisible.Ironically, that is how Adams is most often described. He moved in the shadows, both of society and the sport in which he excelled. “Jayden was a guy of very few words. He was quiet, very shy and the smallest among his teammates,” Brendine Johnson, an Adams family spokesperson, says. “Initially, a lot of people missed his football qualities because of his size, but he had a very good fighting spirit. It just wasn’t always on display.”Adams loved the game dearly and his aunt Monica Thaoge recalled how, as a child, he would kick anything round – “even onions” she said at his memorial. His parents, Juanito and Candice, previously mentioned potatoes as their son’s football of choice. Nobody in the family talks about lacking in financial means because theirs was a community striving to make life better. But there were absences, especially early on.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Mamelodi Sundowns football club carry Jayden Adams’ coffin at the funeral service for the player on Saturday.Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters“Everybody in areas like that is just trying to make ends meet,” says Roger Telemachus, the former South Africa cricketer who grew up on the same street as Adams’s father in Cloetesville. “For the kids, they may not have noticed so much because they were occupied, mostly with playing sport. Some fathers, like Juanito, really encouraged their kids and everyone used to play everything on the street: tennis, football, rugby, cricket. It was also the best way of staying out of trouble.”Problems were there for everyone to see and, according to Telemachus, have got worse “in the last 20 years”. They include gangsterism, substance abuse and crimes that range from petty to serious. Adams was able to escape from that life when he moved to the slightly more affluent area of Ida’s Valley, but still he did not have a life of luxury. For a period, the family of six, which included four children, lived in a two-bedroom place. At other times, they were with his maternal grandmother, Marianna. “He basically grew up in her yard,” says Johnson.Things started to change for Adams when he was picked for the Stellenbosch Academy Under-18 side at the age of 15. “The environment was tough, especially if you are not big or tall enough, but when physicality was no longer the most important thing, people saw that Jayden was technically very good,” says Johnson.His coaches agree. Barker, the nephew of South Africa’s Afcon winning coach, Clive, and the current coach of Simba in Tanzania, gave an emotional assessment of Adams’s skills shortly after his death. “You get many good footballers but you get few great footballers. Jayden was great,” he told Newzroom Afrika.“Jayden had three attributes that set him apart: an incredible first touch, his weight of pass – I’ve never seen anything like it – and he loved the game so much. Being on the pitch was his happy place. He didn’t pass the ball, he used to caress the ball. He was special and his football intelligence was just outstanding.”View image in fullscreenJayden Adams played in South Africa’s World Cup group game against Czechia despite the death of his grandmother the day before.Photograph: Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesIt was under Barker that Adams blossomed. He became the first player from the Stellenbosch Academy to play in South Africa’s top flight, the Premier Soccer League. Five years and an international call up later, the country’s richest club, Mamelodi Sundowns, came calling. This year, at the start of his second season with them, Adams shaved his head, in what he joked was a sign of maturity and called himself a “grootman” (big man). The nickname stuck.Adams never said it, but he may also have realised how much he had grown up. By then, he had been picked, played for and dropped from the national side after arriving late at a training camp and irking the head coach, Hugo Broos. He had also lost two of his academy teammates, including a close friend.In February 2023, Oshwin Andries, who was 19, died from stabbing injuries he sustained in Paarl, which is 16km north of Stellenbosch. Three years later, Jeandre Gaffoor, 20, drowned in the Krom River.When Sundowns won the CAF Champions League in May, Adams dedicated his medal to Andries. To lose so much has weighed on the town, but through Adams they have had reason to celebrate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMembers of Adams’s family, including his father, Juanito (centre left), and mother, Candice (centre right), at his memorial service last week.Photograph: Rodger Bosch/AFP/Getty ImagesHis role in Sundowns’ continental victory and a call-up to the World Cup squad suggested Adams’s career trajectory was rising. After a first season at Sundowns when he was often playing off the bench and his place in the side was questioned, he had become integral to the team. At Adams’s memorial, the Sundowns senior coach, Steve Komphela, called him “the heart of our team and the heartbeat of our playing style” who “understood the game like a coach and played it as a player”.In the past year, Adams was playing to the potential people who knew him well had seen years ago and surprising others with his courage and drive to succeed. South Africa’s captain, Ronwen Williams, recalled an incident at this year’s Africa Cup of Nations when the tiny Adams took on a tall Mali opponent with some choice local words. Williams asked Adams if he knew the size of the player he was sledging, but Adams shrugged it off and replied that the Malian wouldn’t understand anyway.“That was the character he had,” Williams said at the memorial, smiling through his tears as he bade farewell to the teammate he called “my ma se kind” (my mother’s child, a term of endearment used in South Africa).As his star rose, Adams was careful not to advertise his achievements. “Jayden knew what he had, but he never wanted to voice it. He was very competitive, but he would never brag,” says Johnson. “You get people who are very good verbally on social media. Jayden was not like that. And he wanted to give back. After every game, he would be giving away shirts and boots to kids who asked.”He also concentrated on providing for his family because he “always promised them he would change their financial situation”.View image in fullscreenJayden Adams signs a South Africa shirt for a young Mexican fan who arrived at the team’s World Cup hotel. ‘He wanted to give back.’Photograph: SAFAAt the World Cup, Adams played for them, even through immense pain. His grandmother Marianna died the day beforeSouth Africa’s match against Czechiaand Adams opted to remain with the squad. He played that match and appeared in good spirits afterwards and called the 1-1 draw positive, even if he was feeling the opposite way.He also playedthe next game against South Korea, which South Africa won to reach the knockouts for the first time. Post-game footage showed him sitting on his own while the rest of the squad celebrated with a signature song and dance.At the memorial, Komphela offered the Adams family a Bible verse as a comfort, but it may as well be a summary. Psalm 23:4: “Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.”They will know Adams took that walk many times over his short life and he did not fear. He leaves behind his parents, three siblings, a partner, two children and a community who have gone through what no neighbourhood should. In all that, he has gone from not wanting to be known, to entering the footballing world’s spotlight. A minute’s silence was observed at several World Cup games in Adams’s memory. That is not the way his family would have pictured him coming to global attention, but it has shown them that, in football, he was always far more valued than anyone thought.“I don’t think the community knew how big he was and how people enjoyed his football,” says Johnson. “It’s a huge shock.”Explore more on these topicsFootballSouth Africa football teamWorld CupSouth AfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Inter enter talks with Tottenham over signing captain Cristian Romero | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Internazionale have entered talks with Tottenham over the potential signing of captain Cristian Romero
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Internazionale have entered talks with Tottenham over the potential signing of captain Cristian Romero
Content: Cristian Romero helped Argentina to the World Cup final, when they were beaten by Spain.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAView image in fullscreenCristian Romero helped Argentina to the World Cup final, when they were beaten by Spain.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPATransfer windowInter enter talks with Tottenham over signing captain Cristian RomeroInter sporting director confirms attempt to sign RomeroSpurs captain helped Argentina reach World Cup finalPA MediaSun 26 Jul 2026 07.34 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 12.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInter have entered talks with Tottenham over the potential signing of Cristian Romero. The Spurs captain helped Argentina reach a second straight World Cup final this month, but could leave this summer for a significant fee after an eventful five-year spell.The centre-back has made 156 appearances since he joined Tottenham in 2021 and guided the club to Europa League success last year, but served four separate suspensions during a difficult 2025-26 campaign.With Jan Paul van Hecke signed for £52m from Brighton and Marcos Senesi joining as a free agent in June to boost the defensive options of Roberto De Zerbi’s side, Spurs will let Romero depart and his representatives have been in Milan for talks with Inter this weekend.Inter’s sporting director, Piero Ausilio, told Sky Italy: “It’s definitely a deal we are trying to sign with the player and the club. These things take some time but there’s definitely interest. Let’s see.”Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowInternazionaleTottenham HotspurnewsShareReuse this content

title: Real Madrid ready to seal deal for Yan Diomande after PSG pull out of move | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: PSG formally withdraw from race to sign winger with the teenager now expected to complete Bernabéu switch
Author: Mark Dobson
Headline: PSG formally withdraw from race to sign winger with the teenager now expected to complete Bernabéu switch
Content: Yan Diomande has been linked with Liverpool and PSG but looks set for Real Madrid.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyView image in fullscreenYan Diomande has been linked with Liverpool and PSG but looks set for Real Madrid.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyTransfer windowReal Madrid ready to seal deal for Yan Diomande after PSG pull out of movePSG formally withdraw from race to sign wingerTeenager expected to complete Bernabéu switchMark DobsonSun 26 Jul 2026 17.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 18.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReal Madrid look to have won the race for RB Leipzig’s coveted winger, Yan Diomande, afterParis Saint-Germainwithdrew from the bidding war.The Ivory Coast international has been the subject of an intense transfer saga this summer, following a breakout season in the Bundesliga and an impressive World Cup campaign.The 19-year-old was linked with a move with Liverpool early in the window, before the player’s camp revealed he would instead prioritise a switch to Paris. However, with Real now moving ahead of PSG, Diomande looks set for the Bernabéu withthe reported fee “well in excess” of €100m (£85m).Chiesa wants ‘new chapter’ with Iraola after frustrating time under Slot at LiverpoolRead moreThe breakthrough comes just days after Leipzig rejected Madrid’s opening proposal of €90m plus €10m in add-ons. Diomande, who has reportedly already agreed personal terms with Real, is now expected to fly to the Spanish capital for a medical.The deal will come as a blow for PSG, who looked to be the frontrunners, with many reports suggesting they were his first choice if he did leave Germany. However, the European champions were unable to agree a fee and issued a statement on Sunday insisting they will not break their “principles”.The statement read: “Paris Saint-Germain has this evening formally withdrawn its interest in and bids for Yan Diomande. PSG will not break its principles of rational financial management and squad balance.”Meanwhile, Liverpool have turned their attention to PSG’s Bradley Barcola as they continue to search for wingers.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowReal MadridParis Saint-GermainRB LeipzignewsShareReuse this content

title: Chiesa wants ‘new chapter’ with Iraola after frustrating time under Slot at Liverpool | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: The forward, who scored in Liverpool’s friendly win against Sunderland, had a frustrating two seasons under the former head coach Arne Slot
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: The forward, who scored in Liverpool’s friendly win against Sunderland, had a frustrating two seasons under the former head coach Arne Slot
Content: Federico Chiesa (left) celebrates with Dominik Szoboszlai after scoring Liverpool's third goal against Sunderland in Nashville.Photograph: George Walker IV/APView image in fullscreenFederico Chiesa (left) celebrates with Dominik Szoboszlai after scoring Liverpool's third goal against Sunderland in Nashville.Photograph: George Walker IV/APLiverpoolChiesa wants ‘new chapter’ with Iraola after frustrating time under Slot at LiverpoolForward scored in friendly win against SunderlandChiesa had frustrating two seasons under Arne SlotAndy Hunterin NashvilleSun 26 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederico Chiesa has said he wants “a new chapter” atLiverpoolwith Andoni Iraola following a frustrating time under Arne Slot and claimed the club were lucky to qualify for the Champions League last season.The Liverpool forward has been linked with a return to Italy this summer having struggled for minutes during his two years at Anfield. Chiesa made 36 appearances for Slot last season, a healthy return on paper, but only five were starts.Liverpool start Iraola era in style to beat Sunderland but Gomez injury deepens defensive worriesRead moreHe started one Premier League game last season despite the problems Liverpool had in attack because of injuries to Alexander Isak and Hugo Ekitiké, and his last start came in the FA Cup fourth-round winagainst Brighton on 14 February. A change of head coach, Chiesa hopes, will herald a change in fortune as a Liverpool player.“It is always a fresh start at the beginning of the year,” said the 28-year-old, who produced a fine finish inLiverpool’s 4-2 friendly defeat of Sunderlandin Nashville on Saturday. “Maybe there have been too many fresh starts [for him]. But I don’t care, I am trying to do my best for this new manager.“Last season under Arne Slot, I was trying to do my best. Last year I felt ready for a bigger role, then it depended on the coach whether he wanted me to play or not. Of course I wanted to play more but it is what it is. The gaffer had his gameplans, he took his decisions, I have nothing to say about that. It is football. This year, let us say it is a new chapter. There is a new manager and I have to focus on that.”Chiesa admits he has not discussed his future with Iraola since the Basque coachsucceeded Slot in June. “The only conversations I had were about pressing and tactics,” he said. “He put me striker against Sunderland and he wants me there.”But the Italy international, who has two years remaining on his Liverpool contract, claimed his priority is to prove himself to the head coach rather than seek a return to Serie A. Como and former club Juventus have been linked with a move for the forward.“Right now, at the moment, I am happy here at Liverpool,” said Chiesa. “I love the club, I love the fans, I love everything. I am doing the best I can to have a chance here. And then we will see. At the minute, the only thing I am thinking about is Liverpool.”View image in fullscreenFederico Chiesa scored for Liverpool against Sunderland in Nashville on Saturday.Photograph: George Walker IV/APLiverpool secured Champions League qualification on the final day of a troubled season in May in what proved to be Slot’s final game in charge. Chiesa insists that was no cause for celebration at a club of Liverpool’s stature and there must be improvement next term.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe forward said: “Liverpool deserves more. Two years ago, we were Premier League champions. Last year, we almost went out of the Champions League spots. We were battling for fifth, which was enough at the time but as we know usually only four go in. We were lucky.“It was a tough season last year and this season we need to do better, in the Champions League as well. We went out to PSG. We want to go further in that competition and then we want to do even better in the Premier League as well.”Chiesa also hopes to reclaim his place in the national team next season, having missed out on several squads recently. Italy are now searching for a new head coach, having failed to qualify for the World Cup under Gennaro Gattuso.Chiesa said: “The situation is that I spoke to the manager a few times, Gattuso, and I was not ready physically at the time. When I got back in March, unfortunately I got injured. But I am looking forward to playing for the national team. I have won with the national team [the European Championship]. It is always nice to play and win for your national team.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Régis Le Bris says Chelsea’s pursuit of Sunderland captain Xhaka is ‘closed’ | Sunderland | The Guardian
description: Régis Le Bris said: ‘Granit wants to stay in Sunderland,’ denying Chelsea’s Xabi Alonso the chance of working again with the Swiss midfielder
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Régis Le Bris said: ‘Granit wants to stay in Sunderland,’ denying Chelsea’s Xabi Alonso the chance of working again with the Swiss midfielder
Content: Granit Xhaka was instrumental in Switzerland reaching the quarter-finals of the World Cup, where they lost to Argentina.Photograph: Peter Klaunzer/EPAView image in fullscreenGranit Xhaka was instrumental in Switzerland reaching the quarter-finals of the World Cup, where they lost to Argentina.Photograph: Peter Klaunzer/EPASunderlandRégis Le Bris says Chelsea’s pursuit of Sunderland captain Xhaka is ‘closed’Le Bris: ‘Granit wants to stay in Sunderland’Xabi Alonso managed midfielder at LeverkusenAndy Hunterin NashvilleSun 26 Jul 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRégis Le Bris has declared Chelsea’s pursuit of Granit Xhaka “closed” and insisted there is no prospect ofSunderlandselling their influential captain this summer.Xhaka played a major role in Sunderlandqualifying for the Europa Leagueon their return to the Premier League last season, prompting Chelsea to make an £8m bid for the 33-year-old this month. Xabi Alonso, the new Chelsea manager, is keen to be reunited with his former midfielder at Bayer Leverkusen.Inter enter talks with Tottenham over signing captain Cristian RomeroRead moreSunderland, however, immediately rejected Chelsea’s bid and their head coach has emphatically denied that a deal could be revisited before the end of the transfer window.“No, this topic is closed,” said Le Bris after Sunderland’s 4-2 pre-season friendly defeat by Liverpool in Nashville on Saturday. “He has been really clear about his future. He loves Sunderland, he wants to stay in Sunderland. He wants to make the future of Sunderland. He is a good captain. Great leader.”Despite the added demands of European football next season Sunderland have been quiet in the transfer market, signing only the experienced Belgium defender Thomas Meunier on a free from Lille so far. Le Bris anticipates further additions but admits this summer will be nothing like the rebuilding work before Sunderland’s return to the top flight 12 months ago.The Sunderland head coach added: “It’s going to be quiet. Under the radar, right? I won’t give you information. Because I think we are working hard behind the scenes, and it’s really important to be quiet because otherwise it’s a mess. And we are looking at probably a different transfer window if you compare with last season. We had to sign 14 new players. It won’t be the case this year. We’ll see what will happen.”Explore more on these topicsSunderlandChelseaTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Teamwork, tactics and data: behind the scenes at Wigan’s pre-season training | Wigan Athletic | The Guardian
description: Gary Caldwell, who returned to the League One club in February to keep them up, faces a new season with meticulous plans and bright hopes
Author: Sam Dalling
Headline: Gary Caldwell, who returned to the League One club in February to keep them up, faces a new season with meticulous plans and bright hopes
Content: Wigan’s players are put through their paces at their training ground.Photograph: Dom Maltby/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWigan’s players are put through their paces at their training ground.Photograph: Dom Maltby/The GuardianWigan AthleticTeamwork, tactics and data: behind the scenes at Wigan’s pre-season trainingGary Caldwell, who returned to the League One club in February to keep them up, faces a new season with meticulous plans and bright hopesSam DallingSun 26 Jul 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“This is the only rule I’m going to have for yous all season: ‘team first’,” says Gary Caldwell. The Wigan head coach’s Scottish accent booms over the gentle hum of a projector in a darkened classroom at the club’s Christopher Park training ground. “That is the one thing that we cannot ever go against,” he says, pointing to a slide on screen. “The team is the most important aspect of everything we do.”Three rows of professional athletes listen intently, keen to learn not only what the day holds, but about the 10 months ahead.Some shall see it through to next May, others may leave before the 2026-27League Onecampaign begins on 14 August, and new faces will be added.It is pre-season and before the interminable football carousel begins spinning, there is much work ahead.View image in fullscreenGary Caldwell talks tactics with his squad.Photograph: Dom Maltby/The GuardianThe meeting is short, just long enough for Caldwell to zip through a handful of tactical points. As he speaks, the head of performance analysis, Lauren Jones, plays clips from their “best practice bank”.Because she, Caldwell, and the first-team coach, David Perkins, joined from Exeter only in February (the physio, Michael McBride, and goalkeeping coach, Kevin Miller, followed this summer), the bank is small, but growing.There are myriad general football clips that Caldwell could use, but he values “the lads seeing players in Wigan shirts doing what we’re asking of them”.Perkins relays the day’s plan – a 1.5km time trial, several drills, some out-of-possession shape work and an afternoon weights session – before the class is dismissed and told to reassemble on the grass 45 minutes later.There is no idling, though, the entire squad soon beginning self‑led pre-activation (in old money, warming up).Bodies are strewn across the in-house gym with bands, benches and foam rollers used as aids to contort muscles and limbs.Wigan’s facility is, by modern standards, modest but functional. A printed sign sets out the simple rules: £50 fines for anyone with a phone, wearing sliders or sulking.When the centre-back James Carragher discovers the Guardian will be joining the morning’s run, a sanction of double that amount is declared should anyone not beat the guest journalist. At 10.55am, the strength and conditioning lead, Matthew Barrow, explains that the run consists of 15 pitch lengths with 14 turns. “Your choice lads – boots or trainers, but I recommend boots so you don’t lose time on the turn.”“I’m glad I’m not doing it,” Caldwell says, laughing. “It’s a maximal test and anything like that involves people pushing themselves.”Could you survive a professional football pre-season fitness test? – videoIt is not the squad’s first testing of pre-season. Their first day back involved a series of body and strength tests “designed to provide us with a benchmark”, Caldwell says. “If they get injured, we know where we need to get them back to.”But the days of players reporting back overweight are long gone, with only a small number a smidge above their optimum numbers during body composition testing. “That will all have been gone with the first week or so,” Caldwell says.Running for running’s sake is also past practice. Instead, Barrow and the sports scientist Jack Craigie will use the run data to get each individual’s maximum aerobic speed. “From that, we individualise all the running they’ll do,” Craigie says. “For example, if we have a volume session planned, rather than giving a generic number of lengths, we set individual distances based on their results. That way they all get the same stimulus.”By 11am, the players are jogging through a warm-up lap. According to the sign-in sheet outside the staff offices, some arrived on site three hours ago. The physio hub just off the gym has had a steady stream of visitors, a mix of prevention and cure. Breakfast was enjoyed in a canteen acting as a social space for staff and players.It marks a leisurely start when measured against some mornings. With no tour plans, Caldwell is finding alternative ways to avoid monotony. Several 6am meets precede 3.5km runs to a partner gym for intense, Hyrox-style workouts. With players working in trios, staff are as interested in attitude and demeanour as fitness.View image in fullscreenThe players take part in various training drills.Photograph: Dom Maltby/The Guardian“We’re taking the group out of their comfort zone to see how they react under a bit of pressure,” Caldwell says. “We can look at the energy someone brings at 6am when others are tired. That will help us know who is going to pick the group up when we’re a little fatigued.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThose sessions also promote Caldwell’s “team first” ethos. “When you’re ‘off’ you still have a role to play,” he says. “Are you helping your pal get in and out of the straps on the rower more quickly? We want to see how they react in that situation. Come November, when it is cold and we’re struggling in a game, we can remind them of these sessions.”A late-morning run feels tame by comparison, albeit after several pitch lengths that naive notion is dispelled. No one loses £100 to the club kitty.Soon the footballs are out and the group is split into two groups for a series of drills. The energy is impressive, with Max Power, who recently rejoined Wigan for a third spell, among the tone setters.In one exercise he encourages a junior teammate to make a pass, only for a defender to block the space. Rather than get frustrated or dish out abuse, Power immediately finds another opportunity to tee up a similar ball and praises a successful outcome. “The better the player, the less stick they give people, I find,” says one staff member. “They want everyone to improve.”The staff’s challenge is to manage the intensity, building towards a peak. Caldwell avoids directly asking players to hold back, but with a drone monitoring everything and GPS data available in real time, sessions can be adjusted accordingly. Sometimes it is as simple as moving cones in a few yards.For one drill, tape on the grass creates a dozen boxes, within which three banks of four must work to create and find gaps. “Football is sometimes about the chaos,” Caldwell says, grinning. “If we give them more space, they will use it.”View image in fullscreenWigan use the in-house gym during a break from the action on the pitch.Photograph: Dom Maltby/The GuardianBuilding towards a peak is also Wigan’s aim. Supporters want a return to the relatively recent success, which is natural after eight seasons as an established Premier League side.That ended in 2013– the year theylifted the FA Cupat Wembley with Caldwell in the squad.Four Championship relegations and three League One promotions have followed, including in Caldwell’s first full season in management. That was 2015-16 andthe third-tier title was claimed.Caldwell’s immediate challenge last season was avoiding relegation from League One, and patience is required for the next step.After lunch, the day concludes in the gym with a short, sharp, upper body strength session. In one corner, pull-ups, in another perfectly formed jackknives.“Once the season begins, training loads are consistent around games,” Barrow says. “But with the time in here now we can really chase that hypertrophy.”Pre-season was once, in effect, punishment for a summer well enjoyed, but in 2026 is a meticulous, data-driven, foundation-building exercise.The payoff will become known only next May.Explore more on these topicsWigan AthleticLeague OnefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Japan football great ‘King Kazu’ Miura, 59, scores first competitive goal in four years | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The Japanese football legend Kazuyoshi Miura scored his first competitive goal ⁠in nearly four years on Saturday, aged ⁠59 years and 149 days
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Japanese football legend Kazuyoshi Miura scored his first competitive goal ⁠in nearly four years on Saturday, aged ⁠59 years and 149 days
Content: Kazuyoshi Miura is mobbed by his ⁠Fukushima ​United teammates after scoring against Iwaki Furukawa at the age of 59.Photograph: r/soccerView image in fullscreenKazuyoshi Miura is mobbed by his ⁠Fukushima ​United teammates after scoring against Iwaki Furukawa at the age of 59.Photograph: r/soccerSoccerJapan football great ‘King Kazu’ Miura, 59, scores first competitive goal in four yearsKazuyoshi Miura converts cross to score in 52nd minuteFormer Japan international preparing for his 42nd seasonReutersSun 26 Jul 2026 05.14 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 08.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Japanese football legend Kazuyoshi Miura scored his first competitive goal ⁠in nearly four years on Saturday, finding the net at the age of ⁠59 as ⁠Fukushima ​United thrashed Iwaki Furukawa 7-0 to advance in the Emperor’s Cup.Miura, affectionately known ⁠as King Kazu, struck in the 52nd minute to put Fukushima 5-0 ahead, capping a trademark ⁠run into the box by meeting a teammate’s ​cutback with a first-time ‌finish at 59 ‌years and 149 days.The goal sparked celebrations among teammates ‌on the pitch and the bench before the veteran forward was substituted three minutes later.It was Miura’s first competitive goal since November 2022, when he scored for Suzuka PG, now Atletico Suzuka, in ‌a Japan Football League defeat by FC Osaka.The former Japan international is preparing for ​a remarkable 42nd season as a professional after extending his loan spell with third-tier Fukushima United until June 2027.Miura joined the club from Yokohama FC in ⁠December and will remain with Fukushima after making six ​appearances ​during a shortened 2026 ​campaign.With Japan’s professional leagues set to switch ​from a ‌spring-to-autumn schedule to ​an ​autumn-to-spring calendar, Miura will enter his 60s next February still playing professionally, adding another chapter to one of football’s most enduring careers.Explore more on these topicsFootballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tottenham begin tour with victory over Auckland FC in front of record crowd | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: Dane Scarlett and Richarlison were on target as an under-strength Tottenham opened their pre-season tour with a 2-0 win over Auckland FC
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dane Scarlett and Richarlison were on target as an under-strength Tottenham opened their pre-season tour with a 2-0 win over Auckland FC
Content: Richarlison celebrates after scoring the second goal for Tottenham at Eden Park.Photograph: Lynne Cameron/Tottenham Hotspur FC/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRicharlison celebrates after scoring the second goal for Tottenham at Eden Park.Photograph: Lynne Cameron/Tottenham Hotspur FC/ShutterstockTottenham HotspurTottenham begin tour with victory over Auckland FC in front of record crowdScarlett and Richarlison on target in Spurs’ 2-0 victory40,112 a record crowd for a men’s match in New ZealandAFPSun 26 Jul 2026 06.59 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 08.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDane Scarlett and Richarlison were on target as an under-strength Tottenham opened their pre-season tour with an entertaining 2-0 win over the A-League champions,Auckland FC, on Sunday.Roberto De Zerbi rested most of his top players but the Premier League side dominated a match played in damp conditions. The 40,112 who packed into the All Blacks’ famed rugby ground formed the biggest crowd to watch a men’s football match in New Zealand. It surpassed the previous best of 37,034 for a New Zealand World Cup qualifying match against Peru in 2017. They were treated to a fast-paced contest, even if both sides were missing several of their best players.Liverpool start Iraola era in style to beat Sunderland but Gomez injury deepens defensive worriesRead moreTottenham have embarked on an aggressive summer of spending after narrowly avoiding relegation last season, when they finished 17th. However, the only notable new signing to take the field was the former West Ham midfielder Mateus Fernandes, who scored in the 1-0 win over MK Dons in London on Wednesday.De Zerbi said he would ease others into the tour, with Tottenham to play games in Sydney next week against the A-League side Sydney FC and their London rivals Chelsea.“It’s a chance for the young players,” De Zerbi told TVNZ before kick-off, declaring Jan Paul van Hecke, signed from Brighton, and the former Liverpool stalwart Andy Robertson not yet up to speed. “After a very long trip, we can’t take a risk with the players who are not ready to play yet.”The cecord club signing, Sandro Tonali, was not considered because the former Newcastle midfielder had suffered an unspecified injury – “one small problem” – before the team left London, De Zerbi added.Fernandes came on with half an hour remaining and Spurs bagged their second goal shortly afterwards through the work of two other substitutes. Mathys Tel burst into the box and set up a tap-in for Richarlison.Scarlett, one of several Spurs academy players in action, opened the scoring in the 12th minute, pouncing after the Auckland goalkeeper Michael Woud parried Manor Solomon’s shot.Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurAuckland FCFriendliesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We want to win the league’: Arsenal’s new recruits ink in WSL success | Arsenal Women | The Guardian
description: Despite a busy transfer window with Beth Mead moving on and seven new signings, academy graduates such as Lotte Wubben-Moy remain key to trophies
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Despite a busy transfer window with Beth Mead moving on and seven new signings, academy graduates such as Lotte Wubben-Moy remain key to trophies
Content: Georgia Stanway gets ready to hit the new season running for Arsenal.Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorgia Stanway gets ready to hit the new season running for Arsenal.Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesArsenal Women‘We want to win the league’: Arsenal’s new recruits ink in WSL successDespite a busy transfer window with Beth Mead moving on and seven new signings, academy graduates such as Lotte Wubben-Moy remain key to trophiesSuzanne WrackSun 26 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorgia Stanway looks at her arms and then down at her legs on day one of Arsenal’s pre-season. “As you can see, I’m covered in tattoos,” she says. “I only see the bare skin, the space, so I need to keep collecting more.”Tattooing and being tattooed is her creative outlet, her way of expressing herself off the pitch. But seeing space is key to the 27‑year‑old England midfielder being exceptional on the pitch.From Popp to Diani: 10 women’s transfers you may have missed during the men’s World CupRead moreStanway’sunveiling video, after hermove from Bayern Munich, showed a delicate, cursive script reading “whatever the weather” tattooed on her arm. It was a bold statement to get the lyric from North London Forever, Arsenal’s anthem, etched into her skin before she has stepped on to the Emirates Stadium pitch in red and white. “It shows I’m going to give absolutely everything for this club. I want to hit the ground running, play my game, connect with my teammates, connect with the fans and look forward to an exciting future at the club.”Stanway is emblematic of Arsenal’s summer of change, one of seven signings so far. Meanwhile,Lotte Wubben-Moy, a lifelong fan who joined Arsenal’s academy at 13, represents the core and culture that is a point of focus at the club. It is a culture players want to be a part of, so much so it leads to getting a tattoo on day one of being there. “She has set a very high bar,” says Wubben-Moy, with a grin. “That’s Georgia. She goes all in and I like that.”Wubben-Moy is ready to stake a claim in Arsenal’s starting XI after struggling to nail down a position in defence despite having performed exceptionally well when covering for injured players. “I’ve always felt ready,” says the 27-year-old. “When I get my moment, I deliver. Historically, as a club, we’re built on defensive solidity. If we have a solid defence, it allows us to create and score. That should be the stepping stone towards victories. So I will continue to contribute to the defensive solidity in whatever way, shape or form that is. But I want my spot.”View image in fullscreenLotte Wubben-Moy lifts the Champions Cup trophy during the Arsenal trophy parade in May.Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesThere was widespread recognition that Arsenal’s squad needed a revamp, that the age needed to be lowered and changes made if they were going to take the next step. That meant big names leaving, most notablyBeth MeadandKatie McCabe. “They’re both absolute legends of the game and we have so much respect for them,” says Jodie Taylor, the former Arsenal striker who became the club’s technical director in January. “But we always knew this window was going to come with some changes.”“Change is inevitable in women’s football,” says Wubben-Moy. “If you speak to a player and they don’t say they’re nimble, you’ve got someone that’s not built for the game. We’ve become a nimble team, a team that can move with the ebb and flow of women’s football.View image in fullscreenBeth Mead left in a busy summer for Arsenal.Photograph: Rhianna Chadwick/PA“That’s not just within the playing group, it’s something replicated within the staff, the boardroom, the commercial team, the comms team. Everyone is so willing to move and to dictate what we want.“If you’d asked me about change four or five years ago, I’d have been a bit intimidated, but now I know what to do and I’m part of the driver of it. The opportunity we have and that I see for us as a team, as a collective, is something that really excites me.”Arsenal’s approach to Stanway’s recruitment was a contributing factor to her wanting to join the club. “Arsenal came in early doors,” she says. “I really enjoyed they were super loyal from the beginning and wanted me even when I wasn’t available. It’s a nice feeling being wanted.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArsenal continue squad revamp with signing of Spain keeper Misa RodríguezRead more“The last four years in Munich were unbelievable, but I knew I wanted to take the next step and I felt at Arsenal there was an opportunity for me to be able to progress, to make my game better and to play with world-class players.”Arsenal have done most of their business early, with Stanway joined by experienced internationalsSelina Cerci, Géraldine Reuteler,Ona BatlleandMisa Rodríguez, as well as young talents Lisa Baum and Isabella Damm. No major international tournament and seven signings in for day one of pre-season is a big boost for Renée Slegers and her coaching staff, particularly after two seasons of slow starts to domestic campaigns.“The market is not easy, though, it’s constantly changing and the pool of elite talent is small and several clubs are fishing from it,” says Taylor. “You try and plan as much as you can, but you also have to be reactive in the market. We’re always trying to keep an eye on the future, but we have to be quite agile.“We can talk about positional needs, qualities, ages and succession planning, but if a player’s not available or they just don’t exist, it can be like trying to fit square pegs and round holes. As well as looking at current needs and positional profiles, we talk a lot about our core style of play, but we also want to play with variety, be unpredictable and have different qualities in players too.”View image in fullscreenFormer Arsenal striker Jodie Taylor, now technical director, is leading the strong recruitment this summer.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyThe players who have come in have brought energy, says Wubben-Moy, who was on an emotional rollercoaster duringArsenal men’s Premier League and women’s Champions Cup-winning parade, with the bus looping past Highbury Corner, where she filmed her contract renewal video, and past Islington town hall, where she got married to cyclist Tao Geoghegan Hart a few weeks later.“I like to focus on what they’re entering,” says Wubben-Moy, “which is a culture that has been created by history, by players and staff that are the core of this team and who have all lived through the changes to different degrees: Kelly [Smith], Renée, myself, Leah [Williamson], Kim [Little], Jodie too. We’ve been privy to lots of different things but all of us are holding on to and releasing, in a healthy way, the things we know we need to. It’s efficient, we’re focused, we know what we do next.Missing a major football tournament? Fear not, Wafcon 2026 is about to startRead more“It’s like you’re cooking the most beautiful recipe and then you add the final small ingredients that make the marginal difference, that elevate, and you create something that’s beautiful and that you can relish and enjoy. That’s what we’re in the process of now with a beautiful long pre-season. I’m desperate to get it out of the way so we can then serve what we’re cooking to the fans and be like: ‘Let’s eat and we’ll all eat together for the whole year.’”The average attendance of more than 34,000 fans for WSL games at the Emirates last season and the club’s pioneering history in women’s football, as well as theChampions League win in 2025, are huge selling points, and all concerned at Arsenal want more, including a first Women’s Super League title since 2019.“We’re in a great place,” says Taylor. “But we would have liked to have won more trophies last season and that is our huge ambition coming into this year. I’ll flat out say it: we want to win the league. We are an ambitious club and with the signings we’ve made we feel like we’re in a great place to do that.”Explore more on these topicsArsenal WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cam McEvoy says ‘I can’t just cruise’ as he dominates 50m freestyle in Glasgow and eyes Olympics | Australia sport | The Guardian
description: Sprint ace sets new Games record as Australian swimmers bank more gold
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Sprint ace sets new Games record as Australian swimmers bank more gold
Content: Cam McEvoy celebrates after winning the 50m freestyle final in Glasgow and setting a new Commonwealth Games record.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreenCam McEvoy celebrates after winning the 50m freestyle final in Glasgow and setting a new Commonwealth Games record.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPAustralia sportCam McEvoy says ‘I can’t just cruise’ as he dominates 50m freestyle in Glasgow and eyes OlympicsSprint ace sets new Games record as Australian swimmers bank more goldLani Pallister cruises to gold in 1500m as Iona Anderson wins 100m backstrokeBreanna Scott wins individual gymnastics silverGuardian sportand AAPSun 26 Jul 2026 17.36 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 20.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCam McEvoy’s Glasgow gold has him looking to Los Angeles with confidence as he headlined another strong night for Australia’sCommonwealth Gamesswim team.The sprint ace dominated the 50m freestyle final on Sunday night, going under 21 seconds for only the second time. It is McEvoy’s first individual gold medal at his third Commonwealth Games.McEvoy’s Games-record 20.97 seconds follows his 20.88 world record in March and continues his remarkable swimming renaissance.He led home an Australian medal sweep in the event – one of five swimming gold medals on day three – but the time was the bigger deal as he looks to defend his Olympic title at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.Commonwealth Games 2026: day three in picturesRead more“It [gold] is really good, but I’m more excited about ducking under the 21-second barrier,” he said. “A double whammy for me. It was a really good night.“I really wanted to prove to myself that I can consistently get under that [21 seconds]. So to do that for a second time, that brings me a lot of confidence for the world championships next year, LA, moving forward.”View image in fullscreenThe all-Australian podium of Flynn Southam (left), Cam McEvoy (centre) and Jamie Jack.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesAfter a disappointing Tokyo Olympics, McEvoy took a sabbatical and nearly left the sport. He completely overhauled his training and returned for a stunning Paris triumph in the 50m freestyle.“Prior to Paris, I still had the, I guess ... the demons to work with in terms of my Olympic relationship,” he said.“I was able to overcome them, but also I’ve been open-sourcing this type of training for a long time.“The world is getting faster. I can’t just cruise into it.”Flynn Southam won silver and Jamie Jack was third to complete the Australian sweep.Lani Pallister dominates 1500mAs McEvoy ruled the one-lap dash, Lani Pallister remained similarly untouchable in distance freestyle events at the Games and turned the 1500m into a personal time trial and her second Glasgow gold.After taking out the 400m on day one, Pallister won the 1500 by nearly 18 seconds as the women’s event made its debut at the Games.View image in fullscreenLani Pallister was all smiles after winning the 1500m freestyle.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesBut there was no Australian procession in the men’s 4x200m freestyle final.For once, it was a genuine race and England led at the last change before Kai Taylor’s blistering anchor leg delivered the last gold medal of day three and another Games record.Sam Short, Harry Turner, Ed Sommerville and Taylor clocked seven minutes 1.47 seconds to break the Games record Australia set in Birmingham.Iona Anderson had an emotional hug with her Scottish grandmother after winning the 100m backstroke. She had tartan nails as a nod to her heritage.Australia’s opening ceremony baton bearer Tim Hodge successfully defended his Games 100m backstroke S9 title.Australian swimmers have now collected 16 gold medals in three days, entrenching their country atop the overall Games medal standings.But Matthew Temple suffered a bad case of deja vu, the Australian again losing to Canadian star Josh Liendo in a record-breaking 100m butterfly final.Liendo beat Temple by one one-hundredth of a second and fellow Australian Ben Armbruster took bronze.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Olympic silver medallist clocked 50.42 seconds while Temple touched the wall in 50.43, going under the Games record of 50.63 that the Australian had set on day two in the semi-finals.Scott wins gymnastics silver, but Godwin misses podiumDrawing inspiration from her “idol” andteammate Georgia Godwin, Australian gymnast Breanna Scott has broken through for individual all-around silver in Glasgow.All eyes were on defending champion Godwin, but it was Scott who led the charge for Australia as the Canadian great Ellie Black won gold at Glasgow International Stadium.Black’s 16-year-old teammate Lia-Monica Fontaine followed for bronze, while Godwin settled for fifth after guiding Australia to a team gold the day before.View image in fullscreenBreanna Scott alongside Canada’s Elsabeth Black and Lia-Monica Fontaine.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPScott wins her first individual medal at the Games, having won team silver on debut in Birmingham.“It’s pretty crazy. I don’t really think it’s sunk in yet,” Scott said. “There’s been so much that’s happened in the last 24 hours.”The Sydney local credited Godwin and Black for pushing her to the limit in Glasgow.“They’re both like such great role models. Georgia is like basically all of our idols in the team,” Scott said.Georgia Godwin overcomes ‘horrible’ injury to win gymnastics gold as Australian swimmers dominate in GlasgowRead more“We look up to her. She’s just so great to have there. She’s the most supportive person you could have on the team.“And obviously Ellie, like she’s an icon of the sport so it was really great to be competing with both of them.”View image in fullscreenScott performs on the beam during the artistic gymnastics all-around final.Photograph: Stuart Wallace/ShutterstockAfter a quiet start on the vault and uneven bars, beam specialist Scott surged into medal contention after scoring 13.900 points in her pet event.Scott was on target to claim gold at the final rotation after her floor routine netted her 12.800 points, but Canada’s Black did just enough to claim gold.The 24-year-old Australian will again take to the balance beam for the individual apparatus final with teammate Kate McDonald.Explore more on these topicsAustralia sportCommonwealth Games 2026SwimmingCommonwealth GamesGymnasticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Luke Littler defends World Matchplay title after crushing win against Gerwyn Price | Darts | The Guardian
description: Luke Littler set the tournament’s highest average in an 18-9 win, while Beau Greaves beat Fallon Sherrock to lift the women’s World Matchplay title
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Luke Littler set the tournament’s highest average in an 18-9 win, while Beau Greaves beat Fallon Sherrock to lift the women’s World Matchplay title
Content: Luke Littler poses with the World Matchplay trophy after his victory against Gerwyn Price.Photograph: Ben Roberts Photo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLuke Littler poses with the World Matchplay trophy after his victory against Gerwyn Price.Photograph: Ben Roberts Photo/Getty ImagesDartsLuke Littler defends World Matchplay title after crushing win against Gerwyn PriceLittler sets the tournament’s highest average in 18-9 winBeau Greaves beats Fallon Sherrock to lift women’s titlePA MediaSun 26 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 17.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLuke Littler bulldozed his way to a second consecutive World Matchplay title as he crushed Gerwyn Price 18-9 in Blackpool. The 19-year-old averaged 111.53 in the final, setting an average for the tournament as a whole of 111.04 to break Phil Taylor’s record of 106.31.Littler also broke his own competition record for 180s as he hit 12 in the final to reach 66 for the week, as he became only the third man to successfully defend the Matchplay final after Taylor and Michael van Gerwen, who did it most recently in 2016.Oche addicts: how Kenya fell back in love with dartsRead moreIt keeps Littler on course for aclean sweep of trophiesin 2026, having already won the World Championship, UK Open, Premier League and the Masters, while he will defend the Grand Slam, Grand Prix and Players Championship Finals.Littler was on a charge from the start, taking a 3-1 lead with a 167 checkout to leave Price feeding on crumbs. A third bullseye finish of the night made it 11-3, but he twice missed double 10 to allow Price a brief moment of hope, as the Welshman cut the deficit to 14-7. Price hit a 11-darter to get to 15-9 but Littler responded with a 148 before finishing it off in short order.“It’s been a crazy week, one of the best weeks of my life with the darts I’ve played,” Littler said. “It’s not been easy, it’s been tough. The stats make it look easy but when you’re on this stage with how hot it is, I’ve definitely played some of the best darts of my life. I feel like it’s the best version of myself. I have just played so well.”Littler is eyeing a clean sweep of the majors, and will now turn his attention to the Pro Tour in order to qualify for the Player Championship Finals. “I don’t think my dad is too happy because we were meant to be going to Spain but now we will be going to Leicester for some Pro Tours!” he said.Price, appearing in his first final since 2022 having never won the trophy, had said earlier in the week that if he brought his best to the final he could beat Littler, but it was not the case as, even averaging 104.97, the Welshman was blown away.“Luke is one in a million,” Price said. “I think I played pretty decent. “In that game I missed a couple of opportunities but the bull checkouts, the 167, it was a big turning point even though it was early in the game. I didn’t play brilliant, but I played decent.”Earlier, Beau Greaves claimed her third Women’s World Matchplay title in four years as she edged out Fallon Sherrock 6-5.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGreaves started the final with finishes of 148 and 144 in consecutive legs, but Sherrock kept pushing and took back-to-back legs to level at 5-5 and force a decider. They shared maximums but Greaves came out on top with a checkout of 56 to secure the crown.“I’m not one to celebrate but it was relief in the end,” Greaves said. “Fallon is a great lass and an even better darts player. I knew I had to play well but to hit that last dart was an outpouring of relief.”Explore more on these topicsDartsLuke LittlernewsShareReuse this content

title: Adam Ramsay-Peaty armed with ‘battle plan’ for golden revival in 50m breaststroke | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Briton is ready to bounce back after his 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games and he said: ‘The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind’
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The Briton is ready to bounce back after his 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games and he said: ‘The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind’
Content: Adam Ramsay-Peaty is looking for 50m gold after bronze in the 100m breaststroke.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenAdam Ramsay-Peaty is looking for 50m gold after bronze in the 100m breaststroke.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersCommonwealth Games 2026Adam Ramsay-Peaty armed with ‘battle plan’ for golden revival in 50m breaststrokeBriton ready to bounce back after 100m bronze‘The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind’Sean Ingleat the Tollcross International Swimming CentreSun 26 Jul 2026 15.54 EDTFirst published on Sun 26 Jul 2026 10.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdam Ramsay-Peaty has never been one to hide his emotions. He wears them proudly on his sleeve, next to the striking tattoos of a huge lion and Poseidon, the Greek god of the sea.After his shock defeat in the 100m breaststroke final at theseCommonwealth Games, the 31-year-old was back pouring his heart out on Sunday – and insisting he had a “battle plan” to win gold in Monday’s 50m breaststroke final.Tearful Ramsay-Peaty tells critics ‘you can’t hurt me’ after shock Commonwealth bronzeRead moreRamsay-Peaty certainly looked smoother in qualifying third fastest from the semi-finals in 26.82sec. However, he still has a couple of tenths to find on the South African Michael Houlie, who was fastest in 26.61.The Australian Sam Williamson, who is hoping to add the 50m to his 100m crown, also looked good as he won his semi-final in 26.79. Yet Peaty pronounced himself happy with how he had bounced back from Saturday’s shock loss.“It felt much better,” he said. “The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind, but I’m really happy with that. We’re on a great trajectory for tomorrow.“For me, the best way to ever get anything out of my head is just to write it out. When I write down what’s going wrong, what’s going right, what kind of change? What can’t change? Then I’ve got a battle plan.”He added: “People forget that I haven’t done this for two years. And even I forget that. So as you go through heats, semis and finals, it’s quite difficult if you’re not used to it. So I think that perspective is a good thing.”Peaty has stood on the top of the podium 32 times in global championships across his glittering career. Yet he has not won a gold medal since the Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games. That record was extended on Saturday when he could take only bronze in the 100m breaststroke in 59.65, behind Williamson, who won in 59.3, and the brilliant 18-year-old Filip Nowicki from Jersey.Afterwards Ramsay-Peaty was strikingly honest about “all the shit I have been through” to get ready for the Commonwealth Games, including the 5.30am starts, missing family gatherings because of training, and also the amount of abuse he and his family has received on social media.On Sunday he added more context to his struggles, pointing out that he battled with burnout and a broken foot over the past four years, as well as hinting at the much-publicised estrangement with his family.“There have been a multitude of things at play over the last few years – burnout, breaking my foot, fighting against something that you love. It’s been hard,” he said. “Some of it has been quite painful, particularly from that foot injury onwards.“Coming back to where I am now and making the decision to go for LA, I think this is going to be the hardest climb I’ve ever faced and the hardest test. It’s really hard to see the summit because it’s so hard. I don’t think anyone understands.”What was perhaps most striking about that 59.65 was that it was nearly three seconds behind his world record – and slower even than he swam at the British trials in the spring.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I work a lot harder than a 59.6, really. It’s not a good time – we know that,” he said on Sunday. “When your world record is three seconds away, we’ve got to seriously ask what’s going wrong because that’s not me.View image in fullscreenHolly Ramsay-Peaty (centre) watches on as her husband, Adam, prepares for his 50m breaststroke heat.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA“We need to look at it, interrogate it, look at the data, and ask whether it was an issue with race pace, fitness, or something else. I don’t think it was fitness, but there are a lot of components that make us swim, so we really have to analyse it.”He added: “I was fitter in April with less training, which doesn’t really make sense, to be honest. I guess that’s the learning point. Maybe I’m on a plan that I don’t fully understand, and maybe it’ll take another two years to find the right way.”On Saturday, Ramsay-Peaty also took aim at social media and traditional media too, which has become fixated with him and his pregnant wife, Holly – the daughter of the celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay – and his estrangement with his mother.“You don’t know who I am,” he said. “And people who comment, people who see the story because you read a headline, they’ve got to look themselves in the mirror. You can’t hurt me.”He added: “That hasn’t played a part in the sense of what I’ve experienced, because I’m still happy with that result in some sense, but it has to stop. How many athletes, how many people, have to go through this until the media learn their lesson? You have to learn and do better.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Adam Ramsay-PeatyCommonwealth GamesSwimmingnewsShareReuse this content
