title: When the AI bubble bursts, what will Australia do with the tools it built? One man thinks he has the answer | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Journalist and author Cory Doctorow is coming to Australia to spread his message – humans will take their jobs back
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Journalist and author Cory Doctorow is coming to Australia to spread his message – humans will take their jobs back
Content: Journalist and science fiction author Cory Doctorow in his home office in Los Angeles. He says society will have to find a way to recover skills lost to AI once the bubble bursts.Photograph: Jessica Pons/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJournalist and science fiction author Cory Doctorow in his home office in Los Angeles. He says society will have to find a way to recover skills lost to AI once the bubble bursts.Photograph: Jessica Pons/The GuardianAI (artificial intelligence)When the AI bubble bursts, what will Australia do with the tools it built? One man thinks he has the answerJournalist and author Cory Doctorow is coming to Australia to spread his message – humans will take their jobs backFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterSun 26 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 20.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the AI bubble bursts, executives who enthusiastically replaced their staff with AI tools will learn that it takes a “really long time” to replace those lost skills, says Cory Doctorow, a science fiction author and journalist.But those in creative fields should also be warned not to put all their faith in copyright as the best way to safeguard their work, Doctorow warns, just one week after the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese,promised to ramp up protection against AI companies who refuse to pay.In his new book, the Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI, the man who coined the word “enshittification” says the question isn’t “Are we in an AI bubble?” but “When will the bubble burst?”“The thing about bubbles is that after they burst, we look back and we say, ‘Well, obviously that was the weak link,’” he says.The AI bubble is being kept afloat through the massive investments being made from Gulf sovereign wealth funds and billionaires into new datacentres, Doctorow says. If some of those deals begin to collapse, so could the bubble.The circular investment in the AI sector – between thechip manufacturers, AI companies and tech companies using AI– “could easily” be the first domino to fall, he adds. Or if the AI companies including Anthropic and OpenAI continue to delay theirinitial public offeringand struggle to get new funding.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“We can see in retrospect, when we don’t have to continue pretending that this thing is going to go on for ever, that it was always very, very brittle,” Doctorow says. “It was always very fraught.”Executives in industries that were promised by those selling AI that the technology could cheaply replace their workers will find those skills hard to bring back when the dust settles. Workers fired, pushed into retirement or retrained in other fields will leave gaps of knowledge.View image in fullscreenDoctorow in his back-yard bar.Photograph: Jessica Pons/The GuardianDetailed knowledge of business processes can’t be readily transferred or recovered, he says, “and you can’t just recover it like the workers who have it when you scatter them to the four winds”.“It’s going to be a bit a little like Fury Road where there’s just going to be stuff you have but we don’t know how to do again. And it’s going to take a really long time to figure out how to do it again.”Copyright fix on AI ‘won’t solve anyone’s problems’Albaneselast week saidthe Australian government would have “plain as day” laws on copyright to ensure AI companies that train their models on music, books, news and other creative works pay to use it. This followed reports the government was being lobbied by AI companies to introduce a text and data mining exception into Australian copyright law.The announcement was broadly welcomed by creative sectors in Australia. Doctorow argues that using copyright law “won’t solve anyone’s problems” – a position he says doesn’t put him on the side of the AI companies but also doesn’t put him on the side of the large media companies.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s not like the media companies suing the AI companies want to pay media professionals, right? Like, no one has ever accused Rupert Murdoch of feeling that journalists don’t get enough money.“The only other constituency, apart from a few creative workers, for a new copyright is our bosses.”He says ensuring workers have labour law rights over the terms in which they use AI and over their creative output would be better.Doctorow also says governments should not invest in AI right now but should instead wait for the market to crash and build based on open-source AI models when the market shifts.“Let’s not be suckers. We’re going to have tons of hardware. We’re going to have tons of people who know how to use the hardware to do useful things. And we’re going to have means, motive and opportunity to improve these open-source [AI] models.” What will be left for the average person is “a bunch of useful tools”.“Puttingvibe coded stuffinto production [in companies] is creating tech debt at unimaginable scale,” he says. “But vibe coding for the thing that you use to connect your smart alarm clock into your smart coffee-maker is fine.“Who gives a shit if it stops working? You just do it again.”Cory Doctorow appears at Sydney’s Festival of Dangerous Ideas from 22 to 23 August and Melbourne’s the Capitol on 25 August, presented by the Wheeler Centre and Now or Never. The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI published by Verso is released on 4 August and is available for pre-order nowExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingChatGPTAnthropicOpenAIAustralian politicsBusinessfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why does everything feel so joyless? Welcome to the age of decadence without pleasure | Society | The Guardian
description: Decadence in our era comes in technologically mediated forms, emptied of desire and obsessed with self-optimisation
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Decadence in our era comes in technologically mediated forms, emptied of desire and obsessed with self-optimisation
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignThe featured essaySocietyWhy does everything feel so joyless? Welcome to the age of decadence without pleasureDecadence in our era comes in technologically mediated forms, emptied of desire and obsessed with self-optimisationMichèle Mendelssohn and Charlie TysonSun 26 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTShareDo you want to have a good time? You know, really enjoy yourself? Click here, and tell us your desires. Maybe it’s a new outfit, or some exotic cuisine delivered anonymously and steaming hot to your door. Maybe it’s porn or gambling. Perhaps you prefer the infinite scroll, the endlessly unfurling ribbon of glossy images and videos starring people you’ll never meet doing things you’ll never do. Or maybe you favor talking to a chatbot who will assure you that you are the most special of all its users.For anyone with an Internet connection and a little discretionary income, the contemporary moment offers a superabundance of seductive distractions. Why then the pervasive mood of emptiness? Why are so many at once overstimulated and bored?Welcome to the era of decadence without pleasure.The concept of decadence as a marker of cultural decline coinciding with a high level of wealth has been around since the twilight of the ancient Greeks and Romans. After the Roman emperor Elagabalus took the throne at 14, he served flamingo brains, seasoned his food with pearls, and, according to one account, smothered guests to death with an avalanche of rose petals. But his vices were outdone by Nero, who had his enemies sewn into wild animal skins and devoured by dogs in an elaborate garden spectacle.So decadence has an inescapably pejorative ring, suggesting decay, excess and a falling away from norms and ideals. Critics of decadence have usually hailed from the political right, and the same is true today: consider conservative New York Times columnist Ross Douthat’s critique of cultural and economic stagnation in his 2020 book The Decadent Society, or billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s complaints about faltering innovation and the supposed decline of the west. JD Vance likes to invoke the fall of Rome,warning, inhis 2026 memoir Communion, that the US is “a great civilization” tumbling into “disrepair”. But plenty of thinkers on the left also worry that modern wealthy societies have entered a period of paralysis, under the shadow of what the Italian theorist Franco “Bifo” Berardi calls “the slow cancellation of the future”.View image in fullscreenThe Roses of Heliogabalus (1888) by artist Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema, depicting the young Roman emperorElagabalushosting a banquet.Photograph: Studio SebertThat all sounds bad. Yet a passionate minority has sometimes found, in decadence, reasons for hope.Cultures later judged decadent produced extraordinary upwellings of art, like the flare of a dying star. Think of the undulating arabesques of Rococo painting before the French Revolution, or the lush shimmering silks of the late Ottomans, or the experimental cinema and nightlife of Weimar Berlin.Nowhere was the cultural potential of decadence more visible than in the late-19th century. In France, Britain and (with less gusto) in the United States, artists such as Oscar Wilde, Aubrey Beardsley, Joris-Karl Huysmans and Rachilde developed new literary and visual styles championing extravagance, sensuousness and the superiority of artifice. It is to these avant-garde experiments that we owe green carnations (the fakest of flowers), frivolous dandies obsessed with perfumes, a bejeweled tortoise crushed to death by the weight of its splendor, and erotic nightmares including a woman with monstrous flowers growing between her thighs and a male anatomical model whose legs spread at the click of a spring so that he can be penetrated by his female lover. Such taboo-busting grotesquery protested against the inertia of modern civilization by applying moral and aesthetic shock treatment.The decadents, however, were not just provocateurs. Their revolt against Victorian society’s deadening enslavement to usefulness, materialism and conventionality put forward a positive philosophy of life, a certain way of thinking about pleasure. Against their era’s obsession with use-value and profit, the decadents insisted that pleasure was, or ought to be, “useless”, enjoyed for its own sake in life’s passing moments. “Not the fruit of experience, but experience itself, is the end,” intoned the essayist Walter Pater, one of the guiding lights of English decadence, in his masterpiece The Renaissance. A reclusive Oxford don, Pater was said to have once stopped High Street traffic to stroke a cat. Why? For the sensation of fur beneath his fingers. The virtue of decadent pleasure is that it is useless, an end in itself.Our tech overlords are planning for conscious AI to conquer the cosmos. What could go wrong? | Eduardo PorterRead moreThe fixations of fin-de-siècle decadence that inspired Oscar Wilde and company are still with us, but in shrivelled, technologically mediated forms. GLP-1s turn the delights of eating into a problem to be managed. Anti-ageing remedies and “looksmaxxing” turn decadence’s preoccupation with self-styling into a (literally painful) form of self-optimisation. AI restages decadence’s love of artifice by outsourcing human thinking to a chatty, eager-to-please machine butler.The problem with contemporary culture isn’t that we’re too decadent. We have inherited the surfaces of decadence – luxury, excess, artifice, bodily display – but have surrendered the fin de siècle’s commitment to pleasure. The result is a culture in which pleasure is subordinated to programs of optimisation and replaced at scale by numbing algorithmic stimulation and promises of instant gratification. Whether you’re after goods, food, art or ideas, you can get more, faster, now.But quantity and speed can’t make up for the paradox at the heart of today’s decadence: the fact that it’s often “meh” and oddly joyless. It’s a sign of the times that this spring,Amazon’s Chinese rival launchedin the UK and Europe under a name that promises to deliver emotional fulfilment: Joybuy.The ‘looksmaxxing’ eraBryan Johnson, the frequently shirtless tech tycoon who has funnelled his fortune into what he calls the“Don’t Die” movement, has turned his quest for immortality into a prolonged exhibition of ascetic self-management. His lifestyle is harrowingly spartan: he doesn’t drink alcohol, avoids the sun, never goes out in the evening, and subsists primarily on lentils, boiled broccoli and macadamia nuts. Yet his regimen is, in its peculiar way, one of prurient excess. He swallows up to 111 pills a day, tracks his night-time erections, and once tapped his teenage son for blood plasma. His fight against death costs a reported $2m a year.Johnson presents himself as a man of the future, but he has a 19th-century double. While pallid, faintly androgynous men with money and strange habits are not rare in decadent literature, the most famous is Duke Jean des Esseintes, the hero of Joris-Karl Huysmans’s 1884 novel Against the Grain, a work considered the Bible of decadence. The last scion of an aristocratic French family, des Esseintes creates for himself a cloistered world of voluptuous artifice: padded walls, rare books, exotic flowers, fragrant bonbons, subtle liqueurs, perfumes so sweet they verge on rancid.View image in fullscreenBryan Johnson wearing a brain-scanning helmet called Flow during a pilot study involving a ketamine-induced altered state of consciousness.Photograph: Business Wire/APLike Johnson, des Esseintes is medically fragile, obsessed with death, and preoccupied with the minutiae of his private sensations. Like Johnson, he sees his retreat from ordinary society into a tightly controlled artificial environment as an experiment that tests the limits of human possibility. But whereas des Esseintes’s withdrawal is an immersion into the subtleties of sensation, Johnson’s “Don’t Die” movement treats the delights of the senses as suspect, even fatal. Des Esseintes hosts a funeral banquet for his “dead virility” in a dining room draped in black, opening on to charcoaled gardens, with guests dining on black-bordered plates filled with black food (rye bread, caviar, black pudding, cuts of meat dripping with liquorice-coloured sauce). Johnson, by contrast, treats impotence as a technical problem,repeatedly shockinghis penis to increase his erections.double quotation markThese attitudes reflect the fantasies of a narrow elite obsessed with human enhancementJohnson’s programme is extreme, but he is not an anomaly. His lifestyle makes visible, in exaggerated form, new attitudes toward pleasure and embodiment being pushed by today’s tech billionaires. While some superwealthy people in or around Palo Alto are biohacking for longevity with the help of concierge medics, others are treating even sexual pleasure as a domain to be perfected through medical interventions. For example, at Dr Sally Greenwald’s exclusive OB-GYN practice, nicknamed the “Billionaire’s Vagina Club” – Greenwald describes her clientele as “the top 0.001%” – middle-aged women can improve their “sexspan” through bespoke advice, hormonal cocktails and tracking devices. “Sex equals sleep, stress reduction, cardiovascular engagement, relational fulfilment, and pelvic-floor health, and each of those equals health,”Greenwald says.These attitudes reflect the fantasies of a narrow elite obsessed with human enhancement and – above all else – the prolongation of their own survival. The class politics of pleasureless decadence can be roughly summarized as: biohacking and quantified asceticism for the rich, algorithmic stimulation for the rest.In contexts of extreme inequality, rich people tend to set the terms by which pleasure is understood and experienced. The very fact of inequality injures pleasure, because in a stratified society, food, art, travel and other delights can devolve into occasions to demonstrate rank or taste. Our present social order, however, is not just radically unequal; it’s dominated by a ruling class that distrusts pleasure and sensation. What passes for “fun” among today’s top 0.001% amounts to anything but: think of the 80-hour workweeks championed by tech titans like Elon Musk, or Equinox gym’s “Optimize” longevity membership costing $40,000 a year, or courtside seats at Knicks games inside the miniaturesurveillance statethat is Madison Square Garden. And because of their outsized political and cultural influence, their sway over public and private investment, and their habit of not paying their share of tax, the pleasurelessness of the ultra-monied classes trickles down to the rest of us.“I think trying to optimise things … is actually the divine spark within us,” recentlyprofessedthe German biotech billionaire Christian Angermayer, a champion of “humanmaxxing”, the use of drugs and supplements to enhance the body. Divinity aside, it seems pertinent to mention that the person content with every day sensations makes for a poor consumer. But get people outside the plutocratic class to reconceive their minds and bodies as sites of perpetual self-improvement, and you have, in Angermayer’s words, “a total addressable market of ideally 100%”.The most culturally revealing such market is for GLP-1s such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro. One in eight American adults report taking GLP-1 injectables for weight loss, according to a 2025 Galluppoll, and far moreexpress interestin taking them. The global market for this class of drugs isexpectedto reach $190bn by 2035. For many, these medications confer real benefits. Yet it seems fair to ask: what does the widespread embrace of appetite-governing pharmaceuticals suggest about our culture’s handling of pleasure and desire?GLP-1s reshape the felt relation between desire and satisfaction, as research has already begun to show. While more studies are needed, some usersreporta diminution of pleasure across several areas of their lives: they complain of lethargy, decreased libido, emotional flatness and a weakened connection to the social dimensions of eating.View image in fullscreenThe Fruit Bearers (1896) by Aubrey Beardsley.Photograph: AlamyThe decadence of the fin de siècle celebrated cornucopian abundance. Take for example Aubrey Beardsley’s1896 drawingThe Fruit Bearers, depicting two figures bearing colossal bowls of fruit, lush grapes overhanging, a peacock in the background observing the opulent procession. In contrast, today’s anhedonic decadence celebrates the inhibition, even the transcendence, of appetite. While in haute cuisinethe trappings of indulgence are preserved – some upmarket eateries nowoffer“small appetite” menus featuring caviar and foie gras – the tendency is toward delicate minimalism. Because eating is a quintessentially communal activity, an intervention in how people eat is also an intervention in how we socialize.It seems reasonable to expect, meanwhile, that the widespread uptake of such drugs may contribute to a tightening not just of belts but of beauty norms. Looksmaxxing, an online subculture aimed primarily at young men, presents a darker strain of physical perfectionism, treating the body as a site of correction. Of course, women have long been ground down by painful and impossible beauty standards. What’s striking about looksmaxxing is the migration of this kind of disciplinary logic into a male subculture that speaks of beauty in terms of brutal domination: anyone can be “mogged” (outshone by a more handsome man), and one of the purposes of maxxing is to increase one’s “sexual market value”. Key to this subculture is the rejection of subjective taste in favor of mathematical norms (looksmaxxers prize certain ratios of facial proportion, measuring, for instance, the height of the forehead or the distance between the pupils).“[T]o make oneself beautiful is a universal instinct,” a young Max Beerbohm wrote in his 1894 essay A Defence of Cosmetics, a send-up of decadence’s cult of artifice. Whereas the fin-de-siècle decadents with their love of makeup treated the face as a mask to play with or an enigma to contemplate, looksmaxxers recast the face as a set of homogenizing metrics requiring arduous correction. “The men are weeping in the gym,” writes Andrew McMillan in his prescient 2015 poem about punitive male beauty standards:they have got too close to the glassand now they are layingin the broken pools of their own faces.View image in fullscreenThe pleasureless decadence machineThe fin de siècle had its own cult of masculine self-display in the form of the dandy, with his carefully tailored coat, polished shoes and pigskin gloves. The dandy’s concern for appearance was just part of the era’s wide-ranging love of stylization. “The first duty in life is to be as artificial as possible,” Oscar Wilde proclaimed. “What the second duty is no one has yet discovered.” Wilde and other decadents prized the made over the natural. Artifice was a way of intensifying the given world, overlaying the hard facts of life with a glittering sheen or a more pleasant smell. After all, what is the dandy’s perfume but a victory for pleasure over necessity?AI marks a triumph of artifice more sweeping than the old decadents could have imagined. Yet far from bolstering our capacity for perceptual intensity, AI presents new threats to both. Its productions – LinkedIn posts about the virtues of entrepreneurship, cartoon soap operas about the infidelities of anthropomorphized fruits – are eerily hollow, with no felt experience, embodiment or sensation behind them. AI is the pleasureless decadence machine.double quotation markThere is no pleasure or pain for an AI, no skin in the gameCarissa VélizAlready our algorithmically driven culture is saturated with a deluge of slop that promises numbing, empty stimulation. The old decadents were fascinated by the prospect of mental oblivion, the loss of self-control in the face of overwhelming beauty. Today, AI researcherswarnof “human enfeeblement” as tech companies seek to draw users into relations of dependency and infantilization, with machines to do their “thinking” for them.While the fin-de-siècle left imprints on visual art, fashion, music and other art forms, it was primarily as a literary movement that its decadence made cultural interventions. Crucial to decadent writing was a taste for language – lilting rhythms, overheated exclamations – that would affect the reader viscerally, leaving her trembling, her moral assumptions upended. In contrast, LLMs leach language of pleasure by blandifying it: the algorithm steers language away from the idiosyncratic and toward the predictable.Pleasure isn’t just about hedonism or indulgence in “useless” objects. It is one of the principal ways we, as embodied beings, perceive value. Pain teaches us not to touch the hot stove twice; pleasure guides us toward the sweetness of clean water and fresh air. Pleasure is not infallible: some things that feel good are cruel, addictive, or destructive. But the embodied experience of pleasure is crucial to how we learn and how we make judgments about what is good, beautiful and worth pursuing. These are not judgments we can wisely cede to disembodied machines.“There is no pleasure or pain for an AI, no skin in the game,” the philosopher Carissa Véliz writes in her recent book Prophecy. As a result, an AI “cannot care, and therefore cannot value”. Without some felt relation to pleasure and pain, judgments of value and taste become abstract and bloodless.View image in fullscreenReclaiming everyday pleasuresBecause of its commitment to embodied pleasure, fin-de-siècle decadence offers powerful lessons for the increasingly disembodied, tech-optimised world championed by elites. This is not to suggest, however, that the old decadents were living uncomplicated lives of satisfaction and joy. WB Yeats called the poets of 1890s London “the tragic generation”. The decadents could be moody and morbid, susceptible to ennui, spleen and other Baudelairean ailments. In other words, they were all too human. Some died young, succumbing to alcoholism or tuberculosis; others abandoned the religion of art to join the Catholic church. Fin-de-siècle decadence had, moreover, an aristocratic and misogynistic bent. Many of its most influential English champions were highly educated men who regarded ordinary life with aloofness, even contempt.From the start, however, decadence was both an elite and a minoritarian movement, spearheaded largely by men (and some women) of privilege – but responsible for injecting a new awareness of queerness into public consciousness.Oscar Wilde’s 1890 novel The Picture of Dorian Gray is a story of a thrill-seeker’s descent into decadent squalor – hedonism, moral bankruptcy, irresponsible self-indulgence and the exploitation of others – in the name of never ageing. But when Victorian society raged at Dorian’s monstrosity, Wilde countered that “vice and virtue are to the artist materials for an art” that can reveal humanity to itself. Sure, Dorian was a perverted Peter Pan, a bad boy who didn’t want to grow up and face consequences. But his scandalous romp reflected society’s concealed desires back to itself.In fin-de-siècle decadence, we can also see a growing appreciation of female desire. The 1892 poetry collection Sight and Song by Michael Field – the pen name of two lesbian lovers who wrote as one – turns an explicitly female gaze on the art-historical canon. A poem in response to Leonardo da Vinci’s drawing of Leda, the princess seduced by Zeus in the form of a swan, grants Leda all the power: “She draws the fondled creature to her will.” Their Saint Sebastian is, by contrast, a passive icon of masculine beauty, “with body fresh for use, for pleasure fit, / With its energies and needs together knit”.View image in fullscreenLeda and the Swan, 16th century, attributed to the followers of Leonardo da Vinci.Photograph: Heritage Images/Getty ImagesSo too have Black and postcolonial artists drawn from late-19th-century decadence in asserting their own claims to pleasure. Bruce Nugent’s homoerotic story Smoke, Lilies and Jade (1926), one of the more audacious works of the Harlem Renaissance, opens with the Black hero, Alex, lying on his bed, exhaling blue smoke from a cigarette. Alex idly ponders Wilde’s remark that “a cigarette is the most perfect pleasure because it leaves one unsatisfied” before passing into the streets in search of more gratifying pleasures. He meets a white man he callsBeauty, and the two embrace: Alex “could feel Beauty’s body … close against his … hot … tense … white … and soft”. That sentence’s panting prose gives away the game – Alex knows that enjoying the pleasure forbidden to him is the ultimate decadent act.double quotation markIf a New Decadence is to emerge, we need artists to invent it and individuals to ... appreciate its disruptive energiesAnd now? A renewed, democratic decadence could stage a revolt against optimisation, encouraging ordinary people to brace themselves against the siren simulations of the digital world. Because contemporary culture looks decadent but feels punishing and devoid of meaning, a New Decadence could respond powerfully to this essential contradiction. Every day acts of aesthetic perception – such as Walter Pater stopping traffic to stroke a cat – matter. But if a New Decadence is to emerge, we need artists to invent it and individuals to pause and appreciate its disruptive energies.So far, neodecadent energies in art have been submerged in satirical entertainments about rich people behaving badly – films like Saltburnor TV shows like The White Lotus that reproduce the structure of pleasureless decadence by equating pleasure with status, power and consumption.There are signs, however, of something more original and less reactive emerging, an art that foregrounds the senses for an era that distrusts the body. The sensuous cinema ofPeter Strickland; the frightening but gorgeousblood-coloured sculpturesof Anish Kapoor; the reinvigoration of Black decadence in Shola von Reinhold’s novelLote; the Dionysian reimagining of the fin de siècle in John Corigliano’s operaThe Lord of Cries– none of this amounts to a coherent movement. Yet all these works offer, to their respective artforms, materials from which a New Decadence could arise – a movement that could give pleasure back to people, make the social body’s pulses race again, and force fresh blood through today’s complacent, anemic culture.View image in fullscreenA gallery worker poses with the work Mount Moriah at the Gate of the Ghetto by Anish Kapoor at the Hayward Gallery in London on 15 June 2026.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAWalter Pater prefaced his study of the Renaissance with a sort of epicurean pleasure script, a series of diagnostic questions you can ask yourself to get a better handle on what you experience:What is this song or picture, this engaging personality presented in life or in a book, tome? What effect does it really produce on me? Does it give me pleasure? and if so, what sort or degree of pleasure? How is my nature modified by its presence, and under its influence?Your answers to these questions, he argues, have the virtue of satisfying your soul. Giving your attention to what you are feeling, analyzing your impressions, being moved and attentive to life’s everyday experiences – this is where real pleasure lies, so long as your pleasure harms no one else’s.Why strive for pleasure? Why long for it? Because – contra the Bryan Johnsons of the world – we will die. “A counted number of pulses only,” Pater writes, “is given to us of a variegated, dramatic life.” Like Johnson, like the humanmaxxers, Pater counts his pulses. “Our one chance lies,” he writes, “in expanding that interval, in getting as many pulsations as possible into the given time.”How different Pater’s pulse-counting is from that of the biometric ascetics. Against the pressure to optimise life, decadence issues a different command:feel it.View image in fullscreen.

title: Corporate America may be using AI to cut jobs, but small businesses are using it to keep them | Gene Marks | The Guardian
description: Reports of wide-scale replacement of workers by AI are overblown. Small businesses use it to help workers
Author: Gene Marks
Headline: Reports of wide-scale replacement of workers by AI are overblown. Small businesses use it to help workers
Content: Rather than replacing workers, AI is being used by small businesses to help their employees work better.Photograph: Aitor Diago/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRather than replacing workers, AI is being used by small businesses to help their employees work better.Photograph: Aitor Diago/Getty ImagesReworkedUS small businessCorporate America may be using AI to cut jobs, but small businesses are using it to keep themGene MarksReports of wide-scale replacement of workers by AI are overblown. Small businesses use it to help workersSupported byAbout this contentSun 26 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 08.02 EDTShareIrecently met the owner of a company that sells windows and doors. He told me he invested about $10,000 in anAIapplication that is used by his salespeople in his showroom. The application listens to the conversations between the salesperson and the prospective customer and then automatically creates a quote for the salesperson to review and send.“It allows my salespeople to talk to more customers and spend less time doing paperwork,” he said. “And it cuts down on errors.”Another businessperson I know connected Claude to a folder containing the specifications, manuals, instruction guides, technical sheets and other documentation for the equipment her company sells. She says that her customer-support team can now ask Claude questions on any issue and get quick answers. Her next step is to roll out the platform to her customers.There are many more projects like these under way. Last year, most small businesses were using AI to get answers to questions, review contracts, create policies and rewrite emails. Now they’re starting to move into real-life applications that are showing true return on investment.The AI story on Main Street seems so far to not be mass layoffs. It is exhausted owners using technology to help scarce employees do more work, make fewer mistakes and serve more customers.Why a modest US interest rate rise won’t change much for most businessesRead moreSince mid-2021, theDepartment of Laborhas reported an overall 9% increase – not decrease – of people employed. If you don’t believe the government, then read the numbers from HR and payroll processors such asADP,GustoandPaychex, who all report continued job gains among their customers – especially their smaller customers – during the same period of time. Gusto says that small businesses areexpected to hireabout 974,000 recent grads ages 20 to 24 in the 2026 season, up from 962,000 in 2025. There are almost 7.6mjob openingsthis month, an increase from pre-Covid levels andmost predominantlyat small businesses. Andrecent surveysfromnumerous outletshave found that most small businesses – who employ half of the country’s workers – are not only optimistic about their growth but plan to hire more people in the coming months.AI is not replacing people. And, despite media reports and the warnings from pundits, academics and experts, it’s not going to, at least for small companies. Why?For starters, there just aren’t enough people to do the work that needs to be done. The US workforce is expected tosignificantly decline overthe next decade, thanks to an ageing population and a slowdown in birthrates. Immigrant workers who perform much of our services are in short supply. Robot technology – even if a smaller company could afford them – is years away from installing dishwashers, fixing HVAC systems, laying pipes and putting up drywall. Theconstruction industryis desperate for workers. Business owners now view AI as something that can help their workers do their jobs better while they’re easing into retirement.People also adapt. It’s insulting when those experts say that millions will be unemployed, as if humans will just retreat into their darkened living rooms, collect some form of universal income check and watch Netflix all day. Humans aren’t like that.When the tax code was first released in 1913, there were only a few dozen pages. Todayit’s grownto tens of thousands. Twenty years ago, jobs like “social media manager”, “mobile app developer”, “executive coach”, “SEO specialist” and even “cannabis compliance manager” didn’t even exist. With all the automation and technology around us, how many times do you hear that someone is “slammed” or “hasn’t taken a vacation in years”? People want purpose and want to feel needed. They want to be busy. I believe humans will find plenty of other productive things to do with our time. Maybe therecent surgein entrepreneurship is indicative of that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlso, it’s going to take a while to trust AI. My clients don’t. They don’t believe big tech’s promises that their data is protected and private when we regularly read of breaches and models trained on private information. They wonder if, by using AI platforms, their pricing, costs and other propriety information are being exposed for others to see. They’ve been burned by bugs, errors, shutdowns and disruptions before caused by unreliable technology, and they’re not stupid when today’s big tech companies cover up their tracks by saying these are just “hallucinations”. Please. There’s a long way to go before business owners in particular are going to let some bot process their invoices, collect receivables, interact with irate customers or be responsible for shipping products without human oversight.Finally, big companies can lay off thousands of people without flinching because every big company has bloat. These jobs are generally in PR, marketing, IT and customer service and have always been exposed. Big companies often have entire departments where automation can quickly reduce headcount. Small businesses usually don’t. In a 20-person company, there is rarely much slack. Everyone’s valuable and needs to pull their weight. Like the windows-and-doors guy, they want AI to help their staff to do more in a day so they can stop just surviving and start growing.Yes, technology throughout the years has replaced workers and the AI boom will do the same. Corporate America may use AI to cut jobs. Main Street is more likely to use it to save time, save margins and save the employees it already struggled to find. That is the AI story we should be paying more attention to.Explore more on these topicsUS small businessReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)EntrepreneursUS work & careersSmall businessfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on a US-Saudi nuclear agreement: an offer that further erodes international safeguards | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Even if no reactors are built, Donald Trump’s announcement of a double-standards deal with Riyadh has wrought further damage in a new era of proliferation
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Even if no reactors are built, Donald Trump’s announcement of a double-standards deal with Riyadh has wrought further damage in a new era of proliferation
Content: Donald Trump and Mohammed bin Salman at the White House last November.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Mohammed bin Salman at the White House last November.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersOpinionUS foreign policyThe Guardian view on a US-Saudi nuclear agreement: an offer that further erodes international safeguardsEditorialEven if no reactors are built, Donald Trump’s announcement of a double-standards deal with Riyadh has wrought further damage in a new era of proliferationSun 26 Jul 2026 12.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareEven as he threatened to escalate an unlawful war sold in part as preventing Iran from gaining a nuclear weapon, Donald Trump opened the door to proliferation in the region on Wednesday. The US announced that it hadsigned a dealwith Saudi Arabia which would potentially allow the kingdom to enrich uranium in future and to avoid the fullest inspection rights for the international watchdog.Experts have long warned that a civilian nuclear programme could create a path towards a nuclear-armed Riyadh. Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince and de facto leader, hassaidthat if Tehran gets a nuclear weapon, “we will have to get one”. Concerns are magnified by the agreement’s terms. Washington previously argued that the “gold standard” was theUnited Arab Emirates’ agreementto permanently forgo enrichment and accept full monitoring by the UN’s International Atomic Energy Agency. Weakening it sets a precedent that Russia or China could also cite in nuclear deals in future.The turmoil that Mr Trump has created in the Middle East is encouraging governments both to hedge their bets and to tool up. The USpaused attackson Iran at the weekend, after 13 successive days of strikes, amid reports that it is concerned about declining interceptor stockpiles, but no exit is in sight. As António Guterres, the UN secretary general,saidon Thursday, the region “is teetering on the edge of [the] unimaginable … One crisis feeds another. One escalation triggers the next.”View image in fullscreenAntónio Guterres.Photograph: Omar Sanadiki/APGulf statespremised their securityon American-guaranteed order. But Benjamin Netanyahu’sstrike on Hamas leaders in Qatar last yearshowed that the US shield would not protect them from Israel (itself anundeclared nuclear power). The reckless war on Iran has made US military presence an invitation to damage. Washington may be looking to bind Riyadh closer with a reactor deal, though the billions of dollars involved is probably a bigger incentive for Mr Trump. The crumbling of the region’s internal architecture – most visibly with the UAE’s departure from Opec – adds to the dangers of proliferation. Players are acting less predictably.The US president threw the Saudi deal into doubt within hours by declaring it contingent on Riyadh recognisingIsrael. That had long been a precondition for an agreement, but Israel’s war of annihilation in Gaza has shored up the Saudi position that recognition cannot happen without a Palestinian state. Yet even if no reactors are built, the announcement itself acts as legitimation of and encouragement for the pursuit of nuclear capabilities by others. Negotiations produced an Obama-era nuclear deal with which Tehran complied – until Mr Trump trashed the agreement. His war appears to have produced a more aggressive, risk-taking Iranian regime, as foretold; further military action is more likely to spur than end nuclear threat. The prospect of Riyadh acquiring a bomb is further encouragement.Look further afield. The last US-Russia nuclear arms control treatyexpiredin February. China israpidly expandingits arsenal. Asian and European states which counted on the US nuclear umbrella prior to Mr Trump are discussing acquiring or enhancing their own capabilities. Most of them at least understand that diplomacy, multilateralism and global standards are a better choice than a race for the bomb. Mr Trump does not believe in international institutions. But upholding existing nuclear safeguards would be in US interests too as we enter a new age of proliferation.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyOpinionSaudi ArabiaDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsMiddle East and north AfricaIraneditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Pitt is powerful – but it’s the rawness of The Bear that truly portrays hospital work | Seema Jilani | The Guardian
description: Both restaurant work and medicine involve abusive training and relentless devotion to minutiae – and the joy of offering comfort
Author: Seema Jilani
Headline: Both restaurant work and medicine involve abusive training and relentless devotion to minutiae – and the joy of offering comfort
Content: ‘The Bear captures the intimacy of a shared language and bodily familiarity unspoken amongst both doctors and chefs.’Photograph: FXView image in fullscreen‘The Bear captures the intimacy of a shared language and bodily familiarity unspoken amongst both doctors and chefs.’Photograph: FXOpinionDoctorsThe Pitt is powerful – but it’s the rawness of The Bear that truly portrays hospital workSeema JilaniBoth restaurant work and medicine involve abusive training and relentless devotion to minutiae – and the joy of offering comfortSun 26 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.05 EDTShareIpass a mother heaving in grief while her son’s heart monitors flatline. It is the last time she will ever hold his hand. For me, this is another day on call in the intensive care unit as a pediatric physician. For her, this is the day her life shatters.Later that night, a striking, charismatic surgeon from work treats me to an exquisite meal. Served outside a trailer, humidity barreling through our scrubs, the food is neither extravagant nor decadent. It is, however, the most succulent Texas barbecue brisket I will ever taste. This is the night I rest my head on his shoulder and he doesn’t flinch. This is the night an “us” was born.A shared humanity links doctors and chefs. We both craft life’s most tender moments. Some will ricochet off your brain for years, dull with ache. Others will leave you heady, craving more. The television seriesThe Pitthas garnered well-deserved praise for its excellent depiction of an emergency room staff battling insurance companies, mass shootings and mental health crises. In fact, I was one of many healthcare providers who shared my insight for The Pitt, andconsulted to help craft narrativestrue to reality, so I deeply respect its advocacy for destigmatizing mental healthcare for physicians.And yet, I have never been more convinced thatThe Bearis actually the reigning television show for accuracy in its depiction of hospital medicine. From the delayed gratification of abusive, humiliating training to the chaotic intensity of its work-hard-play-hard ethos, training for chefs is, in many ways, comparable to physician pedagogy. Both professions spend infinite hours mastering minutiae no one will ever discern. Both lose themselves in the relentless pursuit of precision, and in their dedication to service, an art form few will appreciate.double quotation markBoth professions spend infinite hours mastering minutiae no one will ever discernWe inhabit two of the last true apprenticeships, marred by years of exploitation, insults and chronic sleep deprivation. It is the perfect recipe for both professions to suffer from disproportionately higher rates of depression, anxiety, addiction, and even suicide. OnThe Bear, Jeremy Allen White’s Carmy once described his former boss at an elite restaurant as: “Very, probably, mentally ill. Dead inside. Cold. Never turns it off. Accomplishes more by 10am than most people do in a lifetime. I don’t think he sleeps. I don’t think he eats. I don’t think he loves.” Ask any doctor about their most feared mentor in residency, and they’d sputter these words out with the same cadence.In one scene, this boss berates his employees for their slowness and orders them to repeat: “Chef, I’m so tough,” while he taunts: “You are not tough ... You are talentless … You should be dead.”It brought to mind the first day of gross anatomy class in medical school. One of our professors joked that if we were to attempt suicide, as many doctors do, that we should at least not shame the profession by surviving. They would gladly show us on a cadaver how to “do it right” so at least we weren’t total failures.We – doctors and chefs - dissolve into our professions chasing illusions of perfection. For me, it is the chance to save your life or to assuage your pain. For a chef, it is the hope that the couple who got engaged at his restaurant retells their proposal story breathlessly for years to come, that he enshrined that memory with the tenderness it deserves.WhileThe Pittis what you might desire from your ideal physician, it’s the frenetic back-of-the-house pulsing turbulence in The Bear that I recognize. The audience gets glimpses of the staff’s camaraderie, which, similar to hospitals, is airtight. These are the only people who truly comprehend the grueling mess it takes to make this look this easy.My patient’s near-death experience in hospital left me with worry and guilt. This is how vicarious trauma starts | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreI remember one night in the ER, a child had been brutally beaten and was dead on arrival. I meticulously washed matted blood from her hair, cloaked her in a hospital blanket and tried to restore some of her dignity. I gave her body, cradled, to her mother, where she lay one last time. And then I hurried along. My next patient was already angry about the wait. This is the raw reality that public-facing professions grapple with. Whether we are wearing scrubs or chef’s uniforms, we serve as punching bags; society has license to exorcise its demons onto us.But The Bear is not only an exacting look in the mirror – not just the mental health woes, not just life’s most dramatic days. It is also a celebration of the joy of the ordinary, luxuriating in the perfect bite. The Bear gets even the most cynical of us to revel in the purest of humanity: offering comfort to another human, hoping that our presence will make their pain more bearable in some way. We show up for life’s most gutting times, but also at its most promising: the moment a baby’s first cry reverberates, or just as the candlelight across the table flickers ever so gently. Food, when done right, offers healing too.The Bear also captures the intimacy of a shared language and bodily familiarity unspoken amongst both doctors and chefs. After working decades alongside one another at godforsaken hours of the night, we know each other’s eyebrow arch. We recognize a vocal tremor infinitesimally longer than it should be. We pick each other up when we fail. We have no choice. It’s a bond borne of collective fatigue, and one of sharing abject frustration and sacred silences in the same day.As for my handsome surgeon, he would later ask me to meet him at a Michelin starred restaurant. I would get my hair done and wear lace. An hour and two glasses into the evening, I would take off my heels as the waiter asked me if I wanted to call it a night. I don’t remember much about that relationship, unceremoniously pronounced dead when he stood me up that night. But I will never bid goodbye to the exquisite flavor of that Texas brisket, which remains a glimmer of magnificence in an otherwise harrowing day. My memories return far more to the taste of that barbecue than to the taste of his kiss, so all things considered? Worth it.Seema Jilani is a pediatric hospitalist who has treated critically ill children on medical evacuation flights. Her humanitarian work has taken her to Afghanistan, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Ukraine, Bosnia, Gaza and the West Bank, and on refugee rescue boats off the coast of Libya. Her radio documentary, Israel and Palestine: The Human Cost of the Occupation, was nominated for the Peabody AwardIn the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. You can also reach Crisis Text Line by texting MHA to 741741. In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978Explore more on these topicsDoctorsOpinionThe PittUS healthcareThe BearUS work & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: From the strait of Hormuz to the North Sea, a global maritime war rages around us – and more than the price of oil is at stake | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: The collapse of the rules-based order is not confined to the land: we’re imperilled as centuries of maritime cooperation sink beneath the waves, says foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: The collapse of the rules-based order is not confined to the land: we’re imperilled as centuries of maritime cooperation sink beneath the waves, says foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: The Russian frigate Admiral Grigorovich off the coast of Tartus, Syria, September 2024.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenThe Russian frigate Admiral Grigorovich off the coast of Tartus, Syria, September 2024.Photograph: APOpinionStrait of HormuzFrom the strait of Hormuz to the North Sea, a global maritime war rages around us – and more than the price of oil is at stakeSimon TisdallThe collapse of the rules-based order is not confined to the land: we’re imperilled as centuries of maritime cooperation sink beneath the wavesSun 26 Jul 2026 07.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 12.47 EDTShareThe US military campaign to protect merchant shipping from Iranian attacks by asserting direct maritime control in the strait of Hormuz is not an idea unique to Donald Trump’s administration. Almost exactly 200 years ago, in the period 1825-27, a powerful US naval squadron led by Commodore John Rodgers was sent to the Mediterraneanto defend American shipsfrom the depredations of Greek corsairs and pirates.For all the new-minted republic’s brave talk of liberty, the US squadron did not assist Greece’s ongoing “regime change” struggle for independence from the Ottoman empire. Its sole, self-serving purpose was to defend US trade, markets and business interests. After abandoning his call for apeople’s revolution in Tehran, this, too, is what Trump’s reckless war with Iran has now boiled down to.Although the US has not ratified the 1982 UN convention on the law of the sea, which establishes a legal right of freedom of passage without interference by littoral states, it has historically upheld the principle of freedom of navigation ormare liberum(the free sea) developed by Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist. Rejecting Iran’s claims, Marco Rubio, US secretary of state,declared in Junethat “no country is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway”.Yet Trump has since suggested the US itself may yet do exactly that and impose tolls. Although helater rowed back, last month’s “memorandum of understanding” with Iran accepts that it has a right, with Oman, to monetise transit through the strait of Hormuz. Despite the resumption of US attacks and Trump’sincreasingly hysterical threats, the MOU currently remains the only basis for a future peace deal.Two-faced Trump’s equivocal stance reflects a wider breakdown in the “free sea” consensus underpinning maritime law – and hastens the overall degradation of the international rules-based order. Trump believes nation states (or at least the US) have an absolute right to act unilaterally in their own interests, unconstrained by laws, treaties or regard for the “global commons” of the high seas.The destabilising ramifications of this approach, emulated by other countries,grow clearer by the day. This new 21st-century war of the sea does not involve titanic clashes between Bismarck-class battleships or huge naval showdowns such as Jutland and Midway. But its frontlines are the same as ever: defence, security, borders, free trade, money, power.Today’s war of the sea has many aspects. One is the spreading impact of precedents set by the Hormuz standoff. In Yemen, Iran-aligned Houthi militias have begun a copycat blockade of the Bab al-Mandab strait, at the mouth of the Red Sea, in reprisal, they claim, for attacks by Saudi Arabia. Two oil tankerswere struck this week, further spooking energy markets and presaging wider escalation.Also potentially fatal for international norms is the post-Hormuz debate in Indonesia about imposingtolls in the strait of Malacca, through which 22% of global maritime shipping passes. Might Turkey adopt the US-Iran approach and charge for passage through the Bosphorus? Or Spain in the strait of Gibraltar? The dire implications for global trade and supply chains are obvious. About80% of goodstraded worldwide by volume go by sea.Friction over seaborne trade aside, overt maritime clashes between regional rivals are increasing, particularly in theSouth China Seaand the waters around Taiwan. Expansionist China’s creation of artificial, militarised islands on obscure reefs and sporadic confrontations with neighbours such as the Philippines are the root cause. Like the US, Beijing rejects international law when it doesn’t suit it – notably the 2016 ruling by the permanent court of arbitration, which found its claim to sovereignty over most of the South China Sealacked a legal basis.China crossed another red line last week when one of its missile destroyersundertook a live-fire drillinside Japan’s exclusive economic zone, about 180km (110 miles) from Okinotori, Japan’s southernmost island. Tokyo and Beijing have longstanding maritime disputes. But tensions rose sharply after Japan’s new prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, suggested a Chinese bid to seize Taiwan could trigger a Japanese military response. Few weeks go by without reports of Chinese air and sea exercises in preparation for a not-so-hypothetical amphibious assault on Taiwan.The fact a Russian frigate accompanied the offending Chinese warship off Japan points to another major actor in the global war of the sea. Vladimir Putin’s once-vaunted Black Sea fleet hassuffered severe losses, caused by Ukraine’s missiles and drones, since 2022. Its ships no longer control the Black Sea, mostly cowering in port. As if to compensate, hybrid “grey zone” Russian military maritime operations against Ukraine’s European alliesare expanding. Baltic undersea pipelines and communications cables have proven vulnerable targets.Russia has also stepped up surface fleet and submarine activities in the North Atlantic approaches, the North Sea and the Channel, where it is suspected of mapping underwater infrastructure with a view to future sabotage. Last Monday, one of its warshipswent a step further, marking Andy Burnham’s first day as UK prime minister with a rare live-fire drill 70kn (45 miles) south of Plymouth, home of the Royal Navy.It was the latest in a string of hostile actions designed to provoke, intimidate and test British and European defences. Last month, a Russian frigatefired warning shotsnear a private yacht off the Isle of Wight. The incident seems trivial until it is set in the wider context of a rapidly building Nato-Russia at-sea confrontation. Then it begins to look scary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe sense of increasing inter-state maritime lawlessness is fed by numerous other recent incidents, such as the unlawful USsinking of an Iranian warshipoff Sri Lanka in March, last week’sbitter clashbetween Chinese and Philippine ships, Trump’s revived threats to forcibly annex the Danish-owned island of Greenland and his bombing of civilian boats off Venezuela. A Chinese nuclear submarine test-fired along-range ballistic missilein the South Pacific this month to the outrage of Australia, which is itselfacquiring nuclear-powered subs.US submarine sinks Iranian warship near coast of Sri Lanka – videoAll this instability is fuelling anaccelerating global arms race. Little wonder Burnham’s revamped government faces pressure togreatly increase defence spending, especially on the badly depleted Royal Navy. Current UK plans include upgrades to the Trident at-sea nuclear deterrent.This many-fronted war of the sea tells a bigger story still: of how centuries-old, hard-won maritime cooperation and collaboration protocols are breaking down, of how international legal norms and rules – whether the issue is free trade, offshore defence, sovereignty, borders, fisheries, deep-sea mining or environmental pollution – are sinking beneath the waves.It’s a story about a world where one country can impose its will on others less powerful and less wealthy, rather than seeking their agreement; where the fundamental concept of global commons or shared space is shot to hell. It’s about Lord Palmerston-style gunboat diplomacy writ large. It’s about a world all at sea.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzOpinionChinaRussiaMilitaryAsia PacificDonald TrumpRoyal NavycommentShareReuse this content

title: How do we defeat authoritarianism? By building a sense of belonging | Julie Fernandes and Katrina Gamble | The Guardian
description: Eighty-five million Americans are disaffected and less likely to vote, our survey found. Our democratic revival depends on a sense of community
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Eighty-five million Americans are disaffected and less likely to vote, our survey found. Our democratic revival depends on a sense of community
Content: ‘They want to see progress on issues they care about. They just don’t see the connection between voting and making their lives better.’Photograph: Eric Risberg/APView image in fullscreen‘They want to see progress on issues they care about. They just don’t see the connection between voting and making their lives better.’Photograph: Eric Risberg/APOpinionActivismHow do we defeat authoritarianism? By building a sense of belongingJulie Fernandes and Katrina GambleEighty-five million Americans are disaffected and less likely to vote, our survey found. Our democratic revival depends on a sense of communitySun 26 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 13.37 EDTShareOur country is at a crossroads between democracy and authoritarianism. And the only antidote is an organized, engaged citizenry. But at this critical moment when we need people to lean into the fight for our future, we find that far too many people have given up.In acomprehensive, multiracial study, Sojourn Strategies, Ariel Research Partners and Richard Shafranekfoundthat 35% of the US electorate – 85 million people – are disaffected, characterized by high levels of disillusionment and low levels of trust in government and politics. Our democratic revival depends on solutions that transform people from disaffected bystanders into powerful civic agents.The desire for community is where we find hope. Almost six in 10 of the disaffected (58%) would like to feel more connected to other people. These feelings provide organizers with an opening to invite new people into community where they can build a sense of belonging and develop collective agency. The research also shows that the disaffected electorate is reachable: they are more likely to act when they feel like they belong and can see the tangible impact of their actions.Americans declared independence from a tyrant once. And we must do that again | Claire FinkelsteinRead moreThe disaffected electorate is the same as the overall population as far as race, ethnicity and gender – although disaffected people tend to be younger, have fewer resources and are less likely to be college educated. What surprised us in the research was the finding that the disaffected are as civically engaged as the general population, with the exception of voting. Disaffected people have almost the same likelihood to talk to a friend or a family member about a political issue (61% of the overall population and 60% of the disaffected electorate) or to search online for information about politics (both at 42%). Yet while 65% of the overall population would vote if the midterm elections were held today, only 56% of disaffected voters say the same.Most institutions, including the traditional political industry, write these folks off as apathetic. But the research shows something very different. They care a great deal about their families, neighbors and communities. They want to see progress on issues they care about. They just don’t see the connection between voting and making their lives better.So, what is going on? A common thread within this group of disaffected people is that they are extremely isolated with no or few friends or organizational affiliations. Almost half (49%) do not belong to an online community, church, mosque or synagogue or other religious groups, a community or political group, a labor union, or other community spaces. But collective spaces that we call“civic homes”are where people develop a sense of belonging and agency that is critical to their belief in the power of voting to drive change. Thus, investment in the organizing groups that operate as civic homes is a critical solution to our current democratic crisis.Civic homes are developed by organizers as places where people can meet each other, feel seen and heard, work together on issues that matter to them, experience concrete benefits and make life better for themselves and the people they care about. Our research shows that even small increases in feelings of belonging within a civic home are associated with significant increases in voting and taking other civic and political actions.Take Angeles in Nevada, for example. She was working long hours as a car wash supervisor, earning wages that never seemed to stretch far enough. Every month, she wondered whether her family would be able to cover rent. A few years ago, an organizer with Make the Road Nevada invited Angeles to a monthly membership meeting. During the discussion, Angeles heard her neighbors sharing similar struggles such as difficulties in making rent, stagnant wages, lack of affordable childcare and a feeling that those in power were not listening. This experience made Angeles feel seen and she began to develop a sense of belonging. She got connected to Make the Road Nevada’s Know Your Rights workshops, which helped her learn about the voting process and made her feel included. This year, Angeles will cast her first ballot as a US citizen. Not because a candidate’s campaign finally reached her. But because her people did.Shared culture creates a feeling of belonging. Familiar food, language, music and even games are what make people feel at home. For example, a non-profit called Power Interfaith is running an innovative Soul Food Dinners program in Pennsylvania. These are nonjudgmental spaces where young, disaffected Black people, especially young men, can have honest conversations about their lives and visions of the future over a meal. Part of the focus is on young Black men who are skeptical about civic engagement and voting, but guided by their faith – a group that is undiscovered and under-researched.The Soul Food Dinner project is similar to Georgia Alliance’s We the People initiative, which hosted intergenerational conversations among younger and older Black people as a strategy for rebuilding a sense of agency and belonging across differences. Older participants often arrived believing young people were disengaged or apathetic, while younger participants frequently viewed older generations as dismissive, out of touch or unwilling to share power. The series created opportunities for participants to ask deeper questions, listen to one another’s lived experiences and recognize shared values beneath different forms of expression. As participants moved beyond stereotypes, the emotional ground softened for collaboration, curiosity and mutual respect. Pre- and post-event feelings of power increased on both sides of the conversations, a measure that correlates to voter turnout in the Black community.In the state next door, game facilitators with North Carolina Asian Americans Together are hosting Mahjong nights with communal hotpot meals for people in their late teens and 20s. The young people who come feel disconnected from traditional politics, but care very much about the cost of living, immigration, healthcare and making life better for their communities. The blend of familiar foods, games and conversations create connections and make people feel comfortable before they are invited into civic engagement, such as registering to vote or attending an organizing meeting.Building trust and belonging that allows people to be transformed into civic agents is deep relational work. And it takes time. But the payoff is powerful. Transactional civic engagement aimed at a discrete outcome is a quick hit, like a sugar rush: it might feel great in the moment, but the long-term effect is weak and empty. Working to support people to become powerful civic actors through belonging and collective agency results in strong, durable architects of a hopeful future.What’s giving us hope nowThe stories of everyday people across the US standing up, getting organized and driving change to make life better for themselves, their families, and their communities is a tremendous source of hope. TakeElnora Gavin in Benton Harbor, Michigan. Working with a local civic organization, We the People Michigan, she organized a base of supporters and won $114m in school debt relief for majority-Black school districts in her state.And she is not alone. More and more people in communities are using organizing strategies to buildpowerful civic homesthat can be containers for people-driven collective action. In these turbulent times, people are choosing to lean into people-centered organizations and movements where they can find belonging, develop collective agency and make a better future possible.Julie Fernandes is managing director of the Democracy & Power Innovation Fund, a community of organizers, researchers and funders who are working together to strengthen state-based community organizing, and associate director of the Rockefeller Family FundKatrina Gamble, PhD, is founder and CEO of Sojourn Strategies, a Black woman-owned social impact consulting firm that brings a people-centered approach to advocacy campaigns, research and philanthropic advisingExplore more on these topicsActivismOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: An act of kindness, or mitzvah, teaches us to be part of something bigger than ourselves | Nomi Kaltmann | The Guardian
description: More than anything, I want my kids to grow into people who notice others and who care about the world around them
Author: Nomi Kaltmann
Headline: More than anything, I want my kids to grow into people who notice others and who care about the world around them
Content: Composite: Nenov/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Nenov/Getty ImagesMaking sense of itJudaismAn act of kindness, or mitzvah, teaches us to be part of something bigger than ourselvesNomi KaltmannMore than anything, I want my kids to grow into people who notice others and who care about the world around themMaking sense of itis a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday lifeSun 26 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 18.59 EDTShareSeveral times a week, I write small notes on pretty stationery for my three-year-old daughter to take to kinder the next day.Sometimes the note is about how she shared a toy with a sibling, other times it is about how she helped someone without being asked. Often it is praising her for saying thank you or please.In our family, we call themmitzvahnotes.The Hebrew word mitzvah is often translated as a good deed but perhaps the best way to describe a mitzvah is an intentional act of goodness and kindness.AI claims to have the answers to life’s big questions. But sometimes not knowing brings us closer to the truth | Amy GallifordRead moreMy daughter proudly takes her mitzvah notes to kinder, where her teacher reads them out loud to the whole class. The notes are then pinned to a wall filled with other children’s mitzvah notes, celebrating the good deeds of her three-year-old peers.So, while other children covet stickers or prizes, my daughter is thrilled when she gets a mitzvah note and loves it when she has one to take to school.As a parent, I spend a lot of time thinking about what values I want to pass on to my kids. Of course, I want my children to be capable and confident, and I want them to work hard and develop resilience. But more than anything, I want them to grow into people who notice others and who care about the world around them. I want them to understand that even the smallest acts of goodness and kindness can have a ripple effect far beyond what we can ever see.There is a verse in the Bible, in the Book of Proverbs, that says: “Train a child according to their path, and even when they are old, they will not depart from it.”I have always loved this quote, because to me it represents the idea that children grow into the identities we help them see in themselves.When I want my children to help clean up their rooms and they are feeling particularly reluctant, instead of focusing on what they are not doing, I usually try to say something like, “I love when you help Mummy clean up your room.”By framing the request like this, I am reminding them of who I think they are. That as their mum, I see them as someone who helps, someone who cares and someone who tries to do the right thing.This is what makes mitzvah notes so powerful. They are not just about praising a single action; they build a mindset where children want to be noticed for the good deeds that they do. They encourage children to look outward rather than inward and they teach every human that they are part of something bigger than themselves.After the Bondi terror attack, many people were left asking what they could do in the face of such darkness.This ancient Jewish tradition brings me closer to my faith and invites me to imagine a better worldRead moreOne response was a renewed focus on acts of kindness, and with consultation from the Jewish community, anational dayto performmitzvotwas announced for people of all faiths to try to bring more light into the world. Across Australia, people volunteered at soup kitchens, cleaned beaches, visited elderly people in nursing homes and found small ways to be kind to others.None of those acts could undo the tragedy that occurred but they reflected a belief that darkness spreads when people withdraw from one another, while goodness grows when people choose to do small acts of goodness and kindness for each other.And perhaps that is why I love mitzvah notes so much.They are small notes, jotted down in a minute or less, yet they carry a much bigger message. They tell a child, “I saw what you did, and I love that you are doing small acts of kindness,” and they encourage them to continue doing small acts of goodness and kindness.And if enough children grow up believing that being kind and thoughtful is part of who they are, then perhaps those small notes are doing far more than recognising a good deed. Perhaps they are helping raise the sort of people our world needs right now.Nomi Kaltmann is an Australian lawyer and journalist. She is a proud member of Melbourne’s Jewish communityExplore more on these topicsJudaismMaking sense of itReligionParents and parentingAustralian educationChildrenFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: Am I a chicken-shop lefty? Here’s what a French fast food row taught me about politics | Coco Khan | The Guardian
description: Feathers are flying over the halal chicken chain Master Poulet opening a branch in gentrified Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine – it’s an issue of wealth and class we know only too well, says writer and podcaster Coco Khan
Author: Coco Khan
Headline: Feathers are flying over the halal chicken chain Master Poulet opening a branch in gentrified Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine – it’s an issue of wealth and class we know only too well, says writer and podcaster Coco Khan
Content: The Master Poulet rotisserie in Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine, near Paris.Photograph: Apaydin Alain/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Master Poulet rotisserie in Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine, near Paris.Photograph: Apaydin Alain/ABACA/ShutterstockOpinionFranceAm I a chicken-shop lefty? Here’s what a French fast food row taught me about politicsCoco KhanFeathers are flying over the halal chicken chain Master Poulet opening a branch in gentrified Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine – it’s an issue of wealth and class we know only too wellSun 26 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareHow do you like your progressive politics? Are you net-zero left or anti-identity politics left? A “legalising drugs” kind of radical or someone whose public sector solidarity includes police? Nato or Nat-no?The reputation for infighting in lefty spaces – where policy disagreements harden into personal tests of morality – needs neither introduction nor encouragement.But reading about the left-on-left battle at Master Poulet, a French chicken chain that just opened its first UK branch, I found myself mulling a question that felt more than a little personal: am I chicken shop left?OK, OK, this might just be ameproblem. I’ve always had an interest in chicken shops. Maybe it’s personal: chicken shops, offering cheap halal takes on mainstream fare, have long been a pursuit of south Asian immigrants who hoped, like my own family, for a better life in this brave new world (talk about a wing and a prayer). But they are also bound up in Black British youth culture: neighbourhood incubators for music, affordable places to hang, landmarks of “the ends”. Chicken shops tell the story of a mixed, working-class Britain, with all its whimsy.Populism unites Le Pen and Farage. But she is a step closer to powerRead moreThere’sMorris CassanovaAKA “Mr Chicken”, the late graphic designer who claimed to have designed 90% of the chicken shop signs in London. Or just the sheer nerve of the Americana. I still chuckle whenever I pass a Dixy Chicken, imagining what the Confederate south might think of a halal business from Solihull bearing its name. Add the peri boom, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s hit YouTube channelChicken Shop Dateand Rishi Sunak discussing his Nando’s order (“It’s good broccoli,” he said), and the chicken shop’s modern cultural legacy is something to crow about.Anyway, back to the boeuf–sorry, I mean poulet – in France. Back in April, Karim Bouamrane, the Socialist party (PS) mayor of Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine, near Paris,tried to block a Master Poulet branchthat had opened outside the town hall. Literally, with concrete blocks at the doors. A court ordered them removed, so he swapped them for giant colourful plant pots. The shop responded withquippy signs(“we are open … no offence to Karim”, read one), delighting French social media with this meta game of chicken. Bouamrane insisted it was all about quality of life, as late deliveries and cooking smells disturbed residents. Not everyone was convinced.Saint-Ouen has transformed in recent years, not least due toregeneration pegged to the Paris Olympics. Critics accuse the mayor of overseeing a gentrification drive that has seen property prices surge, arguingthat’shis real issue: he wants to chase out cheap food (and the sorts of people who eat it). Master Poulet serves a drumstick of rotisserie chicken and potatoes for €4 (£3.40) – cheaper than a McDonald’s and probably no less healthy, yet McDonald’s is not a target. And given the tradition of rotisserie chicken in France, you do have to ask whatexactlyit is about the halal version that prompts complaints about bad odours.Which may explain why politicians from the further-left LaFranceInsoumise (LFI), have waded in, questioning whether Islamophobia and classism are at play, and accusing the mayor of abusing his power. One MP visited the shop in solidarity. His name? Éric Coquerel. I’ll just leave that there.To be clear, I am far from an expert on French politics. The last time I thought much about the LFI and PS was in 2024, when they joined forces in the Nouveau Front Populaire (NFP) to hold back Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally. It worked, prompting many of us in the UK to ask, with Nigel Farage tipped for No 10, shouldn’t we – red, green, yellow or bin – be doing the same?Bouamrane announced last month he would berunning for president. But as I pecked at pommes frites on a warm London evening, it was hard to see how that successful arrangement of NFP could happen again. Bouamrane has since called LFI a colonialist party, for undermining French republicanism with its talk of race; while allegations of racism from LFI continue. Meanwhile, opinion polls put Le Penon trackfor presidential glory.
