What leaves me crestfallen (at this point the puns are involuntary) isn’t the disagreement but what it heralds.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo am I part of the chicken shop left? I don’t know, maybe. But perhaps that’s the wrong question. After the almighty flap over Master Poulet, I’m left feeling that politics should be less “ruling the roost” and more “birds of a feather”. Especially with a far-right fox prowling outside the henhouse.Coco Khan is a freelance writer and co-host of the politics podcast Pod Save the UKDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsFranceOpinionFast foodEuropeFoodcommentShareReuse this content

title: Always remember how Macquarie built its millionaires on outrageous tolls and charges  | John Quiggin | The Guardian
description: As Shemara Wikramanayake retires with shares worth hundreds of millions, the public is left counting the cost of high prices for utilities, roads and airports
Author: John Quiggin
Headline: As Shemara Wikramanayake retires with shares worth hundreds of millions, the public is left counting the cost of high prices for utilities, roads and airports
Content: Outgoing Macquarie boss Shemara Wikramanayake is leaving after nearly 40 years at the ‘millionaires’ factory’.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenOutgoing Macquarie boss Shemara Wikramanayake is leaving after nearly 40 years at the ‘millionaires’ factory’.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersOpinionBankingAlways remember how Macquarie built its millionaires on outrageous tolls and chargesJohn QuigginAs Shemara Wikramanayake retires with shares worth hundreds of millions, the public is left counting the cost of high prices for utilities, roads and airportsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSat 25 Jul 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 23.58 EDTShareThe recent retirement of the Macquarie Group CEO, Shemara Wikramanayake, marks the culmination of a highly successful career. She is leaving the company with shares worth hundreds of millions of dollars after nearly 40 years at the Sydney-based institution. Under her leadership, the “millionaires’ factory” has increased its annual revenue by about 80% and nearly doubled its profit.Wikramanayake has also overseen and consolidated the group’s transition from a firm specialising in privatised infrastructure to a global merchant bank earning profits from commodity trading, specialist asset finance and wealth management.Macquarie shareholders, who have tripled their money over the past eight years (with dividends and capital gains), have plenty of reason to be grateful.The public, in Australia and elsewhere, may take a slightly more jaundiced view. The foundations of the millionaires’ factory were laid through a string of private infrastructure deals that greatly enriched Macquarie while delivering expensive or substandard services.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe biggest disaster of all has been Thames Water,privatisedby the Thatcher government in the UK and acquired by a Macquarie-led consortium in 2006. After extractingbillions in dividendsforitself and other investors, and loading the company with debt, Macquarie sold out in 2017. By that time, the utility’s performance was so dire as to be unsalvageable. Nearly a decade later, the UK government is still grappling with the choice between an unpalatable renationalisation and a hybrid model that is likely to prove unworkable.In June, Andy Burnhamcalled forpublic ownership at Thames Water. As parts of Wales are in drought and the rest of the country is experiencing prolonged dry conditions, about 23 million people across the UKare undera hosepipe ban.Another example worth mentioning is the privatisation of Sydney airport to a Macquarie-led consortium, which promptly raised a wide range of fees and charges. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has repeatedly concluded that the airport is a monopoly and that price monitoring is ineffectual. The issue was predictable – and predicted.Macquarie was also a pioneer of the private toll road industry, which has left Australian cities saddled with costly transport systems, characterised in the words of areview of the Sydney toll-road systemas a “poorly-functioning patchwork”. International deals such asOntario’s Highway 407were even worse for the public, though highly successful for Macquarie’s millionaires.Macquarie Group is not the only corporate giant built on lucrative deals with the public. CSL, one of Australia’s most valuable companies, was created by the privatisation of the Commonwealth Serum Laboratories, which had produced a wide range of innovations. The privatised CSL was awarded a long-term contract to supply products derived from blood plasma at a far higher cost.The resulting cashflow was ploughed into aglobal acquisition programthat made CSL the giant it is today. Meanwhile, research on commercially less attractive products such as antivenoms and vaccines for tropical diseases was scaled down, abandoned or left to universities and public research institutes.Other privatisations have followed a similar pattern of rhetoric about private sector efficiency combined with continued public largesse. Qantas has enjoyed the favoured treatment of a national flag carrier while disclaiming their obligations to either the travelling public or its own employees, beyond those dictated by profit maximisation.Telstraforced us to buy back, at massive expense, the telephone network built under public ownership and sold only a few years previously.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf there is any consolation here, it is that (long after the public) policymakers have finally woken up to the damage done by these deals. Not so long ago, Infrastructure Australia was proclaiming the benefits of innovative finance and universities were offering courses in “financial engineering”. Today these terms are rightly viewed with suspicion. As the UK commentatorAnthony Hilton wroteafter the crash of Carillion (a major participant in private finance initiatives):double quotation markIts demise is also the consequence of the relentless application of a neo-liberal political philosophy that for years has elevated financial engineering above real engineering; off-balance-sheet finance above paying for things openly; and lauded the private sector above the public sector.Ordinary people can express respect for the achievements of Shemara Wikramanayake at Macquarie Group. But every time you pay a toll or an outrageous airport parking charge, remember that the millionaires’ factory was built from the proceeds of charges like these.John Quiggin is a professor at the University of Queensland’s School of EconomicsExplore more on these topicsBankingOpinionAustralian economyThames WaterQantasTelstracommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Andy Burnham can grow a moustache!’: SNL UK’s Paddy Young on breakout stardom – and impersonating the new PM | Saturday Night Live | The Guardian
description: Not even a grisly hand injury could halt the rise of the Saturday Night Live UK comedian. And soon he’ll get to parody the prime minister every week. So why can’t he enjoy the good times?
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: Not even a grisly hand injury could halt the rise of the Saturday Night Live UK comedian. And soon he’ll get to parody the prime minister every week. So why can’t he enjoy the good times?
Content: Paddy Young … ‘I sort of feel like a 68-year-old bloke – like it’s all gone to pot’.Photograph: Sophie GiddonsView image in fullscreenPaddy Young … ‘I sort of feel like a 68-year-old bloke – like it’s all gone to pot’.Photograph: Sophie GiddonsSaturday Night LiveInterview‘Andy Burnham can grow a moustache!’: SNL UK’s Paddy Young on breakout stardom – and impersonating the new PMRachel AroestiNot even a grisly hand injury could halt the rise of the Saturday Night Live UK comedian. And soon he’ll get to parody the prime minister every week. So why can’t he enjoy the good times?Sun 26 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe day before I’m supposed to watch Paddy Young perform a work-in-progress version of his new show Will Sir Be Laughing Alone?, I’m told the gig has been cancelled; the standup has sliced his hand open and is about to have surgery. Soon after, Young shares aphoto of himself on Instagramin a hospital gown, thanking the Australian comedian Sam Campbell for “bringing the sword to my home” – a post quickly rehashed by the tabloids (The Mirror: “SNL UK star Paddy Young hospitalised after samurai sword accident”). When I finally see him on stage a fortnight later, he’s dosed up on codeine, his arm is in a sling and he’s in the uncertain early stages of refashioning this bizarre anecdote into a routine.“You’re getting an exclusive on the hand,” he tells me in an east London coffee shop the next day, after I’ve opened a bottle of water for him. Young and Campbell, who recently collaborated on the winningly madcap Channel 4 series Make That Movie, were preparing to host their occasional comedy night Floggers, which involves them dressing up as old men (fat suits, wigs, prosthetics) and helming a real daytime TV-style auction. Campbell had ordered the sword online as a prop, and when the pair’s Uber arrived Young hurriedly picked up the bag it was in. “Blood splattered up the wall like Kill Bill – we all laughed initially.” When his housemates removed the tea towel they’d wrapped around his hand “they could see yellow, which I think is tendon or muscle. Then I fainted.” He went to A&E for stitches but still did the show afterwards – “I cringe thinking about it because I was basically juggling [in the show]” – returning to hospital later to learn that one tendon was 90% lacerated and required an operation. Just before surgery, Young passed out again.View image in fullscreenHave they got news for you … Paddy with his Weekend Update co-anchor Ania Magliano.Photograph: Sky UKRiding high on the triumph ofSaturday Night LiveUK’s critically acclaimed first series – he co-anchors Weekend Update, the show’s satirical news segment, alongside Ania Magliano – Young was already about to embark on the busiest summer of his life: the Edinburgh fringe, an acting job, a new podcast, numerous Floggers shows. Now he’s cramming various medical appointments into his overstuffed diary, his recovery complicated by his inability to stay conscious. This is partly due to a severe phobia of needles, something that’s making him feel “truly pathetic”. As a veteran fainter myself, I tell him something I only recently discovered; it’s one of the five trauma responses: fight, flight, freeze, fawn and, in this case, flop. The term could describe “how I respond to a lot of things”, nods the 34-year-old. “I’m such a flop it’s unbelievable.”If you’ve only ever seen Young behind his desk at SNL – dapper, puckish, impossibly telegenic and armed with an arsenal of edgy current affairs zingers (plus a faintly worrying fixation with K-pop boyband BTS) – you might struggle to picture him as a failure. But in his sublimely funny standup, he’s a different beast: an indignant northern underdog, a messy millennial manchild of the people, a mordant poster boy for Generation Rent hissing at home-owning audience members. In his 2023 Edinburgh newcomer award-nominated show Hungry, Horny, Scared, he mined comic gold from bleak houseshares (his flat may have been freezing but at least he had an overheating 2012 Lenovo laptop for warmth), interspersed with anecdotes about his medical-grade childhood bed-wetting. (He was eventually assigned a specialist nurse: “How much piss is that? The NHS is getting involved …”)double quotation markYou pat yourself on the back because your video gets 200,000 views but someone getting hit with a frying pan might get 30mI had imagined this low-status shtick was mostly an act, but in person Young really does seem preoccupied with his weaknesses and rotten luck. He possesses none of the himbo-ish mischievousness of his Weekend Update performance. Instead, he’s a fast-talking, winningly candid overthinker with an “incredible talent” for seeing himself as a loser and a compulsion for self-reproach that is both completely ridiculous and extremely relatable. “I feel like I’m constantly either wronging someone or being wronged. I leave most situations thinking I really fumbled and fucked it up – or I’ve been betrayed.” (Same.)Young’s living situation is the overarching theme of his standup; this new show sees him contemplate singledom and his “bachelor” lifestyle (he finds the term amusing). Although he no longer cohabits with strangers in misery – he lives with fellow comedians Horatio Gould and Bebe Cave – he has a grim fascination with “people that have never got out of flatshares. I’ve always thought that’s going to be me.” He’s so fixated on this fate that he often imagines it’s already a reality. “I sort of feel like a 68-year-old bloke – like it’s all gone to pot and it hasn’t at all.” While some of his anxieties stem from his precarious profession, Young’s jokes are ultimately rooted in a near-universal struggle: making ends meet in London if you don’t come “from insane wealth”.View image in fullscreen‘A messy millennial manchild of the people’ … Paddy Young on stage.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanYoung grew up in Scarborough, north Yorkshire. As a schoolboy he was “so small” with no sporting talent, finding a social circle and sense of direction through his drama lessons at the Stephen Joseph theatre. It was helmed at the time by Alan Ayckbourn, one of Britain’s most prolific and popular playwrights, who cast a 10-year-old Young in one of his productions, his first professional acting gig. Ayckbourn even gave Young financial support after he won a placeat Manchester School of Theatre. He was an inconsistent student, he claims; revelling in small comic turns yet performing poorly when cast as a serious lead.After graduating, he tentatively tried standup. He was a comedy obsessive: Laurel and Hardy, Derek and Clive, Blue Jam, his dad’s collection of Viz comics, which “looked like the Beano but they were saying terrible things – that literally changed my brain chemistry”. His “extremely funny” mum was also an inspiration. Yet his early years on the circuit were awful; “going to these rubbish nights and being truly, truly depressed, then bombing and running away”. He has since realised his shtick doesn’t work at the open-mic nights that are a rite of passage for most fledgling comedians because of how he “plays with status” on stage. “I love the game of pretending it’s all falling apart, even though it actually isn’t. That doesn’t work at a gig that is actually bad.” What made him stick with comedy through the tough times? “I’m really fascinated by it – there is nothing else I think about.” He felt “mad” but had a deep-seated conviction he “could be good”.double quotation markShave off my moustache? I don’t know where my career would be without it. It’s like scaffoldingYoung’s career first began gaining traction in 2022, partly as a result of his Instagram sketches with the comedian Ed Night (“The love of my life”), which I return to repeatedly like favourite songs. The pair often parody content creators – conspiracy-minded podcasters, board game influencers and whatever people who make day-in-the-life vlogs are called – whose output Young describes as “the end of culture, but I can’t take my eyes off it”.Yet virality is relative. “You might pat yourself on the back because 200,000 people watch your video but then you scroll down and someone’s getting hit with a frying pan and it’s got 30m.” He doesn’t particularly like social media and thinks he’s “probably doing it completely wrong. It’s geared to be all about consistency” – posting “all the time” – whereas he and Night have a backlog of sketches they’ve never uploaded because they don’t think they’re up to scratch. He also feels slightly unsettled by how little work this kind of content requires compared with crafting an hour of standup. It’s a similar story with his new agony uncle podcast, Paddy Will Help (working tagline: “Oprah for blokes”). When we speak he’s in the process of workshopping the format, but knows he won’t be winging it with the kind of free-flowing parasocial banter his peers churn out. He likes finessing his material. “I couldn’t just be sat on the sofa chatting.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSounds to me as if he’s got integrity, yet Young also sees this as a failure to capitalise on his success (he has learned from friends that standups who pivot to podcasting “earn more than TV comedians”). While his peers discuss their five-year plans and audition strategies, “I’m fumbling in the dark. Everything I do, genuinely, there is no plan.”In the end he didn’t need one. Last year, he was cast in SNL UK: a huge opportunity he knew he was perfectly suited for (when he was told about the British version, his first thought was: “I have to do this. There’s less being made than ever and it just feels like you’re not quite right [for most TV projects],” hetold me in February). The show has offered him unexpected job security, the chance to break out of his own social media bubble – after just one month its sketches had amassed more than 86m online views – and a dose of surreal glamour. “You’re running down the corridor to get a wig fitted and then you pass Louis Theroux chatting to a beefeater. It really does feel like showbusiness, which nothing else does.” That said, being recognised in public isn’t the panacea he imagined. “You feel like someone’s got something on you – they know me and I don’t know them.”Young may need to prepare for more fan encounters: his SNL star is rising. Weekend Update has featured some surprisingly bracing satire and some genuinely great comic writing (“This week, former entertainer and entertainer of sixth-formers, Russell Brand …”). The more I watched, however, the more I became convinced of Young’s ability to sell literally any gag with a choice look or inflection. Initially, he begs to differ: “If it’s a joke I don’t like, I can’t say it – it pains me.” Yet trapped behind his desk, he is gradually finding “a way to pretend” if he’s not fully on board. Although he’s allowed to veto any quips he really doesn’t like – he tries to steer away from poking fun at voters of specific political parties, for example – he thinks it’s important to take this rare chance to really push the envelope. “There are people on set that are 30 years older than me that tell me they’ve never got away with this on TV.”‘How could this be anything other than funny?!’ Behind the scenes of Saturday Night Live UKRead moreOne slightly disappointing thing about the first series of SNL UK was how underutilised Young was as a comic actor. No longer: in the final episode of last season, he played Andy Burnham in a sketch about politicians jostling to become the next prime minister. Given the former mayor of Manchester ascent to the top job, Young looks set to reprise the role regularly next season. His Burnham isn’t a million miles away from his standup persona – they both use “shagger” as a term of endearment and hold southern extravagance in theatrical contempt – but the icing on the cake would be if Burnham “could grow a moustache over the summer”. Couldn’t Young shave his off? Nope – apparently it has talismanic properties. “I don’t know where my career would be without it. It’s like scaffolding.”SNL UK will be back in September and then again in January. In between, Young will tour the UK. It’s a strange sensation, having a full schedule until March. “I’m 34 and I’ve never known what I’m doing for more than six months.” Yet his success still hasn’t sunk in – besides, what if this good fortune is merely a flash in the pan? He’s so haunted by an encounter with an older comic who outlined his rapidly declining income after a career peak (“It’s always those stories that stick with me – any time I hear about someone who earns £5m a year, I forget”) that he’s considering drastic measures in the hope of turning what he fears could be a brief moment in the sun into a lifelong safety net.“I’m not a gambler, but I have thought: do I put all of my pay on red? Insane thoughts like that.” Young may not believe he’s made the big time yet, but I’d still bet against him being in that flatshare at 68.Paddy Youngtours the UKfrom 17 September to 12 December; tour starts Plymouth.Explore more on these topicsSaturday Night LiveTV comedyComedyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Shania Twain’s honest playlist: ‘If Dancing Queen comes on, you rush out’ | Shania Twain | The Guardian
description: The country-pop superstar loves Abba and secretly listens to Lloyd Webber, but which British heartthrob’s single gets her out of bed in the morning?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The country-pop superstar loves Abba and secretly listens to Lloyd Webber, but which British heartthrob’s single gets her out of bed in the morning?
Content: ‘I didn’t realise how powerful music could be until that moment’ … Shania Twain.Photograph: Timothy WhiteView image in fullscreen‘I didn’t realise how powerful music could be until that moment’ … Shania Twain.Photograph: Timothy WhiteHonest playlistShania TwainShania Twain’s honest playlist: ‘If Dancing Queen comes on, you rush out’The country-pop superstar loves Abba and secretly listens to Lloyd Webber, but which British heartthrob’s single gets her out of bed in the morning?As told to Hannah NewtonSun 26 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe song that changed my lifeThere’s many critical songs on The Mission soundtrack, but Gabriel’s Oboe [by Ennio Morricone] hit me hard. I had to pull off the road, I cried like a baby. I didn’t realise how powerful music could be until that moment. I was 22.The first single I boughtAt Seventeen by Janis Ian. I reference it in my album Little Miss Twain and it says so much about the emotions of a teenage misfit. I felt like her, I related – but I was also thinking: “Wow, I have to some day write this well.” It gave me a goal; I was so in awe. I made very little money, babysitting, taking care of my neighbour’s horse, singing in bars. I would get like 20 bucks, that I would mostly give to my family, but I got that record for myself.The best song to play at a partyIf Dancing Queen by Abba comes on and you’re in the bathroom, you rush to get out, you can’t miss a second of it.The song I secretly like, but tell everybody I hateNobody ever wants to listen to The Phantom of the Opera, but I nerd out and listen to the whole album. I have to do it by myself – it’s sort of a secret.The song that gets me up in the morningWhen it comes to getting out of bed, pop always brings me somewhere new, like Harry Styles’s Sign of the Times. I love it.The song that makes me cryMichael Jackson’s Ben used to make me cry as a kid.The song I do at karaokeI was always the kid singing in bars, the last thing I wanted to do was get up and pretend. I was really purist about it. But I realised I’m missing out on all the fun. My favourite is Killing Me Softly by Roberta Flack.The song I want played at my funeralI’ve been through a lot of grief in my life and there are intimate moments where you need to bawl your eyes out. As the dead person, I want to say: this is a moment you cannot control, life goes to shit sometimes. So I would choose Don’t Worry, Be Happy by Bobby McFerrin; some things you can’t change.Shania Twain’s Little Miss Twain is out now.Explore more on these topicsShania TwainHonest playlistCountryPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From author to anime hero: the unlikely revival of a Japanese literary star  | Fiction in translation | The Guardian
description: More than seven decades after they were first released, the dark novels of Osamu Dazai have become a publishing sensation, as a new generation of readers engage with his bleakness, humour and brilliance
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: More than seven decades after they were first released, the dark novels of Osamu Dazai have become a publishing sensation, as a new generation of readers engage with his bleakness, humour and brilliance
Content: Heartfelt desperation … Osamu Dazai.Photograph: Tadahiko HayashiView image in fullscreenHeartfelt desperation … Osamu Dazai.Photograph: Tadahiko HayashiFiction in translationFrom author to anime hero: the unlikely revival of a Japanese literary starMore than seven decades after they were first released, the dark novels of Osamu Dazai have become a publishing sensation, as a new generation of readers engage with his bleakness, humour and brillianceJohn SelfSun 26 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s no question that Japanese literature has been one of the outstanding successes for British bookshops in recent years: in 2024 close to half of the bestselling translated fiction titles were fromJapan. Much of the Japanese fiction translated into English fits into broad categories – cats, crime, coffee shops – but one surprise bestseller stands alone.Sales of books by Osamu Dazai, who killed himself in 1948 aged 38, have rocketed in the last few years. His best-known novel, No Longer Human (1948), has sold more than 75,000 copies in the UK alone. An intense semi-autobiographical account of one man’s alienation, it was the last work of fiction completed before Dazai’s death.Born in the north of Japan in 1909 to a wealthy family, Dazai was a brilliant student, but showed early signs of mental ill health, making two suicide attempts by the age of 21. He lived what his translator Donald Keene called a “life of wild dissipation”, including morphine addiction and a number of relationships.Until recently, Dazai’s work has been available only in imported editions from the US publisher New Directions. But this month, Penguin Classics capitalises on his unexpected popularity by publishing the first UK edition of Dazai’s work in almost 70 years: a collection of short stories from a female perspective, titled Schoolgirl.Polly Barton, who selected and translated the stories into English, tells me that, although Dazai may be relatively new to English-speaking readers, in Japan, he is “one of the big three, along with Yukio Mishima and Ryūnosuke Akutagawa, that everyone talks about as the fathers of modern Japanese literature”.In recent years, Barton adds, he has been discovered by a new generation of younger readers. “The sense I get is that he’s particularly popular with young men – the demographic that we’re constantly told is not reading books.” This is even more surprising, since Dazai’s novels are not traditional bestseller material. They are bleak, nihilistic and riddled with their narrators’ self-loathing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markDazai’s novels are not traditional bestseller material – they are nihilistic and riddled with self‑loathingNo Longer Human comprises a series of notebooks by a formerly “handsome young man”, who declares his incompatibility with the human race. For him, the world is “a place of bottomless horror”; he concludes that “living itself is the source of sin”. The narrator of the title story of Schoolgirl takes a similar view: “the problem is that I’m corrupt. I’m a bad girl.”The relentless pessimism in Dazai’s work risks seeming overwhelming or indulgent but, as Barton puts it, Dazai “leans into [the self-loathing] with a kind of exuberance”. Indeed, his appeal in part lies in this “unashamed emotional quality, but also tempered with enormous intelligence”.Tynan Kogane, the editor-in-chief at New York-based New Directions, agrees. “I think a lot of young readers see themselves in Dazai’s works.” He adds that “there’s a lot of nihilism and despair in Dazai’s work, and it’s unfortunate for our country at the moment, but there’s a lot of nihilism and despair [here too]. The unhappy man in postwar Japan really resonates with a lot of readers.”View image in fullscreenOsamu Dazai in  the 2016 Japanese anime TV series Bungo Stray DogsDazai’s popularity among younger readers may have spread online – on Reddit and TikTok, where commenters praise him as the only person that understands me”. But his renaissance also has unexpected roots in a 2016 Japanese anime TV series called Bungo Stray Dogs, which has fictionalised versions of real writers as its central characters.This bizarre series, featuring a “swashbuckling” version of Osamu Dazai, has been a godsend for book sales, says Chris Wait, an editor at New Directions. Soon after the TV series was released in America in 2018, New Directions noticed sales of Dazai’s books growing.“Before that we were selling dozens or hundreds of copies [a year],” Kogane says. As Bungo Stray Dogs fever grew, Dazai’s sales went stratospheric. “At the height of it,” Wait adds, “the annual figure was something like 150,000 copies, which for us is pretty rare.” Is it true that sales of No Longer Human bought New Directions a new office floor? “Yes,” replies Wait. “And our previous carpeting was very much in need of an update.”But the appeal of Dazai’s work goes much further than this cartoon cameo. His books have both style and substance. There’s “a natural gregariousness to his storytelling,” Wait says, “this raconteurship that keeps you reading no matter what he’s talking about”.Beyond the heartfelt despair of No Longer Human, novellas such as The Flowers of Buffoonery (1935) and The Beggar Student (1940) are frequently playful and funny; self-referential and self-mocking. “Why do I bother writing novels?” the narrator of The Beggar Student asks. “Am I lured by the glory of literary celebrity? Or do I simply want to write bestsellers and cash huge cheques? Let me spare you the theatrics. I want both. So bad it hurts.”Similarly, Schoolgirl, with its exclusively female viewpoints, presents a different side to Dazai. The authenticity of the voice may be in part because the title story, as Barton tells me, “was heavily based on the diary of a real 19-year-old schoolgirl that Dazai was sent in the post”.But Dazai’s most famous book remains inextricably linked with his own life – and death. In No Longer Human, the narrator has survived a suicide pact in which his girlfriend died. Soon after finishing the book, Dazai completed his own suicide pact with his lover Tomie Yamazaki. Their bodies were recovered six days later, on what would have been his 39th birthday. But his work – now more than ever – lives on.Schoolgirl by Osamu Dazai, translated by Polly Barton, is published by Penguin Classics.To order a copy go toguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsFiction in translationFictionJapanShareReuse this content

title: Luke Combs review – regular Joe megastar brings the arena-sized party home | Country | The Guardian
description: Despite his humble persona, the highest-selling country artist of all time has the vocal firepower and heavyweight hits to deliver two hours of crowd-pleasin’ pyrotechnics
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Despite his humble persona, the highest-selling country artist of all time has the vocal firepower and heavyweight hits to deliver two hours of crowd-pleasin’ pyrotechnics
Content: Demanding a sing-along … Luke Combs Live at Murrayfield stadium, Edinburgh.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDemanding a sing-along … Luke Combs Live at Murrayfield stadium, Edinburgh.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The GuardianCountryReviewLuke Combs review – regular Joe megastar brings the arena-sized party homeMurrayfield Stadium, EdinburghDespite his humble persona, the highest-selling country artist of all time has the vocal firepower and heavyweight hits to deliver two hours of crowd-pleasin’ pyrotechnicsKatie HawthorneSun 26 Jul 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first we see of Luke Combs, the North Carolina-born megastar is walking through the stadium crowd. Cap pulled low, with a bashful look on his face, the stunt is less pap walk, more regular Joe dodging a flashmob on his way to work. Combs is now the highest-selling country artist of all time, but he wears his success with humility: when he finally reaches his saloon-themed stage, with near-70,000 screaming fans before him, he keeps that unassuming presence. “Normally I’d ask how you’re feeling tonight, but Iknowhow you’re feeling tonight,” he smiles.This week, Combs will perform to more than half a million fans across just seven dates in England, Scotland and Ireland: a remarkable coronation for an artist yet to have a Top 10 single here. Not that you’d know it, from the way the crowd screams every word to his 2016 hit Hurricane, a soft-rock heartacher about running into your ex in a bar, elevated by a cinematic chorus (“moon went hidin’, stars quit shinin’”) that’s closer to early-doors Taylor than any country-bro machismo.View image in fullscreenA whole lot of show … Luke Combs at Murrayfield stadium, Edinburgh.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The GuardianNamed after recent single My Kinda Saturday Night, this short tour promises – and delivers – a party. Combs brings us three opening acts, lashings of pyro, celebrity cameos, and packs almost 30 songs into two hours. It’s a whole lot of show, but its biggest moments, such as the nostalgic-before-it’s-even-over Tell ’Em About Tonight, deserved more breathing room.It’s a real shame that echoing sound makes it almost impossible to pick out words when Combs speaks, and muddies his more intimate songs, such as the fiddle-laced 5 Leaf Clover. But Combs has one of contemporary country’s most formidable voices, owning an almighty, torn-up roar as well as real tenderness and control, and his hardest-hitting tracks power through regardless.His exuberant band bring power-stance, arena-rock swagger to Back in the Saddle and Beer Never Broke My Heart, while the glittering, tragedy-struck Where the Wild Things Are demands a sing-along that endures as fans walk home. By storming closer Ain’t No Love in Oklahoma (from theTwisterssoundtrack), Combs is crackling with energy, his arms in the air, humbleness be damned – and deservedly so.AtWembley Stadium, London, from 31 July to 2 AugustExplore more on these topicsCountryPop and rockEdinburghreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Keith David on his incredible career: ‘I want you to understand Black men as full-scope human beings’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The hard-working character actor has over 400 screen credits, from The Thing to Platoon to Rick and Morty, and he isn’t slowing down any time soon
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: The hard-working character actor has over 400 screen credits, from The Thing to Platoon to Rick and Morty, and he isn’t slowing down any time soon
Content: ‘One thing I always say is: Don’t quit before the blessing. You never know what it’s gonna take, or what’s in front of you’ … Keith David in The Lowdown.Photograph: FXView image in fullscreen‘One thing I always say is: Don’t quit before the blessing. You never know what it’s gonna take, or what’s in front of you’ … Keith David in The Lowdown.Photograph: FXMoviesInterviewKeith David on his incredible career: ‘I want you to understand Black men as full-scope human beings’Andrew LawrenceThe hard-working character actor has over 400 screen credits, from The Thing to Platoon to Rick and Morty, and he isn’t slowing down any time soonSun 26 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeith David’s voice precedes him. Deep and resonant, with mellifluous notes that hark back to his boys’ choir days, it has spent decades inhabiting warriors, gods, rogues, fathers and a welter of cartoon oddballs. Before David appears in a Zoom window from his Los Angeles home office, his voice reverberates through my tinny laptop speakers like a foghorn. “Can you see me now?” he booms once our connection is established after fits and starts. “OK. Outside of technology, you know I’m … OK.”‘Everything I know about evil I learned in that small town’: John Carpenter on terrifying the world with Halloween, The Thing and The FogRead moreHe fizzes about the project he just wrapped: a dark buddy comedy called My Friend Jim, in which he stars opposite Rob Lowe. It’s the latest entry in a seemingly unstinting slew of productions that have kept him booked and busy since the late 1970s, from The Thing to Platoon to There’s Something About Mary to Nope.“I went to see it last night,” says David, who generally avoids watching his on-screen performances once he’s given them. “I’ll go to a cast and crew screening, and that’s usually the first and last time I’ll see something. Every once in a while if I do something that comes on television that I haven’t seen in a long time, I’ll watch it. Sometimes I’ll look back on a choice I made in a particular scene and go, What the hell was I thinking …?”In an era that venerates stardom, David has made a life’s work of being more recognizable than famous, a character actor nonpareil. The past five decades have seen him amass more than 400 credits – enough to make him a ubiquitous presence in popular culture, even if many people couldn’t place the name behind the voice or the familiar profile – the glasses, the stately bearing and that mischievous grin. His résumé stretches from action movies to animation, Shakespeare to sitcoms; from Ken Burns documentaries to Call of Duty video games.At 70, David remains as in demand as ever, popping up in live-action series like the Ethan Hawke-led noir The Lowdown and Will Ferrell golf comedy The Hawk while his velvet baritone echoes everywhere from the Rick and Morty universe to a straight-to-streaming documentary on the Gettysburg Address. He caught up with the Guardian just before bolting off to San Diego Comic-Con to promote President Curtis, the Rick and Morty spinoff that marks the first standalone lead role of his remarkable career.View image in fullscreenKeith David at The Hawk premiere event.Photograph: Matt Baron/BEI/ShutterstockHe’s in no mood to slow down either, despite recent evidence to the contrary. At his Hollywood Walk of Fame induction in June – on his birthday, incidentally – David was photographed with his right arm in a sling, the result of a workout gone sideways. “I was in the gym fighting with a Bosu ball,” he says of the muscle injury – a line that could have been lifted from one of his animation scripts. “But I’m on the mend. I’m starting some light exercises right now. I keep in shape for whatever role happens to come along.”Work is what keeps him leaping out of bed every morning, thankful that he’s managed to stay in the game this long. If family history is a guide, he reckons he has a fair few productive years still ahead of him. “My grandmothers lived into their 80s and 90s,” he says. “My father is about to be 90. I feel like I’m in good company. There was a time in my life when the men in my family did not live that long. I had some fear of that in the back of my mind – but, you know, you wind up shortening your life, worrying about how long it’s going to be rather than how well you’re going to live.”David knew he wanted to captivate an audience before he knew how or where. The Harlem native might have become a preacher if he hadn’t taken so quickly to a citywide boys’ choir, where that voice first set him apart. By the time the 1970s rolled around and he got started at the High School of Performing Arts – a veritableXavier Institutefor New York City theater kids, where David overlapped with Ben Vereen, Glynn Turman and others – a life in the arts felt more like an inevitability.From there it was on to Juilliard, where he turned a school production of Romeo and Juliet into full-contact sport, tussling with future Tony winner Boyd Gaines. The duel wasn’t quite as drawn out as David’smuch-memed back-alley brawlwith Rowdy Roddy Piper in the 1988 cult classic They Live – but it did earn him and Gaines fight certifications. Two years after barnstorming the country with John Houseman for productions of A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Waiting for Godot, David found himself up for his first ever film part – a sci-fi horror starring Kurt Russell.The role was between David and another Black actor named Roger Mosley, who wound up booking Magnum, PI. The Thing, of course, is sci-fi canon now, a film that has only become more influential over time. But when the John Carpenter film arrived in 1982, David recalls, “it didn’t get the popular vote. It was overshadowed by ET and Poltergeist. Critics didn’t like it. I thought, well, I got an honorable mention [in the reviews]. Maybe I’m not going to have a life in the movies.”View image in fullscreenKurt Russell and Keith David in The Thing.Photograph: Ronald GrantFour years passed before Hollywood called on David again. In between auditions, acting company gigs and a side hustle as a speech teacher, he worked as a shiatsu masseur, charging fellow ensemble members $30 for a session. “The thing with putting out a shingle is that you have to work for anybody who’s got 30 bucks,” he says. “And I didn’t necessarily want to do that. It took me a long time to learn how to work on people’s energy without absorbing it myself. I did it for a while, but I was real selective.”In hindsight, those lean years were teaching David the very discipline that has served him so well over the course of his staggering career: selectiveness.It’s why David has pulled off the ultimate Hollywood sleight of hand: a body of work defined by both quantity and quality. As a young Black actor navigating Hollywood in the 80s and 90s, David understood how easily he could be pigeonholed – into the thug, the soldier, the sidekick, the stereotype. His solution wasn’t to avoid those roles, but to find the humanity within them. “I’ve played hustlers and pimps and all that,” he says. “My criteria is, I need to know why he made those choices so the audience understands the man. I want you to understand Black men as full-scope human beings. I try to go for that as much as possible.”David has a way of lending every character a measure of gravitas, as if the protagonists are interrupting his story. It doesn’t matter if he’s playing the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff in Armageddon, a shady DC alderman in the Chris Rock comedy Head of State or the world-weary Vietnam soldier King in Platoon – the Oliver Stone film that broke David’s four-year slump and set him on a path of near-constant work. But even Platoon could have nearly left him a footnote in a much bigger story.Charlie Sheen credits David withsaving his lifeduring a helicopter scene that nearly turned deadly. It’s the rare story David refuses to embellish. “We were circling back to the set-up point,” he says, “and the chopper tilted at a slightly different angle than before. I just sort of noticed, imperceptibly, he was sliding toward the open door. He didn’t seem to notice it himself, but I’m watching him inch toward that door and I just grabbed him instinctually – or maybe selfishly, because the truth of the matter is I didn’t want to think about what I should have done for the rest of my life. How close did it actually come? I don’t know. We’ll never know. But, praise God, it didn’t happen, and we live to tell the tale.”View image in fullscreenKeith David behind the scenes of Platoon.Photograph: Film PR handoutInterviewing David is a bit like trying to tour the Smithsonian during a lunch break. There’s no getting to everything, let alone all the highlights. But who could skip Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood? After The Thing, David booked a nine-episode arc on the children’s program as Keith, the neighborhood carpenter. The experience – a masterclass in captivating an audience, delivered by a Presbyterian minister no less – is one David still recalls with obvious affection.“One of the ladies in the cast, I believe, now you would say her son had autism,” David says. “He was a wonderful kid, but, you know, he could be all over the place. On set, they had a living room space where the TV was. And when Mr Rogers came on, Brian would sit in front of that television, riveted. He would shush you if you came into the room and made noise. It was really something to see the effect he had on children, on people. It was moving. It was a lesson.”Not every stop in the journey leaves a lasting mark. The Big House – the ill-fated 2004 sitcom that flipped The Fresh Prince’s rags-to-riches conceit and featured Kevin Hart and Leslie Odom Jr in their first on-screen roles – barely registers any more. David doesn’t spend much time dwelling on the misses. The best he can remember is telling himself, “Something else will come along.” And that something else was the 2000 sci-fi sleeper hit Pitch Black.His show business role models were people like Orson Welles, James Earl Jones and Ossie Davis – actors whose voices were instruments unto themselves. “What they were able to do in the realm of voiceover was just fascinating to me,” David says. “I wanted to be able to do that too, just by the voice, take you on a journey.”David had little sense of where that journey would take him when he booked a job on the ensemble sitcom Community. Dan Harmon, the creator and showrunner, called him in to narrate an episode in the elevated style of his Ken Burns collaborations and was blown away by the comedic potential in David’s gravitas and his ability to give fully committed, dead-serious performances in one take. “We had big fun with it,” he says.David was just as game to play around on camera as Elroy Patashnik, Community’s resident IT guy. When that job ended, David quickly found another on Greenleaf, a prestige drama about a Black church in Memphis. More than a starring role as Bishop James Greenleaf, his first true dramatic showcase at the center of a series, it was a prime opportunity on Oprah Winfrey’s young OWN network where he would share the screen with Winfrey, who played his barmaid sister.Did he feel the pressure? “You know, you always have some kind of awareness that that’s true,” David says. “But while she’s sitting at the table read or we’re in the episode, she’s not my boss. There’s no intimidation factor.”But Harmon wasn’t finished with David. Duringa much-publicized hiatus from Community, Harmon developed Rick and Morty, an animated series about a mad scientist and his grandson tearing through space-time and alternate realities. He brought David on almost immediately – first for a one-off role as a parasite giraffe; then as President Curtis, whose access to the government’s deepest secrets puts him on equal footing with Rick Sanchez himself.Together, Harmon and David found a singularity in Rick and Morty’s cosmic playground, where pop culture and chaos theory collide: a genuine breakout character. “The one thing about working with Dan is it can be wacky and crazy, but it’s alwayssmart. It’s the kind of stuff you can laugh at for days after you’ve seen it. Every time you think about a particular moment, you can just break out laughing. It resonates on more than one level.”President Curtis doesn’t just extend the joke. It unleashes the full range of David’s voice: speechifying through White House press room addresses, singing in the shower, one-lining through fight scenes. It’s a first lead role, one where he gets to bring pieces of every bit part he’s played along the way into a single character. Most of all, it’s a handsome reward for sticking it out, for trusting his voice. “You never know in this business. It’s a very funny business. But you gotta be in it. One thing I always say is: don’t quit before the blessing. You never know what it’s gonna take, or what’s in front of you.”President Curtis airs on Adult Swim on Sundays and will be available on HBO MaxExplore more on these topicsFilmUS televisionTelevisioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Curse of Love Island review – the deaths are more complex than this documentary can handle | Television | The Guardian
description: This show tries to grapple with the fact that three people associated with the reality juggernaut have killed themselves. But it forgets that the dating series doesn’t exist in a vacuum
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: This show tries to grapple with the fact that three people associated with the reality juggernaut have killed themselves. But it forgets that the dating series doesn’t exist in a vacuum
Content: The show feels ‘quite toxic’ … former Love Islander Malin Andersson.Photograph: AmazonView image in fullscreenThe show feels ‘quite toxic’ … former Love Islander Malin Andersson.Photograph: AmazonTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Curse of Love Island review – the deaths are more complex than this documentary can handleThis show tries to grapple with the fact that three people associated with the reality juggernaut have killed themselves. But it forgets that the dating series doesn’t exist in a vacuumHannah J DaviesSun 26 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn summer 2015, ITV revived its 00s reality format Celebrity Love Island, a show that was remembered mostly as a drunken, downmarket rival to Big Brother. Its new, slick, civilian Love Island was a slow-burn at first, but by 2017 it was one of British TV’s biggest hits. While it remains among ITV’s hottest properties, viewing figures are now more modest, with 600,000 people tuning in for its 2026 launch. Tastes have changed, but the fact that three people associated with the show – former contestants Mike Thalassitis and Sophie Gradon, and Caroline Flack, the presenter for five series – took their lives, may also have made viewers wary.Timed to coincide with the finale of the latest series of Love Island on Monday, Prime Video has released this two-parter about the apparent “curse” that stalks the programme. It opens with former contestant Anton Danyluk, who appeared on the show in 2019, declaring that there is “no higher high than the summer you’re preparing for Love Island”. But a stint in the show’s Mallorcan villa proved less of a high for some. Luis Morrison – a 2015 Islander – says it feels “disgusting” and “embarrassing” to watch the show back. “Everyone was having sex and stuff,” he says. Malin Andersson, a 2016 contestant, says, looking back, the show feels “quite toxic … so superficial and artificial”. Watching footage of herself coming into the villa for a post-elimination row with her partner, Terry, Andersson alleges there was much meddling on the part of the programme-makers: “The producers are fucking with people who can feel deep things!”View image in fullscreen‘Embarrassing to watch the show back’ … Luis Morrison.Photograph: AmazonSo far, so not shocking; these are all criticisms that could have been levelled at Celebrity Love Island in 2005, or pretty much any other reality dating show. But towards the end of the first episode and into the second, things get darker. Steven Douglass – a close friend of Gradon’s – speaks about her “zest for life” before the show, and the “spark” that faded once she was in the public eye and a victim of relentless trolling. Thalassitis was given the nickname “Muggy Mike” for his apparently sneaky behaviour. Former Big Brother psychologist Linda Papadopoulos says here it was a label that was reductive: “You’re distilling down a multidimensional human being into a catchphrase.” Gradon died in 2018, Thalassitis in 2019. There was, says journalist Caroline Frost, “a pattern forming” around Love Island.The problem, of course, is that such deaths are incredibly complex, and more complicated than The Curse of Love Island is equipped to deal with. Papadopoulos says: “This isn’t about trying to point at a show, or a company, or a person.” Yet much of the documentary concentrates on the programme rather than the online vitriol, financial pressures, family problems, existing mental health conditions, relationship problems, rolling media coverage, or the mind-bending reality of instant renown. Marcel Somerville, who appeared in the 2017 series, says: “If the care that is currently being offered to contestants was being offered back then, it might have had a better bearing for Mike.” Except that the increase in care for Love Island’s contestants – therapy, contact for 14 months, plus advice on finances, social media and adjusting to their new lives – only came about because of those tragedies. We can ask whether more could have been done earlier, but we will never know whether it would have made a difference. Dave Read, who has managed many former Islanders, including Thalassitis, says the media have got it “so wrong” when it comes to plotting a straight line between the show and his death.View image in fullscreenThe show’s saving grace … Anton Danyluk.Photograph: AmazonDanyluk’s frank testimony, rooted in two experiences on the show, is the programme’s saving grace. As reported in the press in 2024, he became a heavy drinker and drug user after Love Island, and tried to take his own life. Incredibly, he would later return for Love Island: All Stars in 2024, unable to shake the feeling that he had more reality mileage left in him, and wanting “to close that chapter of my life”. It was an experience which, he says, felt “a lot more produced” than it had the first time around. There was more support for contestants the second time, but that increased duty of care was, as he tells it, undercut by the producers provoking situations that were “causing a spiral effect online”. “I wouldn’t do reality TV ever again,” he says.Read says: “You need skin like a rhinoceros to be able to deal with this industry. That’s not a Love Island thing, that’s the whole industry. It’s savage.” Indeed, the Curse of Love Island makes many valid points about the difficulties of the reality world, but it seems to forget that Love Island doesn’t exist in a vacuum. The philosopher Mark Fisher wrote in Capitalist Realism in 2009: “Reality TV is continually haunted by questions about fiction and illusion.” In the years since, the massive expansion of social media has only intensified that uncanny boundary between real life and entertainment, performance and documentary, pathos and bathos. Surely the problem here is not so much the Curse of Love Island, but the well-worn curse of overnight fame.The Curse of Love Island is on Prime Video now.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123.In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: V&A workers hold ballot to strike over pay and heatwave conditions | V&A | The Guardian
description: Union calls for museum to become accredited London living wage employer and let staff carry water during shifts
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Union calls for museum to become accredited London living wage employer and let staff carry water during shifts
Content: V&A East in Stratford officially opened in April, having been conceived as a legacy development for the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park area of east London.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenV&A East in Stratford officially opened in April, having been conceived as a legacy development for the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park area of east London.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyV&AV&A workers hold ballot to strike over pay and heatwave conditionsUnion calls for museum to become accredited London living wage employer and let staff carry water during shiftsDiane TaylorSun 26 Jul 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorkers at one of the world’s leading art and design museums are balloting for “heatwave” strike action.The ballot atV&Ais taking place because of concerns about soaring temperatures and access to drinking water, along with pay and conditions.More than 300 workers at four V&A sites inLondon– the museum in South Kensington, V&A East Museum and V&A East Storehouse in Stratford, and Young V&A in Bethnal Green – are taking part in the ballot.The V&A, founded in 1852 after theGreat Exhibition, is described as “a family of museums dedicated to the power of creativity”. Its mission is to “promote art and design for all”.View image in fullscreenV&A East Storehouse in Stratford, east London, a collections and research building, opened in May last year.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe ballot has been launched during a summer ofextraordinarily high temperaturesand is thought to be one of the first to raise concerns about workplace conditions during a heatwave.The Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS) launched the strike ballot on 23 July owing to “serious and unresolved concerns affecting staff across the museum”.While pay rates are an issue, with calls for a minimum 4% pay increase, the union has also raised concerns about heat exposure and access to drinking water.It is calling for management to implement a policy of closing public areas across all four sites when temperatures exceed 30C, introduce heat mitigation measures for back of house workers, and allow staff at V&A East Storehouse to carry and drink water while working in areas where exhibits are on display, rather than waiting for another worker to come and relieve them while they go for a drink.The union is also calling on V&A to become anaccredited living wage employerin London. The current London living wage is£14.80 an hour. The V&A has confirmed that all its staff are paid at least this rate. However, some of the museum’s outsourced contractors arenot in receiptof the living wage and V&A has not so far become an accredited living wage employer, although it says this will be reviewed later this year.V&A Dundee, which is not part of the strike ballot, is an accredited living wage employer.View image in fullscreenPart of the PCS complaint concerns access to drinking water during shifts at museum sites such as V&A East Storehouse (pictured).Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianNick Marro, the culture secretary at PCS, said: “PCS members at the V&A are balloting for strike action because enough is enough. Management refuses to let staff carry or drink water while they work, refuses to become a London living wage accredited employer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom leftwing voters to unions: can Burnham win back Labour bases lost by Starmer? – visualisedRead more“At the same time, it claims it cannot afford a decent pay rise for staff. This is an employer that is failing the very people who keep one of Britain’s most prestigious museums running. It’s unfair, it’s unsafe and our members are prepared to fight back.”The Prospect trade union is alsoballotingmembers for strike action at the V&A over concerns about pay and conditions. Its ballot closes on 29 July.A spokesperson for the V&A said: “The V&A has been in negotiations with the trade union side since February and those negotiations are ongoing. Our offer sees a 3.6% increase in the overall pay bill, an above-inflation pay award as a minimum and 6.9% increase for our lowest-paid colleagues. As always, we have maintained our longstanding commitment to paying at least the London living wage.“The safety and wellbeing of our staff is of utmost importance to the V&A – all our staff have access to water and toilet facilities and regular breaks while at work. Extensive measures were implemented to support our staff during the heatwave, ranging from additional rest breaks, increasing staff rotations across gallery spaces, closing several galleries at V&A South Kensington and closing Young V&A altogether on 11 days during the peak of the heatwave.“To ensure the safety and security of national collections, duringOrder an Objectappointments at V&A East Storehouse, food and drink are not permitted and visitors are accompanied by V&A staff during their appointment.”Explore more on these topicsV&AIndustrial actionLondonMuseumsTrade unionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chuck Russell obituary | Movies | The Guardian
description: Film-maker who reshaped The Mask as an exuberant comic spectacular and launched the film careers of Cameron Diaz and the Rock
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: Film-maker who reshaped The Mask as an exuberant comic spectacular and launched the film careers of Cameron Diaz and the Rock
Content: Chuck Russell, left, with Jim Carrey on the set of The Mask, 1994.Photograph: New Line Productions/Album/AlamyView image in fullscreenChuck Russell, left, with Jim Carrey on the set of The Mask, 1994.Photograph: New Line Productions/Album/AlamyMoviesObituaryChuck Russell obituaryFilm-maker who reshaped The Mask as an exuberant comic spectacular and launched the film careers of Cameron Diaz and the RockRyan GilbeySun 26 Jul 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe film-maker Chuck Russell, who has died aged 74, described himself as “a thrill junkie with a sense of humour”. The proof was in the pudding: his madcap comedyThe Mask(1994) resembled a cinematic knickerbocker glory overflowing with colour, vitality and fun. Its star Jim Carrey called it “one of the jewels of my creative life”.Before Russell was attached to the project, The Mask had been doing the rounds in Hollywood for several years as a horror script. Once he came on board, he persuaded the studio New Line Cinema to let him reshape it as an exuberant comic spectacular. “I wanted to take the various things I know about special effects and apply it to dance and comedy,” he said.The film’s Jekyll-and-Hyde-style story is simplicity itself: when he dons an ancient wooden mask, a timid bank clerk (Carrey) is transformed into an anarchic, lime-faced jester in a banana-yellow zoot suit. Russell created a riotous live-action cartoon that fused Carrey’s gift for physical mayhem with cutting-edge CGI. “I found myself leaning towardsTex Averyphysics,” Russell said; he showed a thumping heart protruding from the actor’s chest, eyeballs flying from their sockets and an elongated tongue unspooling like a red carpet.Between them, he and Carrey developed what the director called a “windup-and-pitch” style of shorthand on set. “I would tell Jim I needed a bigger windup, and he knew he had to cock his head back to give me a greater forward thrust because I was going to extend his entire face five feet by the time I was done with it.”View image in fullscreenRussell on location with Grant Heslov and Dwayne Johnson (the Rock, right) for The Scorpion King, 2002.Photograph: Cinematic/AlamyRussell called Carrey “an uncanny talent … The problem was night shooting, when Jim would crash after ‘lunch’ at 2am. We played a little game to keep him going during the long wait for lighting on those nights. I’d toss out a double impression challenge; not just a celebrity impression, but [something like] ‘Elvis doing Clint Eastwood’… This kept us alert and laughing in the wee hours.”Raking in more than $351m, The Mask became the fourth highest-grossing release of its year. “I designed the film to play internationally,” Russell said. “There is something universal in the … fear of letting loose. The release of all these fears and dreams could be a good thing, it could be a bad thing. You just don’t know. However, it is a dangerous thing. That is a wonderful, universal idea.”It did not hurt that he insisted on pairing Carrey with the charismatic newcomer Cameron Diaz. “It became quite a campaign for me to get the studio to accept using a totally inexperienced actress in a lead role.” He described the chemistry between the leads as “the real ‘special effect’” in The Mask.Launching new acting talent was a speciality of his. He made his directing debut with the horror sequelA Nightmare on Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors(1987), which also marked Patricia Arquette’s movie debut. On the Arnold Schwarzenegger action vehicleEraser(1996), he gave second billing to Vanessa Williams, who had acted sporadically but was better known as a singer.The Scorpion King(2002), a spin-off of The Mummy, provided the wrestler Dwayne Johnson, AKA the Rock, with his first lead role.Born in Park Ridge, Illinois, Chuck (Charles) was the son of Patricia, a travel agent, and Charles Sr, an advertising executive. He was educated at Maine South high school and the University of Illinois. After directing some one-act plays he left Chicago for Los Angeles to try to make it in the movie industry.Like many aspiring film-makers of his era, he served his apprenticeship under the enterprising, low-budget producerRoger Corman, starting out as second assistant director on the violent, futuristic action movieDeath Race 2000(1975).Going on to work in multiple areas of film production, he was an executive producer on the slasher horrorHell Night(1981), where he met Frank Darabont, future director of The Shawshank Redemption, who became his sometime writing partner.View image in fullscreenJamie Campbell Bower in Witchboard, 2024.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyRussell co-wrote the ingenious thrillerDreamscape(1984), a clear precursor to Christopher Nolan’s Inception, starring Dennis Quaid as a psychic who can enter people’s dreams. He also producedBack to School(1986), starring the gurning US comic Rodney Dangerfield as a father enrolling in college classes alongside his own son; Kurt Vonnegut appears briefly, hired by Dangerfield to write an essay on his own novels.Itching to direct, Russell successfully lobbied New Line Cinema for the job of making the third Nightmare on Elm Street movie. He and Darabont also received co-writing credits alongsideWes Craven(the series’ creator) and Bruce Wagner.Their clinching idea was to delve more deeply this time into the dream worlds where potential victims are stalked by the scar-faced, blade-fingered, fedora-wearing killer Freddy Krueger (Robert Englund). This resulted in some disquieting images, including one victim being manipulated like a marionette, his exposed tendons used by Freddy as puppet strings. There was some oxygenating silliness, too: Russell persuadedZsa Zsa Gaborand the talkshow host Dick Cavett to play themselves in a dream sequence.In showing the demise of a heroin addict, the film incorporated a pointed anti-drugs message. The scene in question was among the most disturbing in the series: the holes in the unfortunate addict’s arm start puckering like tiny, ravenous mouths before Freddy, his blades now transformed into syringes, administers the fatal fix.“If I’ve helped at least one person turn their back on the junkie lifestyle, I would … feel I’ve done some good with the picture,” Russell told Starburst magazine.In 1988, he directed his and Darabont’s adaptation of the 1958 monster movie The Blob. While preparing the new version’s gooey special effects, which showed victims being dissolved gruesomely by the gelatinous menace, Russell studied footage of jellyfish, paramecia and Portuguese man-o’-wars ingesting food.View image in fullscreenZsa Zsa Gabor and Robert Englund in Nightmare on Elm Street 3, 1987.Photograph: Cinetext Collection/Sportsphoto/AllstarHe returned to the horror genre inBless the Child(2000), a chiller with Biblical overtones, starring Kim Basinger, andWitchboard(2024).In between, he and Darabont were executive producers on Michael Mann’s thrillerCollateral(2004), starring Tom Cruise as an assassin; Russell had originally hoped to direct the film. Many of the years immediately after The Scorpion King he dedicated to two “epic” personal projects that he planned to make within the studio system; neither came to fruition.He directed John Travolta in two little-seen thrillers,I Am Wrath(2016) andParadise City(2022), the latter co-starring Bruce Willis, and made the Hindi-language martial arts adventureJunglee(2019), in which a veterinarian battles poachers on an elephant reserve. In recent years, Russell devoted time to his companyNeumorphic, through which he hoped to make films built with generative AI.Fangoria magazine described him as “a genial if somewhat guarded man with a playful side”. He certainly knew how to connect with audiences. “I don’t live in an ivory tower,” he said in 2000. “I do ‘pop’ movies – but I tend to do movies that I’m excited about.”He is survived by his wife, Ania Zeyne, whom he married in 2007, and by three children – Carlyn, Riley and Logan – from his first marriage, to Patti Rao, which ended in divorce in 2005.Charles Raymond Russell, film director, born 9 May 1952; died 22 July 2026Explore more on these topicsFilmJim CarreyDwayne JohnsonobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Sinfonia of London/Wilson review – night of Technicolor masterpieces from one of the finest orchestras on the planet | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Verdi’s La Forza del Destino felt vital, cellist Jonathan Aasgaard was immaculate in Walton’s Concerto but it was John Wilson’s wizardly conducting through Respighi’s Roman Trilogy that brought the audience to their feet
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Verdi’s La Forza del Destino felt vital, cellist Jonathan Aasgaard was immaculate in Walton’s Concerto but it was John Wilson’s wizardly conducting through Respighi’s Roman Trilogy that brought the audience to their feet
Content: Playing the Albert Hall acoustic like a fiddle … John Wilson with the Sinfonia of London at the Royal Albert Hall, London.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCView image in fullscreenPlaying the Albert Hall acoustic like a fiddle … John Wilson with the Sinfonia of London at the Royal Albert Hall, London.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCClassical musicReviewSinfonia of London/Wilson review – night of Technicolor masterpieces from one of the finest orchestras on the planetRoyal Albert Hall, LondonVerdi’s La Forza del Destino felt vital, cellist Jonathan Aasgaard was immaculate in Walton’s Concerto but it was John Wilson’s wizardly conducting through Respighi’s Roman Trilogy that brought the audience to their feetClive PagetSun 26 Jul 2026 07.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 26 Jul 2026 10.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnother Sinfonia of London Prom, another five-star concert. Admittedly this programme of Technicolor masterpieces played into the wizardly hands of John Wilson, a conductor whose respect and enthusiasm for the golden age of MGM is legendary. None of this was movie music, however, and Hollywood panache is only a part of what makes this hand-picked ensemble one of the finest orchestras on the planet.View image in fullscreenDelight in the music making  … John Wilson and Jonathan Aasgaard with the Sinfonia of London.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCFirst, there’s that full-fat sound, where every musician is a potential soloist, yet the blend is to die for. Then there’s the parade ground discipline and a willingness to follow Wilson – who seldom lingers – into the very fires of Mordor. The spirit, too, is palpable. Whole sections sway as one, occasionally with broad grins on their faces, such is their delight in the music making.If the conductor has a superpower, it’s an instinct for homing in on tiny details, not just drawing them out but making them reallymeansomething. Take the beautifully articulated rustle of strings underpinning the poignant clarinet melody in the overture to Verdi’s La Forza del Destino. You may have already known it was there, but seldom has it felt so vital or so troubling.A blistering account of the Verdi was curtain raiser to Walton’s Cello Concerto, a golden Mediterranean canvas undercut with sinister ticks and jittery cross-rhythms that feel as if they’ve wandered in from a Hitchcock movie. Principal cellist Jonathan Aasgaard was the generous-toned soloist, articulate and technically immaculate, yet refreshingly undemonstrative.The second half was given over to Respighi’s Roman Trilogy, music with a reputation for cinematic excess, yet works that were embraced by Toscanini who was certainly no vulgarian. Wilson played the Albert Hall acoustic like a fiddle, whether depicting the brazen pomp of the Circus Maximus, Neptune’s chariot emerging from the Trevi Fountain, or nocturnal whisperings on the Janiculum hill, recorded nightingale and all. As the Roman army swept inexorably down the Via Appia, brass bands ricocheting across the balcony, the audience rose as one. All that remained to make the evening complete was a rip-roaring William Tell chaser by way of an encore and cue credits.The Prom is on BBC Four, 26 July at 8pm and available onBBC iPlayerandBBC Sounds(until 12 October). The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicProms 2026Royal Albert HallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Ruth Madeley’s ambitious new drama about the end of the world  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Ruth Jones and Iwan Rheon also star in this story about climate catastrophes and charismatic leaders. Plus: Andrew Lincoln narrates a nature series. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Ruth Jones and Iwan Rheon also star in this story about climate catastrophes and charismatic leaders. Plus: Andrew Lincoln narrates a nature series. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Say what you see … The Rapture on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Mammoth ScreenView image in fullscreenSay what you see … The Rapture on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Mammoth ScreenTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Ruth Madeley’s ambitious new drama about the end of the worldRuth Jones and Iwan Rheon also star in this story about climate catastrophes and charismatic leaders. Plus: Andrew Lincoln narrates a nature series. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Jack Seale,Graeme Virtue,Priya ElanandSimon WardellSun 26 Jul 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Rapture9pm, BBC OneClimate crisis catastrophes, charismatic religious leaders and a troubled girl who reckons she can predict the end of the world … there’s a lot going on in this ambitious new five-part drama. Set in Wales during a brutal heatwave, the story follows Dr Gabs Fox (Ruth Madeley), who is dealing with the trauma of an accident that left her paralysed and her husband dead. As she returns to work as a therapist at a psychiatric hospital, her first case is Bethany Krall (India Amarteifio), a mouthy teenager who draws disturbing sketches and claims they come true. Is there truth to any of it? Ruth Jones, Iwan Rheon and Jack Farthing complete the impressive cast.Hollie RichardsonForce of Nature7pm, ITV1View image in fullscreenIt’s a wash-out … Forces of Nature on ITV1.Photograph: Plimsoll Productions/ITVCats don’t like water at the best of times – so what happens in Kenya when, for the first time, two cheetahs experience a month’s worth of rain in a single day? Andrew Lincoln shows us, as he narrates this striking new nature series that follows the very real impact of the climate crisis on wildlife globally. Luckily, he says of the cheetah brothers, “these old boys have learned a few tricks”.HRJohn Wilson at the Proms8pm, BBC FourThe in-demand British conductor and his award-winning Sinfonia of London play two nights of the Proms this year. Katie Derham presents the first hot-ticket performance, which features Verdi’s overture to La Forza del Destino and Respighi’s Roman Trilogy.HRThe Dark9pm, ITV1In the penultimate episode of the murky thriller, Monica has been played by the killer – all while trying to keep her home life together. Can the stones in the victims’ bodies help identify the perpetrator? And will there be another victim before Monday’s finale?HRThe Piano9pm, Channel 4To York railway station, where the concourse ivories are tickled by the oldest publican in Britain, who ropes the crowd into a traditional bar-room singalong, and a songwriter whose original composition stuns regular judge Mika and this week’s guest expert, jazz pianist Hiromi. Plus, a stunningly gifted 12-year-old musician.Jack SealeThe Idaho Murders9pm, Sky CrimeDays ahead of a rival Netflix series, this true-crime two-parter covers the horrific stabbing of four young students in an Idaho college town in 2022. Part one paints a vivid, heartbreaking portrait of the victims via their social media updates; part two focuses on the hunt to track down the killer.Graeme VirtueTerror in the Skies: Stopping the Liquid Bomb Plot10.20pm, ITV1Using AI reconstruction tech and interviews with spies working at the time, this high-energy documentary looks back at a foiled terror plot in 2006 that could have changed the way we travel for ever. Seven British criminals planned a reign of terror, an expert says, which could have resulted in “a death toll higher than 9/11”.Priya ElanFilm choiceEleanor the Great, 6am, 2pm, 4.10am, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenTwinkly-eyed … Elenor the Great on Sky Cinema Premiere.Photograph: prScarlett Johansson’s directorial debut may be not what you’d expect from the Black Widow: a moving comedy revolving round the lies a 94-year-old woman tells about the Holocaust. June Squibb plays the twinkly eyed Eleanor, who relocates from Florida to live with her daughter in New York after her longtime best friend/housemate Bessie dies. Partly through grief and loneliness – but also to keep the memories alive – Eleanor begins to pass off Bessie’s tales of surviving Nazi atrocities as her own.Simon WardellLive sportThe Hundred Cricket: Manchester Super Giants Women v Birmingham Phoenix Women, 10.45am, Sky Sports CricketManchester Super Giants Men v Birmingham Phoenix Men is at 2pm; Trent Rockets Men v London Spirit Men is at 5.30pm.Formula One Racing: The Hungarian Grand Prix, 1.55pm, Sky Sports Main EventAt the Hungaroring in Mogyoród.The Hundred Cricket: Trent Rockets Women v London Spirit Women, 2.15pm, BBC TwoFollowed by Trent Rocket Men and London Spirit Men at 6pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Oona Doherty: Leather Jacket review – dancers delight in their hard sweaty work  | Stage | The Guardian
